entries.title: Jeremiah 1:1 "The words"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:1 "The words" This Hebrew word (BDB 182) has a wide semantical field and can mean "deeds," "matters," "affairs," or "sayings." This phrase opens the book and closes the message of Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 51:64).

▣ "Jeremiah" This is a very common Hebrew name, but its etymology is uncertain (see Intro. I., B); of all the prophetic books, this one mentions the author more than any other. The book reveals its author's words, thoughts, feelings, and actions more than any other OT book.

▣ "the son of Hilkiah" This name (BDB 324) means "YHWH is my portion." Jeremiah was a Levite (cf. 1 Chr. 6:45), but apparently he was not an active priest because Solomon had exiled his family to Anathoth (i.e. the descendant priests of Eli; cf. 1 Kgs. 2:26-27). There are two men in Jeremiah's day by the same name. His father is not the high priest mentioned in 2 Kgs. 22:4 or 2 Chr. 34:9. The high priest was apparently of the lineage of Zadok, while Jeremiah's father was from the lineage of Abiathar, both descendants of Eli.

From Josh. 21:18, we are told it was a Levitical city in the tribal allocation of Benjamin (i.e. Neh. 11:30-36). Josephus thought it was the more modern city of Anata, but this is still unsubstantiated.

▣ "Anathoth" This name (BDB 779) comes from the Amorite goddess, Anath, who is the sister or consort of Ba'al. She was an active warrior goddess (i.e. Anath, Asherah, Astarte, and Astoreth) called the "Queen of heaven" in the Ras Shamra poetry texts found in the city of Ugarit, north of Israel. A city by this name, Beth-anath, is mentioned in Josh. 15:59; 19:38; Jdgs. 1:33.

▣ "in the land of Benjamin" This was the location of Abiathar's excommunication (cf. 1 Kgs. 2:26-27). It is about three miles from Jerusalem, but its exact location is uncertain.

entries.title: Jeremiah Introduction
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
INTRODUCTION TO JEREMIAH

  1. NAME OF THE BOOK
    1. It was named after the prophet.
    2. The meaning of his name is difficult to ascertain
      1. "YHWH founded" (KB 440)
      2. "YHWH loosens from the womb" (BDB 941)
      3. "YHWH raises up" or "exalts" (BDB 926)
      4. "YHWH hurls" (BDB 941 I, cf. Exod. 15:1)

  2. CANONIZATION
    1. It was part of the "prophet" section of the Hebrew canon.
    2. The Torah or Law ‒ Genesis - Deuteronomy
    3. The Prophets:
      1. Former Prophets ‒ Joshua-Kings (except Ruth)
      2. Latter Prophets ‒ Isaiah-Malachi (except Daniel and Lamentations)
    4. The Writings:
      1. The Megilloth (5 scrolls):
        1. Song of Songs
        2. Ecclesiastes
        3. Ruth
        4. Lamentations
        5. Esther
      2. Daniel
      3. Wisdom Literature:
        1. Job
        2. Psalms
        3. Proverbs
      4. 1 & 2 Chronicles
    5. In rabbinical literature Jeremiah was often considered the first of the prophets (Baba Bathra 14b, cf. Matt. 27:9)

  3. GENRE
    1. This book is made up of several genres:
      1. classical Hebrew poetry (Jeremiah's oracles)
      2. Hebrew prose (written by Baruch in the third person)
      3. summaries of Jeremiah's sermons often in prose (also from Baruch)
      4. autobiographical complaints to God in poetic form (Confessions of Jeremiah, cf. Jer. 15:10-18; 17:9-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18)
    2. The book of Jeremiah includes both oral and written prophecies. Also from chapter 36 we learn that some had to be redictated/recopied. Also, Jer. 52 is a historical addition related to 2 Kgs. 24:18-25:21.
    3. Jeremiah's poetry is not of the same quality as Isaiah and Hosea, but his theology is wonderful.
         This is a comment by Jerome in his introduction to Jeremiah.

      "Jeremiah the prophet. . .is seen to be more rustic in language than Isaiah and Hosea and certain other prophets among the Hebrew, but equal in thought" (quoted from ABD, vol. 3, p. 690).

  4. AUTHORSHIP
    1. Jeremiah did not write Jer. 52 because Jer. 52:31-34 records events which occurred in Neo-Babylon. Jeremiah was taken forcibly to Egypt by renegade Jewish military units after the assassination of Gedeliah, the Jewish governor, appointed by Nebuchandezzar II.
    2. Possible authors/editors:
      1. Jeremiah (Baba Bathra 14b-15a)
      2. Baruch ben Neriah, his scribe
      3. compilers (i.e. "the Deuteronomic historians)
      4. later editors (possibly Ezra or the men of the Great Synagogue)
      5. The Jewish Study Bible, p. 919, mentions that Jer. 51:64 says, "Thus far are the words of Jeremiah." However, the book continues for another whole chapter with 34 verses.
    3. We know more about Jeremiah than any other prophet.
      1. from the priestly (exiled) line of Abiathar, 1 Kgs. 2:26-27)
      2. grew up close to Jerusalem in Anathoth (a Levitical city in the tribal allocation of Benjamin, cf. Josh. 21:17-19)
      3. called by God as a young man, Jer. 1:2; 25:3 (the rabbis estimate he was 18 years old when he was called by YHWH, 627 B.C.)
      4. influenced by the previous writings, especially Hosea and Deuteronomy
      5. contemporary with (see OT Timeline)
        1. Daniel
        2. Ezekiel
        3. Habakkuk
        4. Zephaniah
        5. Nahum
      6. five years after his call "the Law Book" was found in the temple during Josiah's reform. It is surprising that their relationship is never mentioned in Scripture. When the Law Book was found the King consulted a prophetess named Huldah (2 Kgs. 22:14-20), not Jeremiah.
        SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE
      7. his feelings can be clearly seen in his confessions or complaints
        1. Jer. 11:18-12:6
        2. Jer. 15:10-12
        3. Jer. 17:14-18
        4. Jer. 18:18-23
        5. Jer. 20:7-18
      8. he was taken by force to Egypt where he was killed by Jewish refugees, Jer. 43:6
      9. the Jewish Talmudic book of Baba Bathra (i.e. 15a) says Jeremiah wrote
        1. Kings
        2. his own book
        3. Lamentations

  5. DATE
    1. Jeremiah was born in Anathoth between 655-640 B.C. (exact date uncertain).
    2. The book of Jeremiah is dated in Jer. 1:2 and covers the time from the thirteenth year of Josiah (his call) to the time of Gedaliah, 627 B.C. (cf. Jer. 1:1; 25:3) ‒ 582 B.C. How long Jeremiah lived in Egypt with the refugees is uncertain.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY
    3. An ostraca found at Lachnish describes its siege in 587 B.C. The form of its Hebrew text is comparable with Jeremiah.
    4. Jeremiah's messages focus on the events from the fall of Samaria (722 B.C.) to the fall of Jerusalem (586 B.C.)

  6. HISTORICAL SETTING
    1. 686 B.C. ‒ Manasseh (686-641 B.C.)
    2. 664 B.C. ‒ the Egyptian Empire gains strength under Psammetichus (664-610 B.C.; SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF EGYPT)
    3. 648 B.C. ‒ the birth of Josiah (SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY)
    4. 642 B.C. ‒ Amon, king of Judah was killed by his servants (2 Kgs. 21:19-26)
    5. 640 B.C. ‒ the last effective Assyrian ruler, Ashurbanipal, dies (SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA)
    6. 640 B.C. ‒ Josiah becomes a king at 8 years of age (2 Kgs. 22:1)
    7. 628 B.C. ‒ Josiah initiates reform (2 Chr. 34:3ff; 2 Kings 23)
    8. 626 B.C. ‒ the call of Jeremiah (Jer. 1:2)
    9. 626 B.C. ‒ Nabopolassar (626-605 B.C.) becomes king of Neo-Babylon (SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON)
    10. 621 B.C. ‒ the Book of the Law was found by workmen who were remodeling the temple (2 Chr. 34:8ff; 2 Kings 22)
    11. 614 B.C. ‒ the regional capital of Assyria, Ashur, fell to Neo-Babylon
    12. 612 B.C. ‒ Nineveh, Assyria's primary capital was destroyed by Neo-Babylon and Media
    13. 609 B.C. ‒ Josiah was killed at Meggido opposing Pharaoh Necho II (610-594 B.C.) who was  attempting to help the fleeing remnant of the Assyrian army (2 Chr. 35:20-24; II  Kgs. 23:28-30)
    14. 605 B.C. ‒ Neo-Babylon defeats the Egyptians and remainder of the Assyrian armies at  Carchemish
    15. 605 B.C. ‒ Nebuchadbezzar II moves through Palestine demanding tribute payments (taking  Daniel and the first deportation). There were four invasions affecting Judah and  Jerusalem, 605, 597, 586, and 582 b.c.
    16. 601 B.C. ‒ Nebuchadnezzar II lost the battle for control of Egypt (a stalemate)

  7. LITERARY UNITS
    1. The book's structure is topical or thematic, not chronological. It is probably a collection of several different scrolls/messages by Jeremiah, 1-25,30-33, and 46-51 (i.e. an anthology, like Isaiah).
       The UBS' A Handbook of Jeremiah makes the comment,

      "In fact, Jeremiah is not really a 'book' in the sense that most readers today would normally describe a book—it has neither an overall orderly arrangement nor clearly defined contextual settings for interpreting many of its individual parts" (p. 1).

    2. The LXX and the MT differ greatly. Almost 3000 words of the MT are missing in the LXX. Also, the order of the nations in Jer. 46-51 is different, as well as their placement after Jer. 25. Both MSS traditions were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, which implies they are both translations of an early Hebrew text.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT
      SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT
    3. Tentative outline (basically follows R. K Harrison and E. J. Young)
      1. Jer. 1 ‒ Jeremiah's call and provision
      2. Jer. 2-25 ‒ Judah's sin from the early years of Jeremiah's ministry
      3. Jer. 26-29, 34-35 ‒ the personal life of the prophet
        1. YHWH's message to Zedekiah and Hananiah's reaction, Jer. 26-29
        2. the Rechabites, Jer. 34-35
        3. historical events from the reign of Jehoiakim ‒ Zedekiah and Gedaliah and to Egypt, Jer. 36-45
      4. Jer. 30-33 ‒ the promise of the restoration of God's people
        1. physically
        2. spiritually
      5. Jer. 46-51 ‒ prophecies against surrounding nations (also Jer. 25:12-38)
        1. Egypt ‒ Jer. 46 (Isaiah 19; Ezekiel 29-32)
        2. Philistia ‒ Jer. 47 (Amos 1:6-8; Isa. 14:29-32; Ezek. 25;15-17)
        3. Moab ‒ Jer. 48 (Amos 2:1-3; Isaiah 15-16; Ezek. 25:8-11)
        4. Ammon ‒ Jer. 49:1-6 (Amos 1:13-15; Ezek. 25:1-7)
        5. Edom ‒ Jer. 49:7-22 (Amos 1:11-12; Isa. 21:11-12; Ezek. 25:12-14; Obadiah)
        6. Syria ‒ Jer. 49:23-27 (Amos 1:3-5; Isa. 17:1-3)
        7. Arabia ‒ Jer. 49:28-33
        8. Elam ‒ Jer. 49:34-38
        9. Babylon ‒ Jer. 50-51 (Isa. 13:1-14; Hab. 2:6-17)
      6. Jer. 52 ‒ the Fall of Jerusalem (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:18-25:30)
    4. The UBS' A Handbook of Jeremiah makes the comment:
      1. "As is well known, the book of Jeremiah is not put together according to a chronological arrangement, and it is only with difficulty that we can uncover even a topical arrangement of the sayings and deeds recorded in it. However, a recent commentary by Dorsey demonstrates that there are seven fairly well-defined larger units along with an appendix. Each has its own cohesive internal organization. The outline below is based on his analysis:
        1. God will punish Judah (Jer. 1:1-12.17)
        2. The Lord reveals his plans for the fall of Judah (Jer. 13:1-20.18)
        3. God will judge and punish Judah and Jerusalem (Jer. 21:1-29.32)
        4. God will bring his people back to their land (Jer. 30:1-33.26)
        5. Jeremiah delivers messages to Zedekiah and the Rechabites (Jer. 34:1-35.19)
        6. Jeremiah suffers because he delivers the Lord's message (Jer. 36:1-45.5)
        7. God will punish the nations (Jer. 46:1-51.64)
        8. An appendix on the fall of Jerusalem (Jer. 52:1-34)" (p. 1)
      2. "The seven divisions of the book are therefore arranged in a symmetrical pattern (i.e. chiasm; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY). The first and seventh have related themes, as do the second and sixth, and the third and fifth. The fourth, the central division, delivers the central message, that of hope. This is quite different from many of the other prophetic books where the central message is a call to repentance. Further, the book makes clear that God did not fail to protect Judah. Rather, it was he who decreed that Judah should be punished because they failed to obey him. The Lord is above the nations and powers; he is able to punish, but he alone can be trusted to restore the people" (p. 2).
    5. It is interesting to note that in Jer. 1-25 Jeremiah's messages are introduced with the phrase "the word of YHWH came to me," while in Jer. 26-51 they are introduced with "the word of YHWH came to Jeremiah."
    6. Chart of Jeremiah's prophecies by the reigning king:
           E. J. Young       R. K. Harrison
      1. under Josiah (640 b.c.)
      Jer. 1:1-19; 2:1-3:5; 3:6-6:30; 7:1-10:25; 11:1-13:27; 14:1-15:21; 16:1-17:27; 18:1-20:18      		   Jer. 1:1-19; 2:1-3:5; 3:6-6:30; 7:1-10:25; 18:1-20:18
      2. under Jehoahaz (609 b.c.)    
      3. under Jehoiakim (609 b.c.)   Jer. 11:1-13:14;1 4:1-15:21; 16:1-17:27; 22; 25; 26; 27; 35; 36; 45 23; 25; 26; 35; 36; 45; 46-48
      4. under Jehoiachin (598-596 b.c.) Jer. 31:15-27    
      5. Zedekiah (597 b.c.)   Jer. 21:1-22:30; 23; 24; 27; 28; 29; 30-31;  21:1-22:30; 24:1-10; 27; 28; 29; 30-31; 32; 34; 37; 38; 39  32; 33; 34; 37; 38; 39; 49; 50:1-51:64
      6. under Gedaliah   Jer. 40; 41; 42; 43-44:30; 50-52 40:1-42; 43:1-44:30
      7.     Historical Appendix
      Jer. 52:1-34

  8. MAIN THEME
    1. The time of judgment is imminent because Judah would not repent! Jeremiah emphasizes sin, judgment, then restoration; Jer. 1:4-10.
    2. Liturgical or ritual religion without personal lifestyle faith in God is a disaster! (Jer. 7; Isa. 29:13).
    3. Judah had hopelessly lost her way in ritual, idolatry, and sin! She had broken God's covenant, symbolized as a marriage contract (cf. Jer. 2:1-3:5).
    4. Personal repentance and faith are the basis of God's new covenant (Jer. 31:31-34), not family faith (Jer. 31:29; Ezekiel 18).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)
    5. The New Covenant is permanent (Jer. 31:35-37) because it is not conditioned on human performance but on God's grace and power (Ezek. 36:22-38).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

*Although not inspired, paragraph divisions are the key to understanding and following the original author's intent. Each modern translation has divided and summarized the paragraph divisions as they understand them. Every paragraph has one central topic, truth or thought. Each version encapsulates that topic in its own way. As you read the text, which translation fits your understanding of the subject and verse divisions?

In every chapter you must read the Bible first and try to identify its subjects (paragraphs). Then compare your understanding with the modern versions. Only when we understand the original author's intent by following his logic and presentation at the paragraph level, can one truly understand the Bible. Only the original author was inspired-readers have no right to change or modify the message. Bible readers do have the responsibility to apply the inspired truth to their day and lives.

Note that all technical terms and abbreviations are explained fully in the Special Topics: "Brief Explanations of the Technical Resources used in This Commentary," "Brief Definitions of Hebrew Verbal Forms that Impact Exegesis," and "Abbreviations Used in This Commentary."

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.
"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:2 "the word of the Lord came"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2 "the word of the Lord came" The OT prophets repeatedly affirm that their message was from YHWH. This literary formula makes that very clear.

This phrase, "the word of the Lord came," is repeated often in the major prophets. It was a way to clearly denote that the message was YHWH's, not the prophets'. This is similar to Paul's use of being called an Apostle in his letters to establish his authority. For a good brief discussion, see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 66-69.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:2,3 "in the days of Josiah. . .in the days of Jehoiakim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2,3 "in the days of Josiah. . .in the days of Jehoiakim" This forms the beginning and ending dates of Jeremiah's ministry, which is about 627 B.C. to after 586 B.C. Tradition says he went to Egypt with refugees following Gedaliah's assassination (see chapter 40) and was killed by those very refugees.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

▣ "Josiah" This means "YHWH supports" (BDB 78) or "YHWH heals" (BDB 382). He was a godly king who began reigning in 640 B.C. at eight years of age (640-609 B.C.). He started a spiritual reform and the remodeling of the temple. This was when the "Law of the Lord" was found (621 B.C., cf. 2 Kings 22-23).

▣ "in the thirteenth year of the reign" This would be five years after the Book of the Law was found in the temple and when Josiah began his reform. It is unusual that there is no textual connection between Josiah and Jeremiah recorded in the Bible. Even when the Book of the Law was found, it was taken to the prophetess Huldah to interpret, not Jeremiah (cf. 2 Kgs. 22:14-20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:2-3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2-3 The repeated phrase "in the days of. . ." is a way to date the prophetic messages. The opening verses serve to introduce the entire book.

  1. from whom
  2. to whom (cf. Jer. 1:7)
  3. when
  4. why

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:3 "Jehoiakim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3 "Jehoiakim" This was another son of Josiah (Eliakim, cf. 2 Kgs. 23:34) who replaced Jehoahaz (i.e. Shallum, cf. Jer. 22:11) as the ruler of Judah by Pharaoh Necho II (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:31-34; 2 Chr. 36:4).

Notice that there are two sons of Josiah who reigned briefly for three months who are not named in this passage.

  1. Jehoahaz (Shallum) who was exiled to Egypt by Pharaoh Necho II (cf. 2 Kings 23)
  2. Jehoiachin who was exiled to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. 2 Kings 24; 2 Chronicles 36)

▣ "Zedekiah" Zedekiah replaced Jehoiakim on the throne of Judah as a vassal of Nebuchadnezzar II (i.e. 609 B.C., cf. 2 Kgs. 24:17; 2 Chr. 36:10-13).

▣ "the exile of Jerusalem in the fifth month" There were four deportations by Nebuchadnezzar II of the population of Judah to Babylon (i.e. 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.. By far the most destructive was in 586 B.C., when Jerusalem itself fell and the temple was completely destroyed (cf. 2 Kings 25; 2 Chr. 36:9-21; Jeremiah 39 and 52).

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:4 Verses 4 through 10 are the divine call of Jeremiah to prophetic ministry.

SPECIAL TOPIC: OLD TESTAMENT PROPHECY

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:5 "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:5 "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you" This speaks of God's sovereign power over the lives of His human creation (cf. Jer. 43:7; 44:2,24; 49:5). The term "formed" (Qal IMPERFECT, BDB 427, KB 428) is the exact term used in Gen. 2:7,8. God has a plan and a purpose for every human person (cf. Ps. 139:13-16; Isa. 43:7; 49:5; Gal. 1:15).

God had a plan and purpose for this person even before he was born (i.e. notice Paul's words in Gal. 1:15-16). I wonder how many "prophets" and servants of God western culture has aborted in the name of expediency and the individual freedom of their selfish parents. Personal convenience and expedience give a social license to choices that depreciate human worth and dignity!

For a good brief discussion of the Bible texts on the unborn see Millard Erickson, Christian Theology, 2nd ed., pp. 570-572.

▣ YHWH selects four VERBS to describe His personal activity in Jeremiah's life.

  1. I formed ‒ Qal IMPERFECT, BDB 427, KB 428
  2. I knew ‒ Qal PERFECT, BDB 393, KB 390 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW)
  3. I consecrated ‒ Hiphil PERFECT, BDB 872, KB 1073 (i.e. "set apart" for an appointed task," cf. Rom. 1:1; Acts 13:2)
  4. I appointed ‒ Qal PERFECT, BDB 678, KB 733

Note what happens if he does not respond ‒ v. 17.

▣ "to the nations" Jeremiah was not just called to Judah, but was to proclaim God's sovereignty over all nations (cf. Jer. 1:10a; 25:15-29,46-51). This is the theological implication of monotheism.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:6 "Alas"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:6 "Alas" In this first chapter there are several INTERJECTIONS.

  1. "alas" ‒ ההא, BDB 13, KB 18, cf. Jer. 1:6; Jdg. 11:35; 2 Kgs. 3:10; 6:5,15; Joel 1:15; Jer. 1:6; 4:10; 14:13; 32:17. It is translated "ah" in Jeremiah and denotes alarm.
  2. "behold" ‒ הנה, BDB 243, KB 252, cf. Jer. 1:6,9,18; 49:2; Isa. 6:7. This is a way to call attention to a statement.
  3. "see" ‒ in Jer. 1:10 (BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE), also functions as an INTERJECTION
  4. "behold" ‒ הן, BDB 243, Jer. 1:15; 31:8. The UBS Handbook calls it "an emphatic transitional marker" (p. 38).

▣ "Lord God" The Hebrew titles are "Adon" and "YHWH." Since both of these terms are translated "Lord" in English, most English translations use the title "Lord God" (cf. Jer. 4:10; 32:17; Josh. 7:7; Jdg. 6:22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Kurios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "I do not know how to speak" This was the same excuse that Moses used in Exod. 4:10, however, the term used here means "to speak publicly." Moses was claiming to be a stutterer (BDB 546), but Jeremiah was claiming not to be a public speaker (BDB 180, KB 210, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT).

▣ "because I am a youth" His exact age is uncertain, because in Exod. 33:11 Joshua is called a youth and he was 45 years old. Young people in Hebrew culture did not have the status that they do in modern western culture. Jeremiah was afraid that because of his age and because he was unmarried he would not have a strong social or religious platform from which to speak to Judeans.

God regularly uses young people. Here is just a sample.

  1. the spies of Jericho, Josh. 6:23
  2. Samuel
  3. David and Jonathan
  4. Daniel and his three friends
  5. Josiah
  6. Joel 2:28

It is not the age but the heart that is crucial!

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:7 Notice how YHWH answered Jeremiah's reluctance.

  1. do not say, "I am a youth" (Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense)
  2. everywhere I send you, you shall go (two Qal IMPERFECTS)
  3. all that I command you, you shall speak (two Piel IMPERFECTS)

▣ "because everywhere I send you, you will go" God never sends anyone out alone. His greatest provision is His personal presence (cf. Jer. 1:8b,19). He goes along to help (i.e. Matt. 28:20) and to equip for the assigned task (i.e. Eph. 4:12).

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:8 "Do not be afraid of them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:8 "Do not be afraid of them" This is a Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (BDB 431, KB 432). Jeremiah had a hard word to speak to his own people (i.e. exile is coming). They would attack Jeremiah both verbally and physically, but YHWH says "Fear not!" This was a frequent message to YHWH's servants.

  1. Abraham, Gen. 15:1
  2. Isaac, Gen. 26:24
  3. Moses, Num. 21:34; Deut. 3:2,22
  4. Joshua, Josh. 1:5-9; 8:1; 10:8
  5. Gideon, Jdg. 6:8-10
  6. Solomon, 1 Chr. 28:20
  7. Isaiah, Isa. 8:12-15
  8. national Israel, Isa. 41:10,13,14; 43:1,5; 44:2; 54:4
  9. Daniel, Dan. 10:12,19
  10. Mary, Luke 1:30
  11. Simon, Luke 5:16
  12. Paul, Acts 27:24
  13. John, Rev. 1:17

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:9 "the Lord stretched out His hand and touched my mouth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:9 "the Lord stretched out His hand and touched my mouth" Jeremiah becomes YHWH's mouthpiece (cf. Jer. 15:19; Deut. 18:18). Apparently Jeremiah had a vision of God similar to Isaiah's (cf. Isa. 6:6-7). The vision is not elaborated in Jeremiah's call as it is in Isaiah's call (cf. Isaiah 6) or Ezekiel's call (cf. Ezekiel 1).

This is a very anthropomorphic phrase. God is described in human terms.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "Behold I put my words in your mouth" It must be remembered that this was not Jeremiah's message or thoughts, but YHWH's (cf. Jer. 1:2; Deut. 18:18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:10 There is a series of six INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS.

  1. to pluck up ‒ Qal, BDB 684, KB 737, cf. Jer. 31:28
  2. to break down ‒ Qal, BDB 683, KB 736, cf. Jer. 31:28
  3. to destroy ‒ Hiphil, BDB 1, KB 2, cf. Jer. 31:28
  4. to overthrow ‒ Qal, BDB 248, KB 256
  5. to build ‒ Qal, BDB 124, KB 139, cf. Jer. 24:6; 31:4,28; 33:7; 42:10
  6. to plant ‒ Qal, BDB 642, KB 694, cf. Jer. 24:6; 31:28; 32:41; 42:10

The first four speak of judgment, but the last two of renewal and restoration (cf. Jer. 18:7-10; 31:40). It is interesting that Jeremiah repeats this phrasing in Jer. 31:28, where he switches to an emphasis on restoration and deliverance. This phrase then becomes a literary marker for the two opposite prophecies Jeremiah is to speak to "the nations," because YHWH is the true "King" of all nations (cf. 1 Sam. 8:4-9; note Deut. 32:8).

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:11 "What do you see"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:11 "What do you see" There are two visions (Jer. 1:11-12 and Jer. 1:13-19). The time element is uncertain, but they are placed close to Jeremiah's call.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "I see a rod of an almond tree" The term "almond," shaqed (BDB 1052), is related to the VERB "watching" in Jer. 1:12, shoqed (BDB 1052, KB 1638). In this culture the almond tree was called "the watching tree." Apparently this vision was a way to emphasize the surety of God's word through Jeremiah (i.e. "watching over" and "to perform it").

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:13 "a boiling pot, facing away from the north"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:13 "a boiling pot, facing away from the north" Because of Jer. 1:14 it is obvious that this is referring to an invasion from the north. The term "north" became a proverb for "evil" and "invasion" (cf. Jer. 4:6; 6:1,22; 10:22; 25:9) because it was the only land route into Palestine from Mesopotamia because of the desert east of Palestine. The boiling pot pours south (i.e. the advancing Neo-Babylonian army).

There are three words in close proximity that may be sound plays.

  1. נפוח ‒ boiling "pot" (BDB 655, KB 708, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE)
  2. ופניו ‒ facing away from (BDB 815)
  3. הנופצ ‒ the north (BDB 860 I)

These kinds of sound plays are a characteristic of Hebrew poetry.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:15 This invasion from the north into Palestine could refer to

  1. Scythians (Herodotus) in Josiah's reign (628 B.C.)
  2. Egypt, led by Pharaoh Necho II, invaded Judah to stop Assyria in 609 B.C.; possibly Jer. 2:14-15
  3. Neo-Babylon (several times, 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.)
  4. because of Jeremiah's prophetic poetry, possibly an even farther future orientation (i.e. Rome, cf. Dan. 9:24-27)

YHWH uses foreign armies to judge His people because of their covenant disobedience.

  1. Assyria ‒ Israel 732 B.C. - 722 B.C., the fall of Samaria and deportation of most of the population
  2. Neo-Babylon ‒ Judah (605, 597, 586, 582 B.C., finally destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and deported most of the population
  3. Scythians in Josiah's day
  4. Rome in the Jewish Wars of A.D. 66-70 with the destruction of Jerusalem and burning of the temple and the selling into slavery of most of the surviving population
  5. possibly eschaton ‒ Ezek. 38-39; Joel 3

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING, IV.

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:16 Judah's fall came not because of the weakness of YHWH, their God, but the covenant people's idolatry.

  1. they have forsaken Me ‒ Qal PERFECT, BDB 736 I, KB 806
  2. they have offered (lit. "burned incense") to other gods ‒ Piel IMPERFECT with waw, BDB 882, KB 1094
  3. they have worshiped the work of their own hands ‒ Hishtaphel IMPERFECT with waw, BDB 1005, KB 295

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:17 "gird up your loins"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:17 "gird up your loins" This is a Hebrew idiom for "get ready for action" (cf. 1 Kgs. 18:46; 2 Kgs. 4:29; 9:1; Eph. 6:14; 1 Pet. 1:13), which would be similar to our "roll up your sleeves."

Girding up his loins meant to pull one's robe through the legs in front and tuck it into the sash, thereby forming tight-fitting shorts, ready for action. This is not the only preparatory action the prophet is told to do.

  1. arise ‒ Qal PERFECT with waw, BDB 877, KB 1086
  2. speak ‒ Piel PERFECT with waw, BDB 180, KB 210
  3. do not be dismayed ‒ Qal IMPERFECT negated (BDB 369, KB 365) used in a JUSSIVE sense
▣
NASB, NKJV  "or I will dismay you before them"
NRSV, JPSOA, TEV  "I will break you before them"
TEV  "or I will make you even more afraid
  when you are with them"
NJB  "and in their presence I will make
  you fearless"
REB  "or I shall break you before their eyes"
Peshitta  "Lest I confound you before them"
LXX  "For I am with you to deliver you"

Jeremiah's obedience was crucial for YHWH's word and blessing. How could he demand obedience from Judah if he was not obedient himself?

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "and speak to them all which I command you" This shows the purpose of the visions for Jeremiah in Jer. 1:11-16. It was a divine revelatory communication.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "Do not be dismayed before them, or I will dismay you before them" God's service is a double-edged sword, privilege brings responsibility.

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:18 "I have made you today"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:18 "I have made you today" God's provision and protection are emphasized to the prophet.

  1. as a fortified city
  2. as a pillar of iron
  3. as walls of bronze

We must not let the reception of our message affect its proclamation, once we know it is from God! Jeremiah was going to speak to the powerful and elite of his day.

  1. to the kings of Judah
  2. to its princes
  3. to its priests
  4. to the people of the land (wealthy land owners)

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEOPLE OF THE LAND

entries.title: Jeremiah 1:19 "They will fight against you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:19 "They will fight against you" Judah will reject God's message (lit. "wage war," BDB 535, KB 526, Niphal PERFECT with waw). God's people have regularly rejected His message.

▣ "I am. . .the Lord" These are both from the same Hebrew VERB, "to be" (BDB 217, cf. Exod. 3:12-14). Their basic thrust is that YHWH is the ever-living, only-living God. That great God is with Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 1:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.
 

  1. How long did Jeremiah preach?
  2. What does Jer. 1:5 have to say to the abortion issue of our day?
  3. Why did Jeremiah try to excuse himself from God's will?
  4. Explain the two visions and their purposes in Jer. 1:11-16.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:1 This is a literary idiom in the prophets to designate YHWH's message. These were His words not Jeremiah's! It was a very specific revelation. The question is how much of the

  1. genre (poetry)
  2. vocabulary
  3. imagery

is YHWH's and how much is Jeremiah's mind, education, vocabulary, and culture. We simply do not know, but by faith all believers assert it is God's self-revelation (i.e. "Thus says the Lord," Jer. 2:2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "Go and proclaim" One would think these are IMPERATIVES but they are not.

  1. go, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE (BDB 229, KB 246)
  2. proclaim, Qal PERFECT with waw (BDB 894, KB 1128)

▣ "in the ears of Jerusalem" Poetry condenses for emphasis. This phrase is addressing the people of Jerusalem, not a personification of the city. Also the message was for all Judeans not just the capital city.

Does this imply that Jeremiah is speaking only to Judah and that Israel has already been exiled (i.e. 722 B.C.)? It is hard/impossible to date the individual poems of Jeremiah. The word "Jerusalem" is missing in the LXX (which is a different version of an ancient Hebrew text).

▣ In Jer. 2:2 YHWH speaks of the time of the beginning of Israel as a nation (i.e. the exodus and wilderness wandering period of 38 years as a marriage, cf. Isa. 62:4-5).

"I remember" (anthropomorphic imagery, see SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN)

  1. the devotion (hesed) of your youth (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS)
  2. the love of your betrothal
  3. your following after Me in the wilderness

The rabbis called this period "the honeymoon" period between YHWH (husband) and Israel (wife). He provided their every need.

  1. food (manna and quail)
  2. water
  3. clothing
  4. shade (see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADE/SHADOW, I. E. #2)
  5. His personal guidance (see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEKINAH)

In a sense this strophe is like Rev. 2:4, which describes how the OT people of God, like the church at Ephesus, had "left her first love" (i.e. beginning devotion and commitment).

▣ "the devotion of your youth" Devotion is hesed.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS (hesed)

▣ "in the wilderness" The OT presents two differing ways to characterize "wilderness."

  1. during the Exodus it became a place of YHWH's guidance, protection, and provision (cf. Deut. 32:10-14; Jer. 2:1-2; 31:2; also note Rev. 12:6)
  2. it was seen as the haunt of the demonic (cf. Lev. 16:7-8; Isa. 13:21-22; 34:13-15)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WILDERNESSES OF THE EXODUS

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONIC (OT)

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Jeremiah 2:1 through 6:30 possibly occur during the reign of Josiah. Jeremiah was called to be a prophet in the thirteenth year of Josiah's reign (i.e. 627 B.C.)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

  2. Jeremiah 2 is a classic example of Hebrew poetic prophecy.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

  3. The change in the PRONOUNS has caused some to assert that there are several sermons combined, but it seems that Jeremiah switches from speaking to the nation, to individuals and then back to the nation.

  4. Jeremiah 2 is structured in the imagery of a lawsuit (i.e. "rob," BDB 936, #3; cf. Jer. 2:4-8,9,12,29; Isa. 1:2,18; 3:13-15; Hosea 4:1; 12:2; Micah 6:2). This was a major recurrent, prophetic, literary form.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:3 "Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:3 "Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "holy to the Lord" For "holy see SPECIAL TOPIC: HOLY.

For YHWH (Lord) see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "The first of His harvest" This imagery is an allusion to the offering of the first fruits in the temple to the priests, which symbolized YHWH's ownership of the whole crop (cf. Lev. 23:10-11; 1 Cor. 15:20; James 1:18). Here the imagery turns negative. The nations attacked and rejected YHWH by rejecting His chosen vessel of revelation, Israel.

▣ "ate" This term (Qal PARTICIPLE, BDB 37, KB 46) was used in Akkadian for an "illegal invasion," but here it denotes the nations of Palestine's rejection and attack on Israel. This phrase shows Israel's specialness (cf. Gen. 12:3; 27:29; Exod. 19:5-6). She was created and called for a larger purpose.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:4 "Hear"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4 "Hear" This is the theologically significant VERB Shema (Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 1033, KB 1570). Its basic meaning is "to hear, so as to do." It has great importance in Deut. 4:1; 5:1; 6:3,4. Jeremiah was deeply influenced by Deuteronomy (as was Jesus, i.e. He quotes from it several times in His temptation experience, Matthew 4; Luke 4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣ "O house of Jacob. . .families of the house of Israel" These are parallel phrases used of all the seed of Abraham, after the split of the United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon) in 922 B.C. The northern ten tribes are called Israel, Ephraim, or Samaria. This has caused great confusion in the use of the term "Israel."

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:5 "What injustice did your fathers find in Me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:5 "What injustice did your fathers find in Me" This is the literary imagery of a court scene (cf. Jer. 2:4-8). YHWH's true nature is expressed in Deut. 32:4. YHWH asked this same question in Micah 6:3. He was not the problem, they were!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "they went far from Me" The VERB (Qal PERFECT, BDB 934, KB 1221) is in direct contradiction to "follow after Me" in Jer. 2:2.

Also notice the personal element. Not just follow my laws but follow "Me"! Biblical faith is a personal faith, in a personal God, on a daily moment-by-moment basis. It is a faith relationship, but it is personal (i.e. prayer, daily trust, and obedience to the known will of God).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

▣ "walked" This (BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERFECT with waw) is recurrent biblical imagery of lifestyle choices and actions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE WAY. . .THE PATH

▣ "emptiness and became empty" The NOUN (BDB 210 I) and VERB (Qal IMPERFECT with waw, BDB 211, KB 236) are put together for emphasis. This refers to idolatry (cf. Jer. 8:19; 10:3-5,8-10,14-15; 14:22; 16:19-20; 51:17-18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSENQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:6-7 These verses refer to the exodus and wilderness wandering period (i.e. Exodus and Numbers).

Notice the things YHWH did for them as He fulfilled His promise/prophecy to Abraham (cf. Gen. 15:12-21).

  1. brought us up out of the land of Egypt
  2. led us through the wilderness
    1. a land of deserts and pits (natural holes or steep ravines)
    2. a land no one crossed (hyperbole)
    3. a land of drought and deep darkness (see SPECIAL TOPIC: DARKNESS, II.)
    4. a land where no one dwelt (see SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS IN THE OT, B. #6)
  3. brought you into the fruitful land (i.e. Palestine/Canaan)

The exact date, route, and number of the Exodus is uncertain.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE EXODUS (uncertainties)

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:7 Palestine of this period was a very fertile place (cf. Num. 13:23-24,27; Deut. 8:1-9; 11:10-12).

▣ "defiled My land" The VERB (Piel IMPERFECT with waw, BDB 379, KB 375) is used of

  1. sexual defilement ‒ Ezek. 18:6,11,15
  2. murder ‒ Num. 35:29-34; Deut. 21:22-23
  3. idolatry ‒ Lev. 20:3; Ezek. 23:38; 36:17,18
  4. ceremonial uncleanness ‒ Lev. 15:31; Num. 19:13,20

Notice this is God's land (cf. Jer. 12:7-10; 16:18; 50:11) and He will not tolerate those who live inappropriately (cf. Lev. 18:24-30). As He removed the Canaanites (cf. Gen. 15:16) He will remove Abraham's seed if they reject Him (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 28; Jer. 2:6a, 8a).

It must be remembered that the Mosaic Covenant was a conditional covenant.

▣ "abomination" This term (BDB 1072) appears often in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 2:7; 6:15; 7:10; 8:12; 16:18; 32:35; 44:4,22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:8 What a terrible condemnation of the leadership of God's covenant people.

  1. priests (BDB 463) ‒ those who administrate the temple and sacrificial system
  2. those who handle the law ‒ this would refer to Levites who taught and interpreted the law of Moses to the people locally (i.e. Nehemiah 9, later "scribes," cf. Jer. 8:8)
  3. the rulers (lit. "shepherds," BDB 944 I) ‒ this refers to leadership, civil or religious (cf. Num. 27:17; 1 Kgs. 22:17; Isa. 44:28; 56:11; Jer. 3:15; 23:4; Ezekiel 34)
  4. the prophets

Notice their sins.

  1. questioned the presence of YHWH with them (lit. "where is the YHWH," cf. Jer. 2:6a)
  2. did not have a personal faith relationship with YHWH (lit. "did not know Me"; see SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW)
  3. they transgressed His law (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP)
  4. prophesied by Ba'al (i.e. fertility worship, cf. Jer. 2:20; 23:13)
  5. walked after things that did not profit (i.e. adultery, cf. Jer. 16:19; Hab. 2:18)

▣ "things that did not profit" The VERB "profit" (BDB 418 I, KB 420, Hiphil IMPERFECT) is used of idolatry (cf. Isa. 44:9,10; 57:12; Jer. 2:8; Hab. 2:18).

In Hebrew poetry one looks for several markers.

  1. Hebrew parallelism
  2. Hebrew imagery
  3. Hebrew sound plays
  4. parallel passage from Israel's history/wisdom literature, or other prophets
  5. cognate roots

It is surely possible that an intended sound play is here (Jer. 2:8).

  1. profitless ‒ יעל (BDB 418 I)
  2. Ba'al ‒ בעל (BDB 127)

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:9 "contend"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:9 "contend" This VERB repeated twice (Qal IMPERFECT, BDB 936, KB 1224, cf. Jer. 2:29) refers to a legal lawsuit (cf. Jer. 2:35). This literary structure is one of three used by Prophets to communicate their message (lament, legal case, promise oracle). YHWH is divorcing His covenant partner for covenant faithlessness.

This concept of YHWH divorcing His faithless wife (i.e. marriage analogy) is continued in the book of Revelation. I have become a Partial Preterist, which means I think that both the Olivet Discourse of Jesus (cf. Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21), as well as the book of Revelation, refer to this concept of a divorce of Israel and a remarriage to the church. This means the "great harlot" of Revelation is Jerusalem. I hope if you are not familiar with this approach to many of the eschatological passages of the NT, that you will take the time to look at my exegetical verse-by-verse comments on these texts free online (www.freebiblecommentary.org).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVORCE

▣ "with your sons' sons I will contend" This shows that lifestyle priorities are passed on to our children with the result of blessing or cursing (cf. Exod. 34:7; Deut. 5:9). Just an additional thought, I so rejoice in Deut. 7:9, where God's love and mercy extends to the "thousand generations" of those who love and trust Him.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:10 Notice the series of IMPERATIVES.

  1. cross ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 716, KB 778
  2. see ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 906, KB 1157
  3. send ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 1018, KB 1511
  4. observe closely ‒ Hithpolel IMPERATIVE, BDB 106, KB 122
  5. see ‒ same as #2

▣ "Kittim" This (BDB 508) refers to the original Phoenician settlement on Cyprus, but came to refer to all of the islands to the west of Palestine.

▣ "Kedar" This (BDB 871) was an Arab tribe to the east. This entire phrase is used metaphorically for "from east to west." The whole point of the verse is "Ask anyone!" Let anyone be a witness about the things of Jer. 2:11-13.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:11 What a powerful question. Israel had abandoned the only true God (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM) and went after the false, vain, non-existent idols of the surrounding pagan nations (cf. Jer. 2:13). This is not meant to affirm there are no other spiritual beings (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE)

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

▣ "their glory" The NKJV and NRSV capitalize "glory" (BDB 458) thereby showing it is a characteristic title for God (cf. Rom. 1:23). He was Israel's glory! When they reject Him they have no glory (cf. Hosea 4:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: DESCRIPTIVE TITLES FOR GOD

▣ "For that which does not profit" If Jer. 2:8, lines 3 and 4, are parallel, then this may refer to Ba'al worship.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:12 "O heavens"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:12 "O heavens" The heavens are often used as witnesses in God's lawsuit (cf. Deut. 4:26; 30:19; 31:28; 32:1; Isa. 1:2).

Notice that YHWH directs the oldest witness ("O heavens," usually paired with "O earth") to

  1. be appalled ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 1030, KB 1563, cf. Jer. 4:9; 18:16; 19:8; 49:17; 50:13; Ezek. 27:35; 32:10
  2. shudder ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 972, KB 1343, cf. Ezek. 27:35; 32:10
  3. be very desolate, Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 351 II, KB 349 plus "utterly," BDB 547, cf. Isa. 60:12; literally "dry up," cf. Isa. 44:27

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:13 "fountain of living waters"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:13 "fountain of living waters" This may be another descriptive title for God (cf. Jer. 17:13; Ps. 36:9; John 4:10-14; 7:38-39; Rev. 21:6).

▣ "To hew for themselves" This is the problem of fallen humanity, even covenant humanity. They try to run their own lives (cf. Jer. 2:17,19). Their ongoing failure will open the door for YHWH's mercy and grace in the "new covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34 (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:14 Another question starts a new strophe. This question is answered by another rhetorical question in Jer. 2:17. Israel is reaping what she sowed (i.e. the curses of Lev. 26 and Deut. 28, cf. Jer. 17:10; 32:19; see full list of this recurrent theological theme at Gal. 6:7-10). She is no longer what she was when she was formed (i.e. Jer. 2:2-3, devoted, loving, holy to the Lord, the first of His harvest). Now she is a slave who has become a prey (i.e. of other nations and their false gods).

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:15 "young lions"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:15 "young lions" This is imagery for power and strength used of the nations (esp. Assyria, see SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA). Young lions were well known top predators. Here it symbolized Israel's invading enemies. Without her God, she was vulnerable and weak! The false gods she went after who could not see or hear, could not help!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣
NASB   "destroyed"
NKJV, NRSV   "burned"
TEV, NJB   "in ruins"
JPSOA, Peshitta   "desolate"
REB   "razed to the ground"
LXX   "were torn down"

The MT has "burned" (נצתה, Niphal PERFECT, BDB 428, KB 429, but the Masoretic scholars suggested נצתו), which would be translated "are in ruins." Both options fit the context (see above line which is in synonymous parallelism).

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:16 "Memphis and Tahpanhes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:16 "Memphis and Tahpanhes" These were ancient capitals of Egypt (cf. Jer. 44:1). Each city in Egypt had its own patron deity.

▣
NASB, NRSV   "shaved"
NKJV, NJB   "broken"
TEV, NET   "cracked"
JPSOA   "lay bare"
REB   "will break"
LXX   "mocked"
Peshitta   "rule over"

The VERB comes from two possible roots.

  1. BDB 949, KB 1270 ‒ רעע, meaning "to break" (NASB, NJB, REB)
  2. BDB 944, KB 1258 ‒ רעה, meaning "to pasture," "to tend," or "to graze" (cf. Jer. 47:5; 48:37; Isa. 7:20), which in this context denotes slavery (Peshitta)

The UBS Text Project, p. 176, gives option #1 a "B" rating (some doubt). Exile and shame are the fruits of Israel's idolatry.

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:17 See note at Jer. 2:13d. Line 3 of the MT is printed in the NASB. The Septuagint has a totally different line. It is not a textual corruption, but a separate tradition. The DSS have Hebrew copies of both the MT form of Jeremiah and the radically shorter LXX version (see Introduction, VII. B.)

Here is the LXX:

"'Has not your abandoning of Me brought about these things for you?' says the Lord God."

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:18 "on the road to Egypt. . .Assyria"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:18 "on the road to Egypt. . .Assyria" Israel tried to find security themselves by political alliances against Neo-Babylon instead of with faith in YHWH. These alliances included involvement (ceremonies) with their national idols!

▣ "To drink the water" This repeated VERBAL (Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, BDB 1059, KB 1667) is imagery used as voluntary service of another. In a sense this was "self-imposed" exile!

  1. the Nile Shihor (BDB 1009, a branch of the Nile, i.e. Egypt)
  2. the Euphrates (i.e. Assyria)

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:19 Like Jer. 2:13d and 17, this verse emphasizes the terrible results of Israel's choices (cf. Jer. 4:18)! Notice how "wickedness" (BDB 948) and "apostasies" (BDB 1000, cf. Jer. 3:6,8,11,14) will reprove and correct (i.e. personification).

YHWH responds with two Qal IMPERATIVES (i.e. "know" and "see"). They will realize the consequences of their choices.

  1. left YHWH
  2. embraced idolatry

There is no longer an appropriate "fear"/"dread" of YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOSTASY (aphistēmi)

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR

▣ "God of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:20 The first two parallel lines speak of

  1. the Exodus, where God formed Israel into a nation (cf. "planted" in Jer. 2:21) as He promised in Gen. 15:13-16. There are several other texts that use this slavery imagery (cf. Lev. 26:13; Isa. 52:2-3; Jer. 30:8; Ezek. 34:27). Israel traded the slavery of Egypt for the slavery of Mesopotamia!
  2. It is possible that all of v. 20 refers to Israel's rebellion against YHWH.

I think #2 fits the context best..

▣ Lines 4-6 refer to the pervasiveness of the fertility cult of Ba'al and Asherah (i.e. on every high hill, cf. Jer. 3:2,3,6; 17:2; Deut. 12:2; 1 Kgs. 14:23; 2 Kgs. 16:4; 17:10; Isa. 57:5,7; Ezek. 6:13; 20:28; Hosea 4:11-14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣
NASB, NRSV, NJB, REB  "I will not serve"
NKJV  "I will not transgress"
TEV  "refused to obey me and worship me"
JPSOA  "I will not work"
LXX  "I will not be a slave"
Peshitta  "I will never serve another god again"

The MT has "I will not serve" (BDB 712, KB 773, Qal IMPERFECT, NEGATED, but Masoretic scholars suggested "I will not transgress" (see NKJV). But, the first option fits the verse better. Notice all modern translations, except KJV, accept option #1.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:20-25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:20-25 The UBS Handbook on Jeremiah lists the imagery used to describe Israel's apostasy (p. 69).

  1. a rebellious animal, Jer. 2:20a
  2. a prostitute, Jer. 2:20b
  3. a worthless vine from good stock, Jer. 2:21
  4. a guilty person who cannot be washed, Jer. 2:22
  5. a wild camel in heat, Jer. 2:23-24
  6. a fool bent on self-destruction, Jer. 2:25
  7. a thief, Jer. 2:26

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:21 "choice vine"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:21 "choice vine" This is sorek (BDB 977 I), which means "red grape." This was one of the best varieties of grapes available in the ANE (cf. Isa. 5:1-7). But Israel became idolatrous and "turned yourself" (Niphal PERFECT, BDB 245, KB 253) "into the degenerate shoots of a foreign vine" (v. 21d).

▣
NASB  "faithful"
NKJV  "highest quality"
NRSV  "purest"
TEV  "the very best"
REB  "wholly pure"
NJB  "completely sound"
Peshitta  "wholly right"
LXX  "entirely of the right sort"
LXX (footnote)  "all true"

This is an important Hebrew root, אמת (BDB 54, KB 68, cf. Hab. 2:4). It is related to the basic Hebrew root אמן (BDB 52, KB 63, see SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS [OT]).

This form of the root primarily means "faithful" or "true." Israel was not what YHWH expected! She was not "faithful"

  1. as a bride
  2. as a covenant people

even though YHWH metaphorically grew them from a "faithful" stock of grape vines (i.e. sorek, fruitless tree).

Remember, etymology miust be subservient to context. All words have many connotarions. Only context can determine which fits best in this occurrence.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TRUTH/TRUE

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:22 God's people needed a spiritual cleaning (cf. Jer. 4:14; 13:27).

  1. lye (BDB 684) refers to a mineral alkali
  2. soap (BDB 141) refers to an alkali potash soap (cf. Mal. 3:2)

This, of course, is figurative language for "repentance" (cf. Ps. 51:2,7; Jer. 4:14; see Robert Girdlestone, Synonyms of the OT, pp. 147-150).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ "Lord God" This is the common title for Deity using Adon and YHWH in combination.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:23 "How can you say, 'I am not defiled'"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:23 "How can you say, 'I am not defiled'" Here is the real problem (cf. Jer. 2:35). They thought

  1. they were religious
  2. they were worshiping YHWH

Self-deception is the worst possible blindness (cf. Prov. 16:2; 30:12; Luke 16:15; 18:9-14).

▣ "the Baals" This was the male fertility god of Canaan.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "the valley" This is possibly a reference to Ben Hinnom (cf. Jer. 7:31-32; 19:2-6; 32:35; 2 Chr. 28:3; 33:6). It was where Molech, the fertility fire god, was worshiped by child sacrifice (cf. Lev. 18:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?  II. D.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:23-24 "a swift young camel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:23-24 "a swift young camel" This is a sexual, animal imagery for Israel's desire for political alliances (also note at 5:7-8).

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:25 "feet from being unshod. . .throat from thirst"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:25 "feet from being unshod. . .throat from thirst" This refers either to imagery for

  1. running after foreign gods (i.e. political alliances)
  2. slavery
  3. as Rashi believes, it is literal for captivity or exile

I think #1 fits the context best (cf. v. 18).

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:26 These are the same leaders mentioned in Jer. 2:8.

  1. kings
  2. princes
  3. priests
  4. prophets

▣ "is shamed" This VERB (Hiphil PERFECT, BDB 101, KB 116) is also found in Jer. 6:15; 46:24; 48:1,20; 50:2, also notice Jer. 8:9,12! Fear of shame was a powerful motivation for ANE people (i.e. Jer. 15:9; 31:19; 48:13,39; Isa. 1:29; 19:9; 20:5; 23:4; 37:27; 45:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:27 "tree, 'You are my father'. . .stone, 'You gave me birth'"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:27 "tree, 'You are my father'. . .stone, 'You gave me birth'" This is a play on the symbols of the Canaanite fertility gods. Ba'al was symbolized by an uplifted stone (i.e. phallic symbol) and Asherah by a carved stake or live tree (i.e. the tree of life symbol).

▣ "You gave me birth" The MT has the VERB (Qal PERFECT, BDB 408, KB 411, SINGULAR); the Masoretic scholars suggested (Qere) it be changed to the PLURAL.

▣ "they have turned their back to Me" This is another Qal PERFECT (BDB 815, KB 937). It parallels Jer. 32:33. In response YHWH turns His back to them (cf. Jer. 18:17).

▣ There are two IMPERATIVES used to mock what idol worshipers said to their non-existent idols (cf. Jer. 2:28).

  1. arise ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, BDB 877, KB 1086
  2. save us ‒ Hiphil IMPERATIVE, BDB 446, KB 448

Superstition is a sad and powerful reality in our fallen world (cf. Isa. 44:17; 45:20; 46:6-7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

▣ "save us" This is a Hiphil IMPERATIVE (BDB 446, KB 448). In the OT this refers to physical deliverance (also note James 5:14-15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:28 "according to the number of your cities
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:28 "according to the number of your cities

 Are your gods, O Judah" This refers either to the local Ba'als (cf. Jer. 11:13) or as we learn from Ugaritic literature, the Canaanite pantheon, which had 250 gods.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:29 See note at Jer. 2:9.

▣ "You have all transgressed against Me" Sin is personal and it is a rebellion against YHWH (i.e. Gen. 39:9; Ps. 41:4; 51:4; Dan. 9:11). The VERB is a Qal PERFECT (BDB 833, KB 981) denoting a settled attitude of rebellion and disobedience (cf. Jer. 2:8,29; 3:13; 33:8; Isa. 43:27; 66:24; Ezek. 2:3; 20:38; Hosea 7:13).

Notice the word "all," which could refer to

  1. everyone in that generation (cf. Jer. 2:31; 5:1; 6:13)
  2. their ancestors as well

The rebellion of all Israel, and all humans, is clearly seen in Paul's litany of OT verses in Rom. 3:9-18 and the summary statement in Rom. 3:23!

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:30-31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:30-31 YHWH disciplined Israel (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28-29) so that she would return to Him, but she would not. She had forgotten His gracious presence, provision, and protection during her formation (i.e. exodus and wilderness wanderings).

Israel's rejection of their God was surprising and unnatural! They wanted their freedom (i.e. the results of the Fall, cf. Genesis 3; the VERB in Jer. 2:31, line 4, is a Qal PERFECT, BDB 923, KB 1194).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

2:31
NASB  "We are free to roam"
NKJV  "We are lords"
NRSV  "We are our own masters"
NJB  "We are free"
JPSOA  "We have broken loose"
LXX  "We will not be ruled"
REB  "We have broken away"
Peshitta  "We are humiliated"

The VERB רוד (Qal PERFECT, BDB 923, KB 1194, cf. Hosea 12:1) is rare. KB translates the Qal PERFECT as "to roam about freely" (i.e. Jdgs. 11:37).

The UBS Handbook (p. 85) suggests it means "go here and there" (i.e. Arabic root) and links back to the female camel of Jer. 2:23.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:32 "attire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:32 "attire" This (BDB 905) was a sash that shows marital status of women (as does "ornaments," BDB 725). Israel had broken YHWH's covenant symbolized by the marriage contract. This chapter is YHWH's divorce proceedings. See full note at v. 9.

▣ "My people have forgotten Me" This VERB (Qal PERFECT, BDB 1013, KB 1489) is a shocking comment about Israel's relationship to her Deity (the only true Deity). This tragedy continues (i.e. same VERB used in the IMPERFECT stem, cf. Jer. 3:21; 13:25; Ps. 106:21-22).

Here the forgetfulness is a choice not an accident! Israel deliberately chose to leave YHWH, even after all He had done for her.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:33 "You have taught your ways"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:33 "You have taught your ways" Israel was so evil that she taught (Qal PERFECT, twice, BDB 540, KB 531) prostitutes a thing or two about evil. This is an allusion to

  1. fertility worship
  2. foreign alliances

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:34 "lifeblood of the innocent poor"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:34 "lifeblood of the innocent poor" The wealthy and powerful were taking advantage of the poor and powerless, see Jer. 7:6; 19:4; 22:3,17; 26:15; and the book of Amos.

The term "innocent" (BDB 667) does not mean "sinless." See the Special Topic below on the Hebrew concept.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BLAMELESS, INNOCENT, GUILTLESS, WITHOUT REPROACH

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

▣ "You did not find them breaking in" The word translated "breaking in" is a NOUN (BDB 369, KB 573) found only here and in Exod. 22:2, where it refers to the killing of a burglar. These Judeans killed people without even the pretext of necessity.

▣ "But in spite of all these things" The Hebrew phrase is very uncertain. The AB, vol. 21, simply puts it in brackets!

The UBS Text Project has two options.

  1. in spite of all these things (RSV)
  2. on every oak (LXX, NEB)

It gives #1 a C rating (considerable doubt). The UBS Handbook on Jeremiah also prefers #1 as "the least problematic" (p. 88).

The NASB, NRSV, NJB, and NIV connect the last line of Jer. 2:34 with Jer. 2:35.

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:35 This shows the depth of their sin and self-deception as they rationalize their conduct. Possibly their prosperity blinded their eyes as they claimed the promises from Deuteronomy 28-29, but forgot the conditional nature of YHWH's covenant!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:36-37
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:36-37 These verses clearly threaten an exile by Neo-Babylon. The political alliances (i.e. Egypt and the remnant of the Assyrian army, cf. Jer. 2:18) cannot save Israel from Nebuchadnezzar II.

2:36
NASB  "go around so much"
NKJV, Peshitta  "gad about so much"
NRSV  "how frivolously. . ."
NJB  "how lightly you gad about"
JPSOA  "how you cheapaen yourselves"
REB  "why do you so lightly. . ."
LXX  "whatever did you greatly despise"

The root of the VERB is uncertain and the ADVERB, "lightly" (BDB 547), seems to fit well with option #2. Here are the options for the VERB.

  1. אזל ‒ BDB 23, KB 27 ‒ "go"
  2. זלל ‒ KB 272 ‒ "to treat lightly"

entries.title: Jeremiah 2:37 "hands on your head"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:37 "hands on your head" This is a sign of captivity or mourning.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES, #4
