READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Jeremiah 2:1-4:4 forms a literary unit. Identifying literary units is crucial for contextual interpretations. See Introduction, VII.

  2. Jeremiah 3 is a word play on the word shub (שׁוב, BDB 996, KB 1427), which means "to turn," either to something or to someone. The term is used in both religious and non-religious senses. But, its main theological emphasis is a turning from evil and turning to YHWH (cf. Jer. 3:7,10,14; 8:4,6; 18:8; 26:3; 31:19; 44:5).
    SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

  3. The broken covenant is illustrated as a broken marriage resulting in a legal divorce. However, YHWH's grace is so powerful that the Deut. 24:1-4 requirements are annulled (i.e. faithless, idolatrous Israel can return to her first husband, YHWH, v. 1)!
     Israel was almost never faithful to the Sinai covenant. She had such few godly kings. It is surely possible that
    1. YHWH's intent was to use His blessing on Israel to attract the nations, but, they were never faithful and the curses of Lev. 26 and Deut. 28 became a reality.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)
    2. YHWH used Israel, with all of her special blessings (cf. Rom. 9:4-5), to clearly demonstrate that fallen mankind (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND) could never keep the Mosaic Covenant (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP and SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT). Therefore, a new covenant based on YHWH's actions was required (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36). The key was YHWH's "grace" and "mercy" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD) and not human performance!
       The covenant with Israel was a crucial, but temporary, way (cf. Matt. 5:17-19) to demonstrate YHWH's plan for the salvation and restoration to Edenic fellowship.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMTIVE PLAN

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

3:1
NASB  "God says"
NKJV  "they say"
NRSV, LXX, NJB, REB   —omit—
TEV  "The Lord says"
JPSOA  "[the word of the Lord came to me]
  as follows"

The MT simply has the Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (BDB 55, KB 65) "saying." The UBS Text Project suggests (p. 180)

  1. it introduces a principal, a proverb, or judicial statement
  2. it relates to Jer. 2:37

▣ "If a husband divorces his wife" This reflects Moses' statement in Deut. 24:3-4. YHWH uses divorce as imagery of His peoples' "spiritual adultery" (i.e. idolatry). Israelites could not take back a wife after another man had married her (cf. Deut. 24:4), but YHWH's great love will remarry Israel even after her idolatry (Jer. 4:1; Hosea 1-3).

YHWH was stating what had occurred years ago (see full note at Jer. 2:20-25).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVORCE

▣ "Will he still return to her?" This was not allowed (cf. Deut. 24:1-4).

▣ "land be completely polluted" The IMPERFECT VERB and INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root (BDB 337, KB 335) are used to intensify the sense of the idolatrous pollution. This very thing is discussed in Lev. 18:24-28; 19:29; Deut. 24:4.

The LXX (NEB, REB) has "woman," האשׁה, (cf. v. 9), but the MT has "land," הארץ. The UBS Text Project rates "land" as "B" (some doubt); both fit the context.

There are three Hebrew roots that denote pollution and defilement.

  1. BDB 379, KB 375 ‒ pollution by idolatry
    1. Jer. 2:7; 3:9; 16:18, defile the land
    2. Jer. 2:23 ‒ Israel's denial of pollution
  2. BDB 337, KB 335 ‒ polluted by idolatry
    1. Jer. 3:1,2, defiled the land (Ps. 106:38; Isa. 24:5)
    2. Jer. 23:11 ‒ prophets and priests polluted (Dan. 11:32)
  3. BDB 320 II, KB 319 ‒ Jer. 34:16 ‒ pollute the Name of YHWH (cf. Lev. 18:21; 19:12; 20:3; 21:6; 22:2,32; Ezek. 20:39; Amos 2:7

▣ "you are a harlot with many lovers" YHWH is depicted as a husband, possibly based on Deut. 10:20; 11:22; 13:4 (i.e. "cling to Him"). This is one of several anthropomorphic metaphors used of God and His relationship to His faith children.

The shocking imagery of covenant Israel as a "harlot" (i.e. spiritual idolatry with pagan idols) is expanded in the book of Revelation, where, I think, "the great harlot" refers to Jerusalem and the "red beast" on which she rides, refers to the Roman Empire (cf. Rev. 17). In eschatological studies, this position is known as Partial Preterism. Please see my new (2024) verse-by-verse commentary on the book of the Revelation, online at www.freebiblecommentary.org

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣
NASB  "Yet you turn to Me"
NKJV  "yet return to Me"
TEV  "now you want to return to Me?"
LXX, NJB  "would you return to me?"
JPSOA  "can you return to Me?"
Peshitta  "return again to me"

This is the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of a VERB (Qal IMPERFECT, BDB 996, KB 1427) used earlier in the verse (and throughout this chapter). This refers to Israelite worship that had combined the worship of YHWH with pagan worship practices. Its grammatical form can be

  1. "turned to," an IMPERATIVE (NKJV)
  2. "are turned," a VERB (NASB)
  3. "returned," a question (TEV, NJB, JPSOA following the LXX)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:2 "Lift up your eyes. . .see"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:2 "Lift up your eyes. . .see" These are both Qal IMPERATIVES.

  1. lift up ‒ BDB 669, KB 724
  2. see ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, cf. Jer. 1:10; 2:10 (twice), 19, 23, 31

▣ "bare heights" This was the place of the worship of Ba'al and Asherah (cf. Jer. 3:21; 4:11; 7:29; 12:12; 14:6; Hosea 4:11-14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣
NASB  "violated"
NKJV  "lain with men"
NJB, JPSOA, REB  "lain with"
TEV  "acted like a prostitute"
LXX  "contaminated" or "utterly defiled"
Peshitta  "defiled yourself"

The MT has "be ravished" (שׁגל, BDB 993, KB 1415, cf. NASB), but the Masoretic scholars suggest "be lain with" (שׁכב, BDB 1011, KB 1486).

The covenant people were not raped. They voluntarily committed "spiritual adultery" with foreign idols seeking prosperity and fertility of their families, herds, and crops.

▣ "By the roads you have sat" This is an historical/cultural reference to what the prostitutes did (cf. Gen. 38:14; Prov. 7:12ff; Ezek. 16:25).

▣
NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB  "Arab"
NKJV  "Arabian"
NJB  "nomad"
JPSOA  "bandit"
Peshitta  "ostrich"

The MT has "Arabian" (ערבי, BDB 787 IV, cf. Isa. 13:20), but the Septuagint has "raven" (ערב, BDB 788 VI).

The JPSOA interprets the word as a robber (see UBS Handbook, p. 94). The LXX's "raven" could be parallel to "polluted land," as the raven was an unclean scavenger, but it could also mean a supposed helper, cf. 1 Kgs. 17:4.

▣ "harlotry" See SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:3 The first two lines are poetic parallel. God tried to use the cycles of nature to open the eyes of His people (cf. Lev. 26:14-20; Deut. 28:15-68), but they would not see. There are two rainy seasons in Palestine (cf. Deut. 11:14), one at planting time and the other as the plants mature. Most moisture came from daily dew.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

▣ "harlot's forehead" This is a reference either to

  1. characteristic ornamentation (cf. Rev. 17:5)
  2. imagery for stubbornness (JPSOA, "brazenness") and lack of shame (cf. Ezek. 3:7-8)

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:4 "My Father"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:4 "My Father" This is another family image for God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FATHERHOOD OF GOD

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:5 "Will He be angry forever"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:5 "Will He be angry forever" They were trying to take advantage of God's mercy. This same concept is discussed in Ps. 103:8-14. God's mercy was not the issue, but their willful and repeated idolatry (cf. Jer. 3:12-14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "angry. . .indignant" The JPSOA footnote asserts that the MT reflects Akkadian parallels (i.e. "hate" and "rage").

  1. maintain wrath (BDB 643, #1, KB 695, Qal IMPERFECT), cf. v. 12; Ps. 103:9; Micah 7:18 similar statements)
  2. indignant ((BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal IMPERFECT, like #1, means "retain wrath," cf. Amos 1:11

There is a biblical tension between

  1. YHWH's forever judgments
  2. YHWH's willingness to not hold on to His anger

This seems confusing and contradictory to western thinking, but it fits perfectly the eastern mentality of putting truth to tension filled pairs (i.e. paradox), and thereby seeking humans to purposely remain in the tension.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

▣ "spoken. . .done evil" Their lips said one thing, but their actions showed another (cf. Jer. 2:20,23-25; Isa. 29:13).

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:6 "Then the Lord said to me in the days of Josiah the king"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:6 "Then the Lord said to me in the days of Josiah the king" This surely dates the poem and by implication the surrounding strophes.

For the reign of King Josiah see SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY.

▣ "Israel" These are the northern ten tribes. Jeremiah 3:7-8,10,11 show that in light of Israel's sin, Judah should have learned, but she did not, and even copied her sister's sins (cf. Ezek. 16:44-52; 23).

The northern kingdom was known by three titles.

  1. Israel (a collective term)
  2. Ephraim (the largest tribe)
  3. Samaria (the capital city)

▣ "on every high hill and under every green tree" This was the site for Ba'al worship (cf. Deut. 12:7; 1 Kgs. 14:23; 2 Kgs. 16:4; 17:10; 2 Chr. 28:4; Isa. 57:5,7; Jer. 3:2-3,6; 17:2,8; Ezek. 6:13; 20:28; Hosea 4:11-14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:7 "Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:7 "Judah" These are the southern three tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin. Most of the Levites and priests also stayed with the southern tribes.

▣ "she will return to Me" The word "return" (BDB 996, KB 1427) is Hebrew imagery for repentance. It is used several times in this chapter (cf. Jer. 3:1 [twice], 7 [twice], 10, 12,14, 19, 22). The OT, as the NT, is a conditional covenant as it relates to human choices, but an unconditional covenant as to YHWH's plan to redeem those individuals who will turn to Him by repentance and faith (cf. Mark 1:15; Acts 3:16,19; 20:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

3:8
NASB, NKJV, LXX  "I saw. . ."
TEV  "Judah also saw. . ."
NRSV  "She also saw. . ."
NJB, REB, Peshitta  "She saw"
JPSOA  "I noted:""

The MT has "and I saw" (וארא), but the DSS, Peshitta, and the Vulgate versions have "she saw" (ותרא). The UBS Text Project gives the MT a B rating (some doubt).

The next line describes YHWH's actions in light of Israel's response.

▣ "I had sent her away" This links the Assyrian exile (i.e. 722 B.C.) with the imagery of divorce ("send away," BDB 1018, KB 1511, Piel PERFECT, cf. Deut. 22:19,29; 24:1,3; Jer. 3:1).

▣ "writ of divorce" This was a legal document first discussed in Deut. 24:1-4.

  1. involved some legal procedures which took some time so that the couple could work out their differences if possible
  2. another person had to be involved (i.e. a Levite)
  3. involved the restitution of the dowry to the wife or her family
  4. allowed the vulnerable woman to remarry and be a functioning member of that society

SPECIAL TOPIC: CERTIFICATE OF DIVORCE

▣ "yet her treacherous sister Judah did not fear" Israel is described as "faithless" (BDB 1000) in vv. 6,8,11,12. This root denotes apostasy from YHWH and His covenant (cf. Jer. 2:19; 3:22; 5:6; 8:5; 14:7; Hosea 6:7).

Judah, seeing what happened to Israel (i.e. exile), still continued down the same path of threachery (BDB 93, KB 108, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE), especially in marriage (here, spiritual adultery with pagan idols, cf. Jer. 3:20; 9:2). For other usages see Isa. 24:16; 33:1; 48:8; Jer. 3:8,10,11; 5:11; 12:1,6; Hosea 5:7).

Ezekiel discusses this same issue of Judah's lack of understanding about the consequenes of idolatry that fell on the northern tribes (cf. Ezek. 10:44-52; all of chapter 23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

3:9
NASB  "the lightness of her harlotry"
NKJV  "her casual harlotry"
NRSV  "her shameless whoring"
TEV  "was not at all ashamed"
NJB  "she took her whoredom so lightly"
JPSOA  "her casual immorality"
REB  "her casual prostitution"
LXX  "her whoredom came to nothing"

The key word is "so light" (קל, BDB 887, KB 1101 I), found only here. BDB suggests "lightness" or "frivolity."

▣ "stones and trees" This is a reference to the male Canaanite deity, Ba'al, symbolized by an uplifted stone, and the female Canaanite deity, Asherah, symbolized by a live tree or carved tree (cf. Jer. 2:27). These pagan fertility gods were worshiped in every town, either on a manmade, raised platform of cut stones or on a close by hill.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:10 "Judah did not return to Me with all her heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:10 "Judah did not return to Me with all her heart" This may be a reference to the reforms of Hezekiah or Josiah. The reforms of these godly kings were only superficially accepted by the populous.

For "returned" see SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT).

For "heart" see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:11 This is a shocking statement. Judah had more spiritual light and opportunities than did the northern tribes, but she did not learn from YHWH's judgment on them (cf. Ezek. 16:44-52; 23; Luke 12:48).

Israel is "faithless" (BDB 1000, cf. Jer. 3:6,8,12; also note Jer. 2:19; 3:22; 5:6; 8:5; 14:7) but Judah is "treacherous" (BDB 93, KB 108, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, cf. Jer. 3:8,20; 5:11; 12:6; Isa. 21:2; 24:16; 33:1). Both Hebrew roots denote a maintained apostasy. But, Judah had light and was, therefore, more responsible.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:12 "For I am gracious"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:12 "For I am gracious" This is one of the primary presuppositions of the character of Deity. Often in other world religions, deity is capricious, detached, but not so the God of the Bible. Note His repeated characteristics.

  1. compassionate (BDB 933), cf. Exod. 34:6; Deut. 4:31; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13
  2. gracious (BDB 337), cf. Exod. 34:6; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13
  3. slow to anger (BDB 74 CONSTRUCT BDB 60), cf. Exod. 34:6; Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13
  4. abounding in lovingkindness (hesed, BDB 338, see SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS), cf. Exod. 34:6; Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13
  5. abounding in truth ("faithfulness," amen, BDB 54, see SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT), cf. Exod. 34:6; Ps. 86:15
  6. forgiving iniquity and transgression, cf. Num. 14:18
  7. will not (cf. Deut. 4:31)
    1. fail you
    2. destroy you
    3. forget the covenant with your fathers
  8. abundant forgiveness (BDB 699), cf. Neh. 9:17
  9. did not forsake them (BDB 736 I), cf. Neh. 9:17
  10. will not keep His anger forever, cf. Ps. 103:9
  11. relenting of evil, cf. Joel 2:13

Wow! What a wonderful God we trust, serve, and emulate!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:12-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:12-14 The NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB all show these verses in poetic form (like Jer. 3:1-5 and Jer. 3:19-20).

  1. God tells the prophet to
    1. go (Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE)
    2. proclaim (Qal PERFECT with waw)
  2. God tells the northern tribes to
    1. return (Qal IMPERATIVE, see note at Jer. 3:1)
    2. acknowledge (lit. "know," Qal IMPERATIVE; see SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW)
      (1) your iniquity
      (2) that you have transgressed (Qal PERFECT)
      (3) that you scattered your favors (BDB 202) to strangers (i.e. idols)
      (4) that you have not obeyed (Qal PERFECT; see SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP)
  3. If they will obey, God will
    1. not look upon you in anger
    2. not be angry forever (see v. 5)

This literary form has been called "a summons to repentance" in Cracking OT Codes by Sandy and Giese (p. 164). It includes a divine promise, an accusation of sin, and a divine threat of judgment (cf. Isa. 1:19-20; 55:6-7; Jer. 3:12-13; 4:1-4; Joel 2:12-13; Amos 5:4-7,14-15).

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:13-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:13-14 God's people must acknowledge their sin and turn back to faith and faithfulness in YHWH!

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:14 "I am a master to you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:14 "I am a master to you" This is a play on the word Ba'al (BDB 127), the male fertility god of Canaan, whose name means husband (cf. Jer. 31:32), master, lord, owner. This continues the family imagery.

For "sons" (BDB 119), see the same condemnation in Isa. 1:2-3.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:15 God's leaders (i.e. "shepherds," BDB 944), both civil and religious, will

  1. be after YHWH's own heart (BDB 524)
  2. feed the people with knowledge (BDB 395, only here in Jeremiah)
  3. feed the people with understanding (BDB 968, cf. Jer. 9:24)

Numbers 2 and 3 could refer to the shepherds themselves or what they give the people.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:16 "in those days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:16 "in those days" This refers to the New Covenant period (cf. Jer. 3:16-18; 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36) or the Messianic age.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

▣ "ark of the covenant" Whether it was actually missing at this point in time is uncertain; this passage points to internal worship (cf. John 4:23; one wonders if Jesus had this text in mind when He spoke to the woman at the well). There will be no need for a physical object representing YHWH. He Himself will be among His people!

  1. it will not come to mind
  2. you will not rememer it
  3. you will not miss it
  4. you will not make a copy of it

The true hope of Israel was not in the temple (cf. Jer. 7; Acts 7), but in YHWH Himself. Ritual without faith is a barrier to true biblical understanding of YHWH's plan of intimate fellowship with His unique creation (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ARK OF THE COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:17 "Jerusalem"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:17 "Jerusalem" I think this refers to the New Jerusalem (i.e. the new people of God, cf. Rev. 21:1-4). See my full notes in my new (2024) exegetical verse-by-verse commentary on Revelation.

▣ "all nations will be gathered to it" Notice the universal element (cf. Jer. 4:2; 12:15,16; 16:19; Isa. 2:2-4; 25:6-9; 45:22; 49:6; 54:4-5; 56:6-8; 60:3; 66:18,23). This would have shocked and offended these Judean readers/hearers, just as Isaiah's inclusion of the nations shocked the readers/hearers of his day!

It is always difficult to know if these passages refer to

  1. scattered exiles being brought home and rewarded by Gentiles
  2. Gentiles being fully welcomed into YHWH's covenant family
  3. The NT solves this issue by noting God's love for all humans.
    1. no more Jews and Gentiles, Rom. 2:28,29; 9:6; Gal. 3:7-9,29; 6:16; Eph. 2:11-3:13; 1 Pet. 3:6
    2. God's desire for all humans to be saved; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO OT COVENANT PROMISES SEEM SO DIFFERENT FROM NT COVENANT PROMISES?

▣ "nor will they walk any more after the stubbornness of their evil heart" This had been the problem since Genesis 3 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND, cf. Gen. 6:5,11,12; Jer. 11:8)! But the new day will reverse this self-centeredness. Compare Ezek. 18:31 with Ezek. 36:26-27. The new covenant (Jer. 31:31-34) will be based on God's acts, not human acts!

The real question is to whom does "they" refer?

  1. the faithful remnant of Abraham's seed
  2. all of Abraham's seed alive in that day
  3. the Gentiles gathered to Jerusalem

For me, I have been deeply influenced by Rom. 2:28-29; Gal. 3:7-9,28; 6:16; Eph. 3:11-4:13; 1 Pet. 3:6. Abraham is the father of those who believe, not a racial/ethnic group.

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:18 "the house of Judah. . .the house of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:18 "the house of Judah. . .the house of Israel" The reunification of the thirteen tribes into one nation would be the goal of much of Josiah's reform.

The "they" of v. 17 refers to the two nations which split in 922 B.C..

▣ "the land of the north" This is not a reference to a country to the north, but to the route of return of the Jewish exiles (cf. Jer. 31:8).

▣ "to the land that I gave your fathers as an inheritance" See Gen. 12:1-3; 22:16-18; Amos 9:15. YHWH acted toward this generation, and every generation of Abraham's seed, because of His love and promises to the Patriarchs!

God has an eternal redemptive plan that involves Israel and the Messiah. His plan is for all humanity. His plan will not be defeated, delayed, or destroyed!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:19 This verse begins a new strophe (i.e. Jer. 3:19-20). It could refer to

  1. the natural seed of Abraham (i.e. Israel as the firstborn son)
  2. the faith seed of Abraham (cf. Isa. 63:16; Rom. 2:28-29)

Jeremuah 3:20 implies option #1, while Jer. 3:19 implies option #2.  Remember  Jer. 3:16-18 is describing the new age, the new covenant period.

The last two VERBS in Jer. 3:19 are PLURAL in the MT, but the Masoretic scholars suggest a change to the SINGULAR.

The NET Bible (p. 1295) suggests (because of the gender of the VERBS) that "Israel appears to be addressed here contextually as the Lord's wife" and "the imagery here appears to be that of

  1. treating the wife as an equal heir with the sons
  2. giving her the best piece of property"

▣ "Father" See SPECIAL TOPIC: FATHERHOOD OF GOD

▣ "not turn away See SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ 3:20 This refers to the early verses of this chapter.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:21 "A voice"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:21 "A voice" This would be the loud lament of Israel's repentance.

  1. weeping (BDB 113)
  2. supplications (BDB 337)

They are apparently calling out to their pagan gods (because of the first two lines of v. 22 and 3:2).

  1. perverting their way ‒ Hiphil PERFECT, BDB 730, KB 796
  2. forgetting YHWH ‒ Qal PERFECT, BDB 1013, KB 1489, cf. Jer. 2:32; 13:25

▣ "bare heights" This has been used sarcastically of the place of Ba'al worship (see note at v. 2), but here it reflects a place of mourning (cf. Jdg. 11:37).

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:22 The UBS Handbook notes that the words

  1. return (BDB 996, KB 1427)
  2. faithless (BDB 1000)
  3. faithlessness (BDB 1000)

all are based on the same Hebrew consonants, שׁוב (p. 113). Sound plays are very common in Hebrew poetry.

▣ "I will heal your faithlessness" Here, like Ps. 103:3; Isa. 53:4-5; Hosea 14:4, this imagery refers to spiritual healing (i.e. the forgiveness of sin).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:22-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:22-23 These verses have words from

  1. YHWH
    1. return faithless sons ‒ Qal IMPERFECT
    2. I will heal your faithlessness ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. the faithless sons
    1. we come to You ‒ Qal PERFECT
    2. for You are the Lord our God
    3. the hills (i.e. a place of fertility worship) are a deception
    4. salvation is only in YHWH

      Jer. 3:25 continues the words of "the faithless sons" (i.e. their repentance)

    5. let us lie down in our shame ‒ Qal COHORTATIVE
    6. let our humiliation cover us ‒ Piel IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    7. we have sinned against the Lord our God ‒ Qal PERFECT
    8. we and our fathers have sinned since our youth even to this day (cf. Jer. 22:21)
    9. we have not obeyed the voice of the Lord our God

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:23 "surely"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:23 "surely" The ADVERB (BDB 38) occurs twice and gives the words of the people a solemnity!

▣ Lines one and two of verse 23 are depicting Ba'al worship on the mountains of Israel. These worship scenes may be noisy but they cannot save; only YHWH can save (line four).

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:24 "shameful thing"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:24 "shameful thing" This is used sarcastically of Ba'al (cf. Jer. 11:13; Hosea 9:10) or because of the mention of "sons and daughters," it may refer to the worship of Molech.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH.

entries.title: Jeremiah 3:25 "from our youth even to this day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:25 "from our youth even to this day" This rebellion was no new or passing thing. It went back to the wilderness wandering period (i.e. Exodus 32).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. To what is Jeremiah comparing God's people?
  2. What two metaphors does he use of God?
  3. Did His people truly repent? Why or why not?
  4. Does Jer. 3:19-25 reflect the future or post-exilic time?

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:1 "If"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:1 "If" Grammatically there seem to be four "ifs" or conditions in Jer. 4:1-2. This shows the conditional nature of the covenant (i.e. "if. . .then. . .," cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28; also note Deut. 30:15,19; Psalm 1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "return. . .return to Me" The Hebrew root, שׁוב (BDB 996-1000), is used in several words, in several lines in chapters 3:1-4:2.

  1. שׁוב ‒ "return," Jer. 3:1 (twice), 7 (twice), 10,12,14,19,22; 4:1 (twice)

    ‒ "turn away," Jer. 4:8

    ‒ "turn back," Jer. 4:28

  2. שׁובב (BDB 1000) ‒ "faithless," Jer. 3:14,22
  3. משׁובה, (BDB 1000) ‒ "faithless," Jer. 3:6,11,12

    ‒ "backsliding," 3:22

Notice the personal emphasis (cf. Jer. 3:1,4,7,10,19,20). Sin is more than a violation of a law code. It is a personal affront to a personal God (i.e. Gen. 20:6; 39:9; 2 Sam. 12:13; Ps. 41:4; 51:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ Notice the list of things YHWH asks His wayward, faithless, covenant people to do.

  1. return (twice, meaning to repent, that is turn from idols and turn to YHWH)
  2. put away (BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERFECT) your idols (cf. Jer. 7:17-18)
  3. do not waver, that whole hearted repentance, not half-heart pretending
  4. you will swear "as the Lord lives," which is a faith and commitment oath, cf. Deut. 6:13; 10:20; Jer. 12:16)

▣ "Israel" This title (BDB 975, KB 442) can mean

  1. a new name given to Jacob
  2. a collective term for all the children of Jacob
  3. the northern ten tribes after the split of the United Monarchy in 922 B.C. They were later taken captive by Assyria at the fall of the capital, Samaria in 722 B.C.

Context must determine which meaning. This is especially hard in Jeremiah when #2 and #3 are used in isolated poems without their historical setting specified.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "detested things" This is literally "abominations" (BDB 1055) and refers to idols.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

▣ "and will not waver" This VERB (BDB 626, KB 678, Qal IMPERFECT, lit. "wander," cf. Gen. 4:12,14) refers to wholehearted daily activities (i.e. lifestyle).

King David had a whole hearted devotion to YHWH (cf. 1 Kgs. 3:14; 9:4), but his son, Solomon, had only half hearted devotion to YHWH (cf. 1 Kgs. 11:2,4,9). Idolatry destroys faith, trust, and dependence on YHWH and YHWH alone!

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter is a series of poems on different subjects. Verses 5-31 contain several independant poems about Judah's invasion.

  2. Jeremiah 4:1-2 describe repentance and relate to Jeremiah 3, Jer. 4:21-25.

  3. The theme of Judah's rebellion and YHWH's judgment by foreign invasion runs through Jeremiah 6.

  4. Notice the number of ways the God-sent invaders are described
    1. the lion, v. 7
    2. the destroyer, v. 7
    3. he. . ., v. 13
    4. besiegers, v. 16
    5. horsemen and bowmen, v. 28
    6. the killers, v. 31

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:2 "you will swear"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:2 "you will swear" This VERB (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal PERFECT with waw) refers to a verbal act of worship, much like our modern liturgies (cf. Jer. 12:16; Deut. 6:13; 10:20; Isa. 65:16). Idolaters swear by Ba'al, but YHWH's people swear allegiance only to Him! This is theologically parallel to Rom. 10:9-13, which is a quote from Joel 2:32 (cf. Acts 2:21).

▣ "In truth, in justice and in righteousness" This is the attitude of "swear." It refers to a lifestyle response, not only a ritual or periodic emotional experiences. This would describe true repentance. Each of these three words carries theological meaning.

  1. in truth (BDB 54, see Special Topic below)
  2. in justice (BDB 1048, see Special Topic below)
  3. in righteousness (BDB 842, see Special Topic below)

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT, and JUSTICE IN ISAIAH

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "the nations will bless themselves in Him" This is a recurrent theme in Genesis (BDB 138, KB 159, Hithpael PERFECT with waw, cf. Gen. 12:3; 18:18; 22:18; 26:41; 28:14). God's promises to the Patriarchs show Israel's purpose as an instrument of reaching the whole world (cf. Exod. 19:5-6; Isa. 42:6; 49:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

This is such an important theological concept that I have included my notes from Gen. 12:3.

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "and in you all the families
of the earth shall be blessed"
NRSV footnote, JPSOA  "by you all the families of the
earth shall bless themselves"
TEV  "and through you I will bless
all the nations"
TEV footnote  "All the nations will ask me
to bless them as I have
blessed you"
NJB  "and all the clans on earth
will bless themselves by you"
LXX  "and in you shall all the
tribes of the earth be blessed"
REB  "All the peoples on earth will
wish to be blessed as you
are blessed"
REB footnote  "All the peoples on earth will
be blessed because of you"

The Niphal stem is usually PASSIVE (LXX, NASB, "shall be blessed," cf. Jer. 18:18; 28:14), but in Jer. 22:18 and 26:4 the Hithpael PERFECT stem is used, which is REFLEXIVE ("bless themselves"). It is possible that the Hithpael denotes a continuing action through time. It is significant that God includes all nations in His promise to Abram in light of the universal rebellion of chapter 11. God chose Abraham to choose all humans made in His image (cf. Ps. 22:27; 66:4; 86:9; Isa. 25:6-12; 56:6-8; 60:1-3; 66:23; Acts 3:25; Gal. 3:8)! Also see note at Gen. 22:18.

This is really an important passage. It shows clearly God's purpose of using Abram to reach all the world. The universal promise of Gen. 3:15 is being implemented, even amidst the purposeful rebellion of Noah's children (i.e. Genesis 10 and 11). It s not only to those who show favor to Abram, but to those who will show favor to Abram's seed (i.e. the Messiah). There was/is a universal purpose in YHWH's choice of "one" to bring prophesied redemption through the special "One" of his descendants. In the big picture, this is not a text about an attitude toward Jews, but a faith response to the Jewish "promised One."

▣ "in Him they will glory" The VERB (BDB 237, KB 248) is Hithpael IMPERFECT, denoting ongoing action. Followers of YHWH glory/boast in knowing Him and Him alone (cf. Jer. 9:23-24). Notice the wonderful, universal implications of Isa. 45:20-25, especially Jer. 4:25b! Biblical faith is a personal relationship with the one true God!

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:3 "to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:3 "to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem" This shows the collective call to individual repentance, which characterizes Jeremiah and Ezekiel (esp. Ezekiel 18). Biblical faith is corporate but it is entered into by individual choice.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE

▣ "Break up your fallow ground" Verse 3 relates to the agricultural practice of preparing ground for seed. The rabbis use the illustration that our minds are like a plowed field, ready for seed and what one lets in through the eyes and ears falls on that prepared ground. What we think and then dwell on becomes who we are!

Repentance is plowed, good ground, ready for fellowship and obedience in a daily walk with God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:3-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:3-8 This strophe is a warning and call for repentance. Notice the commands.

  1. Jer. 4:3, "break up" ‒ BDB 644, KB 697, Qal IMPERATIVE (metaphor for prepare your heart, cf. Hos.  10:12)
  2. Jer. 4:3, "sow" ‒ BDB 281, KB 282, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (negated, "among the thorns" imagery for established idolatry)
  3. Jer. 4:4, "circumcise yourselves" ‒ BDB 557, KB 555, Niphal IMPERATIVE (imagery for the heart, cf. Jer. 9:25-26; see SPECIAL TOPIC: CIRCUMCISION, III)
  4. Jer. 4:4, "remove" ‒ BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (the literary parallel to "circumcise")

In light of YHWH's warning of judgment (Jer. 4:4c-f), He calls for the proclamation of invasion and action (Jer. 4:5-8).

  1. Jer. 4:5, "declare" ‒ BDB 610, KB 665, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (first of six IMPERATIVES about communication)
  2. Jer. 4:5, "proclaim" ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  3. Jer. 4:5, "say" ‒ BDB 55, KB 65, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. Jer. 4:5, "blow" ‒ BDB 1075, KB 1785, Qal IMPERATIVE
  5. Jer. 4:5, "cry" ‒ BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. Jer. 4:5, "aloud" ‒ BDB 569, KB 583, Piel IMPERATIVE
  7. Jer. 4:5, "say" ‒ same as #3

    The content of their commandment is, act now, judgment is coming (cf. Jer. 4:6c-7)

  8. Jer. 4:5, "assemble" ‒ BDB 62, KB 74, Niphal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 8:14
  9. Jer. 4:5, "let us go" ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal COHORTATIVE, cf. Jer. 8:14
  10. Jer. 4:6, "lift up a standard" ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE (i.e. a military signal)
  11. Jer. 4:6, "seek refuge" ‒ BDB 731, KB 797, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  12. Jer. 4:6, "do not stand still" ‒ BDB 763, KB 840, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (i.e. do not wait!)

    Finally, in light of the coming judgment, they are called on to grieve.

  13. Jer. 4:8, "put on sackcloth" ‒ BDB 291, KB 291, Qal IMPERATIVE (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES)
  14. Jer. 4:8, "lament" ‒ BDB 704, KB 763, Qal IMPERATIVE
  15. Jer. 4:8, "wail" ‒ BDB 410, KB 413, Qal IMPERATIVE

Why? "The fierce anger of the Lord" is coming (cf. Jer. 4:26; 12:13; 25:37,38; 30:24; 49:37; 51:45) and He will not change His mind (cf. Jer 4:28).

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:4 "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord. . .remove the foreskin of your heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:4 "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord. . .remove the foreskin of your heart" This shows that ritual alone was/is never effective, but a daily, internal faith attitude is essential (cf. Deut. 10:12; 30:6).

Other examples of this idiom are:

  1. ears, Jer. 6:10
  2. lips, Exod. 6:12,30
  3. heart, Deut. 10:16; 30:6
  4. flesh, Gen. 17:12

SPECIAL TOPIC: CIRCUMCISION

▣ "My wrath go forth like fire" This is recurrent imagery (cf. Jer. 17:4; 21:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

▣ "And burn with none to quench it" See Isa. 1:31; 66:24; Amos 5:6; Matt. 3:12; Mark 9:43,48; see SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHMENT.

See the word study gehenna in the SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, II. D.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:5 "Blow the trumpet"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:5 "Blow the trumpet" This is the word shophar. It was used as a call to war or for religious observances. Jer. 4:5-9 forms a poem of a watchman.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

▣ "in the land" This is the Hebrew term erets (BDB 75, KB 90). It has a wide semantic field. It is obvious from this context that it means Judah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

▣ "Into the fortified cities" When an enemy approached, all the people of the surrounding unwalled villages rushed to the nearest city with a protective wall (i.e. Jer. 8:14).

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:6 "Lift up a standard"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:6 "Lift up a standard" A standard (BDB 651) serves several purposes.

  1. a call to assemble
  2. a call to gather for war ‒ Isa. 5:26; 13:2; 18:3-4; Jer. 50:2; 51:12
  3. a call to rush to a walled city ‒ Jer. 4:6,21
  4. a call for Gentiles to come to YHWH in peace ‒ Isa. 11:10; 18:3; 49:22; 62:10
  5. YHWH is a banner for His people ‒ Exod. 17:15

▣ "Zion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ZION.

▣ "evil from the north" The "north" was a symbol of evil because it was the route of invasion for the Mesopotamian powers (i.e. Assyria, Babylon, Persia, cf. Jer. 1:14,15; 6:1,22; 10:22; 50:3; Isa. 41:25). Although, some see it as the invasion of the Scythians, according to Herodotus.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:7 "lion"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:7 "lion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣ "a destroyer of nations has set out" This is literally "struck his tents." It refers to Nebuchadnezzar II of Neo-Babylon, who took Judah into exile in 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C., as Assyria did Israel in 722 B.C.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:8 "put on sackcloth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:8 "put on sackcloth" See SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.

▣ "the fierce anger of the Lord has not turned back from us" This is a play on the phrase "turn back" (BDB 996, KB 1427), which is also the term for "repentance," cf. v. 1 (twice). YHWH will not relent of His wrath on His covenant people for their idolatry.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:9 "in that day"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:9 "in that day" This phrase was a way of referring to the special future day of YHWH's visitation (cf. Jer. 4:11a). It can be for blessing or judgment, here judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY

▣ "the king. . .the princes. . .the priests. . .the prophets" This refers to those leaders who rejected Jeremiah's message (cf. Jer. 1:18; 2:8,26; 5:31; 6:13; 8:1,10; 13:13; 14:18; 23:33-34). Judah had no godly leaders!

▣ Notice the parallel VERBS.

  1. fail ‒ BDB 1, KB 2, Qal IMPERFECT
  2. appalled ‒ BDB 1030, KB 1563, Niphal PERFECT with waw (related form "waste" in Jer. 4:7)
  3. astounded ‒ BDB 1069, KB 1744, Qal IMPERFECT (found only here in Jeremiah)

The leadership (civil and religious) will utterly fail and not know what to do in light of the invasion. Their eyes have been blinded by idolatry and false prophets (cf. Jer. 4:10); they cannot find YHWH! Therefore, the common proverb has come true—"As the leaders go, so go the people!"

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:10 "Then I said"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:10 "Then I said" Who is speaking?

  1. the prophet (Jeremiah)
  2. the people of Judah
  3. false prophets (i.e. you will have "peace")

The MT has "Then I said," but the LXX has, "And they shall say."

See my comment in the next item.

▣ "Surely You have utterly deceived this people" Jer. 4:10 is a comment from Jeremiah to YHWH about the message of the false prophets. Jeremiah speaks bluntly and honestly to God (cf. Jer. 12:1; 15:17-18; 20:7-9). This false message of hope and deliverance from invasion was what the false prophets were preaching in God's name (cf. Jer. 6:14; 8:11; 14:13; 23:16-17; 28:1ff). God let this occur but both the speaker and hearer are responsible!

The MT has the Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the Hiphil PERFECT VERB, which was a grammatical way to denote emphasis ("utterly deceived").

One more possibility in understanding this difficult phrase is that the people were clinging to Isaiah's prophecies about the invulnerability of Jerusalem (cf. Isaiah 36-39). Jeremiah would have to remind them that Isaiah's promises were also based on a conditional covenant model (i.e. "if. . .then. . .," cf. Jer. 4:1-2). Judah did not obey the covenant, therefore, its curses, not its promises, were what they would reap (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28-29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "peace" See SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT).

▣ "throat" This is the word nephesh (BDB 659, cf. Gen. 2:7 [of man] and 2:19 [of animals]). It basically means the life on this planet that breathes (related to the Hebrew word for "breath").

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:11 "A scorching wind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:11 "A scorching wind" This refers to the sirocco desert winds, often used in the OT as imagery for judgment (i.e. "not to winnow, and not to cleanse," cf. Jer. 4:12).

▣ "from the bare heights" This was the physical locality of Ba'al worship (cf. Jer. 2:20; 3:2,6; 4:11; 7:29; 14:6; 17:2; Isa. 57:7; Deut. 12:2). It was also the place where winnowing occurred.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "the daughter of My people" See notes at Jer. 46:11.

▣ "not to winnow" The wind will be too strong and too hot for harvesting grain. The last item, "cleanse," probably refers to the process of separating the husk from the grain (DSS).

The implication is that husk and grain (i.e. the faithful and the unfaithful) will both be destroyed.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:12 "at My command"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:12 "at My command" God sent these judgments; they were carried out by Mesopotamian pagan nations! There are consequences to covenant disobedience (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28-29)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:13 This is imagery for God's judgment (i.e. lines a-c refer to the invaders, "he," cf. v. 7) and the results.

  1. woe to us (BDB 17, cf. Jer. 4:31; 6:4; 10:19; 13:27)
  2. we are ruined (BDB 994, KB 1418, Pual PERFECT, same VERB found in Jer. 4:20; 9:19; 10:20; 48:1,15,20; 49:3,10)

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:14 "Wash your heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:14 "Wash your heart" This VERB (BDB 460, KB 459, Piel IMPERATIVE) is an allusion to washing a soiled garment, which is imagery for repentance and cleansing (cf. Ps. 51:2,7; Isa. 1:16; Jer. 2:2). It is a call, like Ezekiel 18, for an individual to turn back to YHWH and change his ways (cf. Jer. 4:3-4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣ "That you may be saved" The Hebrew VERB (BDB 446, KB 448, Niphal IMPERFECT) has two connotations.

  1. physical deliverance
  2. spiritual forgiveness

Both are needed for Judah to avert YHWH's coming judgment!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT term)

▣ "wicked thoughts" Maybe this is best illustrated by Jer. 13:27.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:15 "voice. . .from Dan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:15 "voice. . .from Dan" This was the farthest northern tribe in Palestine. The tribe of Dan, in unbelief, moved from its tribal allocation in the south (i.e. because of the Philistine occupation of their tribal inheritance, cf. Josh. 19:40-48) to the north (cf. Judges 18).

The phrase "from Dan to Beersheba" became a way to denote the whole Promised Land (cf. Jdg. 20:1; 1 Sam. 3:20; 2 Sam. 3:10; 17:11; 24:2; 2 Chr. 30:5; Amos 8:14).

▣ "Mount Ephraim" This refers to the central mountainous (i.e. hill country) region of Palestine, which was the tribal allocation of Ephraim (cf. Josh. 17:15; 19:50; 20:7). The mountains of Ebal and Gerizim (i.e. Samaria) were in this region.

Dan and Ephraim fell to the Assyrians in 722 B.C. Now that destruction would come to Judah and Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 4:16-17) and the northern invaders were close!

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:16 This verse starts with two commands to make known YHWH's coming judgment to Judah.

  1. report ‒ BDB 269, KB 269, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (this could refer to the mercenary invaders, Jer. 4:16c)
  2. proclaim ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

The voice from Dan (Jer. 4:15)

  1. tells the invaders (or the surrounding nations to Judah) they are close to Jerusalem
  2. tells Jerusalem that the invaders are close to them!

▣ "Besiegers come from a far country" The VERBAL (BDB 665, KB 718, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) in this context has the meaning of "besiege" (BDB 666, #5, cf. Isa. 1:8; Ezek. 6:12). It usually is translated "enemies."

  1. The UBS Handbook (p. 133) suggests advanced scouts of the Neo- Babylonian army.
  2. The UBS Text Project, p. 184, suggests it refers to enemy guards who watched besieged cities for those trying to escape.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:17 "Like watchmen of a field"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:17 "Like watchmen of a field" I must admit that I do not understand this phrase in this context. TEV takes it to mean watchmen that surround a field ready to harvest. But here they guard against any persons escaping the besieged city (NET Bible, footnote, #13).

The UBS Handbook (p. 134) suggests that the imagery is connected to the "tents" (booths) of the agricultural watchmen, but here with the army tents of the invaders (v. 7).

▣ "Because she has rebelled against Me" Notice the personal affront that YHWH feels! It is not just the violation of His covenant, but the rebellion against Him, Him as husband, Him as King, Him as the only God! Possibly Jer. 5:20-29 describes the attitude best.

The VERB "rebelled" (BDB 598, KB 632, Qal PERFECT) is also found in Jer. 5:23; Lam. 1:18,20 (twice); and 3:42. However a SYNONYM (BDB 833, KB 981) is used in Jer. 2:8,29; 3:13; 33:8; Lam. 3:42.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:18 The invasion, destruction, and exile of the covenant people from the covenant land and the special covenant city was their own fault. YHWH gave them only what they had sown (cf. Job 34:11; Ps. 28:4; 62:12; Prov. 24:12; Eccl. 12:14; Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:6; 14:12; 1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7-10; 2 Tim. 4:14; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12). For a full list, see Gal. 6:7-10.

▣ "How bitter" This is the result of their rebellion (cf. Jer. 2:19; Amos 8:10). Note Job 20:11-16; sin tastes good initially but becomes poison and brings death!

Their idolatry had spread into their very being (i.e. heart). They were sinful through and through!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:19-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:19-22 This shows the way God truly feels (Jer. 4:22) about bringing judgment to Judah (cf. Hosea 11:8-9). YHWH puts His feeling into the prophet's mind and heart. Jeremiah speaks for Him!

4:19
NASB, NKJV   "My soul, my soul!"
NRSV   "My anguish, my anguish!"
JPSOA   "Oh my suffering, my suffering!"
LXX   "My belly, my belly!"
Peshitta   "I am in pain! I am in pain!"

The MT has a NOUN (BDB 588) which means "bowels" or "inner parts" (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 1012-1013). Here it is parallel with "heart," which is another way of referring to the place of feelings. The ancient Hebrews thought the seat of the emotions was in the lower viscera (BDB 589 #5). This verse is emphasizing the terrible pain of Jeremiah's feelings about YHWH's coming judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INWARD PARTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART

▣
NASB   "I am in anguish"
NKJV   "I am pained in my heart"
NRSV   "how great my agony"
TEV   "I can't bear the pain"
NJB   "I writhe in pain"
JPSOA   "How I writhe"

The VERB in v. 19 could come from

  1. חול ‒ BDB 296, KB 297, Qal COHORTATIVE, "writhe"
  2. יחל ‒ BDB 403 KB 407, Hiphil COHORTATIVE, "wait"

This information is from OT Parsing Guide (revised) by Beall, Banks, and Smith, p. 546. The UBS Text Project and AB do not even mention the option.

▣ "The sound of the trumpet" The JPSOA notes that the MT has "you, O my being, hear," but by a change of vocalization, yields, "I hear the blare of horns, my inner being, alarms of war" (p. 931).

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:20 "Disaster on disaster"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:20 "Disaster on disaster" The NOUN (BDB 991) is repeated for emphasis. This same literary technique was used by isaiah.

Also notice that "devastated" (BDB 994) is also repeated in this verse (v. 30). Both of these similar roots (שׁדד and שׁדר) are used often in Jeremiah.

▣ "tents. . .curtains" The NET Bible (p. 1298) makes the comment that this verse could refer to

  1. the weakness of Judah's defenses
  2. the destruction of a person's home (using an ancient cultural imagery)

The UBS Handbook on Jeremiah (p. 137) suggests that "tents" and "curtain" could be a reference to the temple in Jerusalem.

▣ "in an instant" This is parallel with "suddenly" (v. 20c). The phrase "in an instant" (רגע, BDB 921), with revocalization, can be translated "torn to shreds" (cf. LXX, NEB). This would fit the parallelism as well.

▣ "my. . .My" Apparently, Jeremiah is speaking as a Judean citizen. He is identifying with his people's plight!

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:21 The "standard" and "the trumpet" are military signaling devises, here of the invaders (cf. Jer. 4:19).

The two VERBS of this verse are

  1. see ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense
  2. hear ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal COHORTATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:22 This verse shows God's disappointment in His covenant people in strong images of irony.

  1. they are foolish (BDB 17)
  2. they do not know Me (BDB 393, KB 390, Qal PERFECT)
  3. they are stupid (BDB 698) children (cf. Isa. 1:2-3)
  4. they have no understanding (BDB 106, KB 122, Niphal PARTICIPLE)
  5. they are shrewd to do evil (BDB 314)
  6. they do not know how to do good (BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

Notice how they are described in Jer. 5:21.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:23-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:23-26 This strophe uses original creation in its chaotic state (i.e. "formless and void," cf. Gen. 1:2; "the heavens, and they had no light" before Gen. 1:3) to describe the destruction caused by foreign (Mesopotamian) invasion.

As creation was originally without human habitation, so now the Promised Land is without human habitation. This is not to be taken literally; there were always some Israelites and Judeans not taken captive, but the land looked/seemed empty! (cf. Jer. 4:27).

Also notice the literary structure of "I looked. . ." (BDB 55, KB 65, Qal PERFECT) used four times.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:25 "all the birds of the heavens had fled"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:25 "all the birds of the heavens had fled" This may refer to the fact that even the carnivorous birds have left because there is no more food (i.e. those killed in battle or invasion). Exile had emptied the land.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:27 "Yet I will not execute a complete destruction"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:27 "Yet I will not execute a complete destruction" This refers to hope amidst judgment (cf. Jer. 5:10,18; 30:11; 46:28)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:28 This verse speaks of the determined judgment of God (cf. Jer. 23:20; 30:24; Num. 23:19). There is a greater purpose in the discipline of His covenant people (see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN). His discipline, in reality, was a sign of His parental love. He would not let them continue in their waywardness (i.e. Heb. 12:5-13).

Verse 28 personifies YHWH's creation (i.e. earth and heaven).

  1. The first two created things mourn over the coming judgment of Palestine, and especially of Jerusalem and the temple (possibly Jer. 4:20c and d).
  2. The earth convulses as YHWH approaches (for blessing or judgment), cf. Rom. 8:18-22.

▣ "Because I have spoken" This alludes to the power of YHWH's word (cf. Isa. 55:9-11).

  1. I have spoken
  2. I have purposed
  3. I will not change My mind
  4. I will not turn from it

Judah reaped the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 after repeated warnings.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 4:29 This verse describes what happened when an invading army swept across the land, and smaller unwalled cities were defenseless and had to abandon their homes and shops. They tried to hide or seek the shelter of a walled city.

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:30 This is an allusion to Judah as a harlot. Her lovers are the foreign powers with whom she makes political alliances.

  1. dress in scarlet (BDB 1040)
  2. use gold ornaments (BDB 725 CONSTRUCT BDB 262)
  3. used dark highlighter around your eyes (i.e. with antimony)

This may reflect signs of wealth and social standing or characteristic signs of a prostitute. The second option, in context, seems best. Political alliances were considered "spiritual/political adultery."

entries.title: Jeremiah 4:31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:31 This allusion switches to birth pains (cf. Jer. 4:31; 6:24; 13:21; 22:23; 50:43). Not to bring forth life, but death (cf. v. 30 f,g)! Judah's idolatry and covenant breaking have resulted in destruction, death, and exile!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. List the four conditions God demanded to show repentance (Jer. 4:1-2).
  2. How many separate poems are there in Jeremiah 4?
  3. Briefly express in your own words the central idea that Jeremiah 4 is trying to convey.

entries.title: Jeremiah 5:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:1 Notice the commands in Jer. 5:1 as Jeremiah (or the citizens of Jerusalem, all the VERBS are PLURAL) is instructed to search for one righteous person (obviously, besides himself).

  1. "roam to and fro" ‒ BDB 1001, KB 1439, Polel IMPERATIVE
  2. "look" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. "take note" ‒ BDB 393, KB 390, IMPERATIVE
  4. "seek" ‒ BDB 134, KB 152, Piel IMPERATIVE

This theme of "no righteous person" among the covenant people is repeated several times in the OT (cf. Isa. 59:16; 63:5; Ezek. 22:30). How shocking!

Remember this is poetry, not historical narrative. It is figurative, hyperbolic language to describe the prevalent sin of Judah! There were faithful individuals (i.e. Josiah, his advisers, Jeremiah, Baruch, etc.; see SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)).

Westerners do not understand eastern imagery. Three books have helped me deal with this.

  1. Fee and Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth
  2. G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible
  3. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic

Just as an added thought, I have really enjoyed the writings of R. K. Harrison and John H. Walton. They have tried to understand the OT in light of its day and surrounding cultures.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

▣ "who does justice; who seeks truth" This is the kind of faithful follower mentioned in Jer. 4:1-2. The "if. . .then. . ." of both passages is a literary way to heighten the lack of such a person, who should not have been the exception but the rule for Israel/Judah, who had the benefits of

  1. the Patriarchs
  2. the promises
  3. the covenant
  4. the leaders (Moses, Joshua, David, Hezekiah, Josiah, etc.)
  5. the prophets
  6. YHWH's revelation of Himself and His will (cf. Rom. 9:4)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUSTICE

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "Then I will pardon her" This VERB (BDB 699, KB 757) is a Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense.

Notice one righteous person brings pardon to the whole (i.e. city or nation). This is surely hyperbole (cf. Gen. 18:26,32), but it does show

  1. the sin of Judah
  2. the heart of YHWH

The LXX adds, "says the Lord," which clarifies who the speaker is. It is often difficult to know who is speaking to whom.

This Hebrew concept of corporality can also be seen in Joshua 7 and 2 Chr. 7:14. One can affect the whole for the better or worse! Jesus affected the whole positively (cf. Rom. 5:12-21), as Adam did negatively (cf. Genesis 3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE
