READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Jeremiah 7-10 seems to form a literary unit describing the idolatry of the people of Judah in Jeremiah's day.
    1. Chapter 7 is Jeremiah's famous temple sermon where he confronts the idolatrous people of God at the center of the worship of YHWH. Some believe this sermon extends through Jer. 8:3.
    2. Chapters 8 and 9 form a series of warnings to the people of Jerusalem and Judah which are connected to their abrogation of YHWH's covenant.
    3. Chapter 10 is similar to the sarcastic descriptions of idolatry found in Isaiah 2:20; 31:7; 40:18-20; 41:7; 44:9-20; 45:16; 46:5-7.

  2. As in all of Jeremiah's writings there is a strong Deuteronomic flavor. This can probably be explained by the fact that the prophets went to the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants as a basis for the covenant relationship with YHWH. To this legal and ritual format they emphasized the personal motive and attitude aspect.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:2 "They will spread them out to the sun, the moon and to all the host of heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:2 "They will spread them out to the sun, the moon and to all the host of heaven" Verse 2 shows how involved the Judeans were in astral worship. The VERBS (series of Qal PERFECTS) tell the whole story.

  1. loved
  2. served
  3. gone after
  4. sought
  5. worshiped

The term "host of heaven" (BDB 838 CONSTRUCT 1029) is used in this context for the worship of the stars, planets, moon, and sun (cf. Deut. 4:19; 17:2-20; 2 Kgs. 23:4,5,11; Zeph. 1:5; Jer. 19:13; 32:29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOON WORSHIP

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "They will not be gathered or buried; they will be as dung on the face of the ground" This obviously refers to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. This is one reason why many see the context as running from Jer. 7:1 through 8:3. It was a horror to the Jews to remain unburied. They somehow thought that their afterlife was affected by a proper burial (see IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 649). The imagary "they will be as dung on the face of the ground" is a very striking allusion to their bodies becoming

  1. fertilizer
  2. food for animals

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:3 "And death will be chosen rather than life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:3 "And death will be chosen rather than life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family" Something of the pain of exile can be seen in this hyperbole and in Psalm 137 and also in Lamentations.

For the term "remnant" see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT, THREE SENSES.

▣ "all the places to which I have driven them" YHWH is the one who allowed, even instigated, Judah's exile!

▣ "the Lord of hosts" This is probably a play on the phrase the "host of heaven," found in Jer. 8:2. It was YHWH,  not the planets and stars, who was the creator, sustainer, and guider of the universe (cf. Ps. 19:1-6; Neh. 9:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:4 "Does one turn away and not repent"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:4 "Does one turn away and not repent" There is a play on the phrase "turn back" (BDB 996, KB 1427), found in Jer. 8:4-6 (four times). The exact wording of Jer. 8:4 is somewhat in dispute.

  1. Kimchi translates it as "if a man turns from evil, will not YHWH turn from judgment"
  2. Moore translates it as "if a man repents, He will not repent" (cf. Isa. 55:6)

This seems to be the first allusion to the major theme of Jeremiah 7-10, which is a call to the people of God to turn back to Him. However, Jeremiah knows that at this time their character has already been set and that it is rebellion.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:5 "apostasy"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:5 "apostasy" For the term see SPECIAL TOPIC: APOSTASY .

▣ "They hold fast to deceit" "Hold fast" is literally the Hebrew phrase, "to cling" (BDB 304, KB 302, Hiphil PERFECT) and is used in Gen. 2:24 for the marriage relationship. The imagery of marriage is often used for the relationship between YHWH and His people. This imagery becomes "awhoring after other gods" or spiritual adultery, when used of the fertility cults.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "They refuse to return" The main VERB "refuse" (BDB 549, KB 540) is a Piel PERFECT which denotes a settled attitude!

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:5-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:5-7 YHWH describes the refusal of His people to repent.

  1. they turned away and did not repent, Jer. 8:4
  2. they turned away in continued apostasy, Jer. 8:5
  3. they held fast to deceit, Jer. 8:5
  4. they refused to return, Jer. 8:5
  5. they heard the truth but spoke what was not right, Jer. 8:6
  6. no man repented of his wickedness, Jer. 8:6
  7. they refused to take any responsibility, Jer. 8:6
  8. every one turned to his course, Jer. 8:6
  9. they did not "know" YHWH or His ordinance, Jer. 8:7

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:6 "I have listened and heard"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:6 "I have listened and heard" The Septuagint (LXX) translates this phrase as two IMPERATIVES. The NASB implies that it is God speaking through the prophet, while the Septuagint implies it is God speaking to the people.

▣ "No man repented of his wickedness" This is a different Hebrew word (BDB 636, KB 688) from the word for "repent" and "turn away," which is used four times in Jer. 8:4-6 (BDB 996, KB 1427). However, it is a synonym which also refers to repentance but through the imagery of grief.

▣ "What have I done" This is the big problem! Judah does not even recognize the problem. She is so blind, yet she thinks she sees clearly! One cannot repent of that which they refuse to see or acknowledge (cf. Isa. 6:9-10).

▣ "Like a horse charging into the battle" War horses were trained to charge and fulfill their training. The people of God were trained to love YHWH, but they had totally reverted from their training and were now running with the same intensity toward non-existent idols.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:7 "Even the stork. . .turtledove. . .swift. . .thrush"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:7 "Even the stork. . .turtledove. . .swift. . .thrush" Birds have a natural instinct to migrate at certain times to certain places. This is similar to the animal imagery in Isa. 1:3. However, the people of God had gone totally away from that which was natural and had gone after the fertility gods.

▣ "But My people do not know" There is a play on the word "know" throughout Jeremiah. We learn from Gen. 4:1 that the word "know" can refer to intimate personal relationships such as that between a husband and wife. Again, here is the imagery of God as husband and Israel as wife. However, they had metaphorically lost their intimate relationship. Although the temples may have been full with religious activity, there was no personal relationship with YHWH. They were worshiping the fertility gods of Canaan in YHWH's name!

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

▣ "ordinance" See SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:8-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:8-12 This is a literary unit which describes the religious leaders. This is the first extended mention of a group known as the "scribes" (BDB 707; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SCRIBES). We learn from 1 Chr. 2:55 that scribes developed into families. They do not serve a major function in Israel's faith until after the exile. They seem to have been developed by Ezra into

  1. the synagogue system
  2. rabbinical Judaism
  3. They were basically interpreters of the Mosaic law to local people for specific questions regarding the Torah.

If the leaders are blind, how dark is the darkness? They think they are "wise" and that they "know" the Law of the Lord (cf. Jer. 8:9).

▣
NASB, NRSV, Peshitta  "the lying pen of the scribes
NKJV, NJB  "the false pen of the scribes
TEV  "the laws have been changed
  by dishonest scribes
LXX  "a false pen has become of no
  use to scribes"
JPSOA  "assuredly, for naught has the
  pen labored"
REB  "when scribes with their lying
  pens have falsified it"

This issue is who is being condemned?

  1. the scribes (i.e. equal to "wise men" of Jer. 8:9)
  2. the people (Jer. 8:10)
  3. other religious leaders (Jer. 8:9)

The problem is not the scribes' work (i.e. copying the Law and/or explaining it), but the people's rejecting both the prophetic word and the covenant obligations.

▣ "Has made it into a lie" There is a Hebrew word play between "lying pen" (BDB 1055) and "lie" (BDB 1055). There is often an allusion to Ba'al worship as being "the lie." There may be an allusion here.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:9 "they have rejected the word of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:9 "they have rejected the word of the Lord" They did this at the very time they thought they were upholding the word of the Lord. It would be good to remember Isa. 29:13.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:10 "I will give their wives to others
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:10 "I will give their wives to others

 Their fields to new owners" This refers to the experience of invasion and exile. Notice that wives were listed with a man's property, which was characteristic of ANE patriarchal soceity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:10-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:10-12 These verses are omitted in the Septuagint (LXX) because of their striking resemblance to Jer. 6:12-15. It seems that the book of Jeremiah is a composite book which was edited according to themes, word plays, or subjects, either by Jeremiah, Baruch (his scribe), or someone later in Israel's history. Therefore, there is considerable repetition in the book.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:11 "They heal the brokenness of the daughter of My people superficially"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:11 "They heal the brokenness of the daughter of My people superficially" The religious leaders seem to bring that which will give life, but in reality their message of false hope brings death (i.e. Lam. 2:14). The major truth in this verse is found in the latter part in the false prophets' words, "All is well, all is well" (cf. Jer. 6:14; 14:13,14). The problem was that there was no peace, but impending invasion. Many commentators believe that these false prophets were quoting Isaiah 36-39, referring to God's promises to Hezekiah and the safety of the city of Jerusalem against the invasion of Sennacherib. But, Jeremiah is emphasizing the truth that the covenant has two aspects: God's promises and His covenant people's faith response. Judah had totally abrogated the covenant!

For "the daughter of My people" see full note at Jer. 46:11.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:12 The question of line 1 is answered in an intensified way (i.e. the Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT VERB of the same root, BDB 101, KB 116) in line 2.

▣ "they did not know how to blush" Wow! What strong imagery for willful disobedience. Sin had become a common thing. Idolatry was practiced without a thought!

The word "shame" (BDB 101, KB 116) occurs three times in this verse. God's people knew no shame!

▣ "they shall fall among those who fall" This may be another reference to the previous exile of the northern tribes.

▣ "the time of their punishment" The Neo-Babylonian army took captives from Judah in 605, 597, 586, and 582 B.C. The major deportation was 586 B.C. when the temple and Jerusalem were destroyed.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:13 "'I will surely snatch them away,' declares the Lord
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:13 "'I will surely snatch them away,' declares the Lord

 'There will be no grapes on the vine'" Verse 13, by means of two agricultural imagery, one referring to grapes and the other to figs, implies that no one will be left in the Promised Land and that all will be taken into captivity (i.e. gleaning; see SPECIAL TOPIC: GLEANINGS). Not even a remnant will be left according to this shockingly hyperbolic passage. Palestine was YHWH's special garden but there was no spiritual fruit (cf. Isaiah 5). This is basically the fulfillment of the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28.

The first line of the MT can be understood in several ways:

  1. "I shall put a definite end to them" (RSV, JPSOA)
  2. "I shall gather their harvest" (NEB)
  3. "Their fruit harvest has been" (JPSOA footnote)
  4. "I will surely consume them" (Peshitta, NKJV)
  5. "I shall gather them all in (false religion and its punishment)" (REB)
  6. "When I wanted to gather them. . ." (NRSV)
NASB, Peshitta  "I will surely consume them"
TEV  "I wanted to gather my people, as a
  farmer gathers a harvest"
JPSOA  "I will make an end of them"
NET Bible  "I will take away their harvest"
LXX  "they will gather their produce"
  (i.e. the invaders)

Remember, this is highly emotional poetry! This line can be

  1. positive (i.e. YHWH wants to gather His people to Himself, i.e. repentance)
  2. negative (others will reap their harvest, cf. Jer. 8:12)
▣
NASB  "And what I have given them will pass away"
NRSV  "I have found them people to trample on them"
TEV  "therefore, I have allowed outsiders to take
  over the land"
LXX, REB     —omitted—
JPSOA  "Whatever I have given them is gone"
Peshitta  "and the things that I have given them are passed
  away from them"

The UBS Text Project (p. 200) interprets this ambiguous Hebrew phrase in two ways.

  1. "and I gave them (things which) escape them (i.e. fruits of the earth)"
  2. "and I gave them (precepts which) they have trespassed"

The first option is based on Jer. 8:13, lines 1-4. The second option is related to Jer. 8:8 and refers to the Law (i.e. that which was found in the temple under Josiah's reform and remodeling, cf. 2 Kgs. 22:8).

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:14 "Assemble yourselves, and let us go into the fortified cities"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:14 "Assemble yourselves, and let us go into the fortified cities" In the ancient world, in times of crisis or invasion, the people of the surrounding areas fled into the walled cities. However, the overcrowding exacerbated the problems of food, water, and sanitation. We learn from later history that the siege experience of the people of Judah was so bad that even after the exile they had to cast lots to see who would live in the reconstructed Jerusalem (cf. Neh. 11:1).

YHWH's message of judgment is expressed in three commands.

  1. "assemble yourselves" ‒ BDB 62, KB 74, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  2. "let us go into the fortified cities" ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense
  3. "let us perish" ‒ BDB 198, KB 226, Qal COHORTATIVE

▣ "Because the Lord our God has doomed us. . .

For we have sinned against the Lord" This is the key to understanding God's actions against His own people. God chose them to be a kingdom of priests so that all the world would know Him, Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5,6 (see Special Topic: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN), but the light coming from God's people was anything but complimentary to God! The covenant made with Abraham, and further elaborated at Sinai, was based on the assumption that Israel's life and worship would reveal YHWH to the world. The only way to correct their false message was radical surgery (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

▣ "poisoned water" This (BDB 912 II) is an allusion to "wormwood" or "gall." Many times in the OT "gall" or "wormwood" is mentioned (cf. Jer. 9:15; 23:15; Deut. 29:18; Ps. 69:21; Lam. 3:19; and Matt. 27:34 in the NT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:15 This verse, like Jer. 8:6d,8,11, shows that Judah expected "peace" and was surprised at invasion and exile. This phrase is repeated in Jer. 14:19 and is similar to Job 30:26.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:16 "From Dan is heard the snorting of his horses"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:16 "From Dan is heard the snorting of his horses" We learn that the tribe of Dan moved from its tribal allocation by Joshua in the south to the north (cf. Judges 18). Its capital city became the way for describing the upper limits of the Promised Land (cf. Jer. 4:15). Invading Mesopotamian armies came from the north because of the desert to the east of Canaan. Therefore, when Dan heard the snorting horses it meant the troops from Neo-Babylon were entering Palestine.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:17 "I am sending serpents against you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:17 "I am sending serpents against you" This may be

  1. an allusion to Numbers 21 when God sent serpents to judge His people
  2. simply another kind of poison as in Jer. 8:14

Whichever is true, both images (i.e. poison, snakes) combine to show that there is no hope for the people of God. Here "snakes" refers to the Neo-Babylonian army!

The first line of Jer. 8:18 may go with Jer. 8:17 and be understood as an idiom that the snake bites were fatal (lit. "beyond recovery"). The LXX translated it as "incurable."

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:18-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:18-22 There has been much discussion among commentators as to who is speaking here. Some say that it is the prophet grieving over his people, but it seems, in context, to be God grieving over His people. It is true that God speaks through His prophet throughout this book and it is sometimes difficult to differentiate. However, because of Hosea 11:8,9 and because of the specific references found in Jer. 9:3,6,9,10,11, it seems to me that this is a very significant passage on the heart of God (i.e. Jer. 8:21). Though God was forced to judge His people, it broke His heart to do so. A good way to compare the love and anger of God is by comparing Deut. 5:9 with Deut. 7:9.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

8:18
NASB  "beyond healing"
NKJV  "I would comfort myself"
NRSV  "My joy is gone"
TEV  "can not be healed"
NJB  "incurable sorrow"
REB, NET  "no cure"
Peshitta  "I am weary with. . ."
LXX  "mortally"

The MT has a root that appears only here in the OT, מבליניתי, but some divide and revocalize to מבלי ניתי, "no healing" (KB 514). BDB 114 thinks it means "to shine" or "to brighten." This is an occurance of simply a guess by ancient and modern scholars. But, as usual, the parallelism helps clarify the meaning, and the strophe as a whole is understandable.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:19 By means of a series of questions, the tragedy of Judah's invasion, destruction, and exile are highlighted. Idolatry and rebellion have consequences. This is still true (cf. Jer. 17:10; Gal. 6:7).

The TEV expressed the thought of the verse best.

  1. the people cry out
    1. "Is the Lord not in Zion?"
    2. "Is her King not within her?"
  2. YHWH answers in line 3 (cf. Jer. 7:30-34)

The NASB, "from a distant land," is an incorrect translation. The MT has "from the length and breadth of the land" (cf. NRSV). The people of Judah are speaking; those who remain from the Assyrian exile also. The question, "Where is YHWH?" rang out as the Neo-Babylonian army approached (cf. Jer. 8:16).

▣ "the daughter of my people" See full note at Jer. 46:11.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:19-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:19-20 All of the VEBS are PERFECTS, reflecting settled conditions.

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:20 "Harvest is past, summer is ended
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:20 "Harvest is past, summer is ended

 And we are not saved" This is a reference to the seasons when crops and fruit ripened. When the harvest has passed, there is nothing left!

entries.title: Jeremiah 8:22 "Is there no balm in Gilead"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:22 "Is there no balm in Gilead" Gilead was famous for its healing ointment (cf. Gen. 37:25), but as there was

  1. no way to stop the poisoning of Jer. 8:14
  2. no way to heal the serpent's bite of Jer. 8:17
  3. no cessation of the hunger of Jer. 8:20
  4. there was no doctor's help in Jer. 8:22

The people of God stand judged even though it had not yet happened historically (i.e. Babylonian invasions).

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:1 The prophet is using emotional figurative language to express his pain over YHWH's necessary judgment of His covenant people (cf. Heb. 12:5-11). In reality it is YHWH's pain that the prophet is revealing (cf. Hosea 11:8-9). This same emotion is seen in Jer. 8:18; 13:17; Isa. 22:4; Lam. 2:18.

This verse is one of the sources of Jeremiah being known as "the weeping prophet." He was such because YHWH was weeping through him (cf. Hosea 11:8-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (ANTHROPOMORPHISM)

▣ "the daughter of my people" See full note at Jer. 46:11.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:2 "A wayfarers' lodging place"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:2 "A wayfarers' lodging place" This was a lean-to or an uninhabited wooden shelter used by travelers in desert areas. What shocking imagery that God's prophet wanted to run away from (i.e. two Qal COHORTATIVES, "leave" and "go") the covenant people and hide in the desert. The pain of YHWH's judgment overwhelmed him! YHWH's people surely deserved it, but the curses of Lev. 26 and Deut. 28 were so violent and painful.

▣ "For all of them are adulterers

   An assembly of treacherous men" There is an obvious comparison and play on these two phrases as a title for the people of God. Their lifestyle and attitude reflected both physical and spiritual adultery (i.e. idolatry in general or fertility worship).

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:2-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:2-4 Notice how the prophet/YHWH describes the covenant people.

  1. adulteress, Jer. 9:2
  2. treacherous men, Jer. 9:2
  3. lie, Jer. 9:3
  4. evil to evil, Jer. 9:3
  5. do not know YHWH, Jer. 9:3
  6. untrustworthy, Jer. 9:4
  7. crafty, Jer. 9:4
  8. slanderer, Jer. 9:4
  9. deceiver, Jer. 9:5
  10. do not speak truth, Jer. 9:5
  11. liars, Jer. 9:5
  12. commit iniquity, Jer. 9:5
  13. deceitful, Jer. 9:6
  14. refuse to know YHWH, Jer. 9:6

And these are the people of God. He must do something lest His purpose for this planet is lost (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:3 "They bend their tongue like their bow"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:3 "They bend their tongue like their bow" Their speech showed who and what they really were (cf. Jer. 9:8). This imagery seems to refer to one of three things.

  1. their tongues were bent which reflected the words for sin, a deviation from the standard
  2. they were ready to shoot their words at anyone (cf. Ps. 64:3-4)
  3. it refers to the pain that their lies caused both to God and their fellow Israelites (cf. Lev. 19:15-16)

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH

▣ "And they do not know Me" This is the tragedy—the pain that God felt (cf. Jer. 2:13; 17:13; Hosea 4:1,6; 5:4; 8:2; 11:8-9) after He had given so much to this people and they had knowingly, willfully turned their backs on Him. There is a word to the church today in these verses.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:4 Even among the covenant people, there is no "trust" (BDB 105). They not only lie, cheat, and steal from others, but from each other. The terrible results of the Fall are obvious.

  1. let everyone be on guard against his neighbor ‒ BDB 1036, KB 1581, Niphal IMPERATIVE
  2. do not trust any brother ‒ BDB 105, KB 120, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  3. craftily ‒ this is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 784, KB 872), which shows intensity

The people of God were more like Jacob (supplanter, BDB 784) than Israel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:5 "They weary themselves committing iniquity"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:5 "They weary themselves committing iniquity" What a horrible description of God's people as they go headlong into rebellion and idolatry (BDB 521, KB 512, Niphal PERFECT).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN IN THE OT, A. #2

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:6 "Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:6 "Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit" This describes the covenant people's worldview and daily lifestyle!

▣ "they refuse to know Me" The VERB (BDB 549, KB 540, Piel PERFECT) denotes a settled condition. They are not duped but willful rejecters of truth.

For "know" see SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:7-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:7-9 This is another strophe listing Judah's sins.

  1. liars
  2. ambush neighbors

YHWH must act!

  1. He will refine and assay them (cf. Jer. 6:27)
  2. He will punish them (cf. Jer. 5:9,29)
  3. He will avenge Himself (cf. Isa. 1:24)

YHWH wants to use the covenant people to reach all other nations. He has an eternal redemptive plan. However, His people have not revealed Him, but rather their own weaknesses and failures. Therefore, YHWH Himself must act (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:9 "On a nation such as this"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:9 "On a nation such as this" This is a play on the word goy (BDB 156), which the Jews used in derision for the Gentiles. Here it is used to describe Israel herself.

▣ "Shall I not avenge Myself?" All sin and disobedience of the covenant people was not only against His word but Himself (cf. Jer. 5:9,29).

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:10-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 9:10-11 Again the question arises as to who is speaking in these two verses. The NIV translates Jer. 9:10 as the prophet speaking and Jer. 9:11 as God speaking. But the NASV and RSV translate them as God speaking in both verses. It is basically extended imagery that the land is being affected by the covenant peoples' continuous sin, and there are consequences (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; Rom. 8:18-22).

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:11 "A haunt of jackals"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:11 "A haunt of jackals" This is imagery for ruin and destruction (cf. Jer. 10:22; 49:33; 51:37; Isa. 34:13) and possibly even the presence of the demonic.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEMONIC IN THE OT

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:12-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:12-16 These verses are a strong statement by God (introduced by three questions in Jer. 9:12) on the results of Judah's rebellion. In Jer. 9:13 and 14 the reasons for the exile are enumerated.

  1. they have forsaken My law (written revelation, cf. Exodus 19-20; Deut. 4:8; 5)
  2. they have not obeyed My voice (oral prophetic revelation)
  3. they have not walked according to My voice
  4. they walked after the stubbornness of their heart (cf. Jer. 7:24; 11:8)
  5. they walked after the Ba'als (cf. Jer. 2:8,23; 23:27)

Revelation should result in godly lifestyle (cf. Hosea 14:9)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:14 "walked after the stubbornness of their heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:14 "walked after the stubbornness of their heart" This is a characteristic of the Jewish people delineated in the book of Deuteronomy. God's mercy is seen against the backdrop of their natural tendency to rebellion (cf. Deut. 9:6,13; 10:16; 31:27). It also says that they walked away open-eyed; they were not tricked nor did they do it in ignorance!

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

▣ "and after the Baals" This refers to the fertility worship of Canaan. Originally El and Ashtorah were the chief deities of the Canaanite pantheon (Ras Shamra texts from Ugarit). Ba'al was their son. The myth involved the rising and dying of the agricultural deity every year. By the means of imitation magic, including the sex act, fertility was assured each spring. There was a Ba'al shrine for every city and village.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "as their fathers taught them" This may be an historical allusion to Exodus 32 and Numbers 25. This shows the potential corruption from one generation to the next (cf. Deut. 5:9; Isa. 29:13). Family faith can be a blessing or a curse depending on the content (cf. Jer. 7:18)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:15 "wormwood. . .poisoned water"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 9:15 "wormwood. . .poisoned water" The false family faith of Jer. 9:14b reflects the curse of Deut. 29:18. This was specifically mentioned in Jer. 8:14e. Notice it is YHWH, Himself, who gives it! Sin has consequences, especially for those who know better (cf. Luke 12:48; Rom. 9:4-5).

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:16 "I will scatter them among the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:16 "I will scatter them among the nations" This is either an allusion to the exile of the northern tribes in 722 B.C. by Assyria or it is a prophecy of the exile of the southern tribes by Neo-Babylon in 605, 597, 586 or 582 B.C. Exile was one of the consequences of covenant disobedience in Lev. 26:33; Deut. 28:64.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:17 "the wailing women"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:17 "the wailing women" In the Ancient Near East (ANE) professional mourners were used at funerals (cf. Amos 5:16). Here it is a literary way to highlight the fact that death is coming.

In Jer. 9:20 the daughters are going to be taught how to wail. This is either an allusion to the fact

  1. that the mothers passed on their idolatry to their daughters
  2. that there will be so many dead people that more and more wailers will be needed

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:17-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:17-22 This is a funeral dirge (cf. Jer. 9:20), personifying death. Notice the two terms for professional mourners.

  1. "the mourning women" ‒ BDB 884, KB 1096, Polel PARTICIPLE
  2. "the wailing women" ‒ BDB 314, KB 314 (ADJECTIVE, lit. "unskilled")

Notice the number of commands.

  1. Verse 17
    1. "consider" ‒ BDB 106, KB 122, Hithpolel IMPERATIVE
    2. "call" ‒ BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal IMPERATIVE
    3. "come" ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    4. "send" ‒ BDB 1018, KB 1511, Qal IMPERATIVE
    5. "come" ‒ same as c
  2. Verse 18
    1. "let them make haste" ‒ BDB 554, KB 553, Piel IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    2. "let them take up a wailing for us" ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    3. "let our eyes shed tears" ‒ BDB 432, KB 434, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (NRSV)
    4. "let our eyelids flow with water" ‒ BDB 633, KB 683, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (NRSV)
  3. Verse 20
    1. "hear the word of the Lord" ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE
    2. "let your ear receive the word of His mouth" ‒ BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    3. "teach. . ." ‒ BDB 540, KB 531, Piel IMPERATIVE
  4. Verse 22 ‒ "speak" ‒ BDB 180, KB 210, Piel IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:19 This verse expresses the content of their lamentations.

  1. we are ruined (cf. Jer. 4:13; Deut. 28:29)
  2. we are put to great shame
  3. we have left the land (cf. Jer. 7:15)
  4. our homes are destroyed

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 9:20 This verse is addressed to the professional mourners of Jer. 9:17. See note at Jer. 9:17.

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:21 "For death has come up through our windows"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:21 "For death has come up through our windows" This personification of death (cf. personification of Sheol and death in Hab. 2:5; see SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS) as coming through the windows is very similar to

  1. the Canaanite myth of Ba'al being killed by the god of the underworld, Mot, in the Ugaritic literature found at Ras-Shamra
  2. the Mesopotamian myth of a female demon (Lamashtu) who climbs through the windows to kill babies

This may be an allusion by the prophet to the type of mythology (Canaanite fertility worship, Molech) to which the people of God were listening and sacrificing.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP

▣ "To cut off the children. . .The young men" The last two lines of Jer. 9:21 are a way of saying

  1. that death is no respecter of persons
  2. that death will cut off the next generation

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:22 "The corpses of men will fall like dung on the open field"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:22 "The corpses of men will fall like dung on the open field" This is common imagery for the results of invasion in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 7:33; 8:2; 16:4; 26:23). It was one of the curses for covenant disobedience in Deut. 28:26.

▣ "And like the sheaf after the reaper" This is possibly the origin of the modern personification of death as "the grim reaper," but please note that God, not the evil one, is in control of death (i.e. the death angel of Exodus 12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEATH ANGEL

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:23 "Let not a wise man boast of his wisdom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 9:23 "Let not a wise man boast of his wisdom" The wise person will know that it is not in human might or riches but in YHWH that one's strength lies (cf. Zech. 4:6).

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:23-24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:23-24 This is a beautiful description of true wisdom in contrast with the false wisdom of the scribes mentioned earlier in Jer. 8:8-12. Note the fivefold repetition of "glory" (BDB 237, KB 248).

  1. four Hithpael IMPERFECTS used in a JUSSIVE sense
  2. one Hithpael PARTICIPLE in Jer. 9:24

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:24 "but let him who boasts boast of this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:24 "but let him who boasts boast of this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the Lord"

Notice all the things that humans tend to boast in

  1. wisdom
  2. strength
  3. wealth

are not what should be gloried in, but

  1. that he/she understands Me ‒ BDB 968, KB 1328, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
  2. that he/she knows Me ‒ BDB 393, KB 390, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE

These INFINITIVES speak of human reception of divine revelation. They have heard and responded to the law of YHWH, the voice of YHWH (cf. Jer. 9:13) and the Person of YHWH (i.e. "Me," Jer. 9:24; Hosea 4:1,6; 5:4; 8:2)! This is the opposite of Jer. 9:3d and 6.

Characteristics of YHWH are delineated in this verse. The mandate that believers boast in God is a common biblical theme (cf. Jer. 4:2; Ps. 44:8; Isa. 41:16; 1 Cor. 1:31; 2 Cor. 10:17; Gal. 6:14).

The characteristics of God in Jer. 9:24 can also be seen beautifully expressed in Exod. 34:6,7 and Neh. 9:17.

  1. lovingkindness (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS [hesed])
  2. justice (see SPECIAL TOPIC: JUSTICE)
  3. righteousness (see SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS)

▣ "for I delight in these things" If YHWH "delights" (BDB 342, KB 339, Qal PERFECT) in the above mentioned things, then we should take special notice of them and emulate them (cf. Isa. 58:2; opposite of Jer. 11:10; 13:10; also note Micah 6:8).

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:25-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:25-26 This is a theological contrast between physical circumcision and spiritual circumcision. Circumcision was an outward sign of the covenant between YHWH and Abraham (cf. Gen. 17:10). All of the surrounding nations practiced circumcision, but not for the same spiritual purposes as Israel. The only uncircumcised people in the Ancient Near East that we know of were the Philistines, a group of mercenaries from Aegean Islands who invaded Palestine around the middle of the twelfth century B.C. But, although circumcision was meant to be a sign of the covenant, what God really wanted was an inner attitude of love for Him, as well as the outward covenant stipulations. This is why the Bible repeatedly speaks of different parts of the body being circumcised:

  1. the ears, Jer. 6:10
  2. the lips, Exod. 6:12,30
  3. the heart, Lev. 26:41; Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4; Ezek. 44:7,9

This same radical truth is reflected in the NT in Rom. 2:28,29! As temple ritual and liturgy without faith offered no hope, so too, family liturgy and ritual without faith offered no hope (i.e. Jeremiah 7)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 9:26 "who clip the hair on their temples"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:26 "who clip the hair on their temples" There have been four basic interpretations of this Hebrew phrase.

  1. The NASB, REV, and NJB interpret this as an idolatrous act reflected in Lev. 19:27; Jer. 25:23; 49:32.
  2. It may relate to mourning for the dead (cf. Deut. 14:1).
  3. It may be to a part of the idolatrous worship of the foreign gods (cf. Herodotus 111,8).
  4. The other interpretation is found in the NKJV, NIV, and REB, which translate this as imagery for the universal judgment of God (i.e. NKJV, "and all who are in the farthest corners, who dwell in the wilderness").

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:1 "Hear the word"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:1 "Hear the word" This is the Hebrew word Shema (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE), which means "to hear so as to do." It is a recurrent demand in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 2:4; 5:21; 6:19; 7:2,23; 10:1; 11:2,4,6; 13:15; 17:20; 19:3; 21:11; 22:2; 31:10; 38:20; 42:15; 44:24,26; 49:20; 50:45). YHWH is communicating, but His people are not listening and obeying!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

▣ "house of Israel" The title "Israel" in Jeremiah is so confusing because it is used in two senses.

  1. all of the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob
  2. the Northern Ten Tribes, who split off in 922 B.C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. There is a literary unit from Jeremiah 7 through 10 which deals with Judah's sin and YHWH's judgment (see Contextual Insighst at chapter 8, A).

  2. The poems of Jeremiah are arranged, not by date, but by
    1. word plays
    2. themes

  3. This chapter has many similarities with both Deuteronomy and Isaiah. Two examples:
    1. the rare word (BDB 903 I), "cucumber field," Jer. 10:5 (cf. Isa. 1:8)
    2. the phrase, "none is like You," Jer. 10:6 reflects Deut. 33:26 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM)

  4. Prophetic literature is a genre which modern readers are not familiar with. It must be interpreted in light of
    1. contemporary culture
    2. contemporary idioms
    3. contemporary poetic forms
    4. parallel patterns

      Some resources that have helped me try to put muself back into an ANE mindset are

      1. John H. Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament
      2. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic
      3. G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible
      4. Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How To Read the Bible for All Its Worth

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:2 "Do not learn the way of the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:2 "Do not learn the way of the nations" Chapter 10 addresses the folly of idolatry. It reflects the imagery and sarcasm of Isaiah (cf. Isa. 2:20; 31:7; 40:18-20; 41:7; 44:9-20; 45:16; 46:5-7). YHWH had given them the way in which they should walk (cf. Lev. 18:3; Deut. 12:30; Jer. 12:16), but they chose the way (i.e. lifestyle) of idolatry. This is even reflected in Jer. 10:2 by a seeming allusion to the Babylonian astral deities (i.e. "signs of the heavens," cf. Isa. 47:13; many celestial signs are recorded in Enuma Anu Enlil).

There are two Qal IMPERFECTS used in a JUSSIVE sense (negated).

  1. learn ‒ BDB 540, KB 531
  2. be terrified ‒ BDB 369, KB 365

The pagan nations, without a knowledge of YHWH, were terrified (BDB 369, KB 365, Qal IMPERFECT) by the astrologers (cf. Isa. 47:12-14) and astral events, like meteors, comets, eclipses, weather phenonema. Superstitions are powerful instruments in the hand of Satan to frighten, intimidate, and control humans!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

10:3
NASB  "For the customs of the peoples are
  delusion"
NKJV  "For the customs of the peoples
  are futile"
NRSV, NJB  "For the customs of the peoples
  are false"
TEV  "The religion of these people is
  worthless"
REB  "The carved images of the nations
  are a shame"
JPSOA  "For the laws of the nations are
  delusions"
JPSOA (footnote)  "the objects that the nations fear
  are delusions" (emendation)
LXX  "Because the precepts of the nations
  are vain"
Peshitta  "for the gods of the Gentiles are
  nothing"

The word "customs" (BDB 349) can mean

  1. to inscribe (i.e. a law)
  2. to enact or to decree (i.e. a law)

The term "delusion" means "nothingness" or "vanity" (BDB 210, KB 236, cf. Jer. 2:5; 14:22; 2 Kgs. 17:15). It is quite often used to describe the idols (cf. Deut. 32:21), which were nonentities made by human hands. They had no power to act, in contradistinction to YHWH who acts for His people! Idols cannot hear, see, or act, but they are used by Satan to trick humans from knowing and following the only true God and His Messiah (cf. Eph. 6:10-18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIAH

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:5 "Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:5 "Like a scarecrow in a cucumber field" This is an allusion to idols described as scarecrows. Some translate this as "upright as a palm tree" (NKJV, Peshitta). The LXX omits the phrase.

▣ "They must be carried" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 669, KB 724) used for intensity. Oh, the folly of man-made gods!

▣ "Do not fear them" This is a Qal IMPERFECT (BDB 431, KB 432) used in a JUSSIVE sense. Fear can be paralyzing!

Notice those who know YHWH should not fear because the idols

  1. cannot harm you
  2. cannot do you good

They are non-existent (cf. Isa. 41:23-24; 1 Cor. 8:4; Gal. 4:8). Fear YHWH (cf. Jer. 10:7)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:6 "There is none like You"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:6 "There is none like You" I seems that Jeremiah is speaking. This is an emphasis on the uniqueness of YHWH. It is an affirmation of monotheism. There was only one God (cf. Jer. 10:10).

The Septuagint omits Jer. 10:6-8 and 10; this omission is also in the Dead Sea Scroll manuscripts. Possibly these are based on a different Hebrew text.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS AND DEMONS

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "You are great, and great is Your name" "Great" (BDB 162) is used often in Deuteronomy of YHWH (cf. Deut. 3:24; 5:24; 9:26; 11:2; 32:3). Jeremiah often uses the phrasing and terminology from Deuteronomy.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:7 "King of the nations"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:7 "King of the nations" YHWH is not just the God of Abraham's seed but the God of creation! He is the only true God (cf. Jer. 10:10)!

This emphasis on YHWH as the only true God is difficult to communicate to a post-modern worldview which depreciates absolutes. Yet, this is the question! It is true or it is false. The biblical worldview rests on this basic affirmation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:8 This verse is very difficult to translate, but it seems that the Hebrew is referring to the fact that the Israelites were getting their information and knowledge from a dead stump (i.e. idol).

The second line may be paralleled in v. 3a.

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:9 "Tarshish"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:9 "Tarshish" This was a city in the far west, possibly Spain or Sardinia. Some say it is just a mythological place to describe something far, far away (cf. the book of Jonah and Ezek. 27:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TARSHISH

▣ "And gold from Uphaz" "from Uphaz" (מאופז, BDB 20) is found only here and in Dan. 10:5 as a place name. From 1 Kgs. 9:28 a place called "from Ophir" (פאופיר, BDB 20, cf. Isa. 13:12) has "gold" (cf. Targums, Peshitta, REB). It possibly means "pure" or "fine" gold, thereby functioning as an ADJECTIVVE.

▣ "Violet and purple are their clothing" These were very expensive dyes in the ancient world, originally coming from Phoenicia (i.e. from sea shells). It is simply a way of asserting that no matter how richly or royally they robed their idols, they were still just human-made, inanimate objects!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE SACRED COLORS

▣ "They are all the work of skilled men" The NET Bible (p. 1316, #17) points out the contrast between

  1. the wise men of the nations
  2. the skilled craftsmen

Both use the same root (BDB 314). These idol makers are skillful craftsmen, but they are not wise. True wisdom cannot worship a man-made idol!

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:10 "the Lord is the true God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:10 "the Lord is the true God" The Hebrew word (BDB 54) for "truth" emphasizes trustworthiness, faithfulness, and dependability.

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

▣ "the living God" This seems to reflect the covenant name for God, YHWH, which is from the Hebrew VERB "to be" (cf. Exod. 3:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "everlasting" See SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)

▣ Notice the ways YHWH is characterized.

  1. there is none like You, Jer. 10:6,7 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM)
  2. You are great, Jer. 10:6
  3. King of the nations, Jer. 10:7 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [NT])
  4. the true God, Jer. 10:10
  5. the living God, Jer. 10:10
  6. the everlasting King, Jer. 10:10 (cf. #3)
  7. the creator, Jer. 10:12-13 (SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BEGINNING [physical and spiritual])
  8. the Maker of all is He, Jer. 10:16
  9. the captain of the armies of heaven (i.e. Lord of hosts), Jer. 10:16 (seeSPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts)

YHWH is the God who creates, hears, sees, and acts. The idols are non-existent. They cannot move, hear, see, or act. They will be destroyed! YHWH is the only true, real, live, eternal One!

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [NT]

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:11 This verse is in Aramaic. It is the only verse in Jeremiah in Aramaic (also note Ezra 4:8-6:18; 7:12-26; Dan. 2:4-7:28). Why one Aramaic verse should appear in the midst of a Hebrew book is uncertain. Some of the theories are:

  1. The rabbis say that it was part of a letter sent to King Jehoiachin in captivity in Neo-Babylon.
  2. It was an anti-polytheistic proverb.
  3. It was an exorcism formula (see SPECIAL TOPIC: EXORCISM)
  4. It was a marginal note, later inserted into the text (TEV, NEB).

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:12 "It is He who made the earth by His power,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:12 "It is He who made the earth by His power,

 Who established the world by His wisdom" This is an emphasis on God as creator (cf. Jer. 10:16). Verses 12-16 are repeated in Jer. 51:15-19.

The theological assertion that YHWH established the world by "wisdom" comes from Prov. 8:22-31. This is possibly the OT background for John 1:1-14.

Notice the parallelism of terms used to affirm YHWH as Creator (cf. Jer. 51:15-19; Ps. 104).

  1. He who made the earth
    1. VERB ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal PARTICIPLE
    2. NOUN ‒ "earth" (BDB 75)
  2. who stablished the world
    1. VERB ‒ BDB 465, KB 464, Hiphil PARTICIPLE
    2. NOUN ‒ "world" (BDB 385)
  3. He has stretched out the heavens
    1. VERB ‒ BDB 639, KB 692, Qal PERFECT
    2. NOUN ‒ "heavens" (BDB 1029)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD (several terms)

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BEGINNING (physical and spiritual)

▣ "stretched out the heavens" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH and SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:12-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:12-16 This is a passage about Elohim as creator of both the planet and all celestial objects (cf. Gen. 1:14-19). In this passage it is He who gives and controls water, which was a very important theological issue in the agricultural Ancient Near East. Water was part of the Neo-Babylonian creation myth and the Canaanite creation myth. The Canaanite god, Ba'al, was supposedly the storm god that provided water (i.e. life). Contrary to both of these myths, YHWH is the creator, sustainer, and provider of rain and water.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE CREATION AND FLOOD MYTHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 10:13 This verse may be a parody of the Canaanite fertility god, Ba'al, who was the storm god. YHWH is the One who controls water and the weather, not Ba'al.

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:14-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:14-15 These verses continue the ridicule of idols (cf. Jer. 10:3-5). The term "breath" (BDB 924) is a play on the term for spirit (cf. Ezekiel 37).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:16 "The portion of Jacob is not like these"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:16 "The portion of Jacob is not like these" This refers to the God of Jacob (cf. Ps. 73:26). Jacob's name was changed to Israel (cf. Gen. 32:28).

▣ "Israel is the tribe of His inheritance" The KJV has "the rod of His inheritance." This refers to the rod as a means of measurement or a standard (see BDB 986). However, most English translations follow NASB. Israel is YHWH's own people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:17-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 10:17-18 This strophe starts with an IMPERATIVE, "pick up your bundle" (BDB 62, KB 72, Qal IMPERATIVE) which denotes the imminence of the Neo-Babylonian exile. It shows that the Judean people would go into exile with only that which they could carry; that YHWH is the One who pronounced this judgment because of their sin, not because Marduk was a greater and stronger deity!

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:18 The last line has several translation options.

NASB  "that they may be found"
MT, NKJV  "that they may find it so"
  (from מצא, BDB 592)
NRSV, Peshitta  "that they may find me!"
TEV  "until not one is left"
NJB, JPSOA, NET Bible  "that they shall feel it"
LXX  "that your plague may be
  discovered"
REB, NEB  "squeeze them dry"
  (from מצה, BDB 594)
NIV  "that they may be captured"
JPSOA (footnte)  "that they have to leave"
  (emendation)

Apparently the line refers to the fact that none shall escape capture and exile. Literary context (i.e. Hebrew parallelism) and word root (i.e. Semitic) are the two most helpful ways to determine meaning of a word or phrase in poetry.

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:19 Jeremiah uses sickness or wounds as imagery for sin (cf. Jer. 30:17), as does Isaiah 1:5-6; 53:5; Ps. 103:3 (note the synonymous parallelism). These verses cannot be used as a divine promise of physical healing. However, God still heals.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

▣ The last line of Jer. 10:19 can have several translation options (i.e. different vowels).

NASB, NKJV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "I must bear it"
NRSV  "If this is the worst,
  I can bear it"
TEV  "we thought this was
  something we could
  endure!"
LXX  "it seized me"

Number 1 is the people's resignation to Divine judgment. Number 2 is a belittling of the judgment. I think #1 fits the context best.

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:19-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:19-22 This strophe of lament is similar to Jer. 8:18-22. It seems to reflect the heart of God through the words of Jeremiah. However, the nation is personified. The land suffers from mankind's sin (cf. Deuteronomy 27-28; Rom. 8:18-22). There is a series of nomadic imagery here, particularly related to the "tent" and "flocks."

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:20 Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, p. 13, makes the interesting point about how the poets and prophets used imagery from the nomadic period of Israel's past.

  1. death as a tent being taken down ‒ Job 4:21
  2. security as a tent well grounded ‒ Isa. 33:20
  3. Hezekiah's illness described as a tent being pulled up ‒ Isa. 38:12
  4. restoration of the covenant people as the enlargement of a tent ‒ Isa. 54:2
  5. Judah's invasion and exile as a destroyed tent ‒ Jer. 4:20; 10:20
  6. shepherd imagery ‒ Ps. 23; Isa. 40:11; Jer. 10:21; 23:1-6; Ezek. 34; Zech. 10-12

Only people familiar with nomadic existence can feel the full power and plight of this imagery!

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:22 "A great commotion out of the land of the north"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:22 "A great commotion out of the land of the north" This refers to the coming exile (cf. Jer. 1:14-15; 4:6; 6:1,22). The north was an idiom for invasion since this was the only route that invaders from the Fertile Crescent (i.e. Mesopotamia) could take because of the desert directly to the east of Palestine.

▣ "A desolation, a haunt of jackals" This line of poetry is asserting two realities.

  1. the coming invasion and destruction of Judah's walled cities
  2. the demonic presence in the ruins (i.e. Isa. 34:11-15; Jer. 9:10

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONS IN THE OT

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:23 "a man's way is not in himself;
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:23 "a man's way is not in himself;

Nor is it in a man who walks to direct his steps" This is an affirmation of the truth that God is in control of all things. There is no place to begin a theology except the sovereignty of the Creator God! Humans must trust in Him (cf. Prov. 3:5,6; Ps. 37:23; 66:8,9), for there is no one else to trust!

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:23-25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:23-25 This is a closing prayer for mercy as the prophet speaks on behalf of the people.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:24 "Correct me, O Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:24 "Correct me, O Lord" This is a Piel IMPERATIVE, SINGULAR (BDB 415, KB 418, used in a collective sense, i.e. "us"). It is the emphasis on God as parent (cf. Prov. 3:12; Ps. 103:6-14; Heb. 12:5-13). God is a disciplining parent; He disciplines for the purpose of maturity in righteousness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FATHERHOOD OF GOD

entries.title: Jeremiah 10:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:25 The prophet's prayer to God continues and pleads that He will judge (lit. "pour out," BDB 1049, KB 1629, Qal IMPERATIVE) the nations (and the families) which He used to judge His people (cf. Ps. 79:6-7). The ultimate goal of creation is to know YHWH and have a world that reflects His character.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What metaphor or analogy does Jeremiah use in chapter 8 to describe Judah's reluctance to repent?
  2. Why are the graves opened in Jeremiah 8?
  3. Who are the scribes in Jeremiah 8?
  4. Who is speaking in Jer. 8:18-9:16?
  5. List the judgments that God will send on Judah in Jeremiah 9.
  6. Describe Jeremiah's understanding of circumcision and its purpose.
  7. List the reasons for the futility of idolatry found in Jeremiah 10.
  8. List the attributes of YHWH in Jeremiah 10.
  9. Why did God allow His people to be exiled!
