READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Jeremiah 11-13 is about the Mosaic covenant, which Josiah took seriously, as did the prophets, but the people did not (cf. Jer. 11:7-8)!
    SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TEN COMMANDMENTS
    SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

  2. This discussion of "the covenant" has words and phrasing taken from Deuteronomy.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

  3. The first of several very frank discussions between YHWH and Jeremiah, called "Jeremiah's Confessions," occur in this literary unit (cf. Jer. 11:18-23; 12:1-6; 15:10-21; 17:14-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-13; 20:14-18). Jeremiah felt comfortable being transparent in his conversations with YHWH. This is a perfect example of intimacy!

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:2 "Hear the words"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:2 "Hear the words" This is a Qal PLURAL IMPERATIVE (BDB 1033, KB 1570) which so often introduces a new poem/thought in Jeremiah (see note at Jer. 10:1).

▣ "this covenant" Chapters 11-13 are unified by the term "covenant" (BDB 136, KB 157). This covenant, in context, seems to relate to God's revelation to Moses on Mt. Sinai (cf. Exodus 19-24; Deuteronomy 5). God approached several of the early personages with promises and stipulations (i.e. Noah, Gen. 6:18; Abraham, Genesis 12; 15; 18). These covenants basically involve stipulations with benefits and warnings/cursings for non-performance (i.e. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-29). They exactly follow the Hittite Suzerian Treaty formulas of the second millennium B.C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HITTITE (SUZERAIN) TREATIES

▣ "speak" This VERB has a PLURAL suffix (BDB 180). The question is, "To what/who does this refer?"

  1. the words of the covenant
  2. the Jewish Study Bible, p. 948, says that according to Pesikta Rabbati it refers to the three prophetic speakers of the period.
    1. Jeremiah
    2. Huldah (cf. 2 Kgs. 22:14-20; 2 Chr. 34:22-28)
    3. Zephaniah (cf. Zeph. 1:1)

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:3 "cursed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:3 "cursed" In Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28 Moses lays out the benefits and judgments connected with following YHWH. When Joshua entered the Promised Land, he confirmed this covenant with the people (cf. Josh. 8:30-35). There are consequences to disobedience (i.e. Deut. 27:15-26; 28:15-19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:4 "the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:4 "the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt" It needs to be remembered that YHWH dealt with the Israelites in grace (cf. Gen. 6:1-22; 15:12-21) before He dealt with them in law (cf. Exodus 19-24). The Law was YHWH's way to assure a people who reflected His character to a fallen world! Their purpose is to ensure fallen humans' long term happiness and peace.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "from the iron furnace" This (BDB 468 CONSTRUCT BDB 137) is imagery from the mining industry, a phrase that speaks of processing metal. It is used as imagery for "hard labor" (cf. Isa. 48:10; Deut. 4:20). But here, according to John H. Walton, it denotes a positive imagery of Israel becoming a nation.

▣ "Listen" See note at Jer. 11:2. It is important to remember that God's covenant is both conditional and unconditional. It is conditional on mankind's faith response (cf. Jer. 31:32), but unconditional on God's promise (cf. Jer. 24:4-7). It is important not only to hear (Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 11:2) the Word of God (Exod. 24:3-8), but to act on the Word of God (cf. James 2:14-26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣ "so you shall be My people, and I will be your God" This is covenant language (i..e. Gen. 17:7-8; Exod. 6:7; Deut. 26:17-19; Jer. 7:23; 11:4; 31:1,33). Notice that it is based on Israel's obedience; no obedience — no covenant!

This is why a New Covenant (Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36) was needed. Fallen mankind, even covenant mankind, could not keep God's laws (cf. Gen. 6:5,11-12; Ps. 14:1-3; Acts 15:10; Rom. 3:9-18,23; Galatians 3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:5 "the oath which I swore to your forefathers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:5 "the oath which I swore to your forefathers" This seems to refer to YHWH's call to Abram in Gen. 12:1-3.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "a land flowing with milk and honey" This phrase was a technical name for the land of Palestine in Canaanite, Egyptian, Assyrian, and Babylonian documents (cf. Exod. 3:8,17; Deut. 6:3; 11:9; 26:9,15; 27:3; 31:20).

▣ "as it is this day" This is a combination of BDB 398 and BDB 260, which is used often especially in Deuteronomy (cf. Jer. 2:30; 4:20,38; 5:24; 10:8; 11:4; 27:9; 29:28), but is also found several times in

  1. Joshua ‒ 7:25,26; 14:14; 23:8
  2. Judges ‒ 9:19; 10:15; 12:3; 15:19
  3. 1 Samuel ‒ 14:45; 22:8,13; 24:19; 25:32; 26:21; 27:6; 28:18; 29:3,6,8
  4. 2 Samuel ‒ 16:12; 18:20
  5. 1 Kings ‒ 2:26; 3:2; 8:8,24

Jeremiah, who had access to previous OT books, did not get it uniquely from Deuteronomy, which many modern scholars assume was written in Josiah's day.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PENTATEUCH SOURCE CRITICISM (J,E,D,P)

▣ "Amen" This is a form of the Hebrew term for "faith" (cf. Hab. 2:4). It comes from the root "to be firm" or "to be sure." Its basic affirmation in the OT is "faithfulness" or "trustworthiness" (i.e. this usage may be an allusion to Deut. 27:15-26). Here, and in Jer. 28:6 it is used in the sense of a verbal agreement, as we use it today.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMEN

▣ "Lord" See SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "Lord" See SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:6 This verse may imply an itinerant ministry. There is much about the lives of OT characters that is unknown. The VERB "proclaim" is a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 894, KB 1128, cf. Jer. 2:2; 3:12; 7:2; the same VERB appears in Jer. 19:2, but Qal PERFECT).

Jeremiah speaks on YHWH's behalf with YHWH's words (cf. v. 9).

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:7 "I solemnly warned. . .warning persistently"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:7 "I solemnly warned. . .warning persistently" This first phrase is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and a PERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 729, KB 795), which was a grammatical way to show intensity.

The second phrase is literally "rising early and warning," both Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTES. YHWH repeatedly warned His covenant people by revelations through Moses during the exodus and wilderness wandering period.

YHWH manifested His personal presence then by

  1. the Shekinah cloud
  2. providing water
  3. providing food
  4. clothes
    1. did not wear out
    2. grew with the children
  5. revelations at the tabernacle to Moses

▣ "Listen to My voice" See note at Jer. 11:2. "Voice" would be imagery for all of YHWH's revelations (see above).

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:7-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 11:7-8 These verses are omitted in the LXX (except for "And they did not obey," Jer. 11:8). They are theologically similar to Jer. 7:24-26. Basically they are Judah's response to YHWH's message through Jeremiah.

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:8 This verse describes the covenant people's response to YHWH's revelation.

  1. they did not obey ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal PERFECT (cf. Jer. 7:24; 9:13)
  2. they did not incline their ear ‒ BDB 639, KB 692, Hiphil PERFECT(cf. Jer. 35:15)
  3. they walked, every one, in the stubbornness of their evil heart (cf. Jer. 3:17; 7:24; 9:14; 13:10; 16:12; 18:12; 23:17)

YHWH's response was

  1. to bring the stated curses among them (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-29)
  2. even the curses did not affect their behavior

It must be remembered that biblical faith is not simply cognitive or a crisis experience, but a daily relationship with God through faith and repentance!

▣ "in the stubbornness of their evil heart" God possibly chose Israel because of their rebellious tendencies (cf. Deut. 9:6,7,13,24; 10:16; 31:27), so that the truth of His gracious and patient character (cf. Exod. 34:6-7; Num. 14:18; Deut. 4:31; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8-18; 145:8-13) might shine all the brighter!

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

11:9
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta   "A conspiracy"
TEV   "plotting against"
LXX   "a bond of union"
NET Bible   "plotted rebellion"

The Hebrew NOUN (BDB 905) denotes a "planning together" or "binding" of men to do harm (used often in Kings and Chronicles). It is found only here in Jeremiah. What is shocking is that it was the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem plotting against YHWH!

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:10 "They have turned back to the iniquities of their ancestors"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:10 "They have turned back to the iniquities of their ancestors" The current generation refused to acknowledge the sin and rebellion of their ancestors. They themselves became covenant breakers and idolaters just as their ancestors had (cf. Exod. 20:5). Consequences of sin move through time!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

▣ "the house of Israel and the house of Judah" The Israeli united monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon) split in 922 B.C. over the issue of taxation and forced labor between Solomon's son Rehoboam and the Ephraimatic leader Jeroboam I. From this point on the Northern Ten Tribes are known as Israel (collective term), Ephraim (the largest tribe), or Samaria (the capital city).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

▣ "have broken My covenant" The VERB is a Hiphil PERFECT (BDB 830 I, KB 974), which denotes an intensified, settled condition!

What a shocking phrase. The covenants with the Patriarchs were conditional. Successive generations violated it (the PERFECT denotes a settled condition). It had stated consequences (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-29). YHWH abrogated the covenant (i.e. divorced His covenant wife) and Jeremiah states clearly in Jer. 31:31-34 that a "new" covenant was necessary, one not based on human performance which, because of the Fall (Genesis 3), was impossible. Therefore, YHWH Himself would act redemptively on their behalf (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36). The "new covenant" of Jeremiah is the gospel of Jesus Christ (cf. Rom. 3:21-31; Galatians 3; and the book of Hebrews).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:11 The covenant curses came to fruition (cf. Jer. 6:19).

▣ "though they will cry to Me, yet I will not listen to them" What a shocking phrase! YHWH pleaded again and again with them and they would not listen. Even now, their cry to Him is from the fear of consequences, not true repentance! The covenant is broken! YHWH will not respond (cf. Jer. 11:11; 7:16). Oh my, oh my, "the eternal" covenant (cf. Gen. 17:7,13,19) is abrogated by God.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:12 "will go and cry to the gods to whom they burn incense"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:12 "will go and cry to the gods to whom they burn incense" The lifeless idols cannot hear, see, or save! Oh, the folly of manmade gods! Tradition and superstition are so debilitating (cf. Jer. 7:9; 11:12,13,17; 32:29)!

▣ "they surely will not save them" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 446, KB 448), which shows intensity. There is no possible deliverance from "non-existent" gods made with human hands (cf. Isa. 44:9-20; Jer. 10:2-11)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:13 "For your gods are as many as your cities, O Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:13 "For your gods are as many as your cities, O Judah" Every city had their own Ba'al - Asherah worship site (i.e. "high place," cf. Jer. 2:28).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "the shameful thing" The Hebrews often took the vowels from the Hebrew word "shame" and combined them with the names of foreign deities (i.e. Ishbosheth = "man of shame," cf. 2 Sam. 2:8, instead of Eshbaal, 1 Chr. 8:33). This was done to ridicule the idols. The term "shame" (BDB 102, cf. Hosea 9:10) became a word for the fertility worship of Ba'al and Asherah of the Canaanite pantheon (see W. F. Albright, Archaeology and the Religion of Israel).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:14 "do not pray for this people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:14 "do not pray for this people" The first two VERBS are IMPERFECTS used in a JUSSIVE sense. The time for intercession had passed (cf. Jer. 11:11; 7:16; 14:11). God had set his mind on judgment (cf. Exod. 32:10). It was an act of parental love (cf. Heb. 12:5-11). His people were so sick with sin that only radical surgery could help!

The "for" (BDB 723 III) is read by the LXX as "in the time of."

  1. "for" or "because of," MT ‒ בעד (BDB 723 III)
  2. "in the time of," LXX ‒ בעת, RSV, Peshitta, NRSV (NEB, REB, "in the hour of. . .")

The UBS Text Project, p. 207, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt). Most English translations follow option #1.

A book that has helped me interpret prophecy in light of the original author's intent is by D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks. This is especially true of chapter 4, "How does the Language of Destruction and Blessing Work?" (pp. 73-102). Moderns do not understand ancient eastern ways of imagery. We tend to make everything literal, which is a disaster when interpreting prophetic poetry. I also highly recommend Fee and Stuart, How To Read the Bible For All Its Worth.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:15 "What right has My Beloved in My house"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:15 "What right has My Beloved in My house" This phrasing seems to allude to Isa. 5:1-7. But, now the "Beloved" is the "rejected"!

Jeremiah was obviously familiar with Isaiah and Deuteronomy. Much of his imagery and vocabulary come from these books.

▣ "Can the sacrificial flesh take away from you your disaster" The LXX's understanding of this difficult Hebrew text is that Judah was depending on the ritual of her sacrificial cultus instead of a personal relationship with God. Most modern English translations follow the LXX and see it as relating to Jeremiah's temple sermon in chapter 7.

The MT seems to imply that the people were

  1. taking the sacrificial meat home to eat
  2. eating it at the temple but planning their evil deeds of Ba'al worship activities

In Moses' writings this meat was the privilege of the priests only, except for the peace offering. This showed the people's total disregard for YHWH and His word!

The Expositors Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 455, offers a list of the textual problems.

  1. a MASCULINE PLURAL ADJECTIVE modifying a FEMININE NOUN
  2. a SINGULAR NOUN CONSTRUCE followed by a PLURAL VERB
  3. MT punctuation that does not make sense
  4. an archaic ending to one of the NOUNS
  5. an ADVERB before the last VERB with an unusual meaning

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE OFFERING

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN OFFERING

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:15-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:15-16 These two verses are poetry. God's people are spoken of in the imagery of an unfaithful wife, as in the book of Hosea (chapters 1-3). This shows the intimate interpersonal family relationship that was desired between YHWH and His people (cf. Jer. 2:2).

The shocking notion of YHWH divorcing His covenant wife, in light of this being called "an eternal covenant," has caused great theological confusion. In my opinion, this issue is best discussed in two ways.

  1. YHWH's covenant with the Patriarchs and Moses/Israel were both "conditional" and "unconditional."
    SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT
    SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP
  2. I have recently (2024) become convinced that the book of Revelation also apeaks of YHWH divorcing faithless Israel (i.e. Jerusalem being "the great whore of Babylon") and the Messianic banquet as being the wedding feast of a new marriage to a faithful wife, the Church). Please look at my new Partial Preterist commentary on Revelation (2024) free online www.freebiblecommentary.org, second blue box, "Written Bible Commentaries."

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:16 "A green olive tree"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:16 "A green olive tree" There are two major agricultural symbols used for the nation from Abraham's seed in the OT:

  1. an olive tree (cf. Ps. 52:8; Hosea 14:6; Rom. 11:17-24)
  2. a grapevine (i.e. Isaiah 5)
▣
NASB, LXX   "its branches are worthless"
NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA   "its branches are broken"
TEV   "break its branches"
NJB, REB   "its branches will be consumed"
Peshitta   "its branches are destroyed"

There are three possible VERBS.

  1. רעע ‒ BDB 949, KB 1270, meaning "to break," cf. Jer. 15:12 (alternate form רעה, KB 1264)
  2. רעה ‒ BDB 949, KB 1262, meaning "that which is harmful or useless" (LXX, see Benjamin Davidson, Analytical Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon, p. DCLXXXVI, IV)
  3. בער ‒ BDB 128, KB 145, meaning "to kindle"

The judgment of YHWH (i.e. fire, BDB 77, or possibly lightning) has destroyed the olive tree (i.e. Judah).

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:17 "The Lord of hosts, who planted you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:17 "The Lord of hosts, who planted you" Here again the people are described in agricultural terms as an olive tree or vineyard (cf. Jer. 2:21; Exod. 15:17; Ps. 44:2; 80:8; Isa. 5:2). YHWH is their source and life.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "to provoke Me" This VERBAL (BDB 494, KB 491, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is used often in connection with idolatry (cf. Jer. 25:6,7; 32:30; 44:3,8; Deut. 4:25; 9:18; 31:29; 32:16; 1 Kgs. 16:7; 2 Kgs. 17:15-17; 21:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣ "by offering up sacrifices to Baal" Ba'al was the male fertility god of Canaan (see Ras Shamra Texts, cf. Jer. 7:9; 11:13; and 32:29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE.

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:18-12:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 11:18-12:4 This is the first of several intimate conversations between YHWH and Jeremiah known as "Jeremiah's Confessions" (cf. Jer. 11:18-12:6 [possibly 11:18-23; 12:1-6]; 15:10-21; 17:14-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18 [possibly 20:7-13; 20:14-18]). Verses 18-20 and Jer. 12:1-4 are poems. This first one (or two) deals with the plot from Jeremiah's own kindred in Anathoth to take his life.

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:19 Jeremiah expresses his surprise at the Divine information he received (Jer. 11:18). He was shocked at the intensity of the plot, because he was innocent (i.e. line 1, cf. Isa. 53:7).

Lines 3 and 4 are COHORTATIVES.

  1. let us destroy the tree with its fruit ‒ BDB 1007, KB 1469, Hiphil COHORTATIVE
  2. let us cut him off from the land of the living ‒ BDB 503, KB 500, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense

In Jer. 11:20, line 3, Jeremiah uses a COHORTATIVE directed at those who plotted his death ‒ "let me see Your vengeance on them," BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense.

Just an added note about "with its fruit" (#1 above). This word (בלחמו, BDB 536) usually means "bread" or possibly "food."

  1. REB translated it as "sap," which is a revocalization.
  2. TEV has "while it is still healthy."
  3. NRSV has "in its strength" בלחו).
  4. The UBS Text Project, p. 211, gives "bread/fruit" an A rating (very high probability).

▣ The last two lines of Jer. 11:19 are parallel. The same thought is expressed in two images.

  1. "cut off" ‒ BDB 503, KB 500, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense; this VERB is used in two ways
    1. cut down a tree
    2. cut off a piece of something, here, "the land of the living," cf. Ps. 52:5; Isa. 53:8
  2. "name be remembered no more" ‒ BDB 269, KB 269, Niphal IMPERFECT , cf. Ps. 41:5; 83:4; 109:13

Both of these were imagery for death.

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:20 "O Lord of hosts, who judges righteously"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:20 "O Lord of hosts, who judges righteously" This section deals with the age-old question of why the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper (see John W. Wenham, The Goodness of God and The Enigma of Evil: Can We Believe in the Goodness of God). Jeremiah picks up on God as a righteous judge and in Jer. 12:1 he wants to plead his circumstances before Him. This is reminiscent of the book of Job (see my free exegetical, verse-by-verse commentary on Job online), also note Psalm 37; 73 and Hab: 1:2-4. It is always difficult to face and accept the unfairness of this fallen reality! But the problem is not YHWH but human rebellion (i.e. Genesis 3). This is not the world YHWH intended it to be!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

SPECIAL TOPIC: SUFFERING

▣ "Who tries the feelings and the heart" God does judge (i.e. examine, BDB 103, KB 119, Qal PARTICIPLE, cf. Jer. 6:27) on the basis, not only of actions (see full list of texts on the subject at Gal. 6:7-10), but also motives (cf. Jer. 17:10; 20:12; Ps. 7:9; 17:3; 26:2; 66:10; 139:23).

The word "feelings" (lit. "reins") in the English text is basically the Hebrew word (BDB 480) for the lower viscera. The ancients believed that this was the area where the emotions and motives dwelt (cf. Jer. 12:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INWARD PARTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣ "For to You have I committed my cause" The MT has the VERB "uncovered" (גלה, BDB 162, KB 191, Piel PERFECT, cf. LXX), but most translations have "committed" (lit. "rolled upon," גלל, BDB 164, KB 193, cf. Ps. 22:8).

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:21-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 11:21-23 This is YHWH's response to Jeremiah's prayer of Jer. 11:20. Anathoth was Jeremiah's hometown (cf. Jer. 1:1). There has been much discussion in the commentaries if these threats were based on the ancient rivalry between the two priestly families of Zadok and Abiathar. This connection is not certain in the text, but was obviously an undercurrent. Zadok was the current ruling high priestly family and Abiathar, Jeremiah's family, had been exiled to Anathoth by Solomon (cf. 1 Kgs. 2:26-27).

entries.title: Jeremiah 11:22 "the sword. . .famine"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:22 "the sword. . .famine" In the ANE there was a triad of terms used by Jeremiah to describe coming disaster (cf. Jer. 14:12; 21:7,9; 24:10; 27:8,13; 29:17-18; 32:24,36; 34:17; 38:2; 42:17,22; 44:13).

  1. the sword ‒ invasion
  2. famine ‒ drought or siege
  3. pestilence ‒ insects, sickness, or siege

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. What is a covenant?
  2. Define the Hebrew word "Amen" in Jer. 11:5.
  3. Who is Ba'al and how was he worshiped?
  4. How is Jer. 11:15 related to the book of Hosea?
  5. Why were the men of Anathoth trying to kill Jeremiah?

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:1 "Righteous"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:1 "Righteous" This strophe is similar to Job and Psalm 73 (i.e. why do the wicked prosper?).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS.

▣ "You" YHWH (see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.) is righteous which denotes His justice. This is one aspect of His character. But, Jeremiah feels he has been acted against unfairly.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

▣ "I would plead my case with You" This chapter has three poetic strophes. The first two (Jer. 12:1-4; 5-6) are part of Jeremiah's first confession starting in Jer. 11:18. It is presented as a court case (as is Jeremiah 2). Jeremiah, like Job, wants to take YHWH to court!

Jeremiah almost seems to border on blasphemy in his dialog with God, therefore, the two Jewish exegetists in the Middle Ages, Rashi and Kimchi, try to explain away Jeremiah's hard words. Rashi says that he asked God to know God's ways, while Kimchi says he asked because the prophet was confused. To me the depth of Jeremiah's emotions directed toward God are a sign of their deep interpersonal relationship. I believe God prefers our heartfelt thoughts to false piety!

▣  "Why has the way of the wicked prospered?

Why are all those who deal in treachery at ease" These are in a Hebrew synonymous parallel relationship (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY). This is a major theological question because it seems to be exactly opposite to the Mosaic Law (i.e. the two ways ) and Psalm 1. Humans have always struggled with the unfairness of life (cf. Job; Psalm 73; Habakkuk; Mal. 3:13-15). Psalm 37:7-9 is a good summary of the Bible's advice in this area.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:2 "You have planted them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:2 "You have planted them" YHWH created a nation out of the seed of Abraham (cf. Gen. 12:1-3; 15:12-21). He created/planted (cf. Jer. 11:17) them to be a light to the world, but they became evil and reflected the character of the fallen world instead of YHWH (cf Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣  "You are near to their lips

But far from their mind" They had religion but not relationship (cf. Isa. 29:13; Ezek. 33:30-33; Rom. 2:17-29; 2 Tim. 3:5).

The term "mind" is literally "kidneys" (BDB 480) here, used of human thinking (cf. Ps. 16:7). The root also is used of "feeling" (cf. Job 19:27; Prov. 23:16; Lam. 3:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INWARD PARTS

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:3 Notice the three things Jeremiah says about YHWH's knowledge of him.

  1. He knows me ‒ BDB 393, KB 390, Qal PERFECT
  2. He sees me ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERFECT
  3. He examines my heart ‒ BDB 103, KB 119, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Ps. 7:9

What is amazing, He knows us completely and still loves us and wants us to be with Him!

▣ "You know me, O Lord" The Hebrew word "to know" emphasizes intimate personal relationship (cf. Gen. 4:1; Jer. 1:5). Jeremiah was confident that God knew his motives and his heart (cf. Ps. 139:1,23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

▣ "Drag them off" The last two lines of Jer. 12:3 have two parallel IMPERATIVES.

  1. "drag them off" ‒ BDB 683, KB 736, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  2. "set them apart" (lit. "sanctify") ‒ BDB 872, KB 1073, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

Both call on God (IMPERATIVES OF REQUEST) to actively judge the wickedness of His own people (cf. Amos 3:2; 1 Pet. 4:17).

Jeremiah is much like David (i.e. note Ps. 139:19-22); he is very forceful in his request for vengeance.

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:4 "How long is the land to mourn"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:4 "How long is the land to mourn" Judah's wickedness causes the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28 to fall on Palestine (cf. Hosea 4:1-3). The land of milk and honey has no produce nor flocks! This is exactly the opposite of what YHWH wanted to do!

The same question, "how long," was also asked by Isaiah in Isa. 6:11-13! Judgment is coming on God's covenant people.

The sin of Adam and Eve brought about the disruption of the normal cycles of nature (cf. Rom. 5:12-21; 8:18-25). This is not the world God intended it to be (see John W. Wenham, The Goodness of God and The Enigma of Evil: Can We Believe in the Goodness of God).

The term translated "mourn" (BDB 5, KB 6, Qal IMPERFECT) may be from another Hebrew root of the same three consonants (אבל). This root is used in several ways.

  1. mourn, BDB I, KB I
  2. dry up water, KB II
  3. protected pasture land, BDB II
  4. an ADVERB "truly"
  5. camel driver, BDB III
  6. canal, KB 7

There are several texts where this root is parallel to "wither" (cf. Isa. 24:4; 33:9; Jer. 23:10; Hosea 4:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SUFFERING

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "Because men have said, 'He will not see our latter ending'" This line can have two meanings.

  1. the prophets are giving a false message of peace and prosperity (cf. Jer. 5:31)
  2. the Judean people do not believe YHWH will act against them because of
    1. Abrahamic covenant
    2. the presence of the temple (cf. Jeremiah 7)
    3. earlier statements of Isaiah

There are two textual issues.

  1. who does "he" refer to
    1. Jeremiah ‒ "he" (ambiguous, UBS Text Project, p. 213, gives it a "C" rating)
    2. God ‒ LXX, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, NET
  2. how to translate the last words
    1. our ways (ארחותנו) ‒ LXX, NJB, REB
    2. our latter end (אחריתנו) ‒ MT, NASB, NKJV, JPSOA
    3. our fate ‒ NRSV

The NET Bible (p. 1323) and the IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT) (p. 652) think this line may relate to Deut. 32:20.

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:5-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:5-6 God is answering Jeremiah's complaint (cf. TEV, JPSOA footnote), if you cannot handle the pressure from your hometown, how are you going to handle the pressure from Jerusalem? In reality, God is saying, Jeremiah, are you too impatient or too sensitive? If you think this is bad now, you have not seen anything yet! Problems cause us to depend on God — trials are for training (cf. Heb. 5:8)!

12:5
NASB, NRSV  "you fall down"
TEV  "can't even stand up"
NJB, NET  "you feel secure"
REB  "falling headlong"
JPSOA  "you are secure only"
LXX  "you have been confident"

There are three possible options to translate this root.

  1. בסח ‒ BDB 105, "trust" (Arabic root, "to throw one down upon his face")
  2. בסח ‒ BDB 105, "security," NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 649, cf. Jdgs. 18:10; Isa. 32:9-11; Amos 6:1
  3. בסחה ‒ BDB 105, "confidence," cf. Isa. 32:17
  4. מבסח ‒ BDB 105, "confidence," cf. Isa. 32:18
▣
NASB, NKJV, LXX  "in a land of peace"
NRSV  "in a safe land"
TEV  "in open country"
Peshitta  "on level land"
REB  "in easy country"
NJB  "in a country at peace"
JPSOA  "in a tranquil land"
NET  "in safe and open country"

The MT has "in a safe land" (BDB 1022, cf. Isa. 32:17, "peace"; see SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT)). The NET Bible sees this phrase in contrast to the next poetic line, "in the thicket of the Jordan," which was a place of danger from wild animals and robbers; or imagery for Neo-Babylon, cf. Jer. 50:44.

12:6
NASB  "Even they have cried aloud after you"
NKJV  "yes, they have called a multitude after you"
NRSV  "they will pursue you in full cry"
TEV  "they join in the attacks against you"
LXX  "they too shouted; they were gathered behind you
JPSOA  "they cry after you as a mob"
Peshitta  "yea, they also have gossiped about you"

The MT is ambiguous. The context suggests that after he preached, they (his hometown tribal friends and relatives) chased after him condemning him loudly.

▣ "Do not believe them" The VERB (BDB 52, KB 63) is a Hiphil JUSSIVE. Be careful of the flattery of wicked people (cf. Jer. 9:8; Ps. 28:3; Prov. 26:23,25). Kind words often hide an agenda (cf. Ps. 12:6-8)! The self centeredness of the Fall is a perennial flower.

It seems that Jer. 12:6, lines 1-3, relates to negative things said and done against Jeremiah by his hometown. However, the last line deals with their flattery!

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:7-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:7-13 This is written in a characteristic poetic form which has three beats followed by two beats, denoting a funeral dirge or lament. The VERBS, all mostly PERFECTS, denote a completed action. YHWH's attitude is set on judgment because Judah's attitude is set on sin! In this section God is described as a broken-hearted husband (i.e. "I have come to hate her," Jer. 12:8). This is very similar to Jer. 8:18-9:16 and Hosea 11:8,9.

One wonders if Jer. 12:7-8 is theologically related to Jer. 12:5-6. As Jeremiah was painfully and loudly rejected by his own hometown, YHWH is rejected by His own. As Jeremiah's hometown "cries" against him, YHWH's people "roar" against Him. It is possible that Jer. 12:6, line 3, is hunting imagery, if so, then the animals searching prey in Jer. 12:9 are a literary parallel.

Notice the series of covenant terms used by God to describe Judah:

  1. "My house" (i.e. the temple in Jerusalem, cf. Jer. 7:2,10; 11:15; Hosea 8:1; 9:15)
  2. "My inheritance" (cf. Jer. 12:7,8,9; 2:7; 50:11)
  3. "Beloved of My soul" (cf. Jer. 11:15)
  4. "My vineyard" (cf. Isaiah 5)
  5. "My pleasant field" (cf. Jer. 3:19)

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:7 Notice the parallelism of. Jer. 12:7. YHWH has

  1. forsaken ‒ BDB 736, KB 806, Qal PERFECT (PROPHETIC PERFECT)
  2. abandoned ‒ BDB 643, KB 695, Qal PERFECT (PROPHETIC PERFECT)
  3. given ‒ BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT (PROPHETIC PERFECT)

His people into the hand (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND) of foreign invaders!

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:8-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:8-9 YHWH has rejected them because

  1. they became as a lion to Him, Jer. 12:8 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT)
  2. they became as a bird of prey, Jer. 12:9

The result is that YHWH's love, mercy, and care have changed to "hate" (cf. Hosea 9:15; Amos 6:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HATE

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:9 "My inheritance like a speckled bird of prey to Me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:9 "My inheritance like a speckled bird of prey to Me" The interpretive question is about the word "speckled" (BDB 840, KB 997), which is found only here. It can denote a color (BDB 840, cf. Jdg. 5:30), therefore,

  1. hyena (LXX, REB)
  2. speckled bird of prey (NRSV, NKJV, Peshitta)

JPSOA translates the phrase as "like a bird of prey [or] hyena" (cf. NJB). The LXX translates it as "a hyena's cave." The UBS Text Project gives "speckled" an A Rating, but suggests translating it as ("is my heritage to me) a hyena's lair (with birds of prey [hovering] all about it," p. 214). This is how REB translates it. The consonants are the same in #1 and #2, only vowels are different.

The enemies described here seem to refer to the surrounding nations which were a part of the mercenary army of Neo-Babylon (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:2).

▣ The last two lines of Jer. 12:9 have three IMPERATIVES which are the consequences of covenant violations (cf. Deut. 28:64). The birds and beasts shall eat the flesh of the fallen of Judah (cf. Jer. 7:33; 15:3; 16:4; 19:7; 34:20; Ps. 79:2; Isa. 18:6; 56:9).

  1. go ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. gather ‒ BDB 62, KB 74, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. bring ‒ BDB 87, KB 102, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:10 "Many shepherds have ruined My vineyard"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:10 "Many shepherds have ruined My vineyard" "Shepherds" refers to the spiritual leaders of Judah (i.e. priests and prophets, cf. Jer. 2:8; 10:21; Ezek. 34:1-10). But, because of the context, it could refer to foreign alliances (cf. Jer. 6:3).

▣ "They have trampled down My field" This agricultural imagery denotes a grain field where people have walked through it and knocked down the grain. This same imagery is found in Isa. 5:5; 28:18. YHWH removes all protective barriers.

Other acts of judgment also used this VERB "trampled" (BDB 100, KB 115).

  1. trampled in the mud of the streets, Isa. 10:6
  2. Jerusalem and the temple trampled by Gentiles, Isa. 63:18; Luke 21:24; Rev. 11:2

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:11 "it mourns before Me
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:11 "it mourns before Me

  The whole land has been made desolate" There is a repetition of the root שמס (BDB 1031, cf. Jer. 12:10, line 4).

  1. a FEMININE SINGULAR NOUN ‒ BDB 1031
  2. a FEMININE SINGULAR ADJECTIVE ‒ BDB 1031
  3. a Niphal PERFECT VERB ‒ BDB 1030, KB 1563)

The NASB Study Bible (p. 1075, footnote) mentions that in Jer. 12:11 there are seven "s" sound words and seven "n" sound words.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

▣ Here again (cf. Jer. 12:4) is the theological personification of the land being affected by human sin (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28; Rom. 5:12-21; 8:18-22).

▣ "Because no man lays it to heart" This line can have one of two orientations.

  1. Judah sinned and did not repent so the land suffered (cf. Isa. 42:25).
  2. There was no righteous person to intercede on Judah's behalf (cf. Jer. 5:1; Isa. 59:16; Ezek. 22:30).

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:12 "On all the bare heights in the wilderness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:12 "On all the bare heights in the wilderness" This could refer to

  1. judgment coming from the desert winds, cf. Jer. 4:11-13
  2. the place of Ba'al worship, cf. Jer. 2:20; 3:2,6; 17:2; Deut. 12:2-3
  3. invaders capturing the "caravan trails" (see NASB, NJB footnote) or passes (heights, BDB 1046, cf. Jer. 14:6) through the Judean highlands

▣ "a sword of the Lord is devouring" Remember, this was not the power of the foreign invaders or their gods, but the punishing power of YHWH (cf. Jer. 51:15-23; Isa. 10:5).

▣ "There is no peace for anyone" This may be a play on the message of the false prophets who said "Peace, peace" (cf. Jer. 8:11).

The term "anyone" is literally "all flesh" and could refer to animals and humans. All were suffering because of Judah's idolatry.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:13 "They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:13 "They have sown wheat and have reaped thorns" There have been three ways to understand this.

  1. The farmers sowed but because of the invasion there was no one to work the fields so weeds and thorns flourished (cf. Lev. 26:16; Deut. 28:38).
  2. There was a series of drought seasons (cf. Jer. 12:4; 14:2-4).
  3. Human effort without God will come to naught (cf. Ps. 108:12; 127:1-2).

▣ "But be ashamed of your harvest" The MT has a Qal PERFECT PLURAL (BDB 101, KB 116), but the UBS Text Project suggests (i.e. "B" rating) a Qal IMPERATIVE PLURAL. This refers to their idolatry. They were reaping the results of willful, continual covenant violations (cf. Jer. 11:20; 17:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:14 "all My wicked neighbors who strike at the inheritance"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:14 "all My wicked neighbors who strike at the inheritance" We know from history that nations like Edom and probably some of the other surrounding nations (i.e. Ammon, Jer. 49:1; Moab, Zech. 2:8-11) became mercenaries in the Neo-Babylonian army, and even participated in the siege of Jerusalem and its plunder.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOAB

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMMON

▣ "Behold I am about to uproot them" This imagery is used quite often in the book of Jeremiah to describe the work of the prophet (cf. Jer. 1:10; 18:7).

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:14-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:14-17 This is an extremely important strophe which deals not only with the judgment on the surrounding nations which have participated in or benefitted from the Neo-Babylonian invasion of Judah, but also the hope of their incorporation one day into the people of God. This is a wonderful passage which shows clearly that God desires all humans to be a part of His covenant people. See SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN.

There is a repeated use of "uprooted" (BDB 684, KB 737), the opposite of "planted" (see 1:10).

  1. surrounding nations will be uprooted, Jer. 12:14
  2. Judah will be uprooted, Jer. 12:14
  3. after uprooting them YHWH will have compassion (BDB 933, KB 1216, Piel PERFECT with waw), Jer. 12:15
  4. if they will not listen then He will uproot
    1. that nation, Jer. 12:17
    2. uproot and destroy it, Jer. 12:17

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:15 "I will again have compassion on them; and I will bring them back"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:15 "I will again have compassion on them; and I will bring them back" This is a tremendous statement of hope of restoration, not only for Judah, but for Gentiles as well. This universal theme is found several times in the book of Jeremiah, 3:17,19; 4:2; 16:19; 48:47; 49:6,39. This reflects the recurrent universal theme of the prophet Isaiah (cf. Jer. 2:2-4; 12:4-5; 19:16-25; 25:6-9; 42:6-12; 45:22-23; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 56:6-8; 60:11-14; 66:23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "each one to his inheritance and each one to his land" This seems to be a reference to the LXX of Deut. 32:8, which even suggests "national angels."

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANGELS IN THE BIBLE, I. C. #2

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:16 "they will really learn the ways of My people, to swear by My name"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:16 "they will really learn the ways of My people, to swear by My name" The use of YHWH's name was part of the regular worship liturgy of the temple (cf. Jer. 4:2; Deut. 6:13; 10:20; Isa. 65:16; Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21; Rom. 10:9-13).

Notice that the Lord's compassion (Jer. 12:15) is conditional on "if they will really learn the ways of My people."

  1. "really learn" ‒ this is the intensified form of an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 540, KB 531, cf. Isa. 42:6; 49:6)
  2. notice Judah's faith was meant to be a light and learning for the nations (cf. Ezek. 36:22-38)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CALL ON HIS NAME

▣ "As the Lord lives" This reflects the covenant name for God, YHWH, from the Hebrew VERB "to be," Exod. 3:14.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "to swear by Baal" See SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

▣ "they will be built up in the midst of My people" The VERB "build" (BDB 124, KB 139, Niphal PERFECT with waw) is used several times to describe Jeremiah's ministry (cf. Jer. 1:10; 18:9; 24:6; 30:18; 31:4,28; 32:31; 33:7; 42:10; 45:4). It can be used in a positive or negative way.

entries.title: Jeremiah 12:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:17 The conditional nature of biblical covenants is repeated (i.e. Deut. 30:1-10,15,19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "uproot" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and a PERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 684, KB 737), which denotes intensity. YHWH is abrogating His covenant with Abraham's seed! In their idolatry they could not reveal YHWH to the nations (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36). God's people had forgotten their evangelistic purpose!

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:1 "the Lord said to me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:1 "the Lord said to me" This is a prophetic formula for receiving direct revelation. Notice how often the message from YHWH is noted in this chapter.

  1. "Thus the Lord said to me," Jer. 13:1
  2. "the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying," Jer. 13:3
  3. "the Lord said to me," Jer. 13:6
  4. "the word of the Lord came to me, saying," Jer. 13:8
  5. "thus says the Lord," Jer. 13:9
  6. "thus says the Lord , the God of Israel, Jer. 13:12
  7. "thus says the Lord," Jer. 13:13

This was not Jeremiah's message!

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "Go and buy. . .and put it around. . .but do not put. . ." These VERBALS are translated as IMPERATIVES (cf. Jer. 13:4,6) in English, but in Hebrew they are:

  1. "go" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
  2. "buy" ‒ BDB 888, KB 1111, Qal PERFECT (with waw)
  3. "put" ‒ BDB 962, KB 1221, Qal PERFECT (with waw)
  4. "put" (negated) ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Hiphil IMPERFECT
▣
NASB  "linen waistband"
NKJV  "linen sash"
TEV  "linen shorts"
NRSV, NJB, LXX, JPSOA, REB  "linen loincloth"
Peshitta, ASV  "linen girdle"

This refers to a thigh-length undergarment (BDB 25 CONSTRUCT BDB 833; the depictions of this type of undergarment [Canaan and Egypt] seem more like a short shirt than short pants). The exact meaning of the symbol is uncertain (cf. 2 Kgs. 1:8; Job 12:18; Isa. 5:27; Ezek. 23:15).

  1. Some have said it was used because of its close contact to the body, thereby symbolizing intimacy (cf. Jer. 13:11).
  2. Others say that because it was made of linen it refers to what the priest wore (cf. Lev. 16:4).

It is obvious that God is trying to symbolize Himself and His relationship with Judah by means of this intimate, and possibly priestly, material.

▣ "but do not put it in water" This means "do not wash it." Therefore, it will become soiled and smelly. This is what happened to idolatrous, rebellious, stubborn Israel/Judah. She is unclean (cf. Jer. 13:27) and will not allow YHWH to clean her.

entries.content:

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Jeremiah 13:1-14 is a prose passage with two symbolic acts (also note 1 Kings 22; Isaiah 20; Ezekiel 4,5)
    1. a ruined linen waistcloth, Jer. 13:1-11
    2. a full clay jar of wine, Jer. 13:12-14

  2. The UBS Handbook For Translators of Jeremiah divides the poetic section (Jer. 13:15-27) into three strophes by content (p. 334).
    1. a final urgent warning, Jer. 13:15-17
    2. a word to King Jehoiachin, Jer. 13:18-19
    3. Jerusalem depicted as a "shameless woman," Jer. 13:20-27

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

13:1-7 This is a prophetic, symbolic act involving an intimate piece of clothing. Similar illustrative acts are common in Ezekiel (i.e. chapters 4,5). We would call them "visual aids" (cf. Jer. 19:1ff; 27:2ff).

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:4 There is a series of IMPERATIVES in Jer. 13:4 and 6 that relates to Jer. 13:1 (cf. Jer. 13:5).

  1. take the waistband ‒ BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. arise ‒ BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. go ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. hide ‒ BDB 380, KB 377, Qal IMPERATIVE

Also in Jer. 13:6

  1. arise ‒ BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. go ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. take ‒ BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

▣ "go to the Euphrates" This is the Hebrew word פרת, BDB 832. It is used throughout the OT to refer to the Euphrates River (cf. Gen. 2:14; 15:18; Deut. 1:7; 11:24; Jer. 46:2; 51:63). However, because this would involve a trip of over 350 miles each way, and the context probably refers to two different trips, it seems impossible that this could be the meaning of the term here.

Some have asserted

  1. This was possibly symbolic of the battle of Carchemish (at a place on the Euphrates where there were rocks), which occurred in 605 B.C. whereby Neo-Babylon completely defeated the army of Egypt and the remaining army of Assyria; the enemy from the north comes!
  2. This was possibly a wadi, פרת (BDB 831 II), which flowed from the village of פרה, about five miles northeast of Jerusalem (cf. Josh. 18:23 and DSS of 13:5). It provided water for Jerusalem (IDB, vol. 4, p. 656).
  3. It is a play on the sound of the word "linen" (פשׁת, BDB 833m cf. Jer. 13:1).

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:7 "the waistband was ruined, it was totally worthless"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:7 "the waistband was ruined, it was totally worthless" The first VERB "ruined" (BDB 1007, KB 1469, Niphal PERFECT) denotes that which cannot be used for its intended purpose! This same VERB is used of the clay pot in Jer. 18:4. Israel/Judah's intended purpose was to inform the world about YHWH and help draw them to Him (cf. TEV of Jer. 13:11). Their unrepentant (cf. Jer. 13:10), consistent idolatry thwarted that purpose (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

It is also possible that this text refers to a literal 700 mile trip twice to the headwaters of the Euphrates. It might symbolize:

  1. the invasion, exile, and (i.e. "after many days") dominance of Neo-Babylon. Judah was "ruined" in a physical sense during this period. If so, then the "ruined waistcloth" (cf. Lev. 26:39) symbolizes Judah's temporal destruction.
  2. the spiritual corruption of the Mesopotamian powers through political alliances which involved Judah and introduced their gods to Palestine
13:9
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, LXX, NET  "pride" (twice)
REB  "enormous pride"
Peshitta  "proud men" (twice)
NET  "highly exalted
  position"
JPSOA  "the overweening
  pride"

The MT has the root גאון (BDB 144, KB 169). The basic concept is

  1. pride
  2. exaltation
  3. presumption

Therefore, most translations refer this to the covenant peoples' pride, but NET (p. 1326, #9) relates it to v. 11, where it refers to what YHWH wanted them to be "that they might be a people for renown, for praise, and for glory."

The first option, what they were (i.e. prideful), the second, what YHWH wanted them to be, Lev. 26:19, could relate to either option.

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:10 YHWH characterizes His covenant people as

  1. wicked people
  2. refusing to listen to My words (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR)
  3. walking in stubbornness (see SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNES)
  4. going after other gods
    1. to serve them (BDB 712, KB 773, Qal INIFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
    2. to bow down to them (Hishtaphel, BDB 1005, KB 295, INIFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

▣ "let them be just like this waistband" This is a Qal JUSSIVE (BDB 224, KB 243), denoting invasion from

  1. the enemy from the north is coming
  2. the surrounding nations who will take advantage of the situation as well

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:11 God explains the symbolic actions of Jer. 13:1-7. Verse 10 describes Judah in her rebellion, while Jer. 13:11 describes the purpose that God wanted for them (cf. Deut. 26:19). Israel and Judah were meant to be a light to the nations (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5,6), but they had become totally corrupt. They would not listen and respond to God's word or prophets (cf. Jer. 7:13,24,26; Ps. 81:11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "the whole household of Israel and the whole household of Judah" This terminology denotes the split of the family of the Patriarchs into two distinct nations. This occurred in 922 B.C. when Solomon's son, Rehoboam, raised the taxes and forced labor on all the tribes. Jeroboam I, an Ephramite labor leader who fled to Egypt, led a successful rebellion.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEWS

▣ "clings. . .cling" This VERB (BDB 179, KB 209) is used of

  1. husband and wife in Gen. 2:24 and physical attraction in Gen. 34:3
  2. the tribes holding on to their land allocations in Num. 36:7,9
  3. clinging to the Lord and not the nations in Deut. 10:20; 11:22; 13:4; Josh. 23:8,12

God's people should have clung to Him, should have been close to Him, but they were not! They even went after the gods of Mesopotamia and Canaan.

▣ Notice how YHWH expresses His purpose in calling the seed of Abraham.

  1. a people for Himself (cf. Exod. 19:5-6)
  2. a people of renown (lit. "name," cf. Dan. 9:15; Neh. 9:10)
  3. a people for praise (cf. Jer. 33:9)
  4. a people for glory (cf. Jer. 33:9)

They were to bring honor to YHWH (cf. Isa. 63:12,14) and make Him a "name" (cf. Jer. 32:20)! But they would not "listen" (cf. Ps. 81:11; 106:25; Jer. 7:13,24,26).

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:12 "jug"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:12 "jug" This is the Hebrew term nebel (BDB 614 I), which speaks of (1) a wineskin or (2) the largest earthen container (cf. Isa. 30:14) for liquids, about ten gallons.

The phrase "every jug is to be filled with wine" may be (1) a truism or (2) the hope of drunken revelers. Wine jugs are meant to be filled with wine. So too, should God's people reflect God, however, the opposite was true. This is the thrust of this passage. God will make them drunk (cf. Jer. 25:15-17,27-28; 51:57; Ps. 75:8; Isa. 51:17-20; Ezek. 23:32-34), which was a symbol of judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES (Metrology)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WINE AND STRONG DRINK

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:12 "Do we not very well know. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:12 "Do we not very well know. . ." The Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT of the same root (BDB 393, KB 390 ) intensify the sarcastic response.

They claim to know but, in reality, they know nothing!

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:12-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 13:12-14 This is another symbolic act in the form of a proverb (Luke 21:29). The proverb is recorded in Jer. 13:12 and God's reaction to it in Jer. 13:13-15.

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:13 "inhabitants. . .sit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:13 "inhabitants. . .sit" These are from the same root (BDB 442, KB 444) and are used three times.

  1. Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, "to dwell" (i.e. inhabit, used twice)
  2. Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, "to sit," imagery for the place of power (i.e. throne of the king)

Notice the groups affected.

  1. the Davidic kings (cf. Jer. 17:25; 22:2,4,30; 29:16; 33:21; 36:30)
  2. the priests
  3. the prophets
  4. the inhabitants of Jerusalem

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:14 "dash"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:14 "dash" This VERB (BDB 658, KB 711, Piel PERFECT with waw) was used of the killing of babies by the invaders (i.e. Assyria, Neo-Babylon, cf. 2 Kgs. 8:12; Ps. 137:9; Isa. 13:16,18; Hosea 13:16; Nahum 3:10). The VERB here is a word play on the shattered wine jug of Jer. 13:13 (cf. Jer. 51:20-23).

▣ "father and sons together" Sin, like faith, moves through families.

  1. sin ‒ Deut. 5:9; Jer. 7:18
  2. faith ‒ Deut. 5:10; 7:9

For the balancing truth that each person is responsible only for their own sin, see Ezekiel 18.

▣ "I will not show pity nor be sorry nor have compassion that I should not destroy them" Notice the things YHWH will not do.

  1. show pity ‒ BDB 328, KB 338, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Jer. 15:5; 21:7; Ezek. 5:11
  2. be sorry ‒ BDB 299, KB 298, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Jer. 21:7; Ezek. 5:11
  3. show compassion ‒ BDB 933, KB 1216, Piel IMPERFECT, cf. Jer. 21:7

This same truth is stated in Jer. 16:5 (also note 21:7 about King Zedekiah). There are consequences to the repeated rejection of God's word and will (cf. Lam. 2:17-22; Ezek. 8:18; 9:10; 24:14). But, the OT ends on a promise of YHWH "sparing" in Mal. 3:17!

Remember, this is hyperbolic, anthropomorphic, poetic imagery.

  1. see SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (anthropomorphism)
  2. see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic
  3. see G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:15 "Listen and give heed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:15 "Listen and give heed" These are two Hebrew words for "hear." They are synonymous and both plead for Judah's positive repentant response (cf. Jer. 10:1).

  1. BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR)
  2. BDB 24, KB 27, Hiphil IMPERATIVE , cf. Deut. 32:1; Isa. 1:2

▣ "do not be haughty" The VERB (BDB 146, KB 170) is a Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (negated). The concept of haughtiness and pride are the theme of this particular section (cf. Jer. 13:17). Israel had become so haughty and proud that she would not respond in the appropriate way to God. This word is used of

  1. kings
    1. Uzziah ‒ 2 Chr. 26:15-16
    2. Hezekiah ‒ 2 Chr. 32:25
    3. king of Tyre ‒ Ezek. 28:2,5,17
  2. God's people
    1. Isa. 3:16
    2. Ezek. 16:50
    3. Zeph. 3:11

Haughtiness, pride, and self-directed living are the results of the Fall (cf. Genesis 3; 6:5,11-12; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND and SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP). Apparently even the covenant people could not escape its influence. Therefore, a new creation, a new covenant is mandatory (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36; Rom. 3:21-31; 4-5; Galatians 3; the book of Hebrews).

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:15-27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:15-27 Verses 1-14 are prose but Jer. 13:15-27 forms two or three poetic strophes.

  1. The first strophe is the hopeless call of the prophet for repentance on the part of God's people.
  2. Jeremiah 13:20-27 is a warning of what will happen if they do not repent.

There is a real paradox between the "hear and do" (cf. Jer. 13:15) and the inability to change of Jer. 13:23. It is the tension between

  1. God's sovereignty and human free will
  2. the unconditional and conditional nature of OT covenants

SPECIAL TOPIC: PREDESTINATION vs. FREE WILL

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:16 "Give glory to the Lord your God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:16 "Give glory to the Lord your God" Because of the use of this phrase in Josh. 7:19, many believe this is a call for confession of sin or at least an oath of truthfulness (cf. John 9:24). The grammatical form is a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 670, KB 733).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (kabod, OT)

▣ "deep darkness" This is the Hebrew word salmawet (BDB 853), which is translated in the KJV in Ps. 23:4 as "the valley of the shadow of death." It really means a valley of deep darkness which may describe any and all of life's crises.

The NET Bible has a good note about this word at Jer. 2:6 (p. 1290, #6). It is used in poetic texts of

  1. the darkness of prison, Ps. 107:10,14
  2. the darkness of invasion, Isa. 9:1
  3. the darkness of a mine, Job 28:3
  4. the darkness of a ravine, Ps. 23:4
  5. the darkness of a wasteland and ravines of the Sinai desert, Jer. 2:6
  6. life's tragedies or confusions, Job 3:5; 12:22; 24:17; 28:3; 34:22; Ps. 44:19
  7. the darkness of death, Job 10:21-22; 38:17

Notice the contrast between YHWH's word/truth as light (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LIGHT), but sin as darkness (BDB 364, KB 361, Hiphil IMPERFECT, cf. Isa. 8:22-9:2), deep darkness (BDB 853), and gloom (BDB 791). This darkness imagery is characterized by "stumbling" (BDB 619, KB 669, Hithpael IMPERATIVE). A life of faith is pictured as a person walking on a clearly marked path in light. If one

  1. deviates from the path
  2. stumbles on the path
  3. rejects God's ways (path)
  4. walks in darkness in difficult terrain

judgment is the result.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:17 "if you will not listen to it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:17 "if you will not listen to it" Jeremiah was commanded by God to preach this message of repentance, but he knew the people (i.e. YHWH's flock) would not respond (cf. Isa. 6:9-10). Humans have a choice but their choice has consequences (cf. line 5).

Jeremiah (the weeping prophet) describes his feelings (which mimic YHWH's feelings) about Judah's stubborn, unrepentant, sinful idolatry and its consequences.

  1. my soul will sob in secret
  2. my eyes will bitterly weep (Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal  IMPERFECT from the same root, BDB 199, KB 227)
  3. my eyes will flow down with tears

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:18 "Say to the king and the queen mother"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:18 "Say to the king and the queen mother" Verses 18 and 19 are either a historical allusion to

  1. what happened in the second of Nebuchadnezzar's attacks on Jerusalem in 597 B.C. (cf. Jer. 22:24-26; 29:2), where Jehoiachin and his mother (see similar phrase used of the king of Babylon in Isa. 47:1), Neshushta, are taken into captivity (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:8-17)
  2. a prophecy about the terrible fall of Jerusalem and burning of the temple in 586 B.C. by Neo-Babylon.

Remember, Nebuchadnezzar's army led several deportations, 605, 597, 586, 582 B.C. Whatever the allusion, the king, representing God (cf. 1 Samuel 8), is now humiliated and taken away into captivity and the southern cities (i.e. the Negev) are under siege (cf. Jer. 13:19).

▣
NASB, NJB  "For your beautiful crown
  Has come down from your heads"
NKJV  "For your rule shall collapse the crown of your
  glory
NRSV  "Since your glorious crown has fallen from your
  head
JPSOA  "For your diadems are abased,
  Your glorious crowns"
Peshitta  "For the crown of your glory has fallen from
  your head

The LXX reads, "because your crown of glory has been removed from your head." The MT reads, "for your crown (BDB 912) has come down, the crown of your splendor."

The MT has three VERBS related to what the king and his mother must do.

  1. take a lowly seat
    1. BDB 1050, KB 1631, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    2. BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. because your crown has come down, BDB 432, KB 434, Qal PERFECT

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:19 "the Negev"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:19 "the Negev" This was desert pasture land in south Judah.

▣ "have been locked up" This VERB (BDB 688, KB 742, Pual PERFECT) refers to a siege of a walled city (or fortress in the Negev). The result of these sieges was "exile" (BDB 162, KB 191, Hophal PERFECT, used twice in this verse).

▣ "there is no one to open them" The foreign alliances, in this case Egypt, cannot stop the Neo-Babylonian invasion of Palestine. It was YHWH's will!

▣ "Wholly carried into exile" This is hyperbolic; some of Judah's citizens escaped exile.

The problem with much modern interpretation of Wisdom Literature and Prophetic Literature is western literalism! Prophecy is a hyperbolic genre! See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:20 "Lift up your eyes and see"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:20 "Lift up your eyes and see" These VERBS are both FEMININE SINGULAR IMPERATIVES (kethiv), which refer to the city of Jerusalem. The Septuagint translates this "Jerusalem." The Masoretic scholars put the Qal MASCULINE SINGULAR IMPERATIVES in the margin (Qere). These reflect different Hebrew manuscripts which they consulted.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "from the north" This refers to the imminent invasion by Neo-Babylon. The north was an idiom of evil (cf. Jer. 1:13-15; 4:6; 6:1,22) because it was the invasion route for the empires (both Assyria, Neo-Babylon) of the Tigris-Euphrates River Valley into the land of Palestine.

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:20-27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:20-27 This is the final strophe of chapter 13. Remember, try to identify the main truth of each strophe and let this guide your interpretation of the details.

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:21 "Former companions to be head over you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:21 "Former companions to be head over you" The Hebrew of lines 1-3 is uncertain. This seems to refer to Judah's foreign alliance (cf. Jer. 2:18). The term "companion" is literally the Hebrew "chieftain" (BDB 910). Israel/Judah had many allies but now they have become their masters!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAD

▣  "Will not pangs take hold of you,

 Like a woman in childbirth" Labor pains are often used in the Bible as imagery for judgment (cf. Jer. 4:31; 6:24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIRTH PAINS

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:22 The Judeans were questioning the bad things (invasion and exile) which were about to happen to them, and wondering why! They were God's people! They had the Patriarchal promises; they had the Promised Land; they had the prophets; they had the temple (cf. Rom. 9:4-5). Their judgment became a reality because of

  1. continuing idolatry
  2. unwillingness to listen to God's word or prophet
  3. unwillingness to repent caused the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28 to become a reality

▣ "Your skirts have been removed" This is imagery in the OT for a violent sexual assault (cf. Lev. 18:6-19; 20:17; Deut. 22:30; 27:20; Isa. 47:3; Hosea 2:3,10). Her lovers (i.e. foreign alliances, cf. Jer. 2:17-19) had now become her rapists (TEV).

▣ "And your heels have been exposed" This is a cultural imagery for the act of public exposure, which was considered to be a great shame (cf. Jer. 13:26; Lam. 1:8; Isa. 47:2,3). Sometimes the feet, and here the heels, were used as a euphemism for the human genitalia (cf. Deut. 28:57; Jdg. 3:24; 1 Sam. 24:6; Isa. 6:2).

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 13:23 There are two questions in this proverbial statement which obviously expect "no" answers. This reflects the idea that the Judeans could not change, although God calls to them (cf. NRSV, REB), for they are morally unable to respond. This may be an incipient clue to the need for a new covenant which is based not on the performance of fallen mankind, but on the grace of God (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36; Galatians 3 and the book of Hebrews).

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:24 Invasion and exile are coming, but it is YHWH who initiates and allows it (cf. Jer. 9:16; Lev. 26:33; Deut. 28:64). Notice Jer. 13:25, line 2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:25 "This is your lot, the portion measured to you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:25 "This is your lot, the portion measured to you" Originally Abraham's descendants were considered the "portion of the Lord," but now because of their rebellion, they had become the portion of foreigners (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28).

There has been some question about the word "measure."

  1. MT ‒ "measured out," מדד, BDB 551, MASCULINE NOUN
  2. LXX, REB ‒ "as a rebel," מרד, BDB 597, MASCULINE NOUN

This involves the "r" and "d" confusion in Hebrew transcription. The UBS Text Project, p. 217, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ Two reasons are given why YHWH took His protection from them and energized the invading army.

  1. They forgot YHWH (BDB 1013, KB 1489, Qal PERFECT, cf. Jer. 2:32; 3:21).
  2. They continued to trust in falsehood (BDB 1055, i.e. Ba'al worship and other idols, cf. Jer. 3:23; 5:31; 10:14; 16:19; BDB 105, KB 120, Qal IMPERFECT with waw).

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:26 "So I Myself have also stripped your skirts off over your
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:26 "So I Myself have also stripped your skirts off over your

 face,

 That your shame may be seen" This was the public punishment of a harlot or faithless wife (cf. Hosea 2:3,10; Isa. 47:2,3). The New English Bible translates Jer. 13:22 with the very same imagery.

entries.title: Jeremiah 13:27 "As for your adulteries and your lustful neighings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
13:27 "As for your adulteries and your lustful neighings" This last term means "rutting noises" (BDB 843, cf. Jer. 8;16). The people of God are described in their fertility worship (cf. Jer. 2:20) as mating animals (cf. Jer. 2:24; 14:6).

▣ "On the hills in the field" We learn of the magnitude and grossness of the covenant people's sex sins as they worship Ba'al from Hosea 4:13,14.

▣
NASB, NKJV  "Will you still not be made clean"
NRSV  "How long will it be before you are made
  clean?"
TEV  "When will you ever be pure?"
NJB  "How much longer till you are made clean?"
REB  "How long will you delay?"
JPSOA  "How much longer shall it be?"
LXX  "How long will it yet be?"
Peshitta  "How long will it be until you repent?"

The VERB (BDB 372, KB 369, Qal IMPERFECT) can be used of

  1. freed from leprosy (cf. 2 Kings 5)
  2. ceremonially clean (cf. Leviticus)
  3. freed from idolatry (cf. here and Ezek. 24:13[twice]; 36:25)

This last line is confusing in Hebrew. The LXX translates it as "Because you were not cleaned after me, how long it yet be?"

The very last phrase can be viewed in two ways.

  1. a literary way of asserting it will not happen (if there will be no cleansing)
  2. an attempt to show there is still hope for repentance (but this seems to violate Jer. 13:23)

The problem is the brevity of the MT

  1. a PREPOSITION ‒ BDB 29
  2. an INTERROGATIVE ‒ BDB 607
  3. an ADVERB ‒ BDB 728

The main VERB "be clean" (BDB 372, KB 365, Qal IMPERFECT) is negated. The problem was Jerusalem would not repent. YHWH asks "how long" (i.e. how much judgment) would it take for HIs people to turn to Him?

entries.title: Jeremiah 14:1 "That which came as the word of the Lord to Jeremiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
14:1 "That which came as the word of the Lord to Jeremiah" This is a rather unusual phrase found in Jer. 46:1; 47:1; 49:34. It is an assertion of revelation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "drought" This is literally "droughts" (BDB 131, cf. NKJV, JPSOA). We learn from Lev. 26:19-20; Deut. 11:17; 28:23-24 (the opposite of Jer. 28:12) that drought was one of the covenant curses if the people of God did not fulfill their obligations. Throughout the OT drought is used as a way to force the people of God to depend on Him. The problem here was they thought Ba'al worship was insuring the rains (cf. Jer. 5:24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS
