READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:2 The potter is imagery for YHWH (cf. Isa. 29:16; 30:14; 41:25; 64:8; Zech. 11:13; Rom. 9:21; Rev. 2:27). The VERBAL "formed" (BDB 427, KB 428, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) is often used of YHWH's creative activity (cf. Gen. 2:7,8,19; Isa. 43:1,21; 44:21; 45:9,11,18). YHWH's covenant people were part of a larger purpose (see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN), but their covenant disobedience caused that plan to be damaged (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36). Therefore, the potter starts over again to make a new piece on the wheel (cf. Jer. 18:4). The theological question is "who/what" is the new piece (i.e. restored Judah or all mankind)?

I have come to believe that the events of A.D. 70 (i.e. the Jewish war with Rome, culminating in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple) ended the Mosaic covenant. The church has become the new people of God. This title is no longer national, but "whosoever will" believe in Jesus as the promised Messiah.

I hope if this paragraph shocks you that you will look at my revised verse-by-verse commentary (www.freebiblecommentary.org) on

  1. the Olivet Discourse of Jesus (Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21)
  2. the "man of lawlessness" passage in 2 Thess. 2
  3. my new (2024) exegetical commentary on the book of Revelation
18:3
NASB, Peshitta  "on the wheel"
NKJV  "at the wheel"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, JPSOA, NET  "at his wheel"
LXX  "on the stones"

The MT has

  1. a PREPOSITION
  2. the DEFINITE ARTICLE
  3. dual NOUN "stones" (BDB 6)

This literal translation is followed by the LXX. Potters used two stones

  1. one on which to put the lump of clay
  2. another to turn with the foot

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:4 The problem was defective clay not a poorly skilled potter! The clay was/is fallen (cf. Genesis 3), even with all of YHWH's benefits (cf. Rom. 9:4-5).

The JPSOA translation adds "if," which denotes that not all vessels were "spoiled." But the context suggests YHWH is depicting Judah as a corporate entity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:7 The actions of YHWH are the very actions given to Jeremiah at his call (cf. Jer. 1:10). YHWH exercises interest and control over all nations (cf. LXX, Deut.32:8; all the judgment chapters are addressed to them in the prophets).

  1. to uproot ‒ BDB 684, KB 737, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  2. to pull down ‒ BDB 683, KB 736, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  3. to destroy ‒ BDB 1, KB 2, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

The actions of renewal and rebuilding mentioned in Jer. 1:10 (also note Jer. 31:28) are conditionally stated in Jer. 18:8-9. Faith and faithfulness have consequences, as do idolatry and disobedience (cf. Jer. 18:10). For a good brief discussion of God changing His mind, see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 209-210, 333-334.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT), III.

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:8,10 "if. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:8,10 "if. . ." There are some unconditional promises based on YHWH's desire to redeem mankind. However, they are addressed to nations and individuals on conditional bases (i.e. Jer. 7:3-7; 12:16). This is where the doctrine of "God's Sovereignty" and "Human Freewill" meet!

SPECIAL TOPIC: Predestination (Calvinism) Versus Human Free Will (Arminianism)

SPECIAL TOPIC: Election/Predestination and the Need for a Theological Balance

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:8 "I will relent"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:8 "I will relent" This is the VERB "be sorry" (BDB 636, KB 688, Niphal PERFECT with waw), often translated "repent." It is difficult to speak of YHWH as "repenting." This is obviously anthropomorphic language (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE). YHWH is willing to change (His actions, but not His character, cf. Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29; see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 209-210) based on:

  1. a person's/nation's change of attitude and actions
  2. intercessory prayer

There are several places where this VERB is used of YHWH (cf. Gen. 6:6-7; Exod. 32:14; 1 Sam. 15:11; 2 Sam. 24:16; Ps. 106;45; Jer. 18:7,8; 26:13,19; Amos 7:3,6; Jonah 3:9-4:2,11). However, the opposite is also stated in Scripture (cf. Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29; Ps. 132:11; Jer. 4:28; Ezek. 24:14; Mal. 3:6; James 1:17). YHWH chooses grace over judgment, if humans will only respond in faith and faithfulness. Prophecy (except Messianic) is conditional.

Three good references I trust on this issue are:

  1. F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 129-130
  2. Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 70-75
  3. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, pp. 44-47

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:11 YHWH, like the potter, made and destroyed a piece of defective pottery. The VERBAL (BDB 427, KB 428, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) translated "fashioning" is the same Qal PARTICIPLE translated "potter" (vv. 2, 3, 4 [twice], 6 [twice], 11). It is also used of God's activity

  1. in forming Adam (cf. Gen. 2:7,8)
  2. in forming Jeremiah (Jer. 1:5)
  3. in forming a nation from Abraham's seed (cf. Isa. 27:11; 43:1,21; 44:21; 45:9,11; 64:8).

▣ "I am fashioning calamity against you and devising a plan against you" The OT asserts the full sovereignty of YHWH. His control of "all" events (i.e. one causality in the universe) was a theological way of asserting monotheism. This "one causality" can be seen in 2 Chr. 20:6; Eccl. 7:14; Isa. 14:24-27; 43:13; 45:7; 54:16; Jer. 18:11; Lam. 3:33-38). For a good brief discussion of this see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 305-306. This, in no way, is meant to assert that YHWH is the source of evil!
SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY
SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

The same VERB (BDB 427, KB 426, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) is used of a potter fashioning clay in Isa. 29:16; 41:25; Jer. 18:4 [twice], 6 [twice]). It is used in the famous passage of YHWH's initial creation of human beings in Gen. 2:7,8 and of Jeremiah in the womb in Jer. 1:5.

Here, it refers to YHWH forming, fashioning Israel (cf. Isa. 27:11; 43:1,21; 44:21; 45:9 [twice], 11; 64:7) for His larger purposes of the redemption of all mankind, but they failed!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ There are two IMPERATIVES which describe YHWH's message to Judah.

  1. "turn back" ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERATIVE, see SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)
  2. "reform" (lit. "make good") ‒ BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

Notice that true repentance is not only a turning from evil, but a turning to good! Eternal life has observable characteristics.

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 18:12 This is YHWH's understanding of the unrepentant heart of Judah (cf. Jer. 2:25; 17:1). They will not, they cannot change (cf. Jer. 13:23). They have passed the time of repentance. They continue to walk in open-eyed rebellion (cf. Jer. 7:24; 9:13; 13:10; 16:12)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:13 "The virgin of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:13 "The virgin of Israel" The virgin wife of Israel was a faithless, adulterous wife! See full note at Jer. 46:11.

▣ "a most appalling thing" This phrase is used of a nation changing gods. The word "appalling" (BDB 1045 III, KB 1619 III) has several forms.

  1. שׁערור = horrible things, cf. Jer. 5:30; 23:14
  2. שׁערורי = something horrible, cf. Jer. 18:13; Hosea 6:10
  3. שׁער = rotten figs, cf. Jer. 29:17

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:13-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:13-17 This strophe describes the horrible and unique situation of a nation changing her god/gods (cf. Jer. 2:9-13). YHWH formed/created them but now they have "forgotten" (BDB 1013, KB 1489, Qal PERFECT, cf. Jer. 2:32; 3:21; 13:25) Him, the only true God, the One who brought them into existence, protected them, provided for them, was personally present with them (i.e. Israel as YHWH's wife imagery)!

How could this happen?

  1. They burned incense to worthless gods.
  2. They stumbled from God's clearly revealed way (i.e. ancient paths, cf. Jer. 6:16; Ps. 16:11; 139:24; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY).
  3. They walked in bypaths that were not YHWH's path.

What are the consequences of their choices/actions?

  1. The land of promise will be a desolation (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 28).
  2. It will be a sign of shame and scorn (lit. "shake the head," cf. Jer. 48:27).
  3. They will be scattered (cf. Lev. 26:33; Jer. 9:16; 13:24; 31:10).
  4. YHWH will show them His back and not His face (this is a revocalization of the MT; see JPSOA footnote).

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:14 This verse (a parenthetical statement) is difficult to translate. It obviously describes that which normally or expectedly occurs. Here apparently, the snow stays on Mt. Hermon and its melted waters continually flow down. Nature can be predicted with regularity, but not the seed of Abraham (i.e. Jer. 2:11-13; 8:7; Isa. 1:3)!

▣
NASB  "of the open country"
NKJV  "of the field"
NRSV  "the crags of Sirion"
TEV, REB  "Lebanon's rocky heights"
NJB  "the rocks of its slopes"
JPSOA  "from the mountainous rocks"
Peshitta  "from the mountain"

The MT has "the crags of the field" (BDB 849 CONSTRUCT BDB 961). The word "field" has been interpreted as

  1. field ‒ שׂדי (MT)
  2. Sirion ‒ שׁריון
  3. torrent ‒ שׁדו
  4. Shaddai ‒ שׁדו

The UBS Text Project, p. 234, gives option #4 a "C" rating. It speculates that Shaddai may have been the name of one of the peaks of the Antilebanon mountain range.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:15 "My people have forgotten Me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:15 "My people have forgotten Me" This phrase has several implications.

  1. Israel/Judah have violated their marriage vows with YHWH (i.e. spiritual adultery)
  2. Israel/Judah have violated YHWH's revelation/law (i.e. covenant disobedience)

This is recurrent and powerful imagery of a broken relationship (cf. Deut. 6:12; 8:11; Ps. 106:21; Isa. 17:10; 51:13; Jer. 2:32; 3:21; 13:25; Hosea 2:13; 4:6; 8:14; 13:6). The two exiles (i.e. Assyria and Neo-Babylon) and the foretold destruction of Jerusalem again (cf. Dan. 9:24-27, which became a reality in A.D. 66-70, cf. Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21; 2 Thess. 2; the book of Revelation).

It must be restated again and again that humans were created in God's image and likeness for fellowship, not for dependance on self actualization. We need a vital, intimate, personal faith relationship with our Creator.

▣ "worthless gods" See SPECIAL TOPIC: EMPTY, VAIN, FALSE, NOTHINGNESS

▣ "Not on a highway" Jer. 18:15 resumes the theme of apostasy from Jer. 18:13. The image of a special highway is recurrent in Isaiah (i.e. a way to easity and quickly come to YHWH).

  1. a highway for the exiled Jews to return, Isa. 11:16; 57:14
  2. a highway for Gentile worshipers to come, Isa. 19:23
  3. a highway of holiness, Isa. 26:7; 35:8; 43:19; 49:11; 51:10
  4. a Messianic highway, Isa. 40:3; 42:16

It is possible that this imagery refers to lifestyle faith (i.e. Ps. 1:1-6; Jer. 6:16; 12:16; 31:21). The ancient path is a way of referring to daily covenant obedience. Biblical faith is

  1. a Person to know (i.e. "Me")
  2. truths about that Person's will to believe (i.e. inspired revelation)
  3. a lifestyle of faithfulness to that revelation (#2)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:16-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:16-17 This is exactly opposite of what YHWH wanted to do for His covenant people who He settled in His land. They were to be a light to the nations, but they became an object of scorn (i.e. "perpetual hissing") and astonishment (cf. 2 Chr. 29:8; Jer. 19:8; 25:9,18; 29:18; Lam. 2:15-16; Ezek. 27:36; 36:22-23; Micah 6:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:17 "the east wind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:17 "the east wind" This wind (BDB 924 CONSTRUCT BDB 870) is imagery for the seasonal winds that affect Palestine. The east wind (Arabic sirocco) is a hot, strong desert wind that causes destruction (i.e. Gen. 41:6,23,27; Job 38:24; Ps. 48:7; Isa. 27:8; Hosea 12:2; 13:15; Jonah 4:8).

▣ "I will show them My back and not My face" The MT has "My back and not My face I will show them." This is an idiom for rejection and broken fellowship. It is opposite of the Aaronic blessing of Num. 6:22-26.

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:18 This verse is an introductory strophe to the poem of Jer. 18:19-23. Jeremiah's enemies plan their attack (cf. Jer. 20:10).

  1. come ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. let us devise plans ‒ BDB 362, KB 359, Qal COHORTATIVE
  3. come ‒ same as #1
  4. let us strike at him with our tongue ‒ BDB 645, KB 697, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense
  5. let us give no heed to any of his words ‒ BDB 904, KB 1151, Hiphil COHORTATIVE
    1. stop listening, MT, Peshitta, JPSOA, NRSV
    2. listen and try to find faults, LXX, JB

This is the only verse in the OT where all three means or genres of YHWH's revelation are mentioned together.

  1. the priest ‒ the Law (question about how to apply the law)
  2. the sage ‒ counsel (i.e. Wisdom Literature)
  3. the prophet ‒ the divine word

These are mentioned to assert their belief that Jeremiah's messages are not from YHWH. He is a false prophet (cf. Deut. 13:1-5) and should be killed! Because these false leaders have done this to Jeremiah, YHWH will remove all of His revelation from Judah!

The three groups of leaders are mentioned several times in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 2:8,26; 4:9; 5:31; 8:1; 13:13; 26:16; 28:1).

  1. kings, princes
  2. priests
  3. prophets

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:19-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:19-23 Jeremiah answers their plans with a prayer to YHWH (another of his laments/confessions). It starts out with the same VERB that ends Jer. 18:18 ("heed"). Notice his requests (hyperbolic, prophetic IMPERATIVES, see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, pp. 41-43,46-47,56,99-102,158-160,196-199).

  1. Do give heed to me ‒ BDB 904, KB 1151, Hiphil IMPERATIVE. His enemies will not heed/hear, but YHWH will!
  2. Listen to what my opponents are saying ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE
    1. MT ‒ listen to opponents
    2. LXX ‒ listen to me
  3. Remember how I stood before You for them ‒ BDB 269, KB 269, Qal IMPERATIVE
    1. to speak good on their behalf (i.e. Jer. 14:13-16)
    2. to turn away Your wrath from them (cf. Jer. 15:1)
  4. Therefore, YHWH, respond to them.
    1. give over their children to famine ‒ BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERATIVE
    2. deliver them to the power of the sword ‒ BDB 620, KB 669, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    3. let their wives become childless ‒ BDB 224, KB 243, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    4. let their wives become widows ‒ same as c
    5. let their men also be smitten to death ("by pestilence," BDB 560) ‒ BDB 246, KB 255, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE
    6. let their young men be struck down by the sword ‒ BDB 645, KB 697, Hophal PARTICIPLE
    7. let an outcry be heard from their homes ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Niphal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense. For the NOUN "cry out," see Jer. 20:16; 48:4,34; 50:46; 51:54; Isa. 15:5
    8. do not forgive their iniquity ‒ BDB 497, KB 493, Piel IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    9. Do not blot out their sin from Your sight ‒ BDB 562 I, KB 567, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    10. may they be overthrown before You ‒ BDB 224, KB 243, Qere, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    11. deal with them in the time of Your anger ‒ BDB 793 I, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:20 "Should good be repaid with evil"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:20 "Should good be repaid with evil" Apparently this refers to Jeremiah's prayers ("I stood before You") for Judah (cf. Jer. 17:16), but they responded by trying to kill him.

▣ "they have dug a pit for me" This is an allusion to a hunting technique (cf. Ps. 57:6; 119:85). It may be literal (i.e. they will try to kill him) or figurative (they will try to ruin his reputation, cf. Jer. 18:22, i.e. his prophecies have not occurred, cf. Deut. 13:1-5).

▣ "how I stood before You" The physical position of Jewish prayer was

  1. standing
  2. eyes open
  3. head up
  4. hands outstretched and raised

This implies that prayer is a dialogue with God.

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:21-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:21-22 Jeremiah tried to present YHWH's word to the people of Judah, but they rejected and ignored this revelation. His own family (tribe) even attacked him. Jeremiah's prayers "for" Judah changed to his prayers "against" Judah. This mimicked YHWH's thoughts.

In many ways these calls for judgment reflect the "imprecatory Psalms" (i.e. parts of Psalms 5; 6; 10; 12; 35; 37; 40; 52; 54-59; 69; 70; 79; 83; 94; 109; 129; 137; 139; 140; 143).

These Psalms, as well as the prophetic parallels, are an attempt to arrest people's attention to the "justice" of God. There is a judgment coming for unrepentant, unbelieving, unfaithful humans. These passages are designed to shock and redirect wayward humans.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUSTICE

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT, JUSTICE IN ISAIAH

entries.title: Jeremiah 18:23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
18:23 Is Jeremiah being vindictive? He seems to want justice for Judah's repeated covenant violations. His own circumstances bothered him but Judah's sin bothered him more! There will be justice. There will be a day when humans give an account to God for the gift of life (i.e. Matt. 25:31-46; Rev. 20:11-15). It will be an especially bad day for covenant, informed people (cf. Luke 12:48)!

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:1 Jeremiah 18 and 19 are connected by the use of imagery, "potter" and "pottery jar" (BDB 132 CONSTRUCT BDB 427, i.e. a small drinking flask).

The "pottery jar" would have been a fired clay vessel between 4" and 10" with a narrow neck used for liquids. This type of container was very common in the ANE.

▣
NASB, REB  "earthenware jar"
NKJV  "earthen flask"
NRSV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta  "earthenware jug"
TEV  "clay jar"
JPSOA  "a jug of potter's ware"

The MT has "a flask" (BDB 132) formed (BDB 427, KB 428, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE). This clay object was used for drinking a liquid. Its name is onomatopoeic, from the gurgling sound of drinking (i.e. בקבק, BDB 132). The Arabian cognate is "gurgling sound."

▣ "the elders of the people and some of the senior priests" "Elders" was the title of older, respected, established leadership. It was a carryover from the "tribal days" of Israel's past (cf. Exod. 3:16,18; 4:29; 12:21, etc.).

These two groups would represent the civic and religious leadership of Judah/Jerusalem. This requirement of two witnesses reflects Num. 35:30; Deut. 17:6; 19:15.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELDER

SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVITICAL PRIESTS

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:2 "the valley of Ben-hinnom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:2  "the valley of Ben-hinnom" The following information on Gehenna is taken from the SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEAD, WHERE ARE THEY? , II. D. Gehenna reflects the OT phrase, "the valley of the sons of Hinnom" (south of Jerusalem). It was the place where the Phoenician fire god, Molech (BDB 574) was worshiped by child sacrifice (cf. 2 Kgs. 16:3; 21:6; 2 Chr. 28:3; 33:6), which was forbidden in Lev. 18:21; 20:2-5.

Jeremiah changed it from a place of pagan worship into a site of YHWH's judgment (cf. Jer. 7:32; 19:6-7).  It became the place of fiery, eternal judgment in I Enoch 90:26-27 and Sib. 1:103.

The Jews of Jesus' day were so appalled by their ancesators' participation in pagan worship by child sacrifice that they turned this area into the garbage dump for Jerusalem. Many of Jesus' metaphors for eternal judgment came from this landfill (fire, smoke, worms, stench, cf. Mark 9:44,46). The term Gehenna is used only by Jesus (except in James 3:6).

  1. Jesus' use of Gehenna
    1. fire, Matt. 5:22; 18:9; Mark 9:43
    2. permanent, Mark 9:48 (Matt. 25:46)
    3. place of destruction (both body and soul), Matt. 10:28
    4. paralleled to Sheol, Matt. 5:29-30; 18:9
    5. characterizes the wicked as "son of hell," Matt. 23:15
    6. result of judicial sentence, Matt. 23:33; Luke 12:5
    7. the concept of Gehenna is parallel to the second death (cf. Rev. 2:11; 20:6,14) or the lake of fire (cf. Matt. 13:42,50; Rev. 19:20; 20:10,14-15; 21:8). It is possible the lake of fire becomes the permanent dwelling place of humans (from Sheol) and evil angels (Tartarus, 2 Pet. 2:4; Jude Jer. 19:6, or the abyss, cf. Luke 8:31; Rev. 9:1-11; 20:1,3).
    8. it was not designed for humans, but for Satan and his angels, Matt. 25:41
  2. It is possible, because of the overlap of Sheol, Hades, and Gehenna, that
    1. origiinally all humans went to Sheol/Hades
    2. their experience there (good/bad) is exacerbated after Judgment Day, but the place of the wicked remains the same (this is why the KJV translated hades (grave) as gehenna (hell)
    3. the only NT text to mention torment before Judgment is the parable of Luke 16:19-31 (Lazarus and the Rich Man). Sheol is also described as a place of punishment now (cf. Deut. 32:22). However, one cannot establish a doctrine on a parable.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH

▣
NASB  "the potsherd gate"
NKJV, NJB  "the Potsherd Gate"
JPSOA  "Harsith Gate"
LXX  "the gate Charsith"
Peshitta, KJV  "the east gate"

A gate of Jerusalem by this name is found only here in the OT. Here are the suggestions.

  1. Dung (refuse) Gate of Neh. 2:13; 3:13-14; 12:31 (Jerusalem Targum). This would be the place for garbage to be dumped.
  2. Gate on the south side of Jerusalem, which led to the Hinnom Valley, would be close to the potters' workshops.
  3. The Peshitta gets "east" from the similarity of the Hebrew name with the Greek heres for sun. This is surely inaccurate. The NKJV changes it to "Potsherd Gate."

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:3 "Hear the word of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:3 "Hear the word of the Lord" This is the VERB "hear" or "listen" (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE. It meant "to hear so as to obey."

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

▣ "the Lord. . .the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel" Notice that these are covenant titles and are repeated several times in the chapter. The covenant people are being confronted by the God of the covenant. They have totally failed as YHWH's revelation to "the nations" (cf., Jer. 19:15; Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣
NASB  "a calamity"
NKJV  "a catastrophe"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, JPSOA  "a disaster"
LXX, Peshitta  "evil"

The root (רעה) has several distinct meanings.

  1. pasture, project, or shepherd ‒ BDB 944 I, KB 1258 I, 27 times in Jeremiah
  2. be associated with (i.e. friend or companion) ‒ BDB 945 II, KB 1262 II, used 21 times in Jeremiah
  3. pleasure or desire ‒ BDB 946 III
  4. that which is harmful (from רע, BDB 948, used 32 times in Jeremiah) ‒ BDB 949, KB 1262, used 92 times in Jeremiah. The word is translated by NIV in several different ways.
    1. disaster
    2. wickedness
    3. trouble
    4. evil
    5. punishment
    6. harm
    7. sin
    8. calamity
    9. offense
    10. ruin
    11. crimes
    12. evil deeds
    13. discomfort
    14. destruction
    15. cruelty

▣ "the ears of everyone that hears it will tingle" This is a Hebrew idiom of a surprising judgment (cf. 1 Sam. 3:11; 2 Kgs. 21:12). This is similar to the "lips quivering" in Hab. 3:16.

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:4-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:4-5 The calamity is coming on Judah because

  1. they have forsaken YHWH (cf. Jer. 1:16; 2:13,17,19; 5:7,19; 16:11; 17:13; Deut. 28:20; 31:16; see full note at Jer. 18:15)
  2. they worship foreign gods (cf. Deut. 11:28) in the valley of Ben-hinnom
  3. they have either
    1. sacrificed their children to Molech (Jer. 19:4,5; 2 Kgs. 17:17; Ps106:37)
    2. killed innocent people, cf. Jer. 2:34; 7:6; 12:3,17; 26:15; Ps. 106:38, cf. TEV
  4. they built high places to Ba'al (cf. Jer. 7:9; 11:13,17)
19:4
NASB, NKJV  "an alien place"
TEV, NET  "defiled this place"
NJB  "made this place unrecognizable"
REB  "because of alien worship"
JPSOA  "have made this place alien [to Me]"
Peshitta  "have polluted this place"
LXX, NRSV  "profaned this place"

The MT has "have profaned this place" (BDB 649, KB 699, Piel IMPERFECT with waw). It denoted that which was unclean and polluted by contact with foreign nations and their pagan worship. Judah had committed "spiritual apostasy" with pagan idolatry. This resulted in the shedding of innocent blood.

YHWH's land, and especially His city and temple, had become tainted and impure. It no longer could be used as a place of worship to YHWH.

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:5 "a thing which I never commanded or spoke of nor did it ever enter My mind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:5 "a thing which I never commanded or spoke of nor did it ever enter My mind" This reflects YHWH's thoughts about human sacrifice. It is possible some misunderstood Gen. 22:2 or Exod. 13:2 and used it as a "proof-text" for the child sacrifices to

  1. Molech (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH)
  2. Ba'al (SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE)

Even the death of Job's family (cf. Job 1) could be seen by some as instigated by YHWH to test Job.

The one thing that must be added to this issue is that YHWH will sacrifice His only, unique "Son" (symbolized in Abraham's offering Isaac, cf. Gen. 22:9-19) for the good of the whole (cf. John 3:16; 2 Cor. 5:21). Jesus' death was a human/divine death/gift for human sin (i.e. child sacrifice)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:6-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:6-9 YHWH describes the judgments He will send on them for their wickedness.

  1. the name of the valley of Ben-hinnom will be changed to the valley of Slaughter
  2. the counsel of their wise men will be voided (cf. Jer. 8:8-9)
  3. many will be killed by invasion
  4. there will be no proper burial, cf. Jer. 7:33; 16:4
  5. Jerusalem will be turned into an object of hissing, cf. Jer. 15:4; 18:16
  6. cannibalism will develop (i.e. siege warfare), cf. Lev. 26:29; Deut. 28:53,55,57; Lam. 4:10

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:7 "I shall make void"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:7 "I shall make void" This VERB (בקק, BDB 132 II, KB 150, Qal PERFECT with waw), BDB says it is used "of a mug dipped in water, or emptied of water." Therefore, this is an intentional play on the word for "drinking flask" (בקבק, BDB 132) in Jer. 19:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORROR, REPROACH, RUIN, CURSE

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:10 In chapter 18 the potter remade a lump of clay, but here, after firing, the clay could not be saved, only destroyed! There was no hope of repentance on Judah's part or YHWH's part (cf. Jer. 18:8). Invasion, destruction, slaughter, and exile are coming!

Jeremiah's breaking the clay water flask to symbolize the destruction of Jerusalem is theologically parallel to Ezekiel making a brick to symbolize Jerusalem and then hitting it with a cooking pan (cf. Ezekiel 4).

The image of a broken clay pot as a symbol of judgment and destruction is common in the ANE (i.e. Sumer and Egypt).

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:13 "on whose rooftops they burned sacrifices to all the heavenly host"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:13 "on whose rooftops they burned sacrifices to all the heavenly host" The worship of the lights of the sky was common in the ANE (cf. Deut. 4:19; 17:3; Jer. 8:2; 32:29; 2 Kgs. 17:16; 21:3,5; 23:5,12; 2 Chr. 33:3,5; Zeph. 1:5).

  1. Egypt
  2. Mesopotamia

It was YHWH who created, named, and controlled these objects (cf. Gen. 1:14-19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOON WORSHIP

▣ "to all the heavenly host" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "pour out libations to other gods" This was part of the worship of "the queen of heaven" (cf. Jer. 7:18; 44:18).

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:14 "Topheth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:14 "Topheth" The word (BDB 1075 II) means "fire-place" (possibly from an Aramaic root), which denotes a valley south of Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley. Josiah turned it into a landfill where garbage was burned (see SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, II. D. for Gehenna). It was a place where

  1. the god Molech (cf. Lev. 18:21; see SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH) was worshiped by child sacrifice, cf. Jer. 7:31; 2 Kgs. 23:10 (note Isa. 30:33)
  2. it is imagery for the slaughter of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, cf. Jer. 7:32; 19:6
  3. it is a burial place of the dead of Jerusalem, cf. Jer. 19:11-12

▣ "the court of the Lord's house" The temple of Jeremiah's day was Solomon's temple. It had several outer courts where the people of Israel could gather. Jeremiah is said to proclaim YHWH's message there several times (cf. Jer. 7:2; 26:2).

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:14-15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 19:14-15 Since these two verses are in the third person, possibly they are Baruch's (Jeremiah's scribe) later editorial comments.

entries.title: Jeremiah 19:15 "stiffened their necks so as not to heed My words"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
19:15 "stiffened their necks so as not to heed My words" The covenant people refused to hear and respond to the covenant God (cf. Jer. 7:26; 17:23; Neh. 9:17). They were His people in name only!

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:1 "Pashhur"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:1 "Pashhur" There are several people in the OT with this name (BDB 832).

  1. In this text he was a priest whose task was to maintain order in the temple (cf. Jer. 29:26).
  2. Another was a priest in Jeremiah's day, but with a different father, Jer. 21:1; 38:1; Neh. 11:12.
  3. Another person in Jer. 38:1 (two Pashhurs in this verse).
  4. Head of a post-exilic family in Ezra 2:38; 10:22; Neh. 7:41; 10:3; 11:12.

KB 980 quotes two authors who speculate that Pashhur is an Egyptian name (cf. Jewish Study Bible, p. 966, marginal note), "Portion of Horus." If so, this is a strange name for a priest of YHWH (possibly part of a pro-Egyptian faction). Most scholars simply say the meaning is unknown.

Jeremiah renames him "Magor‒missabib" (i.e. "terror on every side," cf. Jer. 20:3-6).

▣
NASB, NRSV, TEV, REB, JPSOA  "chief officer"
NKJV  "chief governor"
NJB  "the chief of police"
NET  "chief of security"
LXX  "chief"
Peshitta  "governor in charge"

This position (BDB 824, KB 960) is basically someone put in charge of a specific task.

  1. in the temple
    1. the high priest ‒ 2 Chr. 31:10,13
    2. a helper of the high priest ‒ 2 Chr. 24:11
    3. singers/musicians ‒ Neh. 12:42
    4. policing the temple ‒ Jer. 20:1; 29:26
  2. in the civil government
    1. administration ‒ Gen. 41:34; Esther 2:3
    2. governor ‒ Jdgs. 9:28
    3. overseer ‒ Neh. 11:9
  3. military ‒ 2 Kgs. 25:19; Jer. 52:25

▣ "heard Jeremiah prophesying these things" This goes back to Jeremiah 18 or 19, or both.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:2 Although YHWH promised to protect Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 1:18-19), it did not mean he would not emotionally and physically suffer! This is helpful insight to NT believers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SUFFER?

SPECIAL TOPIC: A SUFFERING MESSIAH

▣ "Jeremiah the prophet" There are several terms used to describe those called to give YHWH's revelation. The term here is Nabi (BDB 611, KB 661). For a full list of the descriptive terms, see Special Topic below.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT), I. B. #3

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

▣ "beaten" The VERB (BDB 645, KB 697) is a Hiphil IMPERFECT with waw, probably in the fashion of Deut. 25:2-3. Jeremiah would have been labeled "a wicked man" (i.e. false prophet, cf. Deut. 13:1-5).

▣ "stocks" This word (BDB 246) refers to wooden bars with holes in them for the hands, feet, and neck. These holes were spread widely apart to increase pain and discomfort. The pain was both physical and mental! In 2 Chr. 16:10 a false prophet was put in them (or it). Jeremiah was being treated as a "false prophet." This is what bothered him so badly!

The JPSOA translates this word as "cell" and sees it as a small room of confinement. The LXX also has "dungeon," but "stocks" in a footnote.

▣ "at the upper Benjamin Gate" I like the NET Bible's explanation, p. 1345, #16, "A comparison of Ezek. 8:3 and 9:2 in their contexts will show that this probably refers to the northern gate to the inner court of the temple. It is called Upper because it was on higher ground above the gate in the outer court. It is qualified by 'in the Lord's temple' to distinguish it from the Benjamin Gate in the city wall (cf. 37:13; 38:7). Like the Benjamin Gate in the city wall, it faced north toward the territory of the tribe of Benjamin."

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:4 "to the hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 20:4 "to the hand" This is imagery for "power." See SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND.

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:4-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:4-6 These verses describe the terror (BDB 159 II).

  1. his friends will die by the invaders' (i.e. Neo-Babylon), sword, while you watch
  2. Judah's remaining population will be exiled to Babylon
  3. all the wealth of Jerusalem (including the temple) will be carried to Babylon
  4. Pashhur and his family and friends will be exiled and will die in Babylon

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:6 "you have falsely prophesied"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:6 "you have falsely prophesied" Exactly how this priestly temple official "prophesied" (BDB 612, KB 659, Niphal PERFECT) is uncertain. But he, not Jeremiah, would bear the curse of Deut. 13:1-5 for it! The false prophecy was related to the stability of the temple and Jerusalem (possibly quoting Isaiah's message to Hezekiah, i.e. Isaiah 36-39). It was a message of hope and faith, but at this point in time, it was not YHWH's message (cf. Jer. 14:14-16)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:7-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:7-13 This is another complaint/lament. Even those called by God experience doubt and fear! Jeremiah feels that YHWH has

  1. deceived him ‒ BDB 834, KB 984, Piel PERFECT and Niphal IMPERFECT with waw (this is an intensified form of a strong VERB often used of seduction; it refers to his call in chapter 1)
  2. overcome him ‒ BDB 304, KB 302, Qal PERFECT
  3. prevailed against him ‒ BDB 407, KB 410, Qal IMPERFECT with waw

The results of his prophecies of judgment not occurring (cf. Jer. 20:7-8) are that

  1. he has become a laughingstock all day long (cf. Jer. 48:26,39; Lam. 3:14)
  2. everyone mocks him (cf. Lam. 3:14)
  3. he is reproached
  4. he is derided

This would open him up to the charge of not being a true prophet. The punishment for false prophecy wa death (cf. Deut. 13).

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:7 "You have deceived me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:7 "You have deceived me" The theological issue that comes from this phrase is, "Does God deceive or purposely give false information?" Often, texts such as 1 Kgs. 22:20-23; 2 Chr. 18:18-22; Jer. 4:10; and Ezek. 14:9, are given as evidence.

One way to handle this is to assert the total "goodness" and "changelessness" of God (cf. Gen. 1:31; Mal. 3:6; James 1:17; 1 John 1:5). YHWH is good (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [OT]). We must define these aspects of Deity in such a way as to allow

  1. the Bible's not recognizing secondary causes. All actions and events are attributed to YHWH (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY)
  2. the possibility of prophecy being affected by repentance (i.e. Jonah)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)
  3. the reality of intercessory prayer
    SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER
  4. the conditional nature of the Mosaic covenant
    SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT
  5. defining "goodness," see full not at Mal. 3:6
  6. YHWH does harden some people for His greater purposes
    SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD HARDENED
    SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDAS ISCARIOT

For a good brief discussion, see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 230-231.

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:9 Jeremiah tries to express both the pain and joy of being YHWH's spokesperson. Remember this is highly figurative poetry.

  1. he tries to forget YHWH
  2. he tries not to speak His words anymore

But he cannot! They are like a burning fire shut up in his bones. He cannot hold them back. He must speak (cf. Amos 3:8).

Many of us who feel called to preach/teach/share know these thoughts and feelings.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:10 Verse 10 describes the fear he feels as he hears people whispering their curses.

  1. he has described his own situation by the very words YHWH used to rename Pashhur (i.e. "terror on every side!" v. 3)
  2. they denounce him
  3. his friends are watching for him to fall
  4. they hope to prevail against him
  5. they hope to take revenge against him

Since the current canonical structure of Jeremiah is an anthology of his poetic messages, Jer. 20:7-13 are obviously placed here because of the "catch-word" Magor-missabib of Jer. 20:3 and 10 (cf. Jer. 6:25; 46:5; 49:29).

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:11 Verse 11 describes YHWH as "a dreaded champion" (i.e. the divine warrior, BDB 150 and the ADJECTIVE, BDB 792, cf. Jer. 1:8,19; 15:20; Isa. 59:16-20). Notice what happens to those who oppose him.

  1. they will stumble (BDB 505, KB 502, Niphal IMPERFECT)
  2. they will not prevail (BDB 407, KB 410, Qal IMPERFECT, NEGATED)
  3. they will be utterly ashamed (BDB 101, KB 116, Qal PERFECT; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME)
  4. they will not succeed (BDB 968, KB 1328, Hiphil PERFECT, NEGATED)
  5. they will have an everlasting disgrace (BDB 484, CONSTRUCT BDB 761; see SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)
  6. they will not be forgotten in their shame (BDB 1013, KB 1489, Niphal IMPERFECT, NEGATED)

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:12 Jeremiah describes YHWH.

  1. You test the righteous (BDB 103, KB 119, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
  2. You examine the mind (i.e. kidneys; BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE; see SPECIAL TOPIC: INWARD PARTS)
  3. You examine the heart (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART)
  4. You let me see Your vengeance (BDB 906, LB 1157, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense)
  5. You let me present my cause to You (cf. Jer. 11:20; BDB 162, KB 191, Piel PERFECT). This is similar to Job's request.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD TESTS HIS PEOPLE

▣ Number 5 above has a VERB (BDB 162, KB 191, Piel PERFECT) that can connote several things (see same textual issue at Jer. 11:20).

  1. BDB Piel #3, "make known" or "reveal" (גליתי)
  2. NASB ‒ "set forth"
     NKJV ‒ "have pleaded"
     NRSV, REB ‒ "have committed" (גלותי)
     TEV ‒ "have placed"
     NJB, LXX, Peshitta ‒ "have revealed"
     JPSOA ‒ "lay"

The OBJECT of the VERB is a "law case" or a "cause" (rib, BDB 936).

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:13 This verse starts with two IMPERATIVES.

  1. sing to the Lord ‒ BDB 1010, KB 1479, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. praise the Lord ‒ BDB 237, KB 248, Piel IMPERATIVE

This adulation is because YHWH has delivered the soul of the needy one from the hand of evil doers.

What a wild swing of emotions is expressed in these verses. From complete discouragement in YHWH in Jer. 20:7 to joyous praise in Jer. 20:13. This wild swing continues in the next poem (Jer. 20:14-18). Jeremiah was a highly emotional person.

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:14-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:14-18 These verses continue the lament begun in Jer. 15:10. Remember these are hyperbolic poetic images! The questions are "Why is he so sad? Is it

  1. his personal life
  2. the terrible judgment coming to Judah and Jerusalem?"

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:16 The first two lines refer to YHWH's destruction of the cities of the plain in Gen. 19:24-28, which became a proverb for divine judgment (cf. Isa. 1:9,10; 13:19; Jer. 23:14; 49:18; Matt. 10:15; 11:24).

Some suggest that "man" be emendated to "day," but there is no textual or versional evidence.

▣
NASB, JPSOA  "without relenting"
NKJV  "did not relent"
NRSV  "without pity"
TEV, NJB, REB  "without mercy"
Peshitta  "never reconciled towards them"
LXX  "repented not"

The VERB nacham (BDB 636, KB 688, Niphal PERFECT) basically means "to be sorry." It is used in both a positive way (i.e. Ps. 106:45; Amos 7:3,6) or a negative way (i.e. Gen. 6:7; Jer. 4:28; 15:6; Zech. 8:14).

Modern interpreters must be reminded of Eastern Literature's use of

  1. hyperbolic poetry
  2. assigning human motives to YHWH
  3. presenting truths in dialectical pairs

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 20:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
20:18 Obviously, vv. 14-18 are a word play from Jeremiah's call to prophetic office, recorded in Jer. 1:4-10, esp. v. 5.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:1 "Pashhur"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:1 "Pashhur" This is a different person than the priest/false prophet by the same name in Jer. 20:1 (see note there). He was a grandson of King Zedekiah (cf. Jer. 38).

▣ "King Zedekiah" He was the last of a series of bad Davidic kings.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

▣ "Zephaniah" This priest is also mentioned in Jer. 29:25,29; 37:3; 52:24; 2 Kgs. 25:18-21. He was assistant to the High Priest. This is not the same person as the prophet Zephaniah (cf. Zeph. 1:1).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Brief outline of messages to Judah's royal house, cf. Jer. 21:11-23:8
    1. Zedekiah (Mattaniah, cf. 2 Kgs. 24:17) ‒ Jer. 21:1-14
    2. Jehoahaz (Shallum, cf. 1 Chr. 3:15) ‒ Jer. 22:10-12
    3. Jehoiakim (Eliakim, cf. 2 Kgs. 23:34) ‒ Jer. 22:13-19
    4. Jehoiakim (Coniah) ‒ Jer. 22:24-30; 37:1

  2. Zedekiah (BDB 843), another of Josiah's sons, was placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar II, King of Neo-Babylon (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:17). He reigned from 597-586 B.C. He was king when Jerusalem fell. He was loyal to Neo-Babylon for eight years. Then a pro-Egyptian nationalist party persuaded him to revolt. See Appendix Four: Kings of the Divided Kingdom.

    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

  3. This section of Jeremiah is much more clearly linked to its historical settings. The specifics of
    1. time
    2. place
    3. proper names
      abound!

  4. The house of David had all the wonderful ("eternal") promises of 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Chronicles 17, but they, too, were conditional!

    SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)

    SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

  5. Remember that Nebuchadnezzar's army captured Jerusalem several times: 605 B.C., 597 B.C., 586 B.C., and 582 B.C. They destroyed the city and temple in 586 B.C.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:2 "inquire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:2 "inquire" This Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 205, KB 233) means to petition God on behalf of another (cf. Jer. 37:7; Ezek. 20:1,3). One Aramaic Targum translates it as "pray." Zedekiah requests that YHWH act on Judah's behalf against Neo-Babylon as He had done in the past (i.e. against Assyria, Isaiah 36-39). It was part of the covenant promises especially related to the conquest of Canaan in 2 Kings 18 from Isaiah to Hezekiah.

▣ "Nebuchadnezzar" The spelling here is closer to the Babylonian spelling. It (BDB 613, KB 660) means "Nebo protect the boundary" or "Nebo protect the heir to the crown." The normal Hebrew spelling with an "N" may reflect a sarcastic purposeful corruption, "Nebo protect my mule." The Jews loved to add vowels or consonants that made a name refer to something shameful.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

▣ "wonderful acts" The king was hoping for a repeat of Isa. 37:36-37 or the "Holy War" of the Exodus or Joshua's conquest of Canaan (cf. Jer. 32:16-25).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WONDERFUL THINGS

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:4 "Chaldeans"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:4 "Chaldeans" This was the racial identity of southern Babylon; later the term became the title of the entire nation.

Herodotus (450 B.C.), Hist. I, uses this term to refer to an ethnic group (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:1-4; Dan. 5:30) as well as a priestly class (cf. Dan. 2:2; 3:8; 4:7; 5:7,11) whose usage goes back to Cyrus II. Even before this Assyrian records used the term (BDB 505) in an ethnic sense (cf. R. K. Harrison, Introduction to the Old Testament, p. 1113). Also read the good discussion of the possibility of a confusion of two similar terms (i.e. Kal-du vs. Kasdu) in The Expositors Bible Commentary, vol. 7, pp. 14-15 or Robert Dick Wilson, Studies in the Book of Daniel, series 1.

Because Gen. 11:28 states that Ur of the Chaldeans was the home of Terah and his family, Chaldeans may have been ethnically Semitic (i.e. same racial group as the Hebrews).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:4-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:4-7 This is not the answer from YHWH that Zedekiah was praying for. He wanted covenant mercy without covenant faith and faithfulness!

YHWH spells out in graphic terms the "wonderful acts" He will do to faithless Judah/Jerusalem.

  1. YHWH will not fight for Judah but will be with the Neo-Babylonian army (cf. Jer. 32:5; 33:5; 37:8-10; 38:2,17,18).
  2. YHWH's actions and emotions are described as (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN [anthropomorphism])
    1. an outstretched hand (cf. Exod. 6:6; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND)
    2. a mighty arm (cf. Deut. 4:34; 5:15; 7:19; 11:2; 26:8)
    3. angry
    4. full of wrath
    5. greatly indignant
    6. setting His face against Jerusalem, Jer. 21:10
    7. for harm and not for good, Jer. 21:10
    8. giving Jerusalem to the king of Neo-Babylon to burn, Jer. 21:10
  3. Like "Holy War" (cf. Joshua 6), all that breathes, human and animal, will die.
  4. The Davidic seed, Zedekiah, and his house and the survivors of the siege will be exiled.
  5. Nebuchadnezzar II will act as YHWH's representative in judgment.
    1. will not spare
    2. will not have pity
    3. will not have compassion (cf. Jer. 13:14; 16:5)

This is what the covenant people could not comprehend. YHWH, their God, fighting against them and His own temple! They had missed the key ingredients of

  1. faith
  2. faithfulness

The wonderful covenant with Abraham had conditions (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28) and consequences!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:5 "with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:5 "with an outstretched hand and a mighty arm" See full note at Jer. 27:5.

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:7 There are several groups of Judeans addressed.

  1. the king and his family
  2. the royal servants (BDB 713)
    1. of his house
    2. of the government
    3. religious advisors
  3. the army (lit. "the people," BDB 766 I)
  4. the remaining remnant (lit. "who survive," BDB 983, Niphal PARTICIPLE (see SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT [three senses])
  5. in v. 9 another group is mentioned ‒ those who surrender to the Neo-Babylonians

▣ "pestilence, the sword, and the famine" These are the typical description of the results of invasion and siege warfare (cf. Jer. 14:12). All of the surrounding villages gathered to the walled cities. Therefore, food, water, and sanitation became compromised.

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:8-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:8-10 This describes the conditional nature of the covenant. A good parallel text is Deut. 30:15-18, which Jeremiah seems to allude to. I have included my notes from that commentary here.

Deut. 30:15 "I have set before you today life and prosperity or death and adversity" Even covenant Israel had to choose! This is referring to the blessing and cursing (cf. Deuteronomy 27-28). Remember the choice is set in a covenant of grace. This is very similar to Wisdom Literature's idiom of the "two ways" (cf. Prov. 4:10-19; Jer. 21:8; Matt. 7:13-14). Our choices show who we are! How we respond to life's inexplicable "in and outs" reveals our spiritual orientation!

Deut. 30:16-18 These verses are a summary of covenant conditions and consequences:

  1. the responsibility (cf. Jer. 8:6; 19:9; 26:17; 28:9)
    1. "to love the Lord," Jer. 21:16 (BDB 12, KB 17, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
    2. "walk in His ways," Jer. 21:16 (BDB 229, KB 246, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
    3. "keep His commandments," Jer. 21:16 (BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal INFINITIVE)
  2. the consequences of obedience
    1. "you may live," Jer. 21:16 (BDB 310, KB 309, Qal PERFECT with waw)
    2. "you may multiply," Jer. 21:16 (BDB 915, KB 1156, Qal PERFECT with waw)
    3. "your God may bless you," Jer. 21:16 (BDB 138, KB 159, Piel PERFECT with waw)
  3. the conditions and consequences of disobedience
    1. "if your heart turns away," Jer. 21:17 (BDB 815, KB 937, Qal IMPERFECT)
    2. "if you will not obey," Jer. 21:17; (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERFECT)
    3. idolatry
      (1) drawn away (BDB 623, KB 673, Niphil PERFECT with waw)
      (2) worship (BDB 1005, KB 295, Hishtaphel PERFECT with waw)
      (3) serve (BDB 712, KB 773, Qal PERFECT with waw)
    4. "you shall surely perish," Jer. 21:18 (BDB 1, KB 2, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and Qal IMPERFECT, which expresses intensity)
    5. "you shall not prolong your days," Jer. 21:18 (BDB 73, KB 88, Hiphil IMPERFECT)

Notice how v. 20 reinforces these covenant responsibilities so that the Patriarchal blessing (see SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS) can be fulfilled! This terminology is characteristic of Deuteronomy.

In this context the term "life" refers to physical deliverance from death at the hands of the Neo-Babylonian army. The Deuteronomy passage refers to the blessings of the obeyed covenant of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-29.

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:9 "he who goes out. . .will live"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 21:9 "he who goes out. . .will live" Jeremiah is asserting YHWH's promise that if they surrender (cf. Jer. 38:2; 39:18; 45:5) they will be exiled but will live.

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:11-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:11-14 These are words to the royal Davidic house, who were meant to represent YHWH and fulfill His laws (i.e. Exod. 21:17-22:3). Some English translations have one strophe, some two. The reason this information is important is that each strophe, like each paragraph, has one main truth/point. Outlining by strophe/paragraph facilitates an interpreter finding the intent of the original author more clearly.

See "Bible Interpretation Seminar"

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:12 YHWH seems still to hold open the chance that Judah's leadership may repent, as seen in their possible new actions.

  1. administer justice every morning (BDB 192, KB 220, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 7:5; 22:3; probably at the city gate, early each day)
  2. deliver the person who has been robbed from the power of the oppressor (BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil IMPERATIVE)

If they change (cf. 1 Kgs. 6:12-13), then YHWH will relent of the judgment He plans to send, but if not, "wrath. . .fire" (cf. Jer. 4:4). This is the typical covenantal "if. . .then" pattern of a conditional covenant.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

21:13-14 These two verses address those Judeans who live in the hills and remote valleys of Judah. They thought they would be safe, but not so!

entries.title: Jeremiah 21:14a
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
21:14a This expresses the often repeated biblical truth that "humans reap what they sow." See full list of texts at Gal. 6:7-10.

▣ "fire" See SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE.

▣ "in its forest" The JPSOA (footnote) suggests that this refers to the royal palace which was made of cedars from Lebanon and was called "the house of the forest of Lebanon" (1 Kgs. 7:2; 10:17,21; 2 Chr. 9:16; Isa. 22:8). The house of David is mentioned in Jer. 21:12; also note 22:15b.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:1 "the house of the king of Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:1 "the house of the king of Judah" All of this chapter is a word play on "house" (BDB 108), meaning

  1. descendants (cf. 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17)
  2. king's palace (Jer. 22:13-14 speak of enlarging and beautifying the palace in an attempt to be a great king)

Only God can build a house (cf. Ps. 127:1-2). God's house is depicted as

  1. His temple (cf. 2 Samuel 7)
  2. His king (cf. 2 Samuel 7)
  3. His people

All will be captured, destroyed, or exiled!

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:1-2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:1-2 YHWH's directions to Jeremiah are emphatic.

  1. go ‒ BDB 432, KB 434, Qal IMPERATIVE ("go down" refers to the palace, being on a lower hill than the temple, cf. Jer. 26:10)
  2. speak ‒ BDB 180, KB 210, Piel PERFECT with waw
  3. hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS (repeated from chapter 21)

  1. Brief outline of messages to Judah's royal house, cf. Jer. 21:11-23:8
    1. Zedekiah (Mattaniah, cf. 2 Kgs. 24:17) ‒ Jer. 21:1-14
    2. Jehoahaz (Shallum, cf. 1 Chr. 3:15) ‒ Jer. 22:10-12
    3. Jehoiakim (Eliakim, cf. 2 Kgs. 23:34) ‒ Jer. 22:13-19
    4. Jehoiakim (Coniah) ‒ Jer. 22:24-30; 37:1

  2. Zedekiah (BDB 843), another of Josiah's sons, was placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar II, King of Neo-Babylon (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:17). He reigned from 597-586 B.C. He was king when Jerusalem fell. He was loyal to Neo-Babylon for eight years. Then a pro-Egyptian nationalist party persuaded him to revolt. See Appendix Four: Kings of the Divided Kingdom.

    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

    1. time
    2. place

      abound!

  5. Remember Nebuchadnezzar's army captured Jerusalem several times: 605 B.C., 586 B.C., and 582 B.C. They destroyed the city and temple in 586 B.C.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:3 There is a series of commands addressed to the Davidic King which addresses covenant faithfulness.

  1. do justice ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE, see SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGE, JUDGMENT AND JUSTICE and SPECIAL TOPIC: JUSTICE
  2. do righteousness ‒ same as #1 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS)
  3. deliver the one who has been robbed ‒ BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  4. do not mistreat the stranger, the orphan, or the widow ‒ BDB 413, KB 416, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  5. do not do violence to (the group mentioned in #4) ‒ BDB 329, KB 329, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  6. do not shed innocent blood (lit. "pour out") ‒ BDB 1049, KB 1629, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (this could refer to murder or child sacrifice)

▣ "the stranger, the orphan, or the widow" This is a key phrase from Deuteronomy. It characterized YHWH's action and care (Deut. 10:18; Ps. 146:8-10). It is mentioned several times in Deuteronomy.

  1. help them ‒ Deut. 14:29; 24:17,19
  2. rejoice with them ‒ Deut. 16:11
  3. special offering for them ‒ Deut. 26:12-13
  4. cursings if one distorts their justice ‒ Deut. 27:19

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:4 "if"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:4 "if" The verse states the conditional element which is related to the actual doing of the covenant commands of Jer. 22:4. Verse 4 is first found in Jer. 17:25.

▣ "then" Here are the promises to the king if he will be faithful to the covenant.

  1. kings (i.e. generations of kings) will enter the gates of this house
  2. sit on David's throne
  3. riding in chariots and on horses with his household

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:5 Again the conditional "if." YHWH swears (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal PERFECT) by Himself that if covenant faithlessness continues, Jerusalem and the temple will become a desolation (BDB 352)! YHWH's oath has a sense of certainty and finality (cf. Gen. 22:16; Amos 6:8; Heb. 6:13).

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:6-7 This is a brief poem describing the desolation.

  1. Judah will become a wilderness (BDB 184)
  2. Judah's cities will be uninhabited (BDB 442, KB 444, Niphal PERFECT, Qere)
  3. YHWH will consecrate (i.e. "set apart for His service," BDB 872, KB 1073, Piel PERFECT, with waw cf. Jer. 6:4) the armed destroyers (i.e. this is "holy war" terminology. The point being YHWH is not on Judah's side).
    1. cut down your best forest (i.e. cities, cf. Isa. 10:33-34)
    2. burn them

Just a textual note, the last VERB of Jer. 22:6, "inhabited" (BDB 442, KB 442), in the MT, is a Niphal PARTICIPLE, SINGULAR, but the Masoretic scholars suggested (Qere) a Niphal PERFECT, PLURAL.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

▣ "You are like Gilead to Me" These first two lines of poetry in Jer. 22:6b and c are parallel and address the royal house. The imagery is that as Gilead and Lebanon were beautiful and forested, so too, the house (palace) of Judah. But it will be destroyed! The house of the king (physical and seed) and the house of the Lord will both be destroyed! Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28 have come to painful reality!

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:8-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:8-9 Verse 8 expressed the theological question connected to YHWH's judgment of His own covenant people (cf. Jer. 16:10; Deut. 28:24-26; 1 Kgs. 9:8-9; 2 Chr. 7:20-22).

Moses' prayer of intercession for Israel entreated YHWH about this very issue (cf. Exod. 32:11-13) and YHWH changed His mind (cf. Exod. 32:14). But the covenant people had become so idolatrous (cf. Jer. 1:16; 5:19; 8:2; 16:11) and rebellious that only radical surgery could save their corporate life.

Remember, in that day every nation had its own national deity. The more powerful deity won the battles for its people. Some might think that YHWH was weak because

  1. the northern kingdom (Israel) was exiled by Assyria (722 B.C.)
  2. the southern kingdom (Judah) was defeated and exiled several times by Neo-Babylon (605, 597, 586, 582 B.C.)

The real problem was the sin of the covenant people (cf. Jer. 22:9; 2 Chr. 34:25), not YHWH!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:10-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:10-12 This brief poem and prose conclusion addresses the issue of the Davidic seed (Shallum or Jehoahaz, son of Josiah) exiled! This seems to violate 2 Sam. 7:13-17, but the reality of Ezekiel 18 must also be taken into account. YHWH's promises are sure but they are conditional in relation to individual leaders' volition. Sin has consequences (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28)!

There is a series of commands in Jer. 22:10.

  1. do not weep for the dead ‒ BDB 113, KB 129, Qal IMPERFECT used in a IMPERFECT sense (i.e. this refers to Josiah, who was killed by Pharaoh Necho's army at Megiddo, cf. 2 Kgs. 23:28-30; 2 Chr. 35:20-36:4)
  2. do not mourn for him ‒ BDB 626, KB 678, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  3. weep continually ‒ BDB a Qal IMPERATIVE and INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE from the same root (BDB 113, KB 129; this refers to Jehoahaz/Shallum, who Pharaoh Necho II exiled to Egypt after only a 3 month reign, cf. 2 Kgs. 23:31-35)

The king shall never return from captivity! There may be a word play on "return" (BDB 996, KB 1427), which can mean

  1. repent
  2. return

Although he was Josiah's son, he was capable of neither!

The Anchor Bible Commentary and UBS Handbook for Translators on Jeremiah, and the JPSOA footnote suggest that "the dead" of Jer. 22:10a refers to King Josiah, killed by the Egyptian army at Megiddo in 609 B.C. (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:28-35; 2 Chr. 35:20-25).

The phrase "who departs" (Jer. 22:10b) refers to Jehoahaz (Shallum, cf. 1 Chr. 3:15), who was Josiah's son who succeeded him but was exiled to Egypt three months later by Pharaoh Necho II (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:31-34; 2 Chr. 36:2-4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:13 "Woe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:13 "Woe" The pronounciation of His Hebrew word sounds like exasperated or sorrowful fellings. This term (BDB 222) characterizes the book of Lamentations (cf. Amos 5:24). The Prophets often used the literary form (a 3-2 beat) of a funeral dirge to express the disapproval of God and His coming judgment. This term is recurrent in Isaiah.

  1. negative in the sense of judgment in Isa. 1:4; 5:8,11,18,20,21,22; 10:1; 17:12; 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1; 45:9,10; Jer. 22:13,18; 30:7; 48:1; 50:27; Heb. 2:6,9,12,15,19
  2. neutral in Isa. 10:5
  3. positive in the sense of pity in Isa. 18:1; 55:1; and Jer. 23:1; 34:5; 47:6

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:13-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:13-23 This long strophe is addressed to King Jehoiakim and is related to the Davidic promises of 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17.

Notice the "woe" (BDB 222) of Jer. 22:13 and "alas" (DB 222, four times) of Jer. 22:18. See full note at v. 13.

Jehoiakim is condemned because

  1. he builds his house without righteousness (i.e. 2 Kgs. 23:34-35)
    1. palace
    2. royal family
  2. so opposite of Josiah (cf. Jer. 22:15-16) who "knew" (BDB 395; see SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW) YHWH. To know YHWH is to live in covenant obedience and compassion. David's reign is described by these terms in 2 Sam. 8:15.
    1. Josiah did justice
    2. Josiah did righteousness
    3. Josiah pled the cause of
      (1) the afflicted
      (2) the needy
    4. it was well with him (Jer. 22:15d, 16b)
  3. Jehoiakim (Jer. 22:17)
    1. intent on dishonest gain
    2. shed innocent blood
    3. practiced oppression
    4. practiced extortion (note Jer. 5:20-29, like King, like people)
  4. results
    1. no lament for him in his death (Jer. 22:18)
    2. had a donkey's burial (Jer. 22:19)
    3. no one to lament (Jer. 22:20) because all political alliances (i.e. "lovers") have been crushed
  5. YHWH spoke to him (Jer. 22:21) or a way of referring to Jerusalem
    1. in your prosperity
    2. in your youth 
    3. but he would not (same VERB)
      (1) listen
      (2) obey

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:19 Being improperly buried was viewed in the ANE as negatively affecting one's afterlife. See SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:20 There are three mountain ranges mentioned.

  1. Lebanon (i.e. Mt. Hermon or its foothills)
  2. Bashan (i.e. mountains in TransJordan to the northwest)
  3. Abarim (i.e. mountains of Moab, cf. Num. 27:12; Deut. 32:49)

One wonders why these places?

  1. the higher elevations were used as places of Ba'al worship
  2. these are the places to which some Judeans fled to hide from and escape the invasion
  3. this is sarcasm of the grief Judah felt over the loss of her foreign alliances
  4. they describe the full extent of David's kingdom and the limits of the Promised Land

▣ "your lovers" This refers to all of Judah's political alliances (cf. Jer. 2:25; 3:1). Judah trusted in the armies of foreign nations instead of YHWH (cf. Ps. 20:7; 33:16-17; Isa. 31:1; also note Eccl. 9:11)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:20-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:20-23 The NJB thinks that these verses address Jehoiachin, who reigned only three months, before being removed and exiled by Nebuchadnezzar. However, the TEV and UBS Handbook for Translators on Jeremiah think these verses are addressed to Judah/Jerusalem (FEMININE SINGULAR VERBS).

This is surely imagery of Abraham's seed having become a faithless, disobedient, promiscuous "wife" of YHWH.

It is difficult to know exactly which verses refer to which Davidic king. The NKJV version simply titles the section "Message to the sons of Josiah."

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:21 "I will not listen!
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:21 "I will not listen!

This has been your practice from your youth" The covenant people had been a stiffnecked, rebellious people (cf. Jer. 7:22-26) from the beginning (i.e. two early examples: Exodus 32 and Numbers 16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: STUBBORNNESS (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:22 Notice how "shepherds" (Judah's civic and religious leaders, cf. Jer. 1:18; 2:8; 10:21; 23:2) are paralleled with "lovers" (foreign alliances). What a sad situation! JPSOA footnote suggests a revocalization which yields "paramours."

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:23 "You who dwell in Lebanon,
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:23 "You who dwell in Lebanon,

Nested in the cedars" This seems to be a literary figure of speech referring to the royal family in Jerusalem. The king's palace was known as "the House of the Cedars of Lebanon" (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:2; 10:17).

▣
NASB, NKJV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate  "How you will
  groan"
NRSV  "How gracious
  will you be"
MT, TEV  "How pitied you
  will be"
JPSOA  "How much grace
  will you have"

The MT has נחנת from חנן, BDB 335, KB 334, Niphal PERFECT. The LXX reflects ננחת (there are several roots starting with an "n" meaning "groan" (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3). Either fits the context and parallelism. The UBS Text Project, p. 242, could not decide if the MT reading or the LXX reading was original.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "Pain like a woman in childbirth" This imagery (BDB 408) was used earlier in Jer. 4:31; 6:24; 13:21 (also note Jer. 30:6; 49:24; 50:43). The pain, though expected, is sudden and intense! The imagery is often used in judgment contexts.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIRTH PAINS

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:24 "As I live"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:24 "As I live" This is a recurrent oath formula where YHWH swears by Himself (cf. Jer. 22:5; 44:26; 49:13; 51:14; Gen. 22:16; Deut. 32:40; Isa. 45:23; Amos 6:8). It is a word play on His covenant name, YHWH, from the Hebrew VERB "to be." Covenant people were "to swear by His name" (cf. Jer. 4:2; 12:16; Deut. 6:13; 10:20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:24 "signet ring on My right hand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:24 "signet ring on My right hand" This is Hebrew imagery for the Davidic royal family, especially the current reigning descendant of David (cf. Hag. 2:23).

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:24-30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 22:24-30 This is specifically addressed to Coniah (i.e. Jeconiah, cf. Jer. 24:1), also known by his throne name, Jehoiachin (cf. Jer. 22:24). He was exiled in 597 B.C. to Babylon (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:8-17; 25:27-30). Verses 28-30 are poetry, while Jer. 22:24-27 are prose.

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:25 Notice how specific and repetitive is the reference to Jehoiachin's captors.

  1. into the hand of those who are seeking your life
  2. into the hand of those whom you dread
  3. into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon
  4. into the hand of the Chaldeans

For the idiom using "hand" see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND.

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:27 "they desire"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:27 "they desire" The UBS Handbook for Translators on Jeremiah (p. 489) points out that this English phrase is a translation of a Hebrew idiom "they will lift up their souls" (cf. Jer. 44:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:28-30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:28-30 The poem is addressed to Coniah/Jehoiachin (cf. 1 Chr. 3:16). He has become a vessel of dishonor (cf. Jer. 25:34; Hosea 8:8). The potter (YHWH) makes different vessels. Some are spoiled.

  1. remade (unfired)
  2. destroyed (fired)

The promises of 2 Samuel 7 and 1 Chronicles 17 are vacated and annulled. No more descendants on the throne (i.e. he had children but none ruled, cf. Jer. 22:30)! This was absolutely shocking to Judeans. YHWH's promise nullified! They forgot that the promises to individuals are always conditional. This opens the theological door for a "new" covenant (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36)!

It is very clear who is being described but it is not clear who is speaking.

  1. the people of Judah/Jerusalem
  2. the prophet Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 22:29)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

22:28
NASB, TEV  "shattered jar"
NKJV  "broken idol"
NRSV, NJB, JPSOA, NET  "broken pot"
Peshitta  "useless vessel"
LXX  "good for nothing vessel"

The NOUN (BDB 781 II) basically means that which is formed.

  1. a clay pot, cf. Jer. 50:2; Micah 1:7
  2. an idol, cf. Isa. 46:1; 48:5; Hosea 4:17; 8:4; 13:2; 14:8; Zech. 13:2

There are two terms in this verse that could be translated "jar" (BDB 781 II) or "vessel" (BDB 479). The point is that Jehiochin is

  1. broken (BDB 658 I, KB 711)
  2. despised (BDB102, KB 117)
  3. uncared for (BDB 34 II CONSTRUCT BDB 343)
  4. exiled person and his family (BDB 376, KB 373)

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:29 "O land, land, land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:29 "O land, land, land" The threefold repetition was a Hebraic grammatical feature denoting intensity (cf. Jer. 7:4; Isa. 6:3; Ezek. 21:27), although some grammarians think it was a liturgical chant. It is even possible that "the land" was functioning as a legal witness in this court genre. The land of Palestine is experiencing the judgment of God because of the sin of God's people. The curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28 have come in full force! After one reads this text, they are so grateful for Rom. 8:18-25! The New Covenant is wonderful!

The word translated "land" has several connotations. See SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH (erets)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD (several terms)

entries.title: Jeremiah 22:30 "Write this man down childless"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
22:30 "Write this man down childless" This command from YHWH seems to be unfulfilled because Jehoiachin had several children (cf. 1 Chr. 3:16-17). However, they never sat on David's throne. A good discussion of the seeming contradiction is found in Hard Sayings of the Bible, p. 310. Another good source for interpreting prophetic literature is D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, especially pp. 151-154.

entries.title: Jeremiah 23:1-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
23:1-4 This is a "woe" strophe (i.e. funeral dirge, a 3/2 meter/beat; see full note at Jer. 22:13). The false shepherds (prophets, priests, civic leaders):

  1. are destroying YHWH's flock, Jer. 23:1
  2. are scattering YHWH's flock, Jer. 23:1-2
  3. have not attended YHWH's flock, Jer. 23:2
  4. have driven them away, Jer. 23:2

YHWH will raise up true shepherds.

  1. He will gather His flock, Jer. 23:3
  2. they will be fruitful and multiply, Jer. 23:3 (the expressed desire of YHWH in Gen. 1:22,28; 9:1,7)
  3. good shepherds will tend them, Jer. 23:4
  4. they will not be afraid or terrified any longer, Jer. 23:4
  5. none of them are missing, Jer. 23:4

YHWH's special Davidic leader (cf. Ezekiel 34):

  1. Davidic seed
  2. righteous seed
  3. Branch (cf. Jer. 23:5; 33:15-16; Isa. 4:2; 11:1-5; 53:2; Zech. 3:8; 6:12-13)
  4. He will reign as king, Jer. 23:5
  5. He will act wisely, Jer. 23:5
  6. He will do justice and righteousness, Jer. 23:5
  7. His name will be "the Lord our righteousness," Jer. 23:6

What a contrast!

  1. the wicked leaders do not attend YHWH's flock. He will attend them for their evil deeds, Jer. 23:2
  2. the righteous leader will
    1. save, Jer. 23:6 (i.e. physical deliverance; see SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION [OT])
    2. cause to dwell securely, Jer. 23:6
    3. return them to the Promised Land, Jer. 23:8 (i.e. reflects the land promise of Gen. 12:1-3; see SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS)

The God who acts, will act (cf. Ezek. 36:22-38)! The Good Shepherd will come (John 10), but He will be rejected (cf. Zechariah 11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: OT TITLES OF THE SPECIAL COMING ONE
