READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

BRIEF OVERVIEW

  1. Jeremiah 1-25 is written in the FIRST PERSON, while Jeremiah 26-45 is in the THIRD PERSON. This change is possibly due to Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe (cf. Jer. 36:4,18; 43:3). The book of Jeremiah, like the book of Isaiah, is a collected and edited anthology.

  2. Jeremiah 25 is written in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, while Jer. 26:1 is at the beginning of his reign. Jeremiah is not in chronological order, though many of the early chapters may be.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

  3. Jeremiah 26 is parallel to Jeremiah 7. It possibly records the people at the temple's reaction to Jeremiah's powerful Temple sermon recorded in Jer. 7:2-15.

  4. Jeremiah 27-28 deals with the prophecy concerning the fall of Jerusalem.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:2 "Stand in the court of the Lord's house"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:2 "Stand in the court of the Lord's house" Jeremiah has been directed to share his revelations there several times (cf. Jer. 7:2; 17:19; 19:1-6). From this locale he could address "all the cities of Judah."

▣ "Do not omit a word" This is literally "diminish" (BDB 175, KB 203, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense). It implies a very specific divine message (cf. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Prov. 30:5-6; Eccl. 3:14). This reminds me of

  1. Samuel and Eli in 1 Samuel 3
  2. two verses in Jeremiah, Jer. 1:17 and 42:4
  3. Paul's words in Acts 20:20
  4. Revelation 22:18-19

In Jer. 26:12-13 Jeremiah claims that his words are YHWH's words.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:3 This verse reflects the message of Jer. 25:4-5 (repeated with the same VERBS in Jer. 26:5). The problem is that Judah will not listen and respond (i.e. repent, lit. "turn," BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Jer. 26:13). YHWH will repent (lit. "be sorry," BDB 636, KB 688, Niphal PERFECT with waw) of His decrees of judgment (cf. Jer. 26:4-6) and exile if Judah will turn back to Him. This is the desire of the covenant God! But Judah would not, could not, did not respond!

It is difficult for modern western people to comprehend God "repenting" or "changing His mind" or "being sorry," however, this is an anthropomorphic way of showing His merciful character and His attention to His people's prayers and covenant obedience. Repentance could change prophetic announcements! See Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 108-109.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:4-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:4-5 Notice the covenant criteria YHWH lists as a prerequisite to changing His mind.

  1. if you listen to Me (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR [shema])
  2. if you walk in My law (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY)
  3. if you listen to the words of My servants, the prophets (cf. Deut. 18:19)

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:5 My servants the prophets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:5 My servants the prophets" If the covenant people of Judah will not respond to YHWH's revelation through His "servants" (i.e. the true prophets, cf. Jer. 25:4) who He sent "again and again" (lit. "rising early and sending"), then they will be forced to listen to His appointed invader (i.e., "My Servant," Nebuchadnezzar II, cf. Jer. 25:9; 27:6; 43:10; see SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT).

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:6 "like Shiloh"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:6 "like Shiloh" This was the site of an ancient Jewish sanctuary which was destroyed by the Philistines in 1050 B.C., cf. 1 Sam. 4:1-11; Jer. 7:12,14.

▣ "I will make this house. . .a curse to all the nations of the earth" This hyperbolic language continues from Jer. 24:9 and 25:18. God's people were meant to be a blessing to the world (i.e. Gen. 12:3), but because of their sin, the world (i.e. the nations) saw only the judgment of YHWH, not His grace and mercy (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:7-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:7-8 The different groups of Judah's leadership are condemned (cf. Jer. 1:18; 2:8; 10:21; 23:2,13-15,16,25-26,33-34, 35, etc.).

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:8 "You must die"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:8 "You must die" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 559, KB 562), used for emphasis. The religious leaders considered Jeremiah's message blasphemy (cf. Jer. 26:9; Deut. 18:20) against the Davidic promises of 2 Samuel 7 and Isaiah's theology concerning Jerusalem (i.e. Isa. 33:20 and chapters 36-39). They failed to take seriously the conditional nature of the covenant promises (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28; 30:15-20). This was not the first or last attempt on Jeremiah's life (cf. Jer. 11:19; 18:23).

The NASB Study Bible mentions that the phrase is similar to Exod. 21:15-17; Lev. 24:16-17,21; Deut. 18:20; 1 Kgs. 21:13, all of which describe the ultimate penalty for gross violations of the Mosaic covenant (p. 1098). Because Jeremiah's predictions of judgment did not come to reality for many years, he was considered a false prophet (i.e. Deut. 13:1-5; 18:20).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:10 "sat in the entrance of the New Gate"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:10 "sat in the entrance of the New Gate" The location of the New Gate is unknown (cf. Jer. 36:10). Rashi (a Jewish commentator from the Middle Ages) says it was the rebuilt Eastern Gate.

The gate of the city, or in this case, a gate leading into the temple area, was the location of Jeremiah's trial for the sermon he preached in the temple area in Jeremiah 7. For more information, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 155-157.

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:13,19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:13,19 This repeats the message of Jer. 26:3-6.

Notice the necessary elements for YHWH to "change His mind."

  1. amend your ways (cf. Jer. 7:3,5; 18:11; 35:15)
  2. amend your deeds
  3. obey YHWH's revelatory message from Jeremiah

This required liefstyle change (i.e. Jer. 18:8), not an emotional moment, not a liturgical affirmation, not a cessation of some evil ways, not a heal-heart, but a whole heart devotion ot YHWH.

For a good brief discussion of this issue of God changing His mind, see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 108-109.

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:15 "know for certain"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:15 "know for certain" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 393, KB 390), which denotes intensity.

▣ "innocent blood" This is imagery for premeditated murder. See Jer. 7:6; Gen. 4:10; Deut. 19:10; Prov. 6:16-17.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MURDER

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:16 "in the name of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:16 "in the name of the Lord" See SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH.

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:16-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:16-19 The civil officials and the people are more sensitive to Jeremiah's words than the spiritual leadership (i.e. priests and prophets). They even mention an earlier example of a prophetic message of judgment against Jerusalem (v. 18, cf. Micah 3:12). In a sense this is a call to repentance as in Hezekiah's day (cf. 2 Chr. 29:3-11).

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:17 "elders of the land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 26:17 "elders of the land" This refers to wealthy land owners and influential families.

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:18 "Zion"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:18 "Zion" Jerusalem was built on several hills. One of the tallest was Zion, where the Jebusite fortress was built and later captured by David (cf. 2 Sam. 5:7; 1 Chr. 11:5). Zion became a way of referring to the whole city of Jerusalem (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:1).

The phrase "the virgin daughter of Zion" (i.e. 2 Kgs. 19:21) was a way of referring to God's covenant people whose capital and temple were in Jerusalem.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MORIAH, SALEM, JEBUS, JERUSALEM, ZION

SPECIAL TOPIC: VIRGIN DAUGHTERS OF. . .

▣ The quote in v, 18 is from Micah 3:12. I have included my exegetical notes on this passage below.

Micah 3:12 This must have been an extremely startling statement to the people of Judah. They trusted in God's promises that Jerusalem and the temple would never fall (i.e., Isaiah's promises to Hezekiah, probably based in 2 Samuel 7), and yet, because of their flagrant neglect of the ethical aspects of the covenant, God would take them into exile (cf. Jer. 26:18). Jerusalem would be like Samaria (cf. Mic. 1:6)! This is the first prophetic mention of the fall of Jerusalem ("plowed as a field") and the temple (i.e., overgrown with vegetation, literally "a high place of a forest"). This is theologically parallel to Isaiah 5.

I am sure that Micah was discredited in 701 B.C. when this did not occur (i.e., Sennacherib's army destroyed by God, cf. 2 Kgs. 19:35-37), however, the prophet was vindicated in 586 B.C. when this prophecy was literally fulfilled under the siege of Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon. F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, asserts that the king (i.e., Hezekiah, cf. Mic. 1:1) and people of Judah responded to Micah's message and, therefore, God relented of His judgment (p. 36). Hezekiah's repentance is recorded in 2 Kgs. 20:1-7.

▣ "And the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest" Another translation has, " The temple mount will become a mere wooded ridge" (cf. Micah 3:12). This imagery reflects the worship of "trees" (i.e. Astarte ) located on Ba'al platforms. It would equal the groves "of fertility worship."

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:19 "put him to death"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:19 "put him to death" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 559, KB 562) which denotes intensity. Hezekiah trusted YHWH and did not put Micah to death. The death penalty for false prophets is found in Deut. 13:1-5; 18:20.

▣
NASB, NRSV  "entreat the favor of"
NKJV  "seek the favor of"
TEV  "tried to win his favor"
NJB  "plead with him"
JPSOA  "implore"
REB  "seek to placate"
Peshitta  "prayed before him"

The VERB (BDB 318 II, KB 316, Piel IMPERFECT with waw) was used in the sense of "make the face sweet" (i.e. Aramaic, Arabic). The "face" represents the person (i.e. the Aaronic blessing of Num. 6:24-26). In judgment, the judge could not "lift the face" (i.e. show preferential treatment). Here possibly touch the face (NET Bible, p. 1367 and Expositors Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 541).

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:20 "Uriah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:20 "Uriah" Verses 20-22 function as a parenthesis (cf. TEV, NET). The time frame is uncertain. Apparently Micah is used as an example of a prophet who spoke judgment against the temple and was spared. The priests brought up the example of another prophet who preached judgment against Jerusalem and was executed by the civil leadership.

It is also possible that the reaction of Hezekiah to YHWH's prophet is shown to be different from Jehoiakim's reaction to YHWH's message (cf. NASB Study Bible footnote, p. 1099).

Uriah is otherwise unknown. He was either

  1. a disciple of Jeremiah
  2. another contemporary prophetic voice about YHWH judging Judah

However, Jehoiakim had him killed! Judah was about to kill another prophet!

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:22 "Elnathan the son of Achbor"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:22 "Elnathan the son of Achbor" He is part of a group of godly leaders who (Jer. 36:11-19)

  1. gave Baruch and Jeremiah warning to hide (Jer. 36:19)
  2. encouraged King Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's prophecies (Jer. 36:25)

However, in this context, he was forced to do the king's bidding.

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:23 "the burial place of the common people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:23 "the burial place of the common people" Apparently, those who died in the Jerusalem area and did not have a family tomb, were buried in a certain area (i.e. common trench) in the Kedron Valley (2 Kgs. 23:6). For more information on burial practices of the ANE, see:

  1. Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 57-59
  2. SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

entries.title: Jeremiah 26:24 "Ahikam"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
26:24 "Ahikam" This was the father of Gedaliah, who later became the appointed Babylonian governor of Judah under Nebuchadnezzar II. Also he was part of the deputation to Huldah from Josiah in 2 Kgs. 22:12ff. Jeremiah was not without supporters and advocates.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:1 "Zedekiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:1 "Zedekiah" Most manuscripts of the MT have "Jehoiakim" (JPSOA). However, the Peshitta (Syriac) and the Arabic, along with three Hebrew MSS, have "Zedekiah" because of:

  1. Jer. 27:3,12; 28:1
  2. the internal setting of the chapter fits Zedekiah better (i.e. vv. 3, 12; "Jehoiakim" fits Jer. 26:1 better)
  3. the LXX omitted the verse

The date could be after 597 B.C., possibly 594 B.C. (cf. Jer. 28:1), because an account in the Babylonian Chronicles tells us of the attempted coalition between small western states against Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Jer. 27:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

▣ "Jeremiah" Jeremiah's name (ירמיהו, i.e. Jer. 26:7) is spelled differently in Hebrew (ירמיה, BDB 941), reason unknown. Several names in the OT are spelled differently, examples are Joshua, Nebuchadnezzar.

  1. different scribes translated foreign names differently
  2. Israelites tended to slightly alter names to show disrespect

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
JEREMIAH 27

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
The Nations To Submit to Nebuchadnezzar Symbol of the Bonds and Yokes The Yoke of the King of Babylon
(27:1-28:17)		 Jeremiah Wears An Ox Yoke The Symbolic Yoke and the Message to the Neighboring Kings
27:1-7 27:1-11 27:1-7 27:1-7 27:1-11
27:8-11 27:8-11 27:8-11
27:12-15 27:12-15 27:12-15 27:12-15 27:12-15
27:16-22 27:16-18 27:16-22 27:16-18 27:16-22
27:19-22 27:19-20
27:21-22

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. The LXX text of this chapter is much shorter (LXX chapter 34). The question is
    1. does the LXX simply remove the doublets and repetitions
    2. does the MT expand the text for clarity or current stylistic considerations
      SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

  2. Notice Jeremiah addresses several groups.
    1. the ambassadors from the surrounding nations (cf. Jer. 27:3) who wanted Judah to join their coalition against Neo-Babylon
    2. the king of Judah, Zedekiah, Jer. 27:12-15
    3. the priests, Jer. 27:16
    4. the people, Jer. 27:16

  3. Notice the number of times and the variety of phrasing that Jeremiah used to assure his audiences that he is speaking the message of YHWH, not his own opinion.
    1. this word came to Jeremiah from the Lord, Jer. 27:1
    2. thus says the Lord to me, Jer. 27:2
    3. thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, Jer. 27:4,21
    4. the Lord has spoken to that nation, Jer. 27:13
    5. v. 15 has two disclaimers of YHWH speaking through the false prophets
    6. thus says the Lord, Jer. 27:16
    7. thus says the Lord of hosts, Jer. 27:19
    8. declares the Lord, Jer. 27:22

  4. Jeremiah 27-29 forms a literary unit. Not only does the historical and literary setting establish this, but also the names of both Jeremiah and Nebuchadnezzar are spelled differently in these three chapters.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:3 "bonds and yokes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:3 "bonds and yokes" This refers to oxen yokes (BDB 557). How many Jeremiah made is uncertain, whether one for himself or one for each ambassador. They symbolized servitude (cf. Jer. 27:8; Deut. 28:48; 1 Kgs. 12:4,9,10). Probably the Hebrew "them" of Jer. 27:3 refers to a message, not a yoke.

▣ "by the messengers" This refers to the officials sent by the surrounding nations who were

  1. trying to encourage Zedekiah to resist Babylon, along with them
  2. asked by Zedekiah to form an alliance to resist Neo-Babylon's expansion

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:4 There are several common titles for Israel's Deity used in this verse.

  1. Lord (YHWH), vv. 1,2,4)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.
  2. Lord of Hosts, v. 4
    SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts
  3. God (Eloah) of Israel, v. 4
    SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.
  4. Notice all the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR PRONOUNS (i.e. My)
    1. My great power, v. 5
    2. My outstretched arm, v. 5
      SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD
      SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND
    3. My sight, v. 5
    4. My servant, v. 6
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: DESCRIPTIVE TITLES FOR GOD

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:5 This is the theological assertion that YHWH is the God of creation (cf. Gen. 1:1-2:3). Verses 5-6 also assert His sovereignty over all nations (cf. LXX, Deut. 32:8; Job 12:23; Acts 17:26).

▣ "by My great power and by My outstretched arm" This is a repeated anthropomorphic theme.

  1. YHWH's deliverance of Israel from Egypt, Deut. 4:34; 5:15; 6:21; 9:29
  2. YHWH as creator, 2 Kgs. 19:15; Neh. 9:6; Ps. 102:25; 121:2; 124:8; 134:3; 146:6; Jer. 27:5; 32:17; Acts 14:15; Rev. 14:7
  3. YHWH as against Judah and for Neo-Babylon, Jer. 6:12; 15:6; 21:5; Zeph.1:4

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "I will give it to the one who is pleasing in My sight" This phrase is also used of Cyrus II, King of Persia (cf. Isa. 44:28; 45:1-7), but here of Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Jer. 25:9; 28:14). YHWH is in control of history!

The VERB "give" (BDB 678, KB 733) is used four times in Jer. 27:5-8. The emphasis is not on the power of human kings, but on YHWH's control of nations and events for His redemptive purposes (i.e. Dan. 2:37; 4:14,17,25; 5:18,19,21)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:6 "My servant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:6 "My servant" This is a honorific title used of

  1. the Messiah (cf. Isa. 52:13)
  2. Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Jer. 25:9; 43:10)

God is in control of history, men, nations, and even Satan, who may all be used to accomplish His redemptive purposes!

The footnote of the Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 545, is very helpful as it outlines the different usages of the title "My Servant."

  1. a servant of God as a prophet, cf. Num. 12:7-8; Neh. 1:7; Dan. 9:11
    1. Moses
    2. Daniel, cf. Dan. 9:17
  2. a servant of God as a military leader (i.e. Joshua), cf. Josh. 24:29; Jdg. 2:8
  3. a servant of God as King (i.e. David), cf. 2 Sam. 7:5,8; Psalm 18,36; Ezek. 34:24; 37:24
  4. a servant of God as administrator
    1. Nehemiah, cf. Neh. 1:6
    2. Zerubbabel, cf. Hag. 2:23
  5. all Israel (or Jacob), cf. Isa. 42:1,19; 43:10; 44:1,21; 49:3; Ezek. 28:25; 37:25
  6. the remnant of Israel, cf. Isa. 41:8-10
  7. a godly individual, cf. Job 1:8; 2:3; 42:8
  8. unbelieving rulers who serve YHWH's purposes
    1. Cyrus II, Isa. 44:28; 45:1
    2. Nebuchadnezzar II, Jer. 25:9; 27:6; 43:10

SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

▣ "also the wild animals of the field to serve him" This is a strange phrase. It apparently relates to Jer. 27:5, where it is a way of referring to creation. Here it is used in a series of statements (cf. Jer. 28:14).

  1. creation given, Jer. 27:5
  2. lands given, Jer. 27:6
  3. animals given, Jer. 27:6
  4. nations given, Jer. 27:7

▣ "to serve him" This verb (BDB 712, KB 773, here used of Nebuchadnezzar II) is used eleven times in this chapter.

  1. Qal infinitive construct, Jer. 27:6
  2. Qal perfect with waw, Jer. 27:7 (twice),11 (twice)
  3. Qal imperfect, Jer. 27:8,9,13,14
  4. Qal imperative, Jer. 27:12,17

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:7 "And all the nations will serve him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:7 "And all the nations will serve him" It is obvious from the context that this refers to the nations of the ANE in a geographically limited sense (i.e. also note 1 Kgs. 4:31; 1 Chr. 14:17; Ps. 72:11; Zech. 14:2).

However, usually this phrase (and similar phrases) is used with the universal implications.

  1. judgment ‒ Ps. 82:8; Isa. 2:4; Matt. 25:32
  2. evangelism ‒ Isa. 25:7; 66:18; Matt. 24:14; 28:19; Luke 24:47; Rom. 1:5
  3. salvation/deliverance ‒ Ps. 67:2; Gal. 3:8
  4. worship ‒ Ps. 72:17; 86:9; Isa. 2:2-3; 61:11; 66:23; Jer. 10:7; Mark 11:17
  5. hatred of all nations ‒ Matt. 24:9

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "him, and his son, and his grandson" The LXX omits "grandson." Historically the throne was seized from Nebuchadnezzar's son by a relative. Remember, modern westerners turn Hebrew prophecy into "historical narrative." This phrase is a literary way of asserting Neo-Babylon's domination for a period of time (i.e. 70 years, cf. Jer. 25:11).

Also notice that as YHWH used Nebuchadnezzar II to punish His unrepentant people, the day is coming when YHWH will use Cyrus to judge Neo-Babylon for her sins (cf. Jer. 25:12; chapters 50-51; Isa. 14:4-6).

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:8 "the nation or the kingdom which will not serve him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:8 "the nation or the kingdom which will not serve him" Judah must yield to Neo-Babylon. This is YHWH's will. Judah is being punished for her covenant disobedience. A good example of this is Jeremiah's words to Zedekiah in Jer. 38:17-23.

▣ "sword. . .famine. . .pestilence" This is a common trio used to describe a military takeover and its consequences. It reflects the curses of Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28. See note at Jer. 14:12.

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:9 ▣ "do not listen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:9 ▣ "do not listen" This verb (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal imperfect used in a jussive sense) is repeated in Jer. 27:14,16, and 17! We have a choice who we listen to!

▣ There is a series of forbidden ways to know God's will and manipulate future events (cf. Deut. 18:9-14).

  1. your prophets (BDB 611) ‒ false prophets (cf. Jer. 27:9; 2:8; 23:13-15,26; 29:9)
  2. your diviners (BDB 890) ‒ This is from the Hebrew root for "divine" (BDB 890, cf. Num. 22:7; 23:23; Ezek. 21:21; 2 Kgs. 17:17). It is the general term describing several different methods, but all intent on determining the will of a deity by mechanical or natural means (such as examining the livers of sheep or casting arrows). It is based on the pagan worldview that there is information about the future hidden in natural events and that gifted humans (i.e. false prophets, i.e. Jer. 27:9; 29:8; Ezek. 13:9; 22:28) know it and influence this future.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION
  3. your dreamers (BDB 321) ‒ false revelations (cf. Jer. 23:25-28; 29:8; Deut. 13:1-3; see good brief article in John Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, p. 243). The REB changes the vowels and translates this as "your women dreamers." NEB has "wise women."
    SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION
  4. your soothsayers (BDB 778) ‒ This term (BDB 778 II, KB 857) is related to the term "cloud" (BDB 777). Linguists think the term is related to sound:
    1. the hum of insects
    2. sound of wind in the trees
    3. unknown etymology (if cloud, then related to sight)
      The parallel passage in Moses' writings which prohibits these same pagan practices is in Lev. 19:26-20:8 (see esp. 19:26). This same term is also found in Jdg. 9:37; 2 Kgs. 21:6; 2 Chr. 33:6; Isa. 2:6; 57:3; Jer. 27:9; Micah 5:12.
  5. your sorcerers (BDB 506, the NOUN occurs only here) ‒ This term (BDB 506, KB 503, note Mal. 3:5) basically means "to cut up"
    1. as in the shredding of ingredients for a magical potion
    2. cutting oneself as a way of getting the deity's attention (i.e. Syrian usage, cf. 1 Kgs. 18:28)
    3. This term was used to describe Pharaoh's wise men in Exod. 7:11 and Nebuchadnezzar's wise men in Dan. 2:2.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

▣ ". . .saying, 'You shall not serve the King of Babyon'" This was the extent of the false prophets' message. It seems to reflect 2 Sam. 7; 1 Chr. 17; and Isaiah's messages to Hezekiah. However, Jeremiah's new message reflected the reality of the conditional nature of YHWH's covenant promises. Biblical faith is more than

  1. a national origin
  2. a past religious event
  3. a parroting of liturgy
  4. a pilgrimage to a holy site or event

It is a daily, growing, intimate fellowship with our Creator. Fellowship was the purpose of creation (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: FAITH, BELIEVE, OR TRUST

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:10 "lie"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:10 "lie" This (BDB 1055) is placed first for emphasis.

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:11 This verse is illustrated in Jer. 40:9-12 and alluded to in Jer. 21:9; 38:2. YHWH is true to His promises. Even in judgment, obedience to His word brings its own reward (cf. Num. 21:4-9 [cf. John 3:14-15])!

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:12,17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:12,17 Jeremiah's words to King Zedekiah have urgency.

  1. bring your necks under the yoke ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  2. serve him ‒ BDB 712, KB 773, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. live ‒ BDB 310, KB 309, Qal IMPERATIVE

Several of these IMPERATIVES are repeated in Jer. 27:17 (i.e. #2, #3). Verse 12 is addressed to Zedekiah, while Jer. 27:17 is addressed to the priests and people (cf. Jer. 27:16).

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:15 "for I have not sent them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:15 "for I have not sent them" This statement is repeated in Jer. 23:21 and 29:9. I wonder if the false prophets thought He had or if they knew in their hearts they were speaking only for themselves (or because of political pressure).

I ask that because all speakers for God who do not receive verbal messages must wonder also! My only consolation is that I seek to communicate revelatory Scripture, not cultural or denominational personal opinions. Even then we face the task of application! I rest in the fact that

  1. God knows the heart
  2. the message of the NT is priority
  3. NT prophets are different from OT prophets (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT] and SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [NT])
  4. the Spirit is present with gospel proclaimers

It is uncertain how the inappropriate means of Jer. 27:9 are related to the methods of the false prophets of Judah or the surrounding pagan nations (cf. Jer. 27:3).

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:16 "the vessels"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:16 "the vessels" See Jer. 27:18; 1 Kgs. 7:15-20; Jer. 52:17ff. The first deportation had already occurred (cf. Jer. 27:20). However, the false prophets were asserting these taken items would be returned soon.

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:18 "if they are prophets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:18 "if they are prophets" Jeremiah puts them to the test of Deut. 13:1-3!

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:19 Several of the items of the temple were left.

  1. the pillars (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:15,21,22; 2 Kgs. 25:13,17)
  2. the sea (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:23-26; description in 2 Chr. 4:2-5)
  3. the stands (cf. 1 Kgs. 7:27-39)
  4. the rest of the vessels

See Jer. 52:17-23 where all are taken to Babylon, most placed in Marduk's temple.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 27:20 The exile of Jehoiachin is described in Jer. 22:28; 24:1; 2 Kgs. 24:12,14-16; 2 Chr. 36:10,18.

entries.title: Jeremiah 27:22 "Then I will bring them back"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
27:22 "Then I will bring them back" Here is the hope and promise realized in Ezra 1:7-11; 5:13-15; 7:19! YHWH sends away and YHWH brings back (see 1:10; Isa. 6:9-10)! He is sovereign in world affairs!

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:1 "the prophet"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:1 "the prophet" The LXX has "false prophet."

▣ "Gibeon" This was a Levite city (Josh. 21:17). Both of these "prophets" have the same credentials. Jeremiah was from a city of priests and both are called "the prophet" (cf. Jer. 28:5). Both use the same introductory formula, "Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel" (Jer. 28:2; 27:4,21).

How does the hearer know which to believe? This is a relevant question for believers in every age. I have several suggestions.

  1. my exegetical notes on
    1. Deut. 13:3 (second item)
    2. Deut. 18:20-22
  2. SPECIAL TOPIC: FALSE TEACHERS
  3. SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BIBLE (its uniqueness and inspiration)

▣ "in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying" Hananiah publically confronted Jeremiah, possibly at a yearly or monthly feast at the temple.

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
JEREMIAH 28

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
Hananiah's False Prophecy Hananiah's Falsehood and Doom The Yoke of the King of Babylon
(27:1-28:17)		 Jeremiah and the Prophet Hananiah The Dispute with Hananiah
28:1-4 28:1-4 28:1-4 28:1-4 28:1-4
28:5-9 28:5-9 28:5-9 28:5-9 28:5-9
28:10-11 28:10-11 28:10-11 28:10-11 28:10-11
28:12-16 29:12-17 28:12-16 28:12-14 28:12-14
28:15-16 28:15-16
28:17 28:17 28:17 28:17

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter is the dialog between two priests who both claim to be YHWH's prophets. The word "say" (BDB 55, KB 65) is used sixteen times.

  2. Only an accurate prediction can prove which is the true prophet (cf. Deut. 13:1-3; 18:15-22). Jeremiah's prophecy will be verified within one year.

  3. Hananiah predicts (cf. Jer. 28:1-4) a defeat of Babylon and a return of
    1. Jeconiah and the exiles
    2. temple vessels

  4. Jeremiah predicts the fall of Judah, her destruction, and total exile for seventy years! Who is speaking for God? Time will clearly tell!

  5. Remember, Jeremiah 27-29 is a literary unit.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:2 "The Lord of hosts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:2 "The Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts.

▣ "I have broken the yoke" The TENSE in Hebrew (Qal PERFECT) speaks of the act as already accomplished.

There is a sound play between

  1. "break," שׁבר ‒ BDB 990, KB 1402
  2. "bring back," שׁוב ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427

Both of these are used together two times (Jer. 28:2-4).

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:3-4 "vessels. . .Jeconiah. . .exiles of Judah. . .in two years"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:3-4 "vessels. . .Jeconiah. . .exiles of Judah. . .in two years" This prophecy was very specific and detailed. It spoke to the nationalistic prejudice of the Judean people. It was a repudiation of Jeremiah's sermon in Jeremiah 17. The people of Judah's reaction to this sermon is recorded in Jer. 26.

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:6 "Amen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:6 "Amen" Jeremiah wished Hananiah's message was true, but it was not!

For "amen" see SPECIAL TOPIC: AMEN.

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:8 This shows that the prophets read/knew the prophets before them. Previous revelation is a great blessing. Much of the biblical imagery and idioms is used again and again. The theological message of Jer. 28:8-9 is that the context of the message (i.e. war or peace) cannot be used to determine if the message is from a true prophet. Only accurate fulfillment (or repentance and God changing His mind) can do that!

On the subject of God changing His mind, let me take a moment to clarify.

  1. There are biblical texts that emphatically state God's character and purposes do not change.
    1. Gen. 6:6-7 (see full note there)
    2. Num. 23:19
    3. 1 Sam. 15:29
    4. Isa. 31:2
    5. Mal. 3:6 (see full note there)
    6. James 1:17
  2. There are biblical texts that clearly affirm that repentance and prayer affect God and His actions.
    1. Exod. 32:12
    2. Ps. 106:45
    3. Jer. 18:8; 26:3,13,19
    4. Amos 7:3,6
    5. Jonah 3:9,10; 4:2
      SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)
      SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

This is a good place to assert the often paradoxical nature of Eastern thought.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

▣ "ancient times" This is one use of the word 'olam, which has a wide semantic field.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣
NASB  "of calamity"
NKJV, NJB, JPSOA  "disaster"
NRSV, REB  "famine"
Peshitta  "of evil"

The MT has "of evil" (BDB 949, plus PREPOSITION) but many others suggest an emendation to "famine" (BDB 944).

  1. evil ‒ רעע
  2. famine ‒ רעב

Famine is the normal word used in this triad of plagues for disobedience (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28). The UBS Text Project, p. 257, gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:10 "took the yoke. . .broke it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:10 "took the yoke. . .broke it" This was possibly a violent act!

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:11 "Jeremiah went his way"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 28:11 "Jeremiah went his way" Why we don't know, but possibly because he had to wait for YHWH's reply.

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:12 "Jeremiah. . .Jeremiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:12 "Jeremiah. . .Jeremiah" The use of the personal name of the prophet seems to confirm that this section of chapters was penned by Baruch.

28:13
NASB, NKJV  "you have made"
TEV  "he will replace"
LXX  "I will"
NEB  "I will make"
REB  "you will get"
JPSOA, Peshitta  "you shall make"

The MT has "you" and the UBS Text Project, p. 257, gives it a "B" rating. The LXX seems to catch the meaning better, but usually the more difficult reading is closer to the original (i.e. autogrpah).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM, II. B.

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:14 YHWH will replace the wooden symbol with an iron symbol! Jeremiah's prophecy, not Hananiah's, will come to pass (cf. Jer. 28:15).

Verses 15-17 are YHWH's response through Jeremiah to Hananiah. He will die in the same year. His prophecy was considered "rebellion against the Lord!"

entries.title: Jeremiah 28:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
28:17 The prophecy of Hananiah's death within one year was a way to refute Hananiah's prophecy of "two years" (v. 3).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why was Jeremiah so disliked?
  2. Is all history really controlled by God? If so, think of the implications.
  3. Why is man so obsessed with knowing and altering the future? Is this prevalent today?
  4. Why is it that God's spokesmen are always rejected by their contemporaries?
  5. How do you know the false from the true prophets?
  6. Did Hananiah really believe he was a prophet?

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:1 "to the rest of the elders of the exile"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:1 "to the rest of the elders of the exile" The term "rest" (BDB 451 #1,2) can mean "remnant" or "residue," but also "preeminence" (#3, cf. Gen. 49:3). Some believe that many of the elders or leaders of the Jewish community had already been killed by Nebuchadnezzar II because of their treasonous activity, along with prophets (cf. Jer. 29:21-23; see UBS Text Project, p. 258).

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
JEREMIAH 29

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This is a rare example of personal correspondence during the period of the invasion and fall of the kingdom of Judah. This represents letters between the Jewish exiles in Babylon and the Jews in Jerusalem. There were two previous deportations by Nebuchadnezzar II (605 and 597 B.C.) before the city was completely destroyed in 586 B.C.

  2. There is some conjecture as to how many letters are combined in this chapter. The theories are:
    1. there is only one letter
    2. there are two letters: Jer. 29:1-14 and 29:15-32
    3. there are three letters: Jer. 29:1-15; 29:21-23; 29:31-32
    4. there are four letters: Jer. 29:1-14; 29:15-20; 29:21-23; 29:31-32
      It seems to me that there are probably four pieces of correspondence either being alluded to or comprising this chapter.

  3. Some see the date of this chapter as around 594 B.C.. for the following reasons.
    1. We know from secular literature (i.e. Babylonian Chronicles) that there were internal problems within the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
    2. Some prophets among the Jewish exiles seem to have been killed because they advocated rebellion, Jer. 29:21-22.
    3. This is the year that Zedekiah was required to show loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar II and this may be reflected in the coming of the officials to Babylon, Jer. 29:3.

  4. King Jeconiah, mentioned in Jer. 29:2, is really King Jehoiachin. His father, King Jehoiakim, had paid tribute to Nebuchadnezzar II for three years and then had rebelled. Before Nebuchadnezzar II could come militarily, Jehoiakim died. His son replaced him and apparently ruled with the help of his queen-mother. Nebuchadnezzar II arrived and exiled him to captivity after he had reigned only three months. He was replaced by another relative (uncle) of Josiah, Zedekiah.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NE0-BABYLON

  5. This chapter clearly presents YHWH's sovereignty in the actions of history. Notice the string of "I have. . ." or "I will . .." statements.
    1. I have sent into exile, Jer. 29:4,14,18,20
    2. I have not sent them (i.e. the false prophets in Babylon), Jer. 29:9
    3. I will visit you (i.e. in Babylon), Jer. 29:10
    4. I will fulfill My good word (i.e. to bring you back to Palestine), Jer. 29:10
    5. I have plans for you (two emphatic "I's"), Jer. 29:11
    6. I will listen to you (see note at Jer. 29:11-14), Jer. 29:12
    7. I will restore your fortunes, Jer. 29:14
    8. I will gather you from all the nations. . .where I have driven you, Jer. 29:14
    9. I will send upon them the sword, famine, and pestilence (i.e. the Jews still in Judah), Jer. 29:17
    10. I will make them like rotten fruit (i.e. the Jews still in Judah), Jer. 29:17
    11. I will pursue them with the sword, Jer. 29:18
    12. I sent to them again and again My servants (i.e. the prophets), Jer. 29:19
    13. I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar (i.e. false prophets killed in Babylon), Jer. 29:21
    14. I did not command them (i.e. the false prophets to speak), Jer. 29:23
    15. I am He who knows and am a witness, Jer. 29:23
    16. I am about to punish Shemaiah (i.e. false prophet), Jer. 29:32
    17. I am about to do (good) to My people (i.e. the Jews in Babylon), Jer. 29:32
      YHWH, unlike the lifeless idols, is active in the lives of His people for His larger redemptive purposes!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:2 The NASB and NKJV show Jer. 29:2 as a parenthesis, probably related in 2 Kgs. 24:12-16. The JPSOA has a dash separating Jer. 29:1 from Jer. 29:4. This may be an editorial addition to specify the exact historical setting.

The group of exiled leadership would match the exile of 596 B.C. (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:10-17).

  1. King Jeconiah (i.e. Jehoiachin)
  2. the queen mother (i.e. Nehushta, cf. 2 Kgs. 24:8)
  3. court officials
  4. children of Jeconiah (possibly 605 B.C., cf. Dan. 1:3)
  5. children of powerful families in Jerusalem (possibly 605 B.C., cf. Dan. 1:3)
  6. craftsmen (possibly taken into exile in 605 B.C.)
  7. smiths (possibly taken into exile in 605 B.C.)

▣ "the court officials" This literally is "eunuchs" (BDB 710). It is an Akkadian word which means "the one at the head." Usually this refers to those who had been castrated and put into public service. But, since Potiphar (Gen. 39:1) was married and has this same title, this term may have come to mean simply "a government official."

SPECIAL TOPIC: EUNUCHS

▣ "the craftsmen and the smiths" It is obvious that the first term means "craftsmen" or "artisan" (BDB 360), but the second term (BDB 689) in Hebrew is very uncertain (see note at Jer. 24:1). There is no unanimity about its meaning or origin.

We know that this exile occurred in 597 B.C. (2 Kgs. 24:14) and is alluded to in Jer. 52:28. The number of the exiles is somewhat different in these two passages and scholars are not exactly sure why.

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:3 "Elasah the son of Shaphan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:3 "Elasah the son of Shaphan" This is probably Ahikam's brother of Jer. 26:24, who helped Jeremiah during the royal reaction to his temple sermon. The father mentioned here was probably the scribe of Josiah (cf. 2 Kgs. 22:3,8,12).

▣ "Gemariah the son of Hilkiah" Although we know nothing about this man, his father may have been the high priest who is referred to in 2 Kgs. 22:4, but this is only conjecture.

▣ "whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon" The purpose for this may have been

  1. to pay tribute
  2. to assure Nebuchadnezzar II of Zedekiah's loyalty

These two men are supportive of Jeremiah and willingly, enthusiastically brought his letter to the exiles.

This VERB "send" (BDB 1018, KB 1511; Qal PERFECT) is used an unusual number of times in this chapter.

  1. letter sent, Jer. 29:1
  2. people sent, Jer. 29:3
  3. prophets YHWH did not send, Jer. 29:9,25,31
  4. YHWH sends the sword, famine, and pestilence, Jer. 29:17
  5. YHWH's word sent by His prophets, Jer. 29:19 (twice), 28,31

It is a common VERB but its repetition shows the problem—who speaks for God?

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:4 "whom I have sent into exile"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:4 "whom I have sent into exile" Again, throughout the account of this period God claims to be in control of history (i.e. Isa. 10:5; Jer. 25:9; 27:6). The exile is His judgment on Judah in order to bring His people back to personal faith in Him (cf. Jer. 29:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:5-8 "build houses. . .plant gardens. . .take wives"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:5-8 "build houses. . .plant gardens. . .take wives" Jeremiah's advice is to settle down and make life as normal as possible. Apparently the exiled Judeans were living in makeshift houses and some were even refusing to unpack. Jeremiah advises them to settle down for a long wait (i.e. 70 years). This very message is referred to in the letter by Shemaiah, a false prophet mentioned in Jer. 29:24,31-32. It must have seemed like treason to Judah's leaders.

Notice the commands in Jeremiah's letter (i.e. Jer. 29:5-8; also note Jer. 29:28).

  1. build houses ‒ BDB 124, KB 139, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. live in them ‒ BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. plant gardens ‒ BDB 642, KB 694, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. eat their produce ‒ BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERATIVE
  5. take wives ‒ BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. beget (i.e. have children) ‒ BDB 408, KB 441, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  7. take wives for your sons ‒ same as #5
  8. give your daughters ‒ BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERATIVE
  9. that they may bear ‒ BDB 408, KB 441, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  10. multiply there ‒ BDB 915, KB 1176, Qal IMPERATIVE
  11. do not decrease ‒ BDB 589, KB 611, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  12. seek the welfare of the city ‒ BDB 205, KB 233, Qal IMPERATIVE
  13. pray to the Lord on its behalf ‒ BDB 813, KB 933, Hithpael IMPERATIVE
  14. do not let your prophets. . .deceive you ‒ BDB 674, KB 728, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  15. do not listen to the dreams ‒ BDB 1033, KB 150, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

The whole point is, resume a normal as possible life. You will not be back in Judah until the 70 year prophecy (cf. Jer. 29:10) is fulfilled.

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:7 "seek the welfare of the city. . .and pray to the Lord on its behalf"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:7 "seek the welfare of the city. . .and pray to the Lord on its behalf" This is the only example in the OT of praying for one's enemies, particularly a Gentile city(s) of exile. Some have said that

  1. this refers to prayer at the local synagogue, which would be the beginning of this institution during the exilic period (see SPECIAL TOPIC: SYNAGOGUE)
  2. this may form the basis of the rabbinical admonition, followed by the NT, of praying for civil government (cf. Matt. 22:21; Rom. 13:1)

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:8 "let your prophets. . .your diviners. . .the dreams which they dream"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:8 "let your prophets. . .your diviners. . .the dreams which they dream" This is referring to false prophets among the exiles. Most of the letters recorded in this chapter are either about false prophets or are from false prophets. The list of what the prophets were doing is condemned in Lev. 19:26,31; 20:6; Deut. 18:9-13 (cf. Jer. 27:9-10). For a good discussion of dream interpretation, see John H. Walton, ANE Thought and the OT, p. 243.

It is important to note the biblical material on how to test a true prophet.

  1. OT, Deut. 13:1-5; 18:14-22
  2. NT, Matt. 7:15-27; 1 John 4:1-3)

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:10 "When seventy years have been completed for Babylon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:10 "When seventy years have been completed for Babylon" This same round number is mentioned in Jer. 25:11,12. Some see the time span

  1. from the fall of Nineveh, the capital of Syria in 612 B.C. to the fall of the capital of Babylon in 539 B.C.
  2. from the destruction of the first temple in 586 B.C. to the construction of the second temple in 516 B.C.
  3. from Nebuchadnezzar II becoming king in 605 B.C. to the fall of Babylon in 539 B.C.

The truth of the matter is that there is no literal seventy-year period about which scholars are unanimous. This seems to be a round number which refers to several generations or the normal life span of one individual.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #4

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS

▣ "I will visit you" This visit may be the vision of Ezekiel 1 and 10. YHWH leaves the temple because of its idolatry (Ezekiel 8) and comes to abide with the exiles in Babylon.

▣ "fulfill My good" This is described later in Jer. 29:10 as restoration to the land of promise (cf. Jer. 24:6-7).

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:11 The PRONOUN "I" (אנכי, BDB 59) is repeated twice for emphasis. YHWH will bring about His plans and purposes for His prophet and His people (see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).

YHWH's plan of restoration is clarified

  1. for welfare (BDB 1022, see SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE [shalom])
  2. not for calamity (BDB 449, such a common word in Jeremiah)
  3. give you a future
    1. the people's existence
    2. posterity, cf. Prov. 23:18; esp. 24:14
  4. give you a hope, cf. Prov. 23:18; 24:14; Ezek. 37:11

I remember years ago a student commented to me that this was her life verse. This is a wonderful promise of YHWH to a stressed prophet. The hermeneutical question is, "Can a modern person claim this promise for one's self?"

I remember commenting to this student, "Have you been called by God as a spokesperson? Have you been told not to marry and have children? Have your own family tried to kill you? Have you been rejected by leaders and thrown into a muddy cistern?

Proof texting is a modern problem. Modern intepreters must remember that the original intent is foundational. Every text has one and only one meaning, but many applications or significances!

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:11-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:11-14 This beautiful passage is an affirmation that the covenant has not been totally revoked. God would fulfill His Deuteronomic agreement with His people after this period of judgment (cf. Deuteronomy 27-28,30; Leviticus 26). The emphasis here is that His people must return to Him. Only a spiritually renewed remnant will return and be blessed (see SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT [three senses]).

Notice the conditions of blessing.

  1. you call upon Me ‒ BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal PERFECT with waw (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CALL ON THE NAME)
  2. come to Me ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Jer. 33:3; Isa. 55:6
  3. pray to Me ‒ BDB 813, KB 933, Hithpael PERFECT with waw
  4. seek me ‒ BDB 134, KB 152, Piel PERFECT with waw, cf. Deut. 4:29 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord)
  5. search for Me with all your heart ‒ BDB 205, KB 233, Qal IMPERFECT, i.e. total commitment, cf. Deut. 4:29; Jer. 24:7

All of these denote a worship experience that has become a lifestyle relationship.

Notice how YHWH responds (possible allusion to Deut. 30:3-5).

  1. I will listen to you, Jer. 29:12 ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Jer. 33:3
  2. you will find Me, Jer. 29:13 ‒ BDB 592, KB 619, Qal PERFECT with waw, cf. Deut. 4:29
  3. I will be found by you, Jer. 29:14 ‒ BDB 592, KB 619, Niphal PERFECT with waw
  4. I will restore your fortunes ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal PERFECT with waw (term often used of repenting)
  5. I will gather you from all the nations ‒ BDB 867, KB 1062, Piel PERFECT with waw, cf. Jer. 23:3; 31:8
  6. I will bring you back (i.e. to Palestine) ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427 (see #4), Hiphil PERFECT with waw

Modern Israel cannot be the fulfillment of prophecy because the vast majority of them are secular, non-observant Jews. Only a repentant and covenant-obedient people can claim the promises of YHWH from the Hebrew Bible.

The current theological emphasis on Israel as the "chosen people" is a result of John Darby's (1840's) new theological, eschatological theory called "Dispensationalism." I personally have become a Partial Preterist, which asserts Israel's covenant relationship was once and for all canceled in A.D. 70. If you would like more information on this understanding, please look at my exegetical, verse-by-verse commentaries on:

  1. Jesus' Olivet Discourse (i.e. Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21)
  2. Paul's discussion on "the man of lawlessness" (2 Thess. 2)
  3. John's book of Revelation

Also, please look at my free Bible study website, www.freebiblecommentary.org, for the "Special Topics" (second red box on home page).

  1. SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SECOND COMING
  2. SPECIAL TOPIC: SOON RETURN
  3. SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DELAYED SECOND COMING

In my opinion, there is no future anti-Christ, no seven year tribulation, and no secret rapture!

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:15 This verse seems to be an affirmation for the exiled Judeans that YHWH has true prophets among the exiles. But, the reality is that those who advocate a swift return are false prophets!

It is so difficult for even covenantly informed people to hear judgment oracles. We all want to claim the positive promises but forget the conditional nature of these divine pronouncements.

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:15-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:15-23 These verses seem to involve a second letter. It is interesting that Jer. 29:16-20 is not found in the LXX, which is the Greek translation of the OT (but is in all Hebrew MSS). This section seems to break the sequences between Jer. 29:15 and 21. Possibly these ancient Jewish translators saw this section simply as a repeat of Jer. 24:8-10. There are many repetitious passages in Jeremiah because it is obviously a book later edited around themes, not chronological sequence (an anthology).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:17 "the sword, famine, and pestilence"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:17 "the sword, famine, and pestilence" This is the threefold horror of ancient warfare (see note at Jer. 14:12). It is extremely significant that God's favor rests with Abraham's descendants in exile and not those remaining in Jerusalem. At this time apparently those left in Jerusalem were claiming spiritual superiority because they had been spared captivity, but in reality the opposite was true.

▣
NASB  "split-open"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB  "rotten"
JPSOA  "loathsome"
Peshitta  "bad"

This ADJECTIVE (BDB 1045) has several meanings (KB 1613-1615). The NASB gets its translation from KB 1614 II, Syrian "to split" or Arabic "to break open." This ADJECTIVE is found only here in the OT but bad figs are mentioned in Jer. 24:2.

The same three consonants are found in the word for "horrible thing" (BDB 1045) in Jer. 5:30; 18:13; 23:14, but it is uncertain if it is related etymologically.

As with so many of these rare words, the context is clear even if the word is not. Meaning is not affected!

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:18 See notes at Jer. 24:9-10.

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:19 Here is the recurrent problem. Humans, even covenant humans, do not listen and obey YHWH's words/message/covenant (cf. Jer. 6:19)! Obedience is a marker of devotion (cf. Luke 6:46). SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

Notice that the same series of words beginning with ש is found in Jer. 25:4 (BDB 1018, 1014, 1033).

Also see the note at Jer. 7:13 for the Hebrew idiom "again and again."

▣ "My servants the prophets" See SPECIAL TOPIC: SERVANT LEADERSHIP, I.

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:20 "hear the word of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:20 "hear the word of the Lord" This VERB (BDB 1033, KB 1570; Qal IMPERATIVE) can be translated (examples from NIV):

  1. hear ‒ Jer. 2:4; 5:21; 6:19; 7:2; 10:1; 13:15; 17:20; 19:3; 21:11; 22:2; 31:10; 42:15; 44:24,26; 49:20; 50:45
  2. obey ‒ Jer. 7:23; 11:4,7; 35:13; 38:20
  3. listen ‒ Jer. 11:2,6
  4. proclaim ‒ Jer. 4:5,16; 5:20; 46:14 (twice); 50:2
  5. summon ‒ Jer. 50:29; 51:27

This is the crucial covenant issue! The Mosaic Covenant was a conditional covenant linked to human obedience.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE MOSAIC LAW AND THE CHRISTIAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEW OF THE MOSAIC LAW

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:21 "Lord of hosts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:21 "Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts.

▣ "Ahab. . .Zedekiah" These were false prophets who were in Babylon and who apparently would be publicly executed by Nebuchadnezzar II. We learn from Ezekiel 13 that there were other false prophets in exile also. This entire literary unit, chapters 26-29, seems to be related by the theme of false prophets.

The Expositor's Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 556, and the NASB Study Bible, p. 1103, make the interesting comment that there is a purposeful word play between

  1. Kolaiah ‒ BDB 877, קוליה
  2. curse ‒ BDB 887, קללה
  3. roast ‒ BDB 885 I, קלה

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:22 "May the Lord make you like"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:22 "May the Lord make you like" This verse reflects an ancient proverb and curse formula.

▣ "roasted in fire" We have learned from the Code of Hammurabi (i.e. King of Babylon from 1792-1750 B.C.) that this was a common public means of execution (cf. Section 25:110,157). These prophets betrayed themselves by their lifestyle (cf. Jer. 29:23; 7:15-23; Matt. 7:15-27).

29:23
NASB  "acted foolishly"
NKJV  "disgraceful things"
NRSV  "perpetrated outrage"
TEV  "terrible sins"
NJB  "scandalous things"
REB  "outrage"
JPSOA  "vile"
Peshitta  "have done wickedness"

This NOUN (BDB 615, KB 663) obviously has a wide semantic field, but it denotes some kind of evil thought or act. It denotes someone who acts inappropriately either mentally or morally (cf. Gen. 34:7; Deut. 22:21; Josh. 7:15; Jdg. 19:23-24; 20:6,10; 1 Sam. 25:25; 2 Sam. 13:12; Job 42:8; Isa. 9:17; 32:6). In this context of Jer. 29:23 (its only use in Jeremiah) it describes the actions of two false prophets.

  1. adultery (i.e. spiritual adultery, cf. Jer. 23:14)
  2. spoken falsely in YHWH's name (cf. Jer. 2:8; 23:13)

▣ "in Israel" This does not speak so much of geographical Israel as genealogical Israel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "I am He who knows, and am a witness" This is the affirmation that YHWH judges the heart as well as the deeds (cf. Jer. 7:11; 16:17; 17:10; 32:19; Prov. 5:21; 1 Cor. 4:5; Heb. 4:13). This should be a warning to all those who claim to speak for God!

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:24 "Shemaiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:24 "Shemaiah" This is a reference to another false prophet in exile who apparently wrote letters to the priestly leaders in Jerusalem encouraging them to judge and punish Jeremiah for his treasonous statements (cf. Jer. 29:27).

▣ "the Nehelamite" This refers either to the name of a city whose site is unknown or it is a form of the root "to dream" (Niphal PARTICIPLE), which may refer to his being a prophet (i.e. Deuteronomy 13).

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:25 "Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:25 "Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest" This man is referred to in Jer. 21:1; 37:3; 52:24; 2 Kgs.25:18.

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:26 "Jehoiada"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:26 "Jehoiada" This is possibly the person left in charge of the temple police (cf. 2 Kings 11).

▣ "every madman" The term "madman" (BDB 993), alluding to Jeremiah, was originally used of animal sounds (i.e. pigeon, camel), but came to denote human sounds of a deranged person howling or shouting in anger. It is true that the prophets of the older sections of the OT had these kinds of actions (i.e. 1 Sam. 10:9-13). It was used of prophets in

  1. 2 Kgs. 9:11
  2. Hosea 9:7

It was a slur to discredit the actions and words of a speaker for YHWH, here Jeremiah (i.e. in stocks in Jer. 20:2). It disregarded the message because of the way in which it was delivered. Even though part of Jeremiah's prophecy had come true, the vast majority of the leaders of Judah still thought that Jeremiah was a treasonous, insane person.

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 29:28 This is a reference to Jeremiah's message recorded in Jer. 29:5-6

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:31 "he has made you trust in a lie"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:31 "he has made you trust in a lie" This same phrase is used in Jer. 28:15. It is referring to the messages of peace and rapid restoration coming from the false prophets in both the Jewish community in Babylon and the Judean capital of Jerusalem. Ezekiel well describes these false prophets in Ezek. 13:2-3,22; 22:28.

The concept of "lie" (BDB 1044) can denote

  1. idols (cf. Jer. 10:14; 13:25; 51:17)
  2. false messages (cf. Jer. 14:14; 18:8; 20:6; 23:5,6; 27:10,14,16; 28:15; 29:9)
  3. false testimony (cf. Jer. 5:2; 37:14)
  4. unbelief
  5. rejecting YHWH's true message/messenger for a false one (cf. Jer. 28:16)

entries.title: Jeremiah 29:32 "he shall not have anyone living among this people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
29:32 "he shall not have anyone living among this people" Jeremiah pronounces judgment on this false prophet in the total eradication of all of his relatives and descendants. To a Jew this was a horrifying prospect.

▣ "because he has preached rebellion against the Lord" Notice that the rejection of YHWH's prophet is the rejection of YHWH.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How many letters seems to be involved or mentioned in this chapter?
  2. Explain the historical background of Jeremiah 29.
  3. Why were Jeremiah's words believed to be treasonous?
  4. What are the implications of Jer. 29:7?
  5. Is seventy years meant to be a symbolic or literal figure?
  6. How do you know a false prophet?
