entries.title: Jeremiah 32:1 "the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:1 "the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar" This would make the date 587 B.C. Nebuchadnezzar's father, Nabopolassar (626 - 605 B.C.), was the founder of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. When the last strong king of Assyria (Ashurbanipal) died in 626 B.C.., Nabopolassar rebelled. He started a new empire which was very successful. In 605 B.C., after the death of Nabopolasser, Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 B.C.) returned to Babylon to be crowned. This was after his successful battle at Carchemish, where he defeated the remnant of the Assyrian army and Pharaoh Necho's Egyptian army at the headwaters of the Euphrates. After being crowned king he returned to this area to subdue Palestine.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
JEREMIAH 32

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
Jeremiah Imprisoned Jeremiah Buys a Field Jeremiah Purchases Land in Anathoth Jeremiah Buys a Field Jeremiah Buys a Field in Token of Future Prosperity
32:1-5 32:1-5 32:1-5 32:1-5 32:1-5
32:6-8 32:6-12 32:6-8 32:6-15 32:6-15
32:9-15 32:9-15
32:13-15
Jeremiah Prays and God Explains Jeremiah Prays For Understanding Jeremiah's Prayer
32:16-25 32:16-25 32:16-25 32:16-23 32:16-25
God's Assurance of the People's Return 32:24-25
32:26-35 32:26-35 32:26-35 32:26-35 32:26-27
A Promise of Hope 32:28-35
32:36-44 32:36-41 32:36-41 32:36-41 32:36-44
32:42-44 32:42-44 32:42-44

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Jeremiah 30-33 forms a literary unit commonly referred to as "the Book of Consolation."
    1. Jeremiah 30 and 31 describe God's "new covenant" (i.e. Jer. 31:31-34) with His people
    2. Jeremiah 32 and 33 describe the symbolic act (i.e. the purchase of land right before the exile) which assures His people of future restoration

  2. From other parts of Jeremiah we learn the exact historical setting of Jer. 32.
    1. From Jer. 39:1 we know the exact date that the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar II began, in the ninth year of Zedekiah in the tenth month. This means that we can date Jeremiah 32 to around the year of 588 or 587 B.C.
    2. From Jer. 37:5 we learn that there was a brief respite in the siege of Jerusalem because of the appearance of the Egyptian army in Palestine. However, the Egyptians and Babylonians never fought and the siege of Jerusalem was renewed quickly.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:2 This new place of imprisonment (cf. Jer. 38:13,28; 39:14) was an improvement of the prophet's situation. He had originally been placed in a cistern and was in danger of death (cf. chapter 38).

▣ "the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard, which was in the house of the king of Judah" There seem to be several places of confinement.

  1. a place where (cf. Neh. 3:25) something like house arrest in a royal building (cf. Jer. 32:2,8,12; 33:1; 37:21; 39:14,15)
    1. Jeremiah could receive visitors (cf. Jer. 32:8,12)
    2. his scribe was allowed to be with him
    3. other Judean prisoners, possibly people who agreed with Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 32:12)
    4. he had personal money available (cf. Jer. 32:9)
  2. a place related to a royal son (i.e. Malchijah) which had a cistern in the middle of the courtyard (cf. Jer. 38:6,12,28)
  3. a dungeon in the house of Jonathan the scribe (Jer. 37:15-17); Jeremiah saw this as a death sentence

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:3 This summarizes Jeremiah's prophetic message inside Jerusalem as the Neo-Babylonian army lay siege to the city (cf. Jer. 21:3-7; 27:12-15).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:4 "but he will surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:4 "but he will surely be given into the hand of the king of Babylon" The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Niphal IMPERFECT) is intensified by the addition of the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root.

The term "hand" is a Hebrew idiom for "power." See SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

The term "Chaldean" has several possible meanings.

  1. an ethnic group
  2. a language
  3. a group of Babylonian wise men

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "and he will speak with him face to face and see him eye to eye" This Hebrew idiom speaks of a personal encounter (cf. Jer. 39:5). We learn from 2 Kgs. 25:4-7 that Zedekiah's family was put to death before his eyes and then his eyes were blinded and he was taken into exile.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:5 "until I visit him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:5 "until I visit him" This VERB (BDB 823, KB 955, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is used several times in Jeremiah as both positive and negative constructions. YHWH's "visit" means His presence.

  1. positive (i.e. care for)
    1. Jer. 15:15
    2. Jer. 23:2 (negated but the action is positive)
    3. Jer. 27:22
    4. Jer. 29:10
    5. Ruth 1:6
    6. Psalm 65:19; 106:4
  2. negative (i.e. punish)
    1. Jer. 5:9,29; 6:6,15; 9:9,25; 11:22; 14:10; 21:14; 23:34; 25:12; 27:8; 29:32; 30:20; 32:5; 36:31; 44:13,29; 46:25; 49:8; 50:18,31; 51:44,47,52 (52:11 BDB 824 describes Zedekiah's fate)

Zedekiah was blinded after he was forced to watch his sons killed, along with the princes of Judah. He was exiled to Babylon, where he died in prison (cf. Jer. 52:10-11).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:7 God tells Jeremiah what is going to happen even before the events occur so that he will have confidence in the strange purchase God demands (cf. Jer. 32:8).

▣ "the right of redemption" This is discussed in Lev. 25:25-31 and alluded to in Ruth 4:1-12. It is often called the right of the Go'el (i.e. the Kinsman Redeemer). It is interesting that Jeremiah's family would request that he purchase a field for the following reasons.

  1. Jeremiah had no descendants
  2. his family had betrayed and rejected him earlier

It is important for Jeremiah to accomplish this symbolic act of hope. The closer the fall of Jerusalem came to reality the more Jeremiah's prophecy turned to the hope of restoration (see chapters 30-33, the Book of Consolation).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:8 "Hanamel my uncle's son"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:8 "Hanamel my uncle's son" Jeremiah's cousin from Anathoth came to see him in the court of the guard (i.e. the place of his imprisonment). The very fact that this man could travel and enter Jerusalem shows that the siege had been lifted (i.e. because of the brief appearance of the Egyptian army). Some have asserted that he wanted to sell the land because

  1. he was afraid of the obvious Neo-Babylonian defeat of Judah and Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 32:25)
  2. he was in great debt
  3. he was testing Jeremiah's message about the future hope
  4. the truth is that we do not know the psychological motivations of many of the persons mentioned in the Bible

▣ "Then I knew that this was the word of the Lord" I think we sometimes assume that the OT prophets did not have to live by faith since they were spoken to audibly by God. This is a good example that the prophet had to live by faith also and was not 100% sure that this was the word of God until it was fulfilled. This shows that any dogmatism as to exactly how God communicated with the prophets is probably unfounded.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:9 "Anathoth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:9 "Anathoth" This city, very close to Jerusalem, is where the family of the ousted priestly line of Eli was exiled by the will of Solomon because the current priest from the line of Eli, Abiathar, supported Adonijah's claim to David's throne (cf. 1 Kgs. 1:7; 2:26). Jeremiah was a priest not of the line of Zadok, but of Abiathar.

▣ "weighed out the silver for him, seventeen shekels of silver" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE WEIGHTS AND VOLUMES

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:10-11 "I signed and sealed. . .and called in witnesses, and weighed out. . .the sealed copy. . .the open copy"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:10-11 "I signed and sealed. . .and called in witnesses, and weighed out. . .the sealed copy. . .the open copy" This reflects the ancient legal procedures of buying a piece of property. This has been confirmed archaeologically from the Elephantine Papyri from the fifth century B.C., which was found in Egypt on an island in the Nile River.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:12 "Baruch"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:12 "Baruch" This is the first mention of Jeremiah's private and personal secretary. He was probably the editor and recorder of most of Jeremiah's sermons and messages. He is mentioned in chapters 32; 43; 45, but mostly in chapter 36.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:14 "put them in an earthenware jar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:14 "put them in an earthenware jar" This method of preservation of documents has been confirmed archaeologically, not only by the Elephantine Papyri but also the Dead Sea Scrolls.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:15 "Houses and fields and vineyards"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:15 "Houses and fields and vineyards" It is interesting that "vineyards" are mentioned specifically. It took a number of years for a vineyard to grow and become productive. Judah will be destroyed but a restoration is coming after 70 years.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:16-25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:16-25 Jeremiah bought the field as a symbol of trust in YHWH and His promises, but apparently he still had some degree of doubt. These verses are a strophe recording Jeremiah's prayer to God who tries to assure him:

  1. by using the prophet's very same words from Jer. 32:7
  2. by reminding him of His gracious acts to the seed of Abraham (cf. Neh. 9:9-38)

The Jewish Study Bible, p. 993, has an interesting comment on this paragraph.

"Jeremiah's prayer to God provides the basic outline of God's relationship with Israel from the Exodus and articulates his veiw that the Babylonian invasion and siege is a divinely ordained punishment for Israel's disobedience of God's teaching (v. 23)."

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:17 This verse expresses the recurrent emphasis on YHWH as the creator Deity (i.e. monotheism, see SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM). The idols cannot

  1. act
  2. predict
  3. hear

but YHWH can and does do all these things! He has a purpose for His creation and is actively involved in His world.

▣ "the heavens and the earth" This phrase goes back to Gen. 1:1. Genesis 1 is primarily about the

  1. creation of this planet
    SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN (OT)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH (erets)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH
  2. organization of this planet into a place to sustain plant, animal, and human life. See John H. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One: An ancient Cosmology

▣ "the heavens and the earth" This phrase goes back to Gen. 1:1. Genesis 1 is primarily about the

  1. creation of this planet
    SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN (OT)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY PLANET (erets)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: THE AGE AND FORMATION OF THE EARTH
    SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH
  2. organization of this planet into a place to sustain plant, animal, and human life. See John H. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One: An Ancient Cosmology

▣ "Your outstretched arm" This is an anthropomorphic phrase. See full note at Jer. 27:15.

▣ "Nothing is too difficult for You" This is asserting that YHWH can accomplish Judah's fall and rebuilding (cf. Jer. 1:10; 31:28). This truth clearly states the sovereignty of God (cf. Gen. 18:14; Jer. 32:27; Matt. 19:26).

For the word "difficult" (BDB 810) see SPECIAL TOPIC: WONDERFUL THINGS.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:18 This is a wonderful list of the characteristics of God. Similar lists can be found in Exod. 34:6-7; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8). What a great God. He will not give up on His purpose of fellowship with His fallen human creatures!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "shows lovingkindness to thousands, but repays the iniquity of fathers into the bosom of their children after them" This is an allusion to Deut. 5:9 and 7:9. Jeremiah is a prophet of the Mosaic covenant (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT], IV.) and his phraseology and theology reflect the book of Deuteronomy.

This is a very important quote because it shows the relationship between the wrath of God and the love of God. The wrath of God, based on Deut. 5:9, goes to the third and fourth generations, while the love of God, Deut. 7:9, goes to the thousandth generation.

There is both a corporate aspect to sin and an individual aspect (cf. Ezekiel 18). Both sin and faith run through families!

▣ "lovingkindness" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS (hesed)

▣ "thousands" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

▣ Notice the different phrases in this context for Israel's Deity.

  1. Lord (i.e. YHWH), Jer. 32:1,6,17,26,27,28,42,44; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.
  2. Lord of hosts, Jer. 32:14,15,18; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS
  3. God of Israel (i.e. Elohim), vv.14,15,25,38; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.
  4. Lord (i.e. Adon), Jer. 32:17,25; see SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)
  5. O great and mighty God, Jer. 32:18 (El, see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, A.)
  6. the God of all flesh, Jer. 32:27 (cf. Num. 16:22; 27:16)
  7. the Lord God of Israel (i.e. YHWH and Elohim), Jer. 32:36

One descriptive phrase that is unusual, "with all My heart and with all My soul" (cf. Jer. 32:41). What a shocking physical (anthropomorphic) phrase to describe the trustworthy commitment of the eternal, ever-present, non-corporal Deity (notice the powerful, moving example in Hosea 11:8-9).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:19 "whose eyes are open to all the ways of the sons of men (Adam)"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:19 "whose eyes are open to all the ways of the sons of men (Adam)" There are two ways to understand this phrase.

  1. The Creator cares about His creation, especially His human creatures (i.e. Gen. 1:26-27; 3:8). This seems to be the emphasis of v. 20.
  2. The Creator watches humans to denote their wickedness (i.e. according to their deeds; note Job 34:21-22).

▣ "giving to everyone according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds" This truth is also mentioned in Jer. 17:10 (see full note there). We reap what we sow (see full list of Scripture texts at Gal. 6:7 online). Thank God for grace and forgetfulness (i.e. Isa. 1:18; 38:17; 43:25; 44:22; Ezek. 18:22; 33:16; Ps. 103:10-14; Mic. 7:19).

In the OT this is the obvious outcome of a performance-based covenant (i.e. Mosaic covenant). In the NT it becomes the evidence of a new relationship with God through Christ. Believers are new creatures in Christ, led by the Spirit into daily Christlikeness. Godly living is not the basis of that new relationship, but the natural outcome of a new heart, new mind, new spirit (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36). The good works are the confirmation, the evidence of our free salvation!

Ephesians 1:4 and 2:8-10 have helped me see this truth.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:20 YHWH is active in the lives of the descendants of Abraham. However, He also has a plan (i.e. "among mankind") for all people. He wants His name known among all the nations (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36) that they may come to Him (cf. Gen. 12:3; Exod. 19:5; Ps. 22:27; 66:1-4; 86:9-10; Isa. 2:2-4; 25:6-9; 42:6-10; 45:22-23; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 56:6-8; 60:1-3; 66:23; Micah 4:1-4; Mal. 1:11).

This phrase, "even to this day both in Israel and among mankind," clearly reflects YHWH's wider purpose. Genesis 3:15 is a promise to mankind, not to Abraham's seed only.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ This same imagery used of the Exodus is found in Deut. 4:34; 7:19; 26:8.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:20-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:20-22 This is a reference to the major historical act of YHWH's deliverance from Egypt and bringing the people into the Promised Land as He had promised their forefathers (cf. Gen. 15:12-21).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:22 "a land flowing with milk and honey"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:22 "a land flowing with milk and honey" This is not only a descriptive phrase (cf. Jer. 11:5), but the title for Palestine found in Assyrian documents.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:23 "but they did not obey Your voice or walk in Your law"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:23 "but they did not obey Your voice or walk in Your law" This was the problem. There was a conditional covenant between YHWH and Israel. Israel had failed to keep the conditions (i.e. Jer. 31:32; Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; 30:15,19; Psalm 1). Therefore, the Judean exile reflects YHWH's abrogating (or at least modifying) of this covenant, but He will inaugurate a "new covenant" (Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36). As a Christian I believe this is what Jesus did (cf. Matt. 26:26-29; Luke 22:19-20; 1 Cor. 11:24-26; 2 Cor. 3:6; Heb. 8:7-13; 9:15; 12:24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:24 "the siege mounds"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:24 "the siege mounds" In the ANE walled cities were captured by surrounding them, thereby cutting off the food supply. At the sign of danger the people from the surrounding villages fled to the walled cities. Therefore, the water, sanitation, and food systems were stressed. The enemy built dirt mounds against the wall(s). These mounds supported wooden, mobile A-frames which held a ramming mechanism (cf. Jer. 6:6; 33:4; Isa. 37:33). These rams would hit the stone/brick wall again and again in one place until they crumbled.

▣ "the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans" This VERB "given" (BDB 675, KB 733, Niphal PERFECT is a future event but stated as a current certainty. This grammatical form has been designated a "PROPHETIC PERFECT." God's word is sure.

▣ "Chaldeans" See SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS.

▣ "the sword, the famine and the pestilence" See full note at Jer. 14:12.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:26-44
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:26-44 This is YHWH's reply to Jeremiah's prayer. It covers several aspects of judgment and several wonderful promises of future hope.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:27 "the God of all flesh; is anything too difficult for Me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:27 "the God of all flesh; is anything too difficult for Me" This is God's affirmation that Jeremiah's theology was accurate (i.e. monotheism) and his doubts were unfounded.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:28 Jerusalem will fall to the Neo-Babylonians!

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:29 The city of Jerusalem will be burned because of its idolatrous practices (cf. Jer. 32:30; Ezekiel 8), as the Canaanite cities were burned in the conquest (cf. Deut. 3:6).

▣ "Baal" The worship of Ba'al (the male fertility god of the Canaanites) was somehow connected with the astral deities (i.e. Babylonian, cf. Jer. 8:2; 19:13). Possibly the Babylonian deities (which were called on by name and rituals) became known to Palestine through political alliance treaties.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:30 This is a good place to demonstrate the difficulty in defining "Israel." In this verse it is used both of

  1. the northern ten tribes (i.e. their collective term)
  2. the descendants of Abraham (i.e. "sons of Israel," second usage)

Only context can tell the difference after the United Monarchy, under Saul, David, Solomon, split in 922 B.C. into two separate nations.

  1. Judah, Benjamin, Simeon, and most of the Levitical priests (i.e. Levi) became Judah.
  2. The other ten tribes became Israel, also known as Ephraim or Samaria.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:31
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:31 This is a strange verse! It seems to imply that Jerusalem (and by implication, the temple) was not pleasing to YHWH, even from their beginnings. This is surely hyperbolic, but does clearly show YHWH's reaction to His people worshiping other gods (who are not gods).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:32 The entire population, from king to peasants, were unfaithful, disobedient, and idolatrous. Even those who should have known better (priests, prophets) did not obey!

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:33-35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:33-35 These verses describe how serious their rebellion was.

  1. They turned their backs to God (no respect, cf. Jer. 18:17; no worship, cf. Jer. 2:27).
  2. They should have faced Him (i.e. intimate, personal relationship illustrated in worship and life).
  3. YHWH spoke (through His prophets) again and again (cf. similar idiomatic statements in Jer. 7:13,25; 11:7; 25:3,4; 26:5,19; and also note Hosea 11:2).
  4. They would not listen or heed the words of YHWH.
  5. They put idols in YHWH's temple (cf. Jer. 7:30; 2 Kgs. 23:4; 2 Chronicles 33; Ezekiel 8).
  6. They built high places to Ba'al (cf. Jer. 19:5).
  7. They worshiped, by child sacrifice, the fertility god, Molech (cf. Jer. 7:31; Lev. 18:21; 20:2-5).

The MT, verse 33, has a series of three INFINITIVE ABSOLUTES. This same thing is repeated with different VERBALS in v. 44.

Verse 33 is negative action, while v. 44 is positive action of hope and restoration.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:34 "the house which is called by My name"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:34 "the house which is called by My name" This refers to the temple (cf. Jer. 7:10,11,14,30). This reflects the language of Deuteronomy, "the place I will cause My name to dwell" (cf. Deut. 12:5,11,14,18,21,26; 14:23,24; 15:20; 16:2,6,11,15; 17:8,10; 18:6; 26:2; 31:11).

For more information see Deut. 12:5 and 26:2 online at www.freebiblecommentary.org

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:35 "they built the high places of Baal"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:35 "they built the high places of Baal" YHWH's altars are always constructed with uncut stones (cf. Exod. 20:25; Deut. 27:5-6; Josh. 8:31). However, Ba'al altars were usually located on local high places (i.e. hill, ridge), but if there was no elevation available, the worshipers would build a raised platform of cut (i.e. formed) stones on which to place

  1. an uplifted stone (i.e. phallic symbol) representing the male fertility god
  2. a carved piece of wood or a live tree representing the female fertility goddess, or possibly the "tree of life," which was common imagery in ANE mythology

▣ "which I had not commanded them nor had it entered My mind that they should do this abomination" Child sacrifice was part of the worship of Molech, cf. Lev. 18:21; 20:2-5; Deut. 12:31; 18:10; 2 Kgs. 21:1-7; Jer. 19:5). There may have been some confusion about the child sacrifice being the will of God because of the account of Abraham offering Isaac at God's command in Genesis 22 (or even the death of Job's children in Job 1). A reflection of this misunderstanding is seen in Micah 6:7.

YHWH clearly and emphatically rejects this false understanding of worship.

For "Ben-hinnom" see note at Jer. 31:40 (i.e. "the valley of dead bodies and of the ashes").

For "abomination" see SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:36
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:36 This was Jeremiah's basic message to Judah. It made him

  1. treated as a traitor
  2. rejected by his own family
  3. persecuted by the authorities

But, it was YHWH's message (cf. Jer. 32:24,28).

▣ "by sword, by famine and pestilence" These are the oft repeated idioms involving invasion and siege warfare. The covenant disobedience curses are becoming a reality (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28). The Mosaic covenant is a conditional covenant with consquences, both positive and negative!

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:36-44
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:36-44 As so often occurs in the prophets, a judgment oracle is followed by a promise oracle. The judgment was horrible and deserved (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28), but the restoration is glorious and sure (i.e. Ps. 103:8-14).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:37
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:37 YHWH's mercy (Jer. 32:37c) does not dull His reaction to sin, disobedience, and rebellion.

  1. in My anger
  2. in My wrath
  3. in great indignation

Sin can be forgiven (i.e. Manasseh on his deathbed, cf. 2 Chr. 33:12-13,15-16), but the consequences continue through time.

Verse 37 describes the post-judgment actions of YHWH. This is the future promise.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:38 "They shall be My people, and I will be their God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 32:38 "They shall be My people, and I will be their God" This is covenant language (cf. Jer. 30:22; 31:1). This has always been YHWH's desire. This will be the culmination of the "new covenant" (cf. Rev. 21-22).

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:39 "and I will give them one heart and one way"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:39 "and I will give them one heart and one way" There is a tension between humans making a new heart, Ezek. 18:31, and God giving a new heart, Ezek. 36:26; Jer. 31:33. This paradoxical relationship is normative throughout the Bible (i.e. covenant). God always takes the initiative but humans must respond in faith, repentance, obedience, and perseverance. However, the Fall of Genesis 3 made it impossible for humans, even the faith seed of Abraham, to fulfill God's covenant desires. Therefore, the need of a new heart, new mind, new spirit!

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ Notice what the visible outcome of a "new heart" is.

  1. respect ("fear") of YHWH always (see SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)
  2. the abundance/prosperity/peace of those who know Him (cf. Jer. 32:41a, as a witness to the nations)
  3. stable, happy societies, generation after generation

This was always the desire of God for humanity. We were created for fellowship with Him (cf. Jer. 31:34; Gen. 1:26-27; 3:8).

If there is no visible change, there is no new heart (cf. Matt. 7:15-27 and the NT books of James and 1 John)! God wants a people to reflect His character to a lost and needy world. Conversion demands transformation (cf. Matthew 13; Eph. 2:8-10). Eternal life has observable characteristics!

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:40 "and I will make an everlasting covenant with them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:40 "and I will make an everlasting covenant with them" The new term found here is the term "everlasting" (cf. Isa. 55:3; 61:8; Ezek. 16:60; 37:26). The Hebrew here is rather ambiguous. We know from further history that the returning exiles do not faithfully fulfill the covenant either. There has always been a conditional element built into the covenant. God has always been willing to make the covenant permanent but mankind continues to rebel.

This is a good example of the semantic field of 'olam (BDB 761, KB 798). The older covenants mentioned in the Hebrew Bible were also called "eternal."

  1. Noah (and all mankind) ‒ Gen. 9:11-17 (i.e. the rainbow)
  2. Abraham ‒ Gen. 17:1-8 (esp. v. 7); Ps. 105:9a
  3. Isaac ‒ Gen. 17:19; Ps. 105:9b
  4. to Jacob ‒ Ps. 105:10
  5. aspects of corporate Israel's worship ‒ Gen. 17:9-14; Exod. 31:16; Lev. 24:8
  6. Phineas the priest's actions involving YHWH's wrath on Israel ‒ Num. 25:10-13
  7. David ‒ 2 Sam. 23:1-7 (also note 2 Sam. 7)
  8. Noah's eternal covenant canceled ‒ Isa. 24:1-6
  9. the universal invitation of Isa. 55 (esp. v. 3)
  10. Israel's remnant ‒ Isa. 61:1-9; Jer. 50:4-5
  11. Patriarchal covenants remembered ‒ Ezek. 16:60-63
  12. New Covenant of Jer. 31:31-34 ‒ Jer. 32:40; Heb. 8:6-13

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:41
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:41 We see again an anthropomorphic phrase used for the intensity of God's love for Israel (cf. Hosea 11:8,9; Jer. 8:18-9:16). See SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE.

The last part of this verse has three phrases which describe YHWH's commitment to His gracious acts toward a restored/repentant Judah.

  1. "faithfully" ‒ BDB 54, see SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT
  2. with all My heart" ‒ used only here in the OT, see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART
  3. "with all My soul" ‒ this is another surprising use of a term which is used of humans (Gen. 2:7) and animals (Gen. 1:24; 2:19) ‒ nephesh (BDB 659, KB 711, see notes online at Gen. 35:18; Lev. 11:17; and Ezek. 18:4; and SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH)

YHWH is accommodating Himself to physical human language to make His point to Jeremiah.

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:42
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:42 God is the source of all things (i.e. one causality in the universe). If there is only one God, then basically He either allows or uses both good and evil. This is the affirmation of the OT. The OT recognized no secondary causes!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

entries.title: Jeremiah 32:44
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
32:44 The promises of restoration are multi-fulfillment oracles. These promises were meant to be a reality to the post-exilic Judean community and, in one sense, they were. However, the "eternal covenant" was broken again as the interbiblical (Seleucid) and Roman periods clearly demonstrate. For me these promises to national Israel must be re-evaluated in light of the life and teaching of Jesus. If the NT is revelation, then it must be noted that the national promises have been universalized, which was always YHWH's intent. Please look at the following Special Topic; it shows my biases and meta-narrative orientation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO OT COVENANT PROMISES SEEM SO DIFFERENT FROM NT COVENANT PROMISES?)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:2 This is one of several references in Jeremiah to YHWH as creator.

  1. The first VERB "made" (BDB 793, KB 889, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) is used in a parallel way to "create" (BDB 135, KB 153, cf. Gen. 1:1), which is clearly seen in Gen. 1:7,16,25; 3:1. YHWH made the earth (LXX), which is denoted in the MT by the PRONOUN "it." However, it could refer to His eternal redemptive plan (JPSOA; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN).
  2. The second VERB "formed" (BDB 427, KB 428, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) is also used often of YHWH as creator
    1. Adam ‒ Gen. 2:7,8
    2. Israel as a covenant nation ‒ Isa. 27:11; 43:1,21; 44:21; 45:9,11; 64:8
    3. Jeremiah ‒ Jer. 1:5
  3. The third VERB "to establish it" (BDB 465, KB 464, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) may relate to
    1. the fixed order of nature in Jer. 31:35-37
    2. YHWH establishing the world by His wisdom in Jer. 10:12
    3. YHWH creating the planet (LXX and see Isa. 45:18), where all three VERBS used in v. 2 to describe YHWH's acts of creation, are used
    4. YHWH's eternal plan of human redemption

▣ "the Lord is His name" The "name" represents the Person.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" of YHWH

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:3 Notice the personal element of biblical, covenant faith. Notice the VERB forms.

  1. "call to Me" ‒ BDB 894, KB 1128, Qal IMPERATIVE, SINGULAR, cf. Jer. 29:12 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord)
    1. Jeremiah
    2. His people, collectively
  2. "I will answer you" ‒ BDB 772, KB 851, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense
  3. "I will tell you" ‒ BDB 616, KB 665, Hiphil COHORTATIVE

▣ "Call to Me, and I will answer you" Here again is the sign of the renewed covenant. Earlier Jeremiah had been told not to pray (Jer. 7:16; also note Isa. 1:15), for the people could not repent. Now they are assured that as they sought God, He would respond to them.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CALL ON HIS NAME

▣ "great and mighty things, which you do not know" The term "mighty" is literally "inaccessible" or "fortified" (BDB 130, KB 148, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE). This word was often used for breaking into a fortified city (cf. Jer. 15:20; 52:7; 2 Chr. 32:1; even in this context, v. 4 fits this usage). It refers to that which is beyond human ability ("which you do not know," i.e. Isa. 55:8-11), therefore, here it refers to God's revelation (cf. Isa. 48:6) about future acts for His people.

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:4 The buildings inside the walls of Jerusalem (both of the king's and the citizens') were torn down to

  1. fortify, support
  2. fill in the damage done by the Babylonian siege machines (i.e. A-frames with ropes and logs)
  3. drop rocks on the siege machines placed against the walls

In Jer. 33:5 YHWH will show His wrath on Jerusalem by allowing dead bodies to fill the holes made by the siege machines! The JPSOA and the AB both assert the ambiguity and uncertainty of the end of Jer. 33:4 and the beginning of Jer. 33:5.

JPSOA's translation, "for [defense] against the siegemounds and against the sword, and were filled by those who went to fight the Chaldeans" (p. 995).

AB simply leaves it blank with two blank parentheses (p. 292).

▣ "Against the sword" This is an uncertain Hebrew term (BDB 352, KB 349). The JPSOA indicates thatJer. 33:4c-5a are ambiguous. The Septuagint translates this as "fortifications" (cf. Isa. 22:10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

33:5
NASB, NRSV  "to fill them"
NKJV  "to fill their places"
TEV  "who will fill the houses"
NJB  "to fill the city"
LXX  "to fill it"
Peshitta  "to fill the streets"

The MT has the OBJECT as a FEMININE NOUN which refers to Jerusalem. The Babylonians will fill the streets and houses of Jerusalem with the dead bodies of her citizens.

The places where the buildings were torn down became burial places for the soldiers slain and/or the citizens who died from famine and pestilence.

Notice there are two "fillings."

  1. v. 4 ‒ by the citizens of Jerusalem to support the defenses of the city
  2. v. 5 ‒ to describe the terrible death toll and improper burial of Jerusalem's citizens by the Neo-Babylonian mercenary army

▣ "and I have hidden My face from this city because of all their wickedness" Judah's idolatry and unwillingness to listen to Jeremiah or repent of their wickedness has caused the covenant God to turn His face away (i.e. not to be attentive to the prayers of His people). This imagery begins in Deut. 31:17 and is repeated often in the prophets.

  1. Isa. 1:15; 8:17; 45:15; 54:8; 59:2
  2. Jer. 21:10; 44:11
  3. Amos 9:4
  4. Micah 3:4

As sin drove Adam, Eve, and Cain from the Garden of Eden, it now drives the descendants of Abraham out of the Promised Land! The covenants of the OT are conditional, except for YHWH's unconditional commitment to redeem fallen mankind.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:6-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:6-9 The great and mighty things of Jer. 33:3 are explained in Jer. 33:6-9. Chapters 30-33 are the most positive messages in all of Jeremiah.

Notice what YHWH will do.

  1. bring health (BDB 74) and healing (BDB 951), cf. Jer. 8:22; 30:17 (opposite of Jer. 8:15; 14:19; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING)
  2. bring peace (BDB 1027, possibly "prosperity"; see SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE [OT])
  3. bring truth (BDB 54, possibly "security"; see SPECIAL TOPIC: TRUTH/TRUE)
  4. restore the fortunes of both Judah and Israel (some LXX MSS change "Israel" to "Jerusalem," however, Jeremiah does mention the reunification often, cf. Jer. 3:18; 30:3; 31:27; 33:11,14,17; and possibly Jer. 33:24)
  5. rebuild them both (i.e. completely restore them)
  6. cleanse them from all their iniquity (#6 and #7 are part of the promise of the new covenant in Jer. 31:31-34)
  7. pardon all their iniquities (the first seven above are all PERFECTS with waw)
  8. the restored covenant people will resume their place as a light to the nations (Jer. 33:9; 3:17,19; 4:2; 16:19; see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:8 This is a tremendous affirmation of God restoring His people. It seems to reflect the new covenant (cf. Jer. 31:31-34). All three Hebrew words for sin are found in this verse (as they are in Psalm 51).

  1. iniquity ‒ BDB 730, KB 800
  2. sin ‒ BDB 306, KB 305 (twice), Qal PERFECTS
  3. transgress ‒ BDB 833, KB 981, Qal PERFECT, also translated "rebel"

They all refer to some deviation from the standard of judgment (see SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS) which is God Himself, as revealed in the covenant. However, God affirms that He will cleanse (BDB 372, KB 369, Piel PERFECT with waw) and pardon (BDB 699, KB 757, Qal PERFECT with waw). Wow! What a God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN IN THE OT

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:9 It must be stated with emphasis that God chose Israel to choose the whole world. However, the light that was being revealed to the world was not the wonderful, merciful character of God (cf. Lev. 26:2-13; Deut. 28:1-6; 30:1-20) that He wanted to reveal (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36). Because of Israel's and Judah's disobedience the only aspect of YHWH' character the nations saw was judgment. God wanted to use Israel as a kingdom of priests (cf. Exod. 19:5-6, note the phrase's use in 1 Pet. 2:5,9; Rev. 1:6) to reach the whole world (cf. Jer. 3:17,19; 4:2; 16:19). In my opinion the church has become that evangelistic light (cf. Matt. 28:18-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8), but the same warning (cf. Rom. 11:18-22; James 2:14-26) that was given to Abraham's physical seed is obviously appropriate for Abraham's spiritual seed (cf. Rom. 2:28-29; 9:6; Gal. 3:7-9,29; 6:16; 1 Pet. 3:6).

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:10-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:10-11 What a contrast Jer. 33:10 is to Jer. 33:11! Verse 10 expresses the tragedy of the destruction and exile of Jerusalem/Judah. The human population and their flocks and herds are all gone! One note I would add is that even though there are no domesticated animals left, there is also no mention of wild animals inhabiting the site. These wild animals often denoted the presence of the demonic (cf. Jer. 9:11; 10:22; Isa. 13:22; 34:11-15; Zeph. 2:14).

Verse 11 is a threefold litany of the joys of normal social activities (i.e. weddings, feast days). This is a clear reversal of Jer. 7:34; 16:9; 25:10. This joy is possible because YHWH has brought His people back to their land and He dwells with them (i.e. the temple). This theme of joy is recurrent in the prophets (i.e. Jer. 31:12; Isa. 12:1-6; 25:9; 35:10; 51:3,11; 65:18; 66:10; Zeph. 2:6-7). A new day is coming because a new covenant is coming. That new covenant is Jesus Christ and salvation by grace through faith (cf. Eph. 2:8-10), which issues in Christlikeness (i.e. personal holiness, cf. Lev. 11:44-45; 19:2; 20:7,26; Jer. 33:15; Matt. 5:49; Rom. 8:28-30; 2 Cor. 3:18; Gal. 4:19; Eph. 1:4; 4:13; 1 Thess. 3:13; 4:3; 5:23; 1 Pet. 1:15).

The voice of joy (a command of thanks, BDB 392, KB 389, Hiphil IMPERATIVE) is also found in Ps. 106:1; 107:1; 118:1; 136:1. So, the three poetic line quote must have been a well known poem/proverb/ritual affirmation!

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:11 "to the Lord of hosts "
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:11 "to the Lord of hosts " See SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

▣ "For the Lord is good" This characterization of YHWH (BDB 373, #9, b) is a common ADJECTIVE used in several senses.

  1. pleasant
  2. agreeable
  3. good
  4. kind

This is the term used of initial creation (i.e. Gen. 1:4,10,12,18,21,25,31). It came to be used of other aspects of God's character as well as His creation.

  1. God Himself ‒ 1 Chr. 16:34; 2 Chr. 5:13; 7:3; 30:18; Ezra 3:11; Ps. 25:8; 34:8; 86:5; 100:5; 119:68; 135:3; Jer. 33:11; Nah. 1:7. It is used as an introductory affirmation in Ps. 106:1; 107:1; 118:1; 136:1.
  2. God's words/promises ‒ Josh. 21:45; 23:14,15; 1 Kgs. 8:56; Jer. 29:10; 33:14
  3. God's purposes for His people ‒ Jer. 24:6; 29:10; 33:14

▣ "His lovingkindness is everlasting" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS and SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

▣ "a thankful offering" See SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE OFFERING.

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:12-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 33:12-13 The strophe further explains Jer. 33:10-11.

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:13 "will again pass under the hands of the one who numbers them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:13 "will again pass under the hands of the one who numbers them" This refers to the daily actions of shepherds (cf. Lev. 27:32; Ezek. 20:37; this imagery is the background of John 10:1-18).

  1. making sure that all of the sheep were in the pen at night
  2. a way of counting the sheep for tithing purposes
  3. the Aramaic Targums specifically attribute this action to the Messiah

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:14-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:14-16 This passage is absent in the LXX. Some scholars postulate that the reason it is omitted in Jeremiah 33 is because it seems to be a development and repetition of the same truth found in Jer. 23:5-6 (this is a characteristic of the LXX; see notes at Jer. 23:5-6).

However, this is a tremendous Messianic passage which promises a future fulfillment, not only of the exiled seed of Abraham to the Promised Land, but also of the restoration of the Davidic seed and the restored temple.

R. K. Harrison is one of my favorite authors. In his commentary (Tyndale OT series) on Jeremiah he gives a list of all the descriptive titles and phrases Jeremiah uses of the coming Davidic seed/Messiah (p. 144).

  1. the Fountain of living waters, Jer. 2:13; 17:13
  2. the good Shepherd, Jer. 23:4; 31:10 (3:15, PLURAL)
  3. the righteous Branch, Jer. 23:5; 33:15
  4. the Redeemer, Jer. 50:34
  5. the Lord our righteousness, Jer. 23:6; 33:16
  6. David the king, Jer. 30:9
  7. agent of the new covenant, Jer. 31:31-34

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:15 "In those days and at that time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:15 "In those days and at that time" This refers to a future period. It and similar phrases are used often in chapters 30-33.

  1. Jer. 30:3,24
  2. Jer. 31:27,29,31,33,38
  3. Jer. 32:14
  4. Jer. 33:14,15,16

The exact time element is not stated but since it is the "new covenant period," Christian scholars believe it refers to the New Testament and Jesus (Zerubbabel is in the genealogy of Jesus, cf. Matt. 1:12-13; Luke 3:27), while Jewish scholars believe it refers to the post-exilic period (i.e. Zerubbabel and Joshua, cf. Zech. 6:12). If it is post-exilic then even though it is not stated in the "if. . .then" format, it is a conditional covenant (i.e. future Seleucid and Roman defeats). Here, one's meta-narrative structures the text to fit a particular worldview. My biases are spelled out in the SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN.

▣ "I will cause a righteous Branch of David to spring forth" This is the same Davidic Messianic imagery used in Jer. 23:5-6 and 30:9-11. It was also favorite imagery of

  1. Isaiah, cf. Jer. 4:2; 53:3; also note Jer. 11:1-5
  2. Zechariah, cf. Jer. 3:8; 6:12,13

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE BRANCH OF THE LORD

SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS THE NAZARENE

▣ "He shall execute justice and righteousness on earth" This Messianic period is described in Isa. 9:6-7; Micah 5:2-5.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUSTICE

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "earth" This is the term erets, which has a wide semantic field. Here, it could refer to Palestine or all the earth.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD (several terms)

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:16 "the Lord is our righteousness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:16 "the Lord is our righteousness" This phrase is a title of

  1. the restored city of Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 31:23)
  2. the Messiah in Jer. 23:6
  3. It is later transferred to the repentant and obedient people of God (cf. Isa. 45:24-25).

The goal of God is a people who reflect His character to a lost and needy world!

For Hebrew people a change of name marked a significant event in the life of a person (cf. Gen. 32:28). A significant, permanent change has occurred to the nation personified in this title (also note the title in Jer. 31:23 for Jerusalem).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: DESCRIPTIVE TITLES FOR GOD

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:17 "For thus says the Lord, 'David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel'"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:17 "For thus says the Lord, 'David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel'" This refers back to the prophecy of 2 Sam. 7:11-16; 23:5; 1 Chronicles 17 (cf. Ps. 89:30-37). Note the conditional element emphasized again in 1 Kgs. 8:25.

However, we learn from history that Jerusalem did fall, the temple was destroyed and the Davidic seed was carried into captivity in Babylon. This section certainly reflects the Messiah (i.e. Jesus, the line of David, Matthew 1; Luke 2), but some see it as referring to Zerubbabel as the Davidic branch (i.e. "Prince," possibly Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel are the same person or relatives, cf. Ezra 1:8; 5:14) who returned after the exile (cf. Zech. 4:6-10; 6:12). See full notes online in Ezra.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL COVENANTS (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:18 "the Levitical priests shall never lack a man before Me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:18 "the Levitical priests shall never lack a man before Me" There has been much discussion about this promise of a renewed Levitical priesthood. Some say it means that there will be sacrifices in the end-time period. However, my understanding of Jesus as fulfilling both the roles of king and priest (cf. Heb. 1:2-3) probably makes this a spiritual promise instead of one to be literally fulfilled (see the book of Hebrews). There are several places in the OT where the Messiah has both a priestly and royal aspect (cf. Ps. 110:1-3 [royal], then 4 [priestly]; also Zerubbabel [royal] and Joshua [priestly], cf Zechariah 4, esp. Jer. 33:14; 6:9-15).

Remember that Melchizedek, in Gen. 14:17-24, was the priest/king of Salem. The NT book of Hebrews, particularly chapters 5-7, asserts that the Messiah's twin roles (priest/king) is foreshadowed in him. This same priest/king combination is revealed in Psalm 110 and Zechariah 3 and 4. The Dead Sea Scroll community expected two Messiahs, one from the tribe of Judah (Gen. 49:8-12) and one from the tribe of Levi.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: MELCHIZEDEK

SPECIAL TOPIC: LEVITICAL PRIESTS

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:19-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:19-22 This strophe claims that the new covenant is going to be permanent because the order and cycles of nature are permanent (cf. Jer. 31:35-37). Western science was developed on this premise of the regularity of God's creation (i.e. uniformitarianism, cf. Jer. 33:25; Gen. 8:22; Ps. 74:16-17; 89:36-37).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEWS OF THE MOSAIC LAW

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE AGE AND FORMATION OF THE EARTH

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:22 "counted. . .measured"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:22 "counted. . .measured" These are both Niphal IMPERFECTS. They are the same imagery (i.e. stars and sand) used in the promises to the Patriarchs about the number of descendants to

  1. Abraham ‒ Gen. 13:16; 15:5; 22:17
  2. Isaac ‒ Gen. 26:4
  3. Jacob ‒ Gen. 28:14; 32:12
  4. all of them ‒ Exod. 32:13

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "My servant" See SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:23-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:23-26 This strophe expresses the same truth as Jer. 33:19-22.

Grant Osborne, The Hermeneutical Spiral (p. 216), calls this strophe a "disputation speech" (cf. Isa. 28:14-19; Ezek. 18:1-20) where the prophet uses the opponents' own words to show their sin and rebellion. Each of their statements is answered by the prophet and a future setting/outcome is revealed.

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:24 "this people. . .My people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:24 "this people. . .My people" The first use of "people" refers to unrepentant Jews who are about to be destroyed and the second uses refers to the repentant remnant which will one day return.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (three senses)

▣ "the two families" This may refer to

  1. Abraham ‒ Gen. 13:16; 15:5; 22:17
  2. Isaac ‒ Gen. 26:4
  3. the tribes of Judah (royal) and Levi (priestly), cf. Jer. 33:7,14
  4. Jacob and David ‒ cf. Jer. 33:26
  5. David and Levi ‒ cf. Jer. 33:21
  6. Judah and Israel (after 922 B.C.)

entries.title: Jeremiah 33:26 "I will restore"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
33:26 "I will restore" The MT has "restore" (BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERFECT) but the Masoretic scholars suggested instead "bring back" (BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil IMPERFECT, cf. NKJV, NJB); both concepts are found together in Jer. 29:14.

The concept of "restore" is mentioned in Jer. 29:14; 30:3,18; 31:23; 32:44; 33:7,11. It refers to the covenant blessings given to the Patriarchs. The concept of "bring back" is included in this larger agenda.

The VERB "I will have mercy" is a family term (BDB 933, KB 1216, Piel PERFECT with waw, cf. Ps. 103:13; Isa. 49:15). What a great affirmation that God will not leave His people totally defenseless. But, notice the conditional element that they must repent and that the time of judgment was necessary to pull them away from the idolatry and ritualism to which they had fallen.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How are Jeremiah 30-33 related?
  2. Why is Jeremiah's symbolic act of buying a field so significant?
  3. How has archaeology confirmed the historicity of Jeremiah 32?
  4. Why is the close of Jer. 32:8 so spiritually significant?
  5. How are the gods Ba'al and Molech related?
  6. How do we explain Jer. 32:39 in light of Ezek. 18:31?
  7. List and define the three Hebrew words for sin found in Jer. 33:8
  8. Why is Jer. 33:14-18 so significant and how does it impact our understanding of the end-time?

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
JEREMIAH 34

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
A Prophecy Against Zedekiah Zedekiah Warned by God Warning to Zedekiah A Message to Zedekiah The Fate of Zedekiah
34:1-5 34:1-5 34:1-5 34:1-5 34:1-5
34:6-7 34:6-7 34:6-7 34:6-7 34:6-7
Treacherous Treatment of Slaves Manumission of Slaves and Perfidy of the Jerusalemites Deceitful Treatment of Slaves The Episode of the Liberated Slaves
34:8-11 34:8-11 34:8-22 34:8-11 34:8-16
34:12-16 34:12-16 34:12-22
34:17-22 34:17-22 34:17-22

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

34:1
NASB, NKJV, TEV, NJB  "Nebuchadnezzar"
NRSV, JPSOA, REB  "Nebuchadrezzar"

#1 with an "n" in Jer. 27:6,8,20; 28:3,11,14; 29:1,3 (most common spelling outside Jeremiah)

#2 with an "r" in Jer. 21:2,7; 22:25; 24:1; 25:1,9; 29:21; 32:1,28; 34:1; 35:11; 37:1; 39:1,5,11; 43:10; 44:30 and several more (but only in Jeremiah and 4 times in Ezekiel)

The MT follows option #2. In Jeremiah the word is spelled both ways.

It is difficult to transcribe ancient names from one language to another, but it is surprising that two different spellings occur in one author. This may be a textual hint of a later editor/compiler.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

▣ "all his army with all the kingdoms of the earth" The military force was made up of

  1. Babylonians
  2. mercenaries
  3. vassal people (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:1-2)

This descriptive phrase links up with Jer. 1:15. This is a good example of biblical hyperbole. See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp.110-117,133

▣ "were fighting against Jerusalem and against all its cities" This terrible judgment event is recorded in gruesome detail in 2 Kgs. 25 and Jer. 52. This probably occurred in the early spring of 588 B.C., just before the Egyptian army briefly approached (see IVP Biblical Background Commentary [OT], p. 667).

The curses of covenant disobedience from Lev. 26 and Deut. 28 have now become reality because of the continuous, open-eyed rebellion of both Israel and Judah.

The Mosaic covenant had blessings and judgments related to obedience!

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:2 "the Lord God of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:2 "the Lord God of Israel" The use of "Israel" in this characterization of YHWH denotes

  1. the use of the collective title referring to the Patriarch Jacob
  2. the promise of a restored covenant people; the split of 922 B.C. will be healed

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C., D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah" This chapter refers to two different messages given to Zedekiah, the last king of Judah.

  1. his personal fate and the fate of Jerusalem
  2. the fate of his leaders who broke their covenant with YHWH and their servants

▣ "hand" A Hebrew idiom of "power" (cf. Jer. 34:3,21; 21:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "he will burn it with fire" This was a

  1. means of total destruction (i.e. uninhabited, cf. Isa. 34:11-15; Zeph. 2:13-15)
  2. symbol of the judgment of God

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:3 "you will not escape"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:3 "you will not escape" The "you" is emphatic! There are three accounts of Zedekiah's capture in the OT (cf. Jer. 39:4-7; 52:7-11; 2 Kgs. 25:4-7). It was God's will that Neo-Babylon succeed (cf. Ezek. 17:11-21). Only capitulation could have saved the city from destruction.

▣ "you will surely be captured" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 1074, KB 1779), used for emphasis.

▣ "face to face" Zedekiah was brought before Nebuchadnezzar. They had a personal encounter (cf. Jer. 32:4).

  1. "mouth to mouth," BDB 804
  2. "eye to eye" (BDB 744)

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:4 This chapter is characterized by VERBS being doubled.

  1. captured, Jer. 34:3
  2. die, Jer. 34:4-5
  3. speak, Jer. 34:5-6
  4. turn, Jer. 34:11
  5. proclaim, Jer. 34:17
  6. give, Jer. 34:17-18
  7. pass over, Jer. 34:18-19

"Says" is often found side by side (cf. Jer. 34:1-2,2,12-13), but these other VERBS being doubled form a characteristic of Jeremiah's writing or speaking style.

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:4-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:4-5 Zedekiah will experience

  1. the death of his sons
  2. the death of all the princes (the royal family or leaders in general)
  3. being blinded
  4. exiled in chains
  5. put in prison in Babylon until his death

However, at his death in Babylon (cf. Jer. 52:7-11) he was honored as a royal Judean king.

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:5 "burn spices for you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:5 "burn spices for you" Literally this is the VERB "to burn" (BDB 976, KB 1358, Qal IMPERFECT). Exactly what, why, or how is not specified, but it must be stated, it does not refer to cremation (see cremation (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CREMATION). It may be a reference to

  1. large amounts of spices burnt in honor of the dead king as a symbol of prayers on his behalf (cf. 2 Chr. 16:14; 21:19). The people did this not so much to mourn for him personally but for the memory of their homeland's once-proud heritage. This was just opposite of Jehoiakim's funeral (cf. Jer. 22:18-19).
  2. This is a conditional promise (though the "if. . .then" is not stated) message which did not come to pass because Zedekiah would not heed YHWH's words from Jeremiah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT), VI., VII.

▣ "alas" This INTERJECTION (i.e. "alas," "woe," "ah," BDB 222) is used in several senses.

  1. at a funeral (i.e. "Alas")
    1. royal ‒ 1 Kgs. 13:30; Jer. 22:18; 34:5
    2. non-royal ‒ Amos 5:16
  2. declaration of the sins of Judah ‒ Isa. 1:4
  3. judgment of Assyria ("Woe") ‒ Isa. 10:5
  4. judgment of rich Judean exploitation of the poor and helpless ("Woe") ‒ Isa. 5:8,11,18; Jer. 22:13; Hab. 2:6,9,12
  5. judgment of Judean idolaters ("Woe") ‒ Isa. 29:15; 45:9,10; Hab. 2:19; Ezek. 13:18
  6. judgment on Judean leaders who seek an alliance with Egypt ("Woe") ‒ Isa. 31:1 (also note Zech 11:17)
  7. judgment ("Alas") ‒ Jer. 30:7; 48:1
  8. a way of attracting attention ("Ho," "Ah") ‒ Isa. 18:1; 55:1; Jer. 47:6; Zech. 2:10,11

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:7 "Lachish"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:7 "Lachish" Archaeologists have found letters (i.e. the Lachish Letters on 21 ostraca) from this siege period. The city was larger than Jerusalem during this time. It is about 23 miles southwest of Jerusalem. These two cities were the main coastal plain (cf. Shephlah) defensive positions of Jerusalem.

▣ "Azekah" This city was about eleven miles southwest of Jerusalem. This verse implies that all other cities of Judah had already been destroyed.

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:8-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:8-11 This paragraph describes one example of the evil and disrespect for YHWH that existed among the leadership of Jerusalem. They made a public commitment to YHWH and His law (i.e. setting slaves/ servants free, cf. Jer. 34:14; Exod. 21:1-11; Lev. 25:39-55; Deut. 15:12-18), but when the circumstances seemed to change they reversed their actions.

For a good discussion of slavery among the covenant people, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 80-90.

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:8 "covenant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:8 "covenant" This word (BDB 136, KB 157, cf. Jer. 34:13,15,18; 31:32) is not a Hebrew word. Its etymology is uncertain, possibly

  1. "to cut," cf. Jer. 34:18-19
  2. "to bind" from Akkadian
  3.  to establish a covenant with an oath" from Akkadian
  4.  to eat a meal together," which sealed the covenant (BDB 136 I, ברה), 1 Kgs. 8:25

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:9 "Hebrew"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:9 "Hebrew" See SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW PEOPLE.

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:10-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:10-11 Jeremiah's poetry often used words that sound alike. Notice

  1. hear, Jer. 34:10 ‒ שׁמע (twice), BDB 1033
  2. send away, Jer. 34:10,11 ‒ שׁלח (twice), BDBB 1018
  3. turn, Jer. 34:11 ‒ שׁוב (twice), BDB 996

If you go back to Jer. 34:9, there are eight words from Jer. 34:9-11 that begin with שׁ.

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:11 "afterward they turned around and took back the servants"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:11 "afterward they turned around and took back the servants" Jeremiah 37:7-10,11 and 34:21-22 tell us that the arrival of the Egyptian army in Canaan was the cause of the siege being broken off briefly.

The Mosiac law allowed a Hebrew to sell himself or herself for a set period of time, six years. They were to be released at the end of one year of rest following the six of labor (cf. Exod. 23:10-11; 21:2-11; Lev. 25:39-46; Deut. 15:1,12-18). The rich people of the city vowed this act to impress God but when the siege was lifted they reneged!

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:14 "end of seven years"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:14 "end of seven years" The LXX has "six years" (RSV). The meaning is "at the beginning of the seventh year." This reflects the ancient law (cf. Exod. 21:2-11; Lev. 25:39-46; Deut. 15:1,12-18).

▣ "did not obey Me or incline their ear to Me" This same reluctance to hear and obey is seen in Jer. 7:24-26; 17:23; 19:15. It was not an issue of ignorance of God's will but willful, recurrent disobedience.

  1. "obey" ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal PERFECT, lit. "hear" (Shema, cf. Deut. 6:4)
  2. "incline" ‒ BDB 639, KB 692, Hiphil PERFECT, cf. Josh. 24:23; Ps. 119:36

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:15 "in the house which is called by My name"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:15 "in the house which is called by My name" This Deuteronomic language refers to the temple, which will eventually be in Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 7:10-11,14,30; 32:34).

The concept of the temple as "house" is the word play from 2 Sam. 7:2,13,16 (i.e. building vs. dynasty).

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:16 "profaned My name"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:16 "profaned My name" This root (BDB 320 III, KB 319, Piel IMPERFECT with waw) means "to pollute," "to defile," or "to profane" (cf. Lev. 18:21; 19:12; 20:3; 21:6; 22:2,32; Ezek. 20:39; 36:20-23; Amos 2:7; Mal. 1:12; 2:10). This was a serious covenant breach (cf. Exod. 20:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CALL ON HIS NAME

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:17 The leaders of Jerusalem swore in God's name to "release" (BDB 204 I, twice) their Hebrew slaves but they did not. Now YHWH will "release"

  1. the sword (BDB 352)
  2. pestilence (BDB 184)
  3. famine (BDB 944)

on them (see note at Jer. 14:12).

▣ "and I will make you a terror to all the kingdoms of the earth" This same phrase is used in Jer. 29:18 and Deut. 28:25. God's covenant people were meant to be a light to the nations but they had become a proverb of disaster! This was an exact reversal of God's purposes (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:18 "transgressed My covenant. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:18 "transgressed My covenant. . ." This common VERB (BDB 716, KB 778, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) basically means "to pass through." Usually, it is used literally. However, it can denote the violation of a known legal, moral boundary, which denotes intentional actions/choices. The problem was not information, but purposeful violations (cf. Dan. 9:11; Hosea 6:7; 8:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SIN IN THE OT, B. #1

▣
NASB, NKJV, Peshitta  "when they cut the calf"
NRSV  "I will make like the calf"
TEV  "I will do to these people what they
  did to the bull"
NJB, REB  "I will treat them like the calf"
JPSOA  "[like] the calf which they cut in two"

The MT is ambiguous. There have been two ways to interpret this phrase.

  1. a reference to the way treaties, covenants, agreements were ratified (i.e. cut an animal in two, cf. Gen. 15:19-21)
  2. the ones who broke the covenant with YHWH would become like the animal that was cut in two

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:18-19 "who passed between the parts of the calf"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:18-19 "who passed between the parts of the calf" This was an ancient method of ratifying a covenant (i.e. Gen. 15:9-10,17).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:19 "and all the people of the land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:19 "and all the people of the land" This designation changes over a period of time from common non-government citizens to wealthy leadership.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PEOPLE OF THE LAND

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 34:20 An improper burial was a horror to ANE people (cf. Jer. 19:7; 1 Sam. 17:44,46; 1 Kgs. 14:11; 16:4). It functioned as a threat and curse which affected one's afterlife.

entries.title: Jeremiah 34:22 "I will bring them back to this city"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
34:22 "I will bring them back to this city" As Nebuchadnezzar II was besieging Jerusalem in 588 B.C., the Egyptian army appeared in Judah. The Babylonians withdrew their siege of Jerusalem for a brief period to meet the new threat (cf. Jer. 37:5,7,11), but there was no battle and the siege of Jerusalem was quickly reestablished.

Notice it is YHWH (lit. "I am going to command" ‒ BDB 845, KB 1010, Piel ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) who directs the Neo-Babylonian military (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:3). Remember the concept of monotheism is often communicated by the absence of secondary causes! YHWH is in control of individual, national, and international events!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:1 "Jehoiakim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:1 "Jehoiakim" When one compares Jer. 34:2 it is easy to see how the book of Jeremiah is out of chronological order (chapters 35-36 precede 32-34). Someone compiled and edited his work, probably Baruch (cf. Jer. 32:12,13,16; 36:4,5,8,10,13,14,15,16; 43:3,6; 45:1,2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHT

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
JEREMIAH 35

PARAGRAPH DIVISIONS OF MODERN TRANSLATIONS

NASB NKJV NRSV TEV NJB
The Rechabites' Obedience The Obedient Rechabites The Symbol of the Rechabites Jeremiah and the Rechabites The Example of the Rechabites
35:1-11 35:1-11 35:1-11 35:1-5 35:1-5
Judah Rebuked 35:6-11 35:6-11
35:12-17 35:12-17 35:12-17 35:12-17 35:12-17
35:18-19 35:18-19 35:18-19 35:18-19 35:18-19

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter is built around the faithfulness of the Rechabites to not drink wine.
    1. VERB ‒ "give to drink" ‒ BDB 1052, KB 1639, Hiphil PERFECT with waw, Jer. 35:2
    2. VERB ‒ "drink" ‒ BDB 1059, KB 1667, Jer. 35:5,6 (twice), 8,14 (twice)
      The Rechabites are in contrast to the people of Judah who were not obedient to what they had heard. This chapter is not about total abstinence (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM). This chapter is about faithfulness to a message. Be careful not to read your modern issues (total abstinence from the American temperance movement) into these ancient texts, where wine drinking was the societal norm.

  2. The VERB "hear" (BDB 1033, KB 1570) is used many times in this chapter (Jer. 35:8,10,13,14 [twice],15,16,17,18). The Rechabites "hear" but Judah does not!
    SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR

  3. There is a sound play on words with שׁ (cf. Jer. 25:3-5; 29:19-20; 34:9-11).
    1. drink, שׁתה (twice), BDB 1059
    2. hear, שׁמע (twice), BDB 1033
    3. send, שׁלח (twice), BDB 1018
    4. rise early, שׁכם (twice), BDB 1014
    5. turn, שׁוב, BDB 996

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:2 "the house of"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:2 "the house of" This idiom means "the family of."

▣ "Rechabites" We do not know much about them (cf. 1 Chr. 2:55; Jdg. 1:16). They seem to be a nomadic Arab tribe related to Midionites or Kenites, the in-laws of Moses' first wife. Moses' father-in-law goes by four names — Jethro, Jether, Reuel, Hobab (cf. Exod. 2:18; 3:1; 4:18; Num. 10:29; Jdg. 4:11 and two titles — the Kenite, Jdg. 1:16 and "priest of Midian," Exod. 3:1; 18:1). For a good brief discussion, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, pp. 14-15.

It is obvious that YHWH is commanding the testing of the family traditions of this family group. The test is intensified by

  1. bring them to the temple
  2. take into a private chamber
  3. tempt them with an abundance of wine to drink (IMPERATIVE in Jer. 35:5)

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:4 "the man of God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:4 "the man of God" This phrase is used of Moses (cf. Deut. 33:1; Josh. 14:6) and prophets (cf. 1 Kgs. 12:22; 17:18,24; 20:28) but here it is used of one of their godly ancestors (i.e. Hanan).

▣ "the door keeper" This phrase (BDB 1036 CONSTRUCT BDB 706 II) denoted a very important position in the temple (cf. Jer. 52:24; 2 Kgs. 12:9; 25:18). This position was part of the Levitical temple police.

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:5 "pitchers"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 35:5 "pitchers" This Egyptian loan word (BDB 149, cf. Gen. 44:2,12) refers to very large bowls.

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:6 "Jonadab"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 35:6 "Jonadab" This man is mentioned in 2 Kgs. 10:15-27).

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:6-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:6-7 There is a series (Qal IMPERFECTS) of things the original father of the family commanded his descendants not to do (i.e. stay nomadic).

  1. do not drink wine, Jer. 35:6c
  2. do not build a house, Jer. 35:7
  3. do not sow seed
  4. do not plant a vineyard
  5. do not own a vineyard
  6. live in tents

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:7 "that you may live many days in the land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 35:7 "that you may live many days in the land" This phrase is similar to the phrase in Deuteronomy about honoring parents. This brings about a stable society. This is not a promise of a long life to individuals. (cf. Deut. 5:16,33; 4:40; 11:9).

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:11 Like so many of the people of the land, this family fled into the walled city of Jerusalem for protection.

▣ "before the army of the Chaldeans and before the army of the Arameans" The locality from which this faction of Neo-Babylon's mercenary military came is uncertain. Apparently, there was a nation north of Babylon and an ethnic group within Mesopotamia. They must have had a large enough affect and influence to be named in conjunction with the "Chaldean army."

Also the nomadic family of the Rachabites to enter a walled city—it must have been a major military crisis!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 35:13 This is the key verse as to the theological point of the chapter (cf. Jer. 35:16-17). This family obeyed their father but Judah did not obey their Father (i.e. YHWH).

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 35:14 God sent His spokesperson again and again (lit. "rising up early"), but Judah would not hear and obey!

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:15 "I have sent to you all My servants the prophets, sending them again and again"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:15 "I have sent to you all My servants the prophets, sending them again and again" This is a recurrent theme of Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 7:13,25; 11:7; 25:3-4; 26:5; 29:19; 32:33; 35:14-15; 44:4).

The Recabites heard and responded to one message by an ancient ancestor, but Judah rejected again and again the message of their God!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERVANT LEADERSHIP

▣ A sample of the message is recorded in Jer. 35:15.

  1. (an implied "if") turn ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 18:11
  2. amend ‒ BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 7:3; 18:11
  3. do not go (walk) after other gods ‒ BDB 229, KB 240, Qal IMPERECT used in a JUSSIVE sense, cf. Jer. 7:6 (see note below)
  4. then you shall dwell in the land ‒ BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERATIVE

The conditional element of the message has been violated as the last line of Jer. 35:15 shows (cf. Jer. 7:24)!

▣ "go after other gods" This phrase first occurs in Deut. 11:28; 28:14 (the vocabulary and idioms used in Jeremiah are found in Deuteronomy). In Deuteronomy the phrase refers to

  1. knowing YHWH's commands
  2. but knowing and following another path (i.e. 1 Kgs. 14:8; 18:15,21)

Note the usages in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 7:6; 8:2; 11:10; 13:10; 16:10; 25:6; 35:15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:17 Notice the threefold emphasis on the One who is speaking the message.

  1. the Lord (YHWH), see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.
  2. the God of hosts (usually YHWH of hosts, cf. Jer. 35:18; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS)
  3. the God of Israel (Elohim of Israel, cf. Jer. 35:18; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.)

He "spoke" and "called," but Judah would not "listen" or "respond" (cf. Jer. 7:13,26,27; 26:5).

entries.title: Jeremiah 35:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
35:19 YHWH's promise is not that this family group will be a priest (i.e. "to stand before Me") in the temple, but that they will continue to be a family through time (including this crisis). There is no reasosn to think the prohibition to drinking wine is connected to either

  1. a priestly prohibition, Lev. 10:9
  2. the Nazarites, Numbers 6

but to a prohibition to not settle down in one place and plant a vineyard. YHWH promises that this family group will survive the siege.

▣ "always" This is literally "all the days." This is an idiom of permanence (cf. Jer. 31:36; 32:39).

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:1 "In the fourth year of Jehoiakim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:1 "In the fourth year of Jehoiakim" This is the same introductory phrase used in Jeremiah 25, 45, and 46. The year is 605 B.C.. This was the year of the Battle of Carchemish in which the Neo-Babylon army defeated the Egyptian and the remnants of the Assyrian armies. Daniel had been in exile for one year (cf. Dan. 1:1). This Judean king was a son of the godly King Josiah. He grew up under godly teachers but his heart turned away from God. Ezekiel 18 uses him and his father or Hezekiah and Manasseh as types.
