FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:2 Jeremiah's message was not his own! YHWH wanted His message delivered to that generation in writing so it could be a witness to us also (cf. Rom. 4:23-24; 15:4; 1 Cor. 10:6,11; 1 Pet. 1:10-12). He spoke to a particular culture, at a particular time, but the basic message has relevance for all believers for all times! The best book I have read that discusses this issue is Gordon Fee, Gospel and Spirit. I commend it to you.

▣ "concerning Israel and concerning Judah, and concerning all the nations" What a tremendous statement! YHWH is not a God of the Israelites only but a God of all the world (cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3; Exod. 19:5; Ps. 22:27; 66:1-4; 86:8-10; Isa. 2:2-4; 12:4-5; 25:6-9; 42:6-12; 45:22-23; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 56:6-8; 60:1-3; 66:23; Jonah; Micah 4:1-4; Mal. 1:11; John 3:16; 4:42; 12:47; Rom. 5:18; 1 Tim. 2:4; 4:10; Titus 2:11; 3:4; 2 Pet. 3:9; 1 John 2:2; 4:14)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "from the day I first spoke to you, from the days of Josiah, even to this day" This is a reference to the introduction to the book at Jer. 1:2-3.

  1. from the 13th year of Josiah, the last godly king of Judah (2 Chr. 34:1-3); this 13th year would have been 627 B.C.
  2. to the 11th year of Zedekiah, son of Josiah, when Jerusalem fell to Neo-Babylon (586 B.C., cf. 2 Kgs. 25; 2 Chr. 36:17-20)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:3 "all the calamity which I plan to bring on them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:3 "all the calamity which I plan to bring on them" This is a difficult phrase to understand. Does this mean that every physical tragedy is from the hand of God? I think not! But sometimes it is or at least He allows the consequences of a fallen world to manifest in the lives of nations and individuals. If this occurred every time we sinned, we would all live in constant crises. Here is a problem.

  1. God does use problems (physical, emotional, relational, spiritual) to cause us to recognize His presence and purpose for our lives. There are consequences for disobedience (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28,30).
  2. Everything that happens to us in our lives is not the hand of God but the consequences of living in a fallen world.
  3. I never know if what happens to me is a result of #1 or #2, so I choose to use the circumstances (good or bad) to seek God and His will for my life. He is with us and for us (my worldview). I filter everything through this truth.
  4. In the OT all causality is attributed to God to affirm monotheism (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM). The OT does not recognize or designate "secondary causes"!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

▣ "every man will turn from his evil ways" This is a continuing emphasis of individual responsibility (i.e. a conditional covenant, cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 18:2-4). Notice how YHWH desires that all Judah repent, one person at a time. Biblical faith is both individual and corporate!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

▣ "I will forgive their iniquity and their sins" This is the continuing promise of the graciousness of God, that if humans (i.e. in this context, Judeans, cf. Jer. 18:7-12; 26:3) will turn to Him in repentance and faith (cf. Jer. 7:5-7; 26:3; Ps. 103:6-14; Isa. 1:16-19; Mark 1:15), He will turn to them (cf. Zech. 1:3; Mal. 3:7). Note the implied "if. . .then" conditional covenant.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: FORGIVENESS IN THE OT

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:4 "Baruch"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:4 "Baruch" This man functions as Jeremiah's scribe. He was from an important family in Jerusalem (i.e. his brother, Seraiah, was a high official, cf. Jer. 51:59). It is uncertain how much he contributed to the book (i.e. helped grammatically, lexically, structurally), but Jer. 36:17-18 implies he simply wrote down what Jeremiah said to him.

▣ "on a scroll" This scroll would have been written on

  1. long pieces of leather with the writing in small columns. The leather scroll of Isaiah, found in the Dead Sea Scrolls, is 29 feet long.
  2. papyrus pages glued together. Papyri pages could be written easily on only one side.

This phrase (BDB 166 CONSTRUCT BDB 706) is found only here and in Ps. 40:7; Ezek. 2:9.

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:5 "I am restricted"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:5 "I am restricted" The root term is "debarred" (BDB 783, KB 870, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE). It means

  1. he had been put under house arrest (cf. Jer. 32:2; 33:1) and barred from the temple area
  2. he had become ceremonially unclean and, therefore, could not enter the temple area

▣ "on a fast day" Which fast day is not specified. Originally, there was only one fast day a year (i.e. the Day of Atonement, Lev. 16), but as the generations passed, more and more were added.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FASTING

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, I. E. #2

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:7 Notice the interplay between the corporate ("everyone") and individual ("his"). I often wonder if God holds me responsible, not only for my own sins but also the sins of my culture/society. Often in the OT God's leaders prayed for their sins and their people's sins! Somehow these are related. The same theological question could be asked about Adam/Eve's sin. Am I responsible for Adam's sin or my own? Yes!

▣ "for great is the anger and the wrath" This is anthropomorphic language.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:9 "in the ninth month"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:9 "in the ninth month" This is the first mention in the OT of the Babylonian calendar (NET Bible #11, p. 1398). In this same month, Ashkelon, a major Judean city forty-five miles from Jerusalem, fell to Neo-Babylon. This may be the reason for this fast (i.e. not "the Day of Atonement," Leviticus 16 or the fall of Jerusalem in 605 to Babylon).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANE CALENDARS

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEASTS OF ISRAEL, I. E. #2

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:10 "Shaphan, the scribe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:10 "Shaphan, the scribe" This was an official in Josiah's court. He was comparable to modern America's Secretary of State (cf. 2 Kgs. 22:3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCRIBES

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:12 "all the officials were sitting there"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:12 "all the officials were sitting there" This was an official meeting of the leaders of both the temple and the royal court (cf. Jer. 26:20-23).

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:14 "Jehudi"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:14 "Jehudi" His name means "man of Judah" (BDB 397 II). His lineage is listed to the third generation because

  1. he was a man of some renown
  2. he was of the royal line (cf. Zeph. 1:1)
  3. he had an ancestor name Cush (i.e. "black" or from Cush, cf. Gen. 10:6-8)

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:15 "Sit down, please, and read it to us"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:15 "Sit down, please, and read it to us" Apparently these leaders were very cordial to both Baruch and to Jeremiah. This shows that at some level the leadership recognized the truthfulness of Jeremiah's prophecy.

The LXX and Aramaic Targums change the vowels to read "read it again." They had heard it before but wanted to hear the message of doom again (cf. Jer. 36:10-11). They were hoping and praying for royal repentance (cf. Jer. 36:24-25).

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:16 Notice the reaction of these leaders to Jeremiah's message — "they turned in fear (BDB 808, KB 922, Qal PERFECT) one to another."

▣ "We will surely report all these words to the king" The INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 616, KB 665) are used to denote the urgency and intensity of their feelings about Jeremiah's prophecy.

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:17-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:17-18 Apparently these leaders wanted to know how Baruch received this message. Baruch assures them that these are exactly the words Jeremiah spoke to him with the implication that these are the very words YHWH spoke to Jeremiah.

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:19 "Go, hide yourself, you and Jeremiah, and do not let anyone know where you are"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:19 "Go, hide yourself, you and Jeremiah, and do not let anyone know where you are" "Go" (BDB 229, KB 246,Qal IMPERATIVE) and "hide" (BDB 711, KB 771, Niphal IMPERATIVE). These are their strong suggestions because they feared the King's reaction (i.e. Jer. 36:26; 26:23) and wanted to protect Jeremiah and Baruch.

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:22 "winter house"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 36:22 "winter house" This was not a separate structure but a two story dwelling. In the summer the ancients lived on the second story which had many open windows, and in the winter on the first floor which had few windows.

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:23 "read three or four columns"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:23 "read three or four columns" Remember this was a scroll written in columns on rolled material. As the scroll was unrolled several columns would appear. The king would cut off the columns that had just been read and burn them. Thus, bit by bit the whole scroll was destroyed!

The word translated "columns" is literally "doors" (BDB 195). It is used in this sense only here. The columns of the scroll would be the same dimensions (i.e. rectangular) as a door.

▣ "a scribe's knife" This was a small penknife used to sharpen quills for writing. This word is found only here (BDB 789 CONSTRUCT BDB 707).

▣ "the scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the brazier" Why did the king do this?

  1. to physically show his rejection of both Jeremiah and his message (symbolic act so often used by Jeremiah)
  2. to use an ANE method of counter-cursing. By burning the predictive scroll, its contents would be null and void.

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:24 What a contrast between the leaders' hearing of the prophecy (cf. Jer. 36:16) and the king's (cf. Ps. 36:1). It may also be a purposeful contrast to Josiah hearing God's message read in 2 Kgs. 22:11.

For the phrase "rend their garments," see SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:26 "the king's son"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:26 "the king's son" This was probably not a true son of the king but a title for a member of the royal family or even possibly an official at court (cf. Jer. 38:6; 1 Kgs. 22:26; 2 Chr. 28:7).

▣ "but the Lord hid them" This is similar to YHWH's protection of Elijah from King Ahab in 1 Kgs. 17:3-7. As Hebrews 11 shows, some prophets are killed and some are spared! Either way, YHWH is in control. Circumstances do not affect the love and presence of YHWH.

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:29 "the king of Babylon will certainly come"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:29 "the king of Babylon will certainly come" This is the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 97, KB 112) used for certainty/emphasis.

▣ "destroy this land" The VERB (BDB 1007, KB 1469) form is Hiphil PERFECT with waw. The destruction will be complete and assured (i.e. a PROPHETIC PERFECT)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:30 "He shall have no one to sit on the throne of David"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:30 "He shall have no one to sit on the throne of David" Was this a false prophecy? Jehoiakim was succeeded by his son, Jehoiachin, for three months before he was taken into exile by Nebuchanezzar II.

It has been a lifelong process for me to understand OT prophetic literature. A book that has really helped me is D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic. For this subject chapters 6 and 7 are especially helpful. Modern westerners expect literal, complete fulfillment of every detail, but ancient easterners did not. They recognized the hyperbolic and idiomatic nature of this genre.

▣ "his dead body. . ." This was a curse that even affected one's afterlife. Improper burial, especially for a royal Davidic king, was a sign of God's displeasure and judgment. It is one of the specific curses recorded in Deut. 28:26.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

entries.title: Jeremiah 36:32 "and many similar words were added to them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
36:32 "and many similar words were added to them" It is almost a good thing that the king burned Jeremiah's prophecy because his second copy included many more words. It is not certain what part of our current book of Jeremiah was included in this scroll, although many scholars believe the LXX, which puts the judgment of the nations (i.e. Jeremiah 46-51) after chapter 25, is the original form.

Obviously, Jeremiah used some notes to help recall YHWH's messages. Moderns are not certain how or when the OT books were collected and edited. It is a faith presupposition that they are uniquely inspired and preserved at every stage of their development. For a good book on how ancient oral cultures passed on their traditions, see John H. Walton and D. Brent Sandy, The Lost World of Scripture.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Did King Zedekiah heed Jeremiah's warnings?
  2. Why was the removal of the Babylonian army so badly misinterpreted by the defenders of Jerusalem (cf. Isa. 33:20)?
  3. Does Jeremiah 35 speak to the modern use of alcohol?
  4. Why do the Rechabites in Jeremiah 35 want to continue in their nomadic existence?
  5. List God's terms for "forgiveness" in Jer. 35:15.

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:1 "king of Babylon had made king"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:1 "king of Babylon had made king" Zedekiah was Jehoiachin's uncle (Mattaniah, cf. 2 Kgs. 24:17) who was made a vassal king by Nebuchadnezzar II. See 2 Kgs.24:17 for the historical account.

▣ "Coniah" This is the contracted name for Jeconiah, whose throne name was Jehoiachin (cf. Jer. 22:24,28; 24:1; 52:31; 2 Kgs. 24:12; 1 Chr. 3:16; 2 Chr. 36:9,10). It has been eighteen years since the events recorded in chapter 36 (i.e. 605 B.C. - 586 B.C..).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:2 "the people of the land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:2 "the people of the land" This phrase (BDB 766 I CONSTRUCT BDB 75) is used in two distinct senses:

  1. pre-exilic, "landed gentry"
  2. post-exilic, "common poor people"

Here it seems to refer to all the people of Jerusalem, therefore, a third usage.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PEOPLE OF THE LAND

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:3 "Jehucal"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:3 "Jehucal" Jehucal is one of the leaders who asserts that Jeremiah should be put to death for treason (cf. Jer. 38:1-4).

▣ "Zephaniah" In Jer. 52:24 he is called the "second priest." He seems to have been favorable to Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 21:1; 29:25-29).

▣ "please pray to the Lord" This must have been a request for a special prayer for the protection of Jerusalem, but Jeremiah had already proclaimed its defeat (cf. Jer. 21:1-14). The request does show that Zedekiah believed Jeremiah was a true prophet.

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:5 "Pharaoh"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:5 "Pharaoh" In the Bible this Pharaoh is called "Hophra" in Jer. 44:30. He is also known as Apries (i.e. Herodotus 2.161; 4.159). He ruled from 589-570 B.C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF EGYPT

▣ "the Chaldeans" In this passage this title is synonymous to "Babylonians," but at one time it referred to wise men from Media.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "they lifted ths siege" However, a battle between Egyptian and Neo-Babylonian armies did not occur (or at least is not recorded) and the siege of Jerusalem was quickly restored. It lasted from 588 b.c. until 586 B.C., when the city fell (cf. Jeremiah 52; 2 Kings 25; 2 Chr. 36:17-21).

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:8 All the VERBS are PERFECTS denoting completed future action. Grammarians call them "PROPHETIC FUTURES." They all have "waws," which show the actions are linked.

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:9 "Do not deceive yourselves"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:9 "Do not deceive yourselves" This refers to false hope. The VERB (BDB 674, KB 728, Hiphil IMPERFECT is used in a JUSSIVE sense. They had convinced themselves of a falsehood! The falsehood is "The Chaldeans will surely go away from us." This is expressed emphatically by the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 229, KB 246).

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:10 This imaginary assertion is hyperbolic imagery, given to assure the Judeans that Jerusalem would be destroyed, along with YHWH's temple. Egypt cannot help (cf. Isa. 30:6-17). Judah's army cannot help!

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:12 "to take possession of some property there among the people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:12 "to take possession of some property there among the people" The Hebrew is ambiguous but possibly somehow related to Jer. 32:1ff, although this chapter predates that account.

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:13 "Gate of Benjamin"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:13 "Gate of Benjamin" This was the gate of Jerusalem to the north.

▣ "You are going over to the Chaldeans" This accusation was not unreasonable when one compares Jer. 21:8-10.

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:15 "the officials"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:15 "the officials" This (BDB 978) is a different group of officials than is mentioned in Jer. 36:11-12.

▣ "beat. . .put in jail" Jeremiah had no easy life. His messages from YHWH were viewed as treason by most Judeans, even his own family in Anathoth.

▣ "Jonathan the scribe" This position was like modern America's Secretary of State.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCRIBES

37:16
NASB  "the dungeon, that is, the vaulted cell"
NKJV  "the dungeon and the cells"
NRSV  "the cistern house, in the cells"
TEV  "an underground vault"
JPSOA  "the pit and the cells"
REB  "a vaulted pit beneath the house"

This (BDB 333, KB 333, occurs only here in the OT) is possibly a cistern, converted into a place of solitary confinement.

▣ "stayed there many days" Jeremiah thought he would die there (cf. Jer. 37:20).

Whenever I read about the hard lives of OT prophets, I am reminded of Paul's life, described in 2 Cor. 4:7-11; 6:3-10; 11:23-28. Suffering does not come to all believers but we must be ready (cf. 1 Pet. 4:12-16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SUFFER?

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:17 "Is there a word from the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:17 "Is there a word from the Lord" The message had not changed! Zedekiah, for all his weakness, still sought YHWH, but he would not act on YHWH's message! Good intentions do not replace obedient actions!

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 37:19 This is a good question. Why have not all those false prophets been put in prison or killed (cf. Deuteronomy 18)? His message was obviously true, why is he being persecuted?

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:20 This verse has several commands that denote a polite request from Jeremiah to Zedekiah.

  1. please listen ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. please let my petition come before you ‒ BDB 656, KB 709, Qal JUSSIVE
  3. do not make me return ‒ BDB 996, KB 1427, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

entries.title: Jeremiah 37:21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
37:21 Zedekiah sent Jeremiah to "the court of the guardhouse," which was a much better situation than the dungeon. The king also commanded that he be given bread as long as supplies lasted.

▣ "bakers street" This shows that merchants (i.e. guilds) of one trade lived in close proximity to one another, usually on one street or in one section of a city.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:1 "Shephatiah the son of Mattan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:1 "Shephatiah the son of Mattan" He was a member of the royal servants/counselors of Zedekiah during the invasion of Judah by Neo-Babylon.

He was an enemy of Jeremiah and thought he was a traitor deserving death.

▣ "Gdealiah the son of Pashhur" He was of the same group and held the same opinion of Jeremiah as did Shephatiah.

▣ "Jucal the son of Shelemiah" This man also goes by the name "Jehucal" in Jer. 37:3, where he is a royal messenger sent to Jeremiah and asking him, on the king's behalf, to pray for the crisis situation.

𘅋 "Pashhur the son of Malchijah" This royal servant is also mentioned in Jer. 21:1, as well as here. He is not the same person as Pashhur the priest, mentioned in Jer. 20:1-6.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. The Anchor Bible Commentary by John Bright says that Jer. 37:11-21 is the first recorded interview of Jeremiah face to face with Zedekiah and Jer. 38:1-28 is a second account.

  2. R. K. Harrison, in the Tyndale OT Series lists the similarities of Jer. 37:11-21 and Jer. 38:1-28.
    1. Jeremiah charged with treason
    2. Jeremiah imprisoned
    3. Jeremiah has a secret meeting with Zedekiah
      However, there are also differences which leave open the possibility of separate events (p. 154).

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:2 "die"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:2 "die" This chapter uses this VERB "die" (BDB 559, KB 562) often.

  1. those who stay in Jerusalem will die, Jer. 38:2
  2. those who desire to kill Jeremiah, Jer. 38:4
  3. Jeremiah's death as a result of being put into the empty cistern, Jer. 38:9,26
  4. desire to save Jeremiah, Jer. 38:10
  5. Jeremiah's message to Zedekiah, Jer. 38:15
  6. Zedekiah's response to Jeremiah, Jer. 38:16
  7. Zedekiah's threat to Jeremiah, Jer. 38:24
  8. the official's threat to Jeremiah, Jer. 38:25

▣ "the sword and by famine and by pestilence" These are the three killers of the siege experience. See full note at Jer. 14:12.

▣ "live" As "die" is used often in this chapter, so too, "live" (BDB 310, KB 309).

  1. In Jer. 38:2
    1. "will live" ‒ The Kethiv (written in the MT) has it as a Qal IMPERFECT but the Qere (suggested in the margin by MT formatters) has a Qal PERFECT, which matches the next two VERBS.
    2. The second use of "will live" is a Qal IMPERFECT.
  2. in Jer. 38:17 (twice) are Jeremiah's words to Zedekiah.
  3. in Jer. 38:20 are Jeremiah's words to Zedekiah.

Obedience to YHWH's message through Jeremiah brings life, but disobedience brings death. In a sense it reflects the "two ways" of Deut. 30:15-20 (cf. Jer. 21:8). Life is a gift of which we are stewards. There are consequences, both temporal and eternal, connected to human choices and actions (i.e. Psalm 1)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:3 "This city will certainly be given"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:3 "This city will certainly be given" The prophecy by Jeremiah of the complete destruction of Jerusalem by Neo-Babylon has not changed (cf. Jer. 21:20; 32:28; 34:2; 37:8; 38:3)!

The VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Niphal IMPERFECT) is matched by the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root which denotes certainty! There was no hope for Jerusalem and the temple to be spared.

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:4 "the men of war who are left"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:4 "the men of war who are left" Apparently there had been casualties and desertions. The other option is that Judah had no regular military except volunteers who went by the name, "men of war."

▣ "this man is not seeking the well-being of this people" These court officials still totally misunderstood Jeremiah and his message. They purposefully ignored the promise of "life" in Jer. 38:2.

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:5 This verse shows the weakness of Zedekiah (so too, Saul, cf. 1 Sam. 15:24 and even of David, cf. 2 Sam. 3:39).

Notice the play on "hand."

  1. "discouraging" of Jer. 38:4 is literally "weakening the hands"
  2. "all the people" of Jer. 38:4 is literally "the hands of all"
  3. "he is in your hands" of Jer. 38:5 is an idiom of power over someone

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:6 "the king's son"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:6 "the king's son" This was an official title, not necessarily a blood relationship, but probably someone of the royal family (cf. Jer. 36:26).

▣ "Jeremiah sank into the mud" Josephus adds the tradition that it was up to his neck (Antiq. 10.7.5). He was meant to die there (cf. Jer. 38:4). The "mud" would have been the sediment which had collected in the bottom of a cistern. Cisterns caught and stored the runoff of rain water.

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:7 "Ebed-melech"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:7 "Ebed-melech" This term (BDB 715) is literally "servant of the king." It is not a name but a title also found in other Semitic cultures.

This man helps Jeremiah and is rewarded with his life (cf. Jer. 39:16-18).

▣ "Ethiopian" This (BDB 469 I) is often translated "Cushite" (cf. Jer. 13:23), which denotes a person from the nation just south of Egypt. This was a foreign servant/official in the Judean palace.

▣ "a eunuch" This term can be translated "official" (BDB 710). Physical castration was often involved (cf. Isa. 56:3-5), but not always (i.e. Potiphar in Gen. 39:1ff).

▣ "the king was sitting in the Gate of Benjamin" The gate was the place of social and legal activities. Apparently Zedekiah, the King, was holding public court.

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:8 "spoke to the king"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:8 "spoke to the king" Either he was a trusted official who had the ear of the king or he took advantage of public court to speak.

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:9 The reason for Jeremiah's feared death is stated as famine. Conditions are much worse now than in Jer. 37:21.

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:10 "thirty men"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:10 "thirty men" One Hebrew MS and the LXX have "three" (cf. NRSV, TEV, NEB, NIV). The UBS Text Project, p. 278, gives "thirty" an A rating (very high probability; MT and Peshitta).

38:11
NASB  "beneath the storeroom"
NKJV, Peshitta  "under the treasury"
NRSV  "to a wardrobe of the storehouse"
TEV  "the palace storeroom"
NJB  "the treasury wardrobe"
JPSOA  "a place below the treasury"
LXX  "the underground chamber"
JPSOA footnote  "the wardrobe of the treasury"

The exact site is uncertain. It refers to a cistern somewhere in the palace. The MT has "under the treasury," to which the UBS Text Project, p. 278, gives a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

  1. underneath the treasury ‒ אל - תחת האוצר
  2. towards the wardrobe of the treasury ‒ אל - מלתחת האוצר

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:12 "put these worn-out clothes and rags under your armpits"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:12 "put these worn-out clothes and rags under your armpits" Apparently a room close by had some worn out clothes that could be used to cushion Jeremiah as he was pulled from the cistern. This shows the man's concern for Jeremiah. This is an eyewitness detail!

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:13 He was rescued from the cistern but would stay in custody!

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:14 "the third entrance"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:14 "the third entrance" Zedekiah was a conflicted, weak ruler!

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:15 Zedekiah still holds Jeremiah in a sacred position (i.e. Herod and John the Baptist).

  1. meets with him secretly (cf. Jer. 38:16,24-27)
  2. but will not act on his words

He wants to know the word of YHWH (cf. Jer. 38:14) but he will not do it (James 1:22). He apparently feared the Neo-Babylonian army and a faction within Judah (cf. v. 16).

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:16 The king promises

  1. not to kill Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 38:15-16)
  2. not to turn him over to his officials who want to kill him (cf. Jer. 38:4)

Zedekiah swore by the covenant Deity's name ("As the Lord lives") and His creative action ("who gave us life/breath"). Zedekiah was a religious man but a weak, indecisive one!

▣ "this life" See SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:17 Notice the three titles of the One in whose name (cf. Jer. 35:17) Jeremiah speaks.

  1. YHWH (Lord); see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.
  2. God of hosts; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS
  3. God of Israel; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

The VERB "go out to" means "surrender" (BDB 422, KB 425, QalM IMPERFECT) in this context. It is intensified by the presence of the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root!

Notice, if the king will respond appropriately, even at this late date, to YHWH's words, there is hope for the city/temple! But if not—Jer. 38:18!

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:18 "the Chaldeans"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:18 "the Chaldeans" See SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 38:19 As Zedekiah was afraid of the officials in Jer. 38:4-5, now he is afraid of the Judean deserters! He should have been afraid of YHWH! If only he would have trusted in YHWH's promise (cf. Jer. 38:20). Divine promises are linked to human choices!

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:20 This reaffirmation of YHWH's promise has

  1. a command to obedience ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP)
  2. two conditional JUSSIVES
    1. it may go well with you ‒ BDB 405, KB 408, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    2. you may live ‒ BDB 310, KB 309, Qal JUSSIVE (cf. Jer. 38:2)

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:21-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:21-23 YHWH's promises, ignored or refused, result in consequences.

  1. women of the palace will be given over to the officials of the Neo-Babylonian army
  2. they will accuse the king of vacillation and weakness to his counselors ("your feet were sunk in the mire" is an idiom of indecision)
  3. Zedekiah's wives and children will be exiled. The VERB may imply
    1. sexual abuse
    2. humiliation
    3. exile
  4. Zedekiah will be tortured as he feared
  5. the city and temple will be destroyed

Verse 22 includes a poem at the end which is purported to be from the palace women given over to the Neo-Babylonian officers. It addresses a group of people called "your close friends."

  1. royal counselors who favored an alliance with Egypt
  2. royal counselors who wanted Jeremiah killed for treason
  3. false prophets who gave a supposed divine message absolutely opposite of Jeremiah's message of defeat and exile

entries.title: Jeremiah 38:26 "you are to say to them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
38:26 "you are to say to them" Jeremiah agrees to the cover story. He did ask the king this very question in Jer. 37:20.

The "cover story" involved the location of Jeremiah's confinement (cf. v. 28).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. How much time separates chapter 36 from 37?
  2. What does Jer. 37:3 and 17 imply about the king?
  3. Why was Jeremiah arrested in chapter 37?
  4. Did the officials have any grounds for his arrest?
  5. What does Jer. 37:20 say about Jeremiah?
  6. Why do some scholars see chapters 37 and 38 as two accounts of one occurrence?
  7. In which verse of chapter 38 does the weakness of Jeremiah show clearly?
  8. Why did the officials want to kill Jeremiah?
  9. Who is Ebed-melech?
  10. Did Jeremiah lie in Jer. 38:27?

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:1 "Jerusalem was captured"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:1 "Jerusalem was captured" Jerusalem fell in 586 B.C. (there are parallel accounts in Jeremiah 52 and 2 Kgs. 25:1-12).

▣ "in the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month. . .laid siege to it" The siege began in January of 588 B.C. It lasted over a year and a half (i.e. July of 586 B.C., cf. Jer. 52:4-6; 2 Kgs. 25:1-3).

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:3 The names and titles of the Neo-Babylon officials mentioned in Jer. 39:3 (cf. Jer. 39:13) are very confusing.

  1. the Septuagint, King James, and American Standard versions list six men
  2. Josephus (Antiq.10.7.2) and the Peshitta list five men
  3. the Revised Standard Version and Jewish Publication Society of America Bible list four men
  4. the New International Version, the New English Bible, and the Revised English Bible list three
  5. the New Jerusalem Bible lists two men
39:3
NASB  "sat down"
TEV  "took their places"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "sat in"
REB, NJB  "came in and took their seats"
NET  "set up quarters"
JPSOA  "took up quarters"

The MT has the VERB "sat," "sit" (BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERATIVE with waw). The NET Bible, p. 1407, #4, mentions that John Bright, in his commentary on Jeremiah, p. 243, asserts this phrase refers to the Neo-Babylonian leaders setting up provisional military governent in Jerusalem after its fall.

▣ "the Middle Gate" This designation is mentioned only here, so the location is uncertain.

▣ "Nergal-sar-ezer" This (BDB 669) is possibly the same as Neri-glissar, who was the successor to Nebuchadnezzar's son, Evil-merodach.

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:4 "they fled and went out of the city at night"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:4 "they fled and went out of the city at night" Josephus tells us that it was midnight (Antiq. 10.7.2, cf. Jer. 52:7; 2 Kgs. 25:4).

▣ "by way of the king's garden" From Neh. 2:14; 3:15; 12:37 it appears that this is the fountain of the Pool of Siloam.

▣ "Arabah" This refers to the great rift valley that runs from above the Sea of Galilee down into the Sinai. Here it would refer to the forested valley east of Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 39:5).

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:5 "the Chaldeans pursued"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:5 "the Chaldeans pursued" This is predicted in Jer. 32:4-5; 38:18,23. Josephus tells us that Jewish deserters informed the Neo-Babylonian officials of their flight.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "he passed sentence on him" Josephus tells us that it was for

  1. ingratitude
  2. treason

His sentence is spelled out in graphic detail in Jer. 39:6-7; 52:10-11; and 2 Kgs. 25:7.

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:6 "Riblah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:6 "Riblah" This was a city in a district of Syria. It was where Nebuchadnezzar's main expeditionary military camp was located. It is about fifty miles north of Damascus. Pharaoh Necho II also used this area as headquarters during the Carchemish campaign, where he was defeated (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:33)

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:8 "the houses of the people"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:8 "the houses of the people" The Masoretic Text is SINGULAR (UBS Text Project, p. 282, gives it a B rating) and, therefore, could mean

  1. a meeting hall
  2. the temple
  3. following the Talmud, the main synagogue
  4. Kimchi, a Jewish exegete of the Middle Ages, translates this phrase, "the peoples' houses" (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:9). This translation has influenced all English translations.

▣ "broke down the walls of Jerusalem" When limestone is exposed to high heat it loses its strength and cannot be reused for construction. The walls themselves were pulled down (BDB 683, KB 736, Qal PERFECT) the slopes so that it would be very difficult to raise them.

Jerusalem was totally destroyed and left uninhabited and uninhabitable!

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:9 "Nebuzaradan the captain of the bodyguard"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:9 "Nebuzaradan the captain of the bodyguard" It is uncertain whether this title (BDB 913 II CONSTRUCT BDB 371, literally "the chief slaughterer") refers to an executioner or the chief cook.

It is uncertain how many groups of people are exiled. There are two other groups.

  1. those left in the city (RSV)
  2. those who deserted

There is either a repeated reference to #1 or a third group which the NJB and REB identify as "artisans," which involves an emendation of the MT, but fits with the parallel of Jer. 52:15. See UBS Text Project, p. 283.

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:10 One way for the Neo-Babylonians to leave a loyal people who would pay taxes was to give the land to those who had nothing (i.e. the poor of the countryside). None of them were owners nor producers!

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:11-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:11-14 Jeremiah 40:1-6 seems to be a different account of the same event (similar to chapters 37 and 38). Some have asserted that these are in sequential order and others see two different accounts of the same event. At this point we just do not know. Moderns tend to read ancient literature through the filter of their own culture, era, and literary methods. See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:12 Nebuchadnezzar II must have heard about Jeremiah's prophetic message from

  1. Daniel
  2. Jewish deserters
  3. spies in the city of Jerusalem

He gives several orders.

  1. take him ‒ BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE (meaning "locate him")
  2. look after ‒ BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. do nothing harmful to him ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal JUSSIVE
  4. deal with him just as he tells you ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:14 "Gedaliah, the son of Ahikam"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:14 "Gedaliah, the son of Ahikam" Later Gedaliah was appointed the Neo-Babylonian governor of Judah (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:23; Jer. 40:5,7). He was not of the lineage of David. His father had been friendly to Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 26:24; 2 Kgs. 22:12-14).

▣ "take him home" At this point Gedaliah chose the city of Mizpah (cf. Jer. 40:5,8) to be his headquarters. Mizpah means "watchtower" and there were many towns by this name in Palestine.

Apparently, Jeremiah was taken to Gedaliah's new residence.

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:15-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:15-18 This paragraph is out of chronological order. Remember, the book of Jeremiah, like Isaiah, is an anthology of his messages over years of his ministry. YHWH's gracious attitude and actions toward Ebed-melech are because of his kind treatment and intercession on behalf of His prophet, Jeremiah while in the cistern (cf. Jer. 38:7-13).

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:17 "I will deliver you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 39:17 "I will deliver you" This VERB (BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil PERFECT with waw) is a promise that YHWH will deal kindly and with special protection to this foreigner (non-Jew). In Jer. 39:18 he is said to have trust (BDB 105, KB 120, Qal PERFECT) in YHWH (cf. Jer. 17:7,8).

entries.title: Jeremiah 39:18 "I will certainly rescue you"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
39:18 "I will certainly rescue you" This is a literary parallel to Jer. 39:17. The VERB (BDB 572, KB 589) is intensified by the INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and the IMPERFECT VERB of the same root.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:1 "The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:1 "The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord" Notice no word/message is recorded. One wonders if the theological quote from Jer. 40:2-3 were a part of that message. The theology recorded is so specific and unexpected from the lips of a Babylonian military commander.

This phrase, "the word of the Lord came," is repeated often in the major prophets. It was a way to clearly denote that the message was YHWH's, not the prophets'. This is similar to Paul's use of being called an Apostle in his letters to establish his authority. For a good brief discussion, see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 66-69.

▣ "Nebuzaradan captain of the bodyguard" From 2 Kgs. 25:3,8 it seems that this man came one month after the capture of Jerusalem to oversee the complete destruction of the city.

▣ "Ramah" This city was on the route of the Judean exiles to Babylon (cf. Jer. 31:15).

▣ "he had taken him bound in chains" The Jewish Midrash says Jeremiah saw the young men in chains and joined them. But it seems he was mistakenly arrested and taken as far north as Ramah before Nebuchadnezzar's orders (cf. Jer. 39:11-14) were finally carried out.

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:2-4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:2-4 These verses are often rejected by scholars because of their high theological content. It is quite possible that Jeremiah's prophecies were relayed to the Neo-Babylonians

  1. by spies in Jerusalem
  2. after the city's downfall

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:4 This verse has several idioms and IMPERATIVES.

  1. "if you would prefer" is literally "it is good in your eyes"
  2. "came. . .came" ‒ This is a Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT and a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 97, KB 112)
  3. "I will look after you" is literally "set my eyes on"
  4. "if you would prefer" is literally "it is evil in your eyes"
  5. "never mind" is literally "cease" ‒ BDB 292, KB 292, Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. "look" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE
  7. "go. . .to go" ‒ This is an INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT and Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 229, KB 246). This same phrase is repeated in Jer. 40:5.
40:5
NASB  "Jeremiah was still not going back"
NKJV  "now while Jeremiah had not yet gone back"
NRSV  "if you remain"
TEV  "when I did not answer"
REB  "before Jeremiah could answer"
NJB  "before Jeremiah retired"
Peshitta  "then he said to him again"

It is obvious the phrase is ambiguous. The MT has "and still he will remain." This phrase seems to reflect some hesitation on Jeremiah's part on where to go. The UBS Text Project discusses the options on p. 285. It gives the MT a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "Gedaliah the son of Ahikam" This man's father was a supporter and helper of Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 26:24). Gedaliah was entrusted with Jeremiah's care in Jer. 39:14. He came from a godly family (cf. 2 Kgs. 22:14).

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:6 "Mizpah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 40:6 "Mizpah" This means "watchtower" (BDB 859). There are several cities by this name (see The MacMillan Bible Atlas, p. 211). One of them was the location of Saul being chosen as king (cf. 1 Sam. 10:17ff). It became a central meeting place for the tribes (cf. Jgds. 20:1-3). This is where Gedaliah had his headquarters. It was about 8 miles north of Jerusalem in the tribal allocation of Benjamin.

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:7 "the commanders of the forces that were in the field"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:7 "the commanders of the forces that were in the field" This refers to Jewish military units not captured by Nebuchadnezzar's army because they were not in Jerusalem when it fell.

▣ "those of the poorest of the land who had not been exiled to Babylon" This links with Jer. 39:10.

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:8 "and their men"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:8 "and their men" There are at least two ways to understand this phrase.

  1. There were Judean military units in the countryside that escaped the Neo-Babylonian invasion.
  2. The "men of war" were country folk who, in times of crisis, became part time soldiers, but after the crisis returned to their vocations.

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:9 "Gedaliah. . .swore to them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:9 "Gedaliah. . .swore to them" The new governor's first responsibility was convincing the Jewish forces to lay down their arms (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:23-24).

Notice what Gedaliah swore (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal IMPERFECT with waw).

  1. do not be afraid ‒ BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  2. stay in the land ‒ BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. serve the king of Babylon ‒ BDB 712, KB 773, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. that it may go well with you ‒ BDB 405, KB 408, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
▣
NASB, NJB  "serving the Chaldeans"
NKJV, NRSV, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "tp serve the Chaldeans"
TEV  "to surrender to the Babylonians"

The Septuagint (LXX) has "do not be afraid of the Chaldean officials" (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:24). The UBS Text Project, p. 286, gives the MT VERB "to serve" (BDB 712, KB 773, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) a "B" rating, instead of "the servants" (NEB).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:10 "to stand before the Chaldeans"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:10 "to stand before the Chaldeans" This term (BDB 763, KB 840, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is often used of priests standing before God on behalf of sinful humans. Therefore, we can understand the word to mean "mediator" in this context.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

▣ "gather in wine and summer fruit and oil" The war had left the fields unattended. If this fruit was not gathered it would spoil and they would have no food for winter.

There are three commands in Gedaliah's statement.

  1. gather ‒ BDB 62, KB 74, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. put ‒ BDB 962, KB 1321, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. live ‒ BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:11-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 40:11-12 Many Jewish exiles in the neighboring countries returned to take advantage of the free land and prepare for winter by harvesting the ripe crops.

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:14 "Are you well aware"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:14 "Are you well aware" Johanan thought that it was common knowledge that Ishmael was going to attempt to assassinate Gedaliah. This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 393, KB 390), used for emphasis.

▣ "Baalis the king of the sons of Ammon" Baalis' name is related to the Canaanite fertility god Ba'al. The Jewish Study Bible (p. 1008) asserts that he may be the "ba'alyash" from a 6th century Ammonite seal impression (also note NASB Study Bible, p. 1122 footnote).

▣ "Ishmael" Ishmael was of the Davidic line (cf. Jer. 41:1; 2 Kgs. 25:25). The exact reason for his assassination of Gedaliah is uncertain.

  1. attempt to restore the ancient covenant promises to the house of David
  2. jealousy because he had been overlooked (he, not Gedaliah, was of the lineage of David)
  3. acting on behalf of Baalis, King of Ammon
    1. to take over control of Judah at this weakened moment
    2. to help restore Davidic rule
  4. he was just a cruel man (cf. Jer. 41:4-10)

▣ "did not believe them" The reason is not stated. Maybe he felt YHW had brought him to a time like this.

entries.title: Jeremiah 40:15-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
40:15-16 Gedaliah did not believe the rumor about Ishmael. He did nothing to protect himself.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:1 "Now it came about"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:1 "Now it came about" Jeremiah 41 continues the literary unit which began in Jeremiah 40, specifically about the plot to assassinate Gedaliah (Jer. 40:13-16).

▣ "while they were eating bread together there at Mizpah" The viciousness of this act can only be seen in the eastern culture's attitude toward the importance of eating together (i.e. Ps. 41:9).

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:2 "arose and struck down Gedeliah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:2 "arose and struck down Gedeliah" The exact date is uncertain but it preceded the deportation of 582 B.C. (cf. Jer. 52:30). The time can be from

  1. three months after the fall of Jerusalem (586 B.C.)
  2. four years after the fall of Jerusalem (the deportation of 582 B.C., cf. Jer. 52:30).

▣ "struck down Gedaliah" Josephus, who recorded the current Jewish thoughts of his day, comments that Gedaliah was drunk (Antiq. 10.9.4).

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:3 "and the Chaldeans who were found there, the men of war"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 41:3 "and the Chaldeans who were found there, the men of war" As we learn from Jer. 41:18, the remaining Jews were afraid of Neo-Babylon's reprisals (cf. Josephus, Antiq. 10.9.5).

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:5 "Shechem. . .Shiloh. . .Samaria"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:5 "Shechem. . .Shiloh. . .Samaria" These were three northern cities. Samaria was the ancient capital of the Northern Ten Tribes, established by Omri. This area was devastated and the people exiled by Assyria in 722 B.C.

The people from these cities in the northern kingdom (now exiled) still viewed Jerusalem as YHWH's special city and the temple as His special meeting place! It is this theology that expected and demanded a reunification of the tribes of Jacob.

▣ "with their beards shaved off and their clothes torn and their bodies gashed" These were Jews going to Jerusalem to bemoan the destruction of the temple. The gashing of their bodies is related to pagan mourning rites. These mourning rites are mentioned often in Job 1:20; Isa. 22:12; Jer. 16:6; 47:5; 48:37; Ezek. 7:18; Amos 8:10; Lev. 19:28; 21:5; Deut. 14:1; 1 Kgs. 18:28. The elements of the amalgamated worship of YHWH and the gods of Canaan continue.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:6-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:6-10 Something of Ishmael's personality can be seen.

  1. fake crying, Jer. 41:6
  2. killing 70 innocent mourners, apparently just to cover up his slaughter of Gedaliah
  3. sparing ten people for their hidden supplies or for ransom
  4. polluting the water supply of Mizpah with the dead corpses
  5. kidnapping the remainder of the population of Mizpah, for what reason is unsure, possibly to sell into slavery or as a gift to Baalis

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:8 "oil and honey hidden in the field"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 41:8 "oil and honey hidden in the field" This was a usual procedure both for keeping the food cool and for hiding it in times of war.

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:9 "because of Gedaliah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:9 "because of Gedaliah" The Masoretic Text has "by the hand of Gedaliah." This is obviously an impossible translation. There are several suggestions.

  1. a Ugaritic root to translate "because of Gedaliah" (NKJV)
  2. BDB 390 #3 suggests "by the side of"
  3. the LXX has the phrase "this is a large well" (NJB, REB, NRSV, NET)
  4. the JPSOA has "in the affair of Gedaliah"
  5. the Peshitta has "with Gedaliah"

▣ "the one that King Asa had made on account of Baasha, king of Israel" See the account in 1 Kgs. 15:17-22; 2 Chr. 16:1-6.

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:10 "all the remnant of the people who were in Mizpah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:10 "all the remnant of the people who were in Mizpah" This group must have included Jeremiah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (three senses)

▣ "the king's daughters" This could refer to

  1. some of the literal royal family left in Gedaliah's charge
  2. some of the line of David returning from the surrounding countries
  3. It could refer to the daughters of the "princes" of Judah.

▣ "to cross over to the sons of Ammon" This implies that he traveled to the east and planned to cross the Jordan River into the trans-Jordan region controlled by Baalis (cf. Jer. 40:14).

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:12 "the great pool that is at Gibeon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 41:12 "the great pool that is at Gibeon" Archaeology has found a large rock cistern seventy to eighty feet deep at Gibeon (cf. 2 Sam. 2:12-16).

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:13 "they were glad"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:13 "they were glad" This must refer to those taken forcibly from Mizpah (cf. Jer. 41:10,16).

41:16
NASB, NKJV  "the people whom he had recovered
  from Ishmael"
NRSV  "the people whom Ishmael. . .had carried
  away captive"
TEV  "took charge of the people whom Ishmael
  had taken away as prisoners"
REB, JPSOA  "all the survivors who he had rescued from
  Ishmael"
NJB  "then rallied all the remaining people whom
  Ishmael. . .had taken as prisoners"
Peshitta  "took all the remnant of the people whom
  he had recovered from Ishmael"
NET  "led off all the people who had been left
  alive"

The MT has "all the rest of the people whom he recovered from Ishamel." This phrase is ambiguous, but the larger context helps the understanding. This is a good example of the crucial hermeneutical aspect of both

  1. historical setting
  2. literary context

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

entries.title: Jeremiah 41:17 "Geruth Chimham"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
41:17 "Geruth Chimham" The first word (BDB 158) means "lodging place" or "inn." It denoted a caravan camping place (possibly had a well or natural protection from the wind).

The second word (BDB 484) can be

  1. a location near Bethlehem
  2. a person (cf. 2 Sam. 19:37,38,40, an attendant of David)
  3. Josephus calls the place "Mandara" (Antiq. 10.9.5)

Its location is unknown. The name is found only here in the Hebrew Bible.

▣ "in order to proceed into Egypt" This shows that Johanan had already made up his mind to go to Egypt, and also sets the stage for Jeremiah 42. They went to Egypt out of fear of Nebuchadnezzar's reprisals!

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:1 "Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:1 "Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah" The person mentioned in Jer. 42:1 seems to be the same as in Jer. 43:2. The Septuagint (NRSV) has "Azariah" in both places. The UBS Text Project, p. 287, gives "Jezaniah" a "B" rating.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

▣ "both small and great" There are several forms of this Hebraic idiom which denote all the people (cf. Jer. 6:13; 8:10; 42:8; 44:12). This is a hyperbolic, inclusive idiom which does not mean every person. Hyperbole is such a common ANE literary form and it is so misunderstood by westerners. See G. B. Caird, The Langauge and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 110-117 and D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, especially chapter 5.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:2 "Jeremiah the prophet"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:2 "Jeremiah the prophet" This designation is repeated in Jer. 42:4. There is no doubt now, after the fall of Jerusalem to the Neo-Babylonian army, that Jeremiah was a true prophet (cf. Deut. 13:1-5). All that he had predicted came true. This is also a warning to those remaining Judeans who seek YHWH's counsel through him (cf. Jer. 42:4).

In a sense this chapter is an example of a reverse "exodus." The Judeans refused to trust YHWH and stay in Palestine! Disobedience remains the problem!

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIFFERENT HEBREW TERMS FOR PROPHET, #3

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT)

▣ "the Lord your God" The use of the PERSONAL PRONOUN "your" is not a theological statement of the petitioner's lack of faith in YHWH, but simply a cultural idiom (cf. 1 Kgs. 13:6; Jer. 37:3; 42:3,6, and esp. Jer. 42:20).

▣ "for all this remnant" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (three senses), A. #2

▣ "because we are left but a few out of many" This may be an allusion to Deut. 28:62. The covenant people were to be as the stars of heaven, the sand in the seashore (cf. Gen. 13:16), but they rebelled and violated the covenant.

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S COVENANT REQUIREMENTS OF ISRAEL

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:3 This is false piety. They really did not want to know YHWH's will. They wanted Him to affirm their decision of fleeing to Egypt. They had not followed YHWH's will (expressed through Scripture and the prophets) up to this point in their history. This is a sample of "fox-hole" faith (i.e. faith in crisis) that only lasts until the crisis has passed!

▣ "walk" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:4 Jeremiah agrees to pray on their behalf. He will pass on their words to YHWH and will give them "exactly" His words!

The last phrase of this verse, "I will not keep back a word from you," reminds one of the interchange between Eli and Samuel in 1 Sam. 3:17-18.

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:5 These are two theologically significant words, "true" and "faithful," which are forms of the same root.

  1. true ‒ BDB 54, cf. Jer. 2:21; 4:2; 9:5; 10:10; 14:13; 23:28; 26:15; 28:9; 32:41; 33:6; 42:5
  2. faithful ‒ BDB 52, cf. Jer. 12:6; 15:18; 40:14; 42:5

SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:5-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 42:5-6 These verses are a tremendous statement of faith, but just not true! They really wanted God to approve their plans. Words of faith do not replace lives of faith!

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:6 "that it may go well with us when we listen to the voice of the Lord our God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:6 "that it may go well with us when we listen to the voice of the Lord our God" The phrase "go well" is an idiom from Deuteronomy (cf. Deut. 4:40; 5:16,29,33). It is used in Jeremiah in Jer. 7:23; 38:20. Remember, the desire of YHWH for His covenant people is "blessing" so that the nations may be attracted to Him. This is part of the OT's "two ways" (cf. Deut. 30:15-20, Psalm 1).

For "listen" see SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema).

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:7 "at the end of ten days the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:7 "at the end of ten days the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah" Notice that Jeremiah had to wait for YHWH to respond. He could not voice his own opinion.

For "ten" see SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:10 "If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:10 "If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down" This is related to Jeremiah's call in Jer. 1:10. This is a tremendous promise of restoration and divine protection!

The first of v. 10, in the MT, has the VERB shub (שׁוב, BDB 996, KB 1427, Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE, but Masoretic scholars suggest it should be the VERB "remain" (ישׁב, BDB 442, KB 444), which matches the IMPERFECT VERB, making this an intensified statement (i.e. NASB, "if you will indeed stay in the land"). Notice lthe conditional nature of YHWH's response!

▣ "I will relent" This is literally "to be sorry" (BDB 636, KB 688, Niphal PERFECT; cf. Jer. 4:28; 15:6; 18:8; 20:16; 31:15,19; Joel 2:13; Amos 7:3,6; Jonah 3:10; 4:2). God does change His mind, based on human repentance! If prayer and repentance do not change God, why do believers pray?!

Remember all characterizations about Deity are communicated in human language. A change of heart and mind in a human triggers a positive response from God! Most prophecies are conditional (even when not stated). They express what will happen if the current attitude and actions continue. But if repentance occurs the future changes (i.e. Jonah)! See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic.

It is a tenet of hermeneutics that a literary context must also be interpreted in a larger historical context. The ANE, particularly Sumer and Babylon, record that pagan deities also grieved over the judgment they allowed to occur. See The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 674.

Several of my favorite commentators try to interpret the Bible in light of its cultural setting.

  1. R. K. Harrison
  2. Roland deVaux
  3. John H. Walton
  4. Kenneth E. Bailey

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: INTERCESSORY PRAYER

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:11 What a wonderful encouragement.

  1. do not be afraid of the king of Babylon ‒ BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (cf. Jer. 1:8; also note 2 Chr. 32:7-8)
  2. whom you are now fearing ‒ BDB 431, KB 432, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  3. do not be afraid of him (repeated for emphasis; note Rom. 8:31-39)
  4. I am with you (i.e. there is no greater promise)
    1. to save ‒ BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (Jer. 15:20)
    2. to deliver ‒ BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (cf. Jer. 1:19; Isa. 43:2,5)

This was YHWH's word to them! Would they believe it and obey it by faith? They said they would (Jer. 42:5-6), but they would not!

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:12 YHWH promises that as He shows compassion/mercy (BDB 933, KB 1216), He will guide His servant Nebuchadnezzar II to show mercy to the remaining remnant of Judeans (there are textual variants related to the PRONOUNS "he" and "I." YHWH will direct Nebuchadnezzar).

The phrase "I will restore you to your own soil" may reflect that

  1. Jeremiah wrote this text while in Egypt
  2. it is idiomatic for their own personal ancestral property

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:13-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:13-17 The conditional nature of YHWH's answer to their prayers through Jeremiah is clearly spelled out in these verses. Rejection of YHWH's repentance and mercy becomes the curse of judgment (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-30). There is an awesome responsibility in seeking YHWH's guidance!

The IMPERATIVE of "listen" ("hear," BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE) in Jer. 42:15 has consequences (cf. Luke 12:48).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:15 "remnant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:15 "remnant" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT, three senses, A. #2.

▣
NASB  "if you really set your mind"
NKJV  "if you wholly set your faces"
Peshitta  "if you set your faces"
JPSOA  "if you turn your faces"
NRSV, TEV, REB, NJB, NET  "if you are so determined"

These translations reflect a common Hebrew idiom involving the use of "face" as denoting a personal decision. Here, it denotes a decision against the revealed will of YHWH. These people said one thing but did another!

  1. human decisions ‒ 2 Kgs. 12:17; Jer. 42:17; 44:11; Dan. 11:17
  2. divine decisions ‒ Lev. 26:17; Jer. 21:10; 44:11

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:16 Notice the personification of the means YHWH will use for His judgment.

  1. the sword ‒ will overtake you (BDB 673, KB 727, Hiphil IMPERFECT
  2. the famine ‒ will follow closely after you (BDB 179, KB 209, Qal IMPERFECT

See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp. 136-137.

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:18 "the Lord of hosts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:18 "the Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts.

▣ "you will see this place no more" This is God's stern warning that if they violated His words, there would be no restoration for them!

Notice the list of negative consequences for disobeying YHWH's revealed will (see Ps. 24:9).

  1. as My anger and wrath (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD) have been poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so too, on you
  2. "a curse" ‒ BDB 46, #4, "excretion," cf. Num. 5:27; Deut. 29:21; Jer. 29:18; 42:18; 44:12
  3. "an object of horror" ‒ BDB 1031 I, "apallment," "horror" ‒ cf. Deut. 28:37; 2 Kgs. 22:19; 2 Chr. 29:8; 30:7; Jer. 5:30; 25:9,11; 29:18; 42:18; 44:12,22; 49:13,17; 50:23; 51:37,41; Micah 6:16; Zeph. 2:15
  4. "an imprecation" ‒ BDB 887, cf. Deut. 11:26,28; 21:23; 23:5; 28:15,45; 2 Kgs. 22:19; Ps. 109:17,18; Jer. 24:9; 25:18; 29:22; Zech. 8:13
  5. "a reproach" ‒ BDB 357, #3, "a taunt," cf. Ps. 31:11; 44:13; 69:10; 79:4; 89:41; 109:25; Isa. 30:5; Jer. 6:10; 20:8; 24:9; 29:18; 44:8,12; 49:13; Ezek. 5:14,15; Dan. 9;16; 12:2
  6. you will become a reproach (BDB 357, cf. Jer. 6:10; 24:9; 29:18; 42:18; 44:8,12; 49:13)
  7. you will see this place (i.e. Judah) no more (see SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS)

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:19 "clearly understand"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 42:19 "clearly understand" This is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 393, KB 390) used for emphasis. For even added emphasis, it is repeated twice (Jer. 42:19 and 22). These Judeans asked for YHWH's guidance and now they were knowingly rejecting it! Ignorance is one thing, but open-eyed disobedience is another.

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:20 "you have only deceived yourselves"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:20 "you have only deceived yourselves" How characteristic of fallen mankind! We tend to do what we want to do! We only appear to be religious (i.e. Isa. 29:13)!

▣ "we will do it" They were planning incredible disobedience in light of Jer. 42:5 and 6!

entries.title: Jeremiah 42:21 "you have not obeyed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
42:21 "you have not obeyed" Literally "listened to." See SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema) and SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:1 "Jeremiah, whom the Lord their God had sent"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 43:1 "Jeremiah, whom the Lord their God had sent" This phrase, like "Jeremiah the prophet" in Jer. 42:2,4, affirms the true status of Jeremiah. He was YHWH's spokesperson to them. He was the giver of the "voice of YHWH" (cf. Jer. 42:13,21). To disobey his prophecy was to disobey YHWH!

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. There is little historical evidence for an invasion of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar II.
    1. fragment of Nebuchadnezzar annals from the 37th year (568-567 B.C.)
    2. Herodotus, History
    3. Ezekiel 29:19-21

  2. The invasion may have been a punitive raid which, after initial success, was suspended. After this the political relationship between Egypt and Neo-Babylon improved.

  3. There was another military campaign against Egypt by Nabonidus (550-539 B.C.) in the closing days of the Neo-Babylonian Empire which lasted ten years.

  4. Jeremiah 43 and 44 are a literary unit but deal with two different groups of Judean refugees.

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:2 "Azariah the son of Hoshaiah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
43:2 "Azariah the son of Hoshaiah" This is probably the brother of Jezaniah (i.e. Jer. 42:1).

▣
NASB, TEV, NJB, JPSOA  "the arrogant men"
NKJV  "the proud men"
NRSV  "the insolent men"
Peshitta  "the wicked men"
REB  "their party"
LXX  "all the men who had spoken"

The Hebrew word (BDB 267) has the connotation of those who knowingly reject YHWH's word/message (cf. Ps. 119:21; Prov. 21:24; Mal. 4:1 [MT 3:19]).

This type of person is described in Jer. 5:12-13. The consequences of this attitude was clearly stated in Jer. 42:15-16.

▣ "you are telling a lie" They knew that Jeremiah was a prophet because all of his predictions had come true concerning the Neo-Babylonian invasion (i.e. Deuteronomy 13), yet they had already made up their minds (cf. Jer. 41:17). They wanted the pretense of spirituality but not the demanded obedience! Rejecting Jeremiah was tantamount to rejecting YHWH!

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:3 "but Baruch is inciting you against us"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 43:3 "but Baruch is inciting you against us" This shows that Baruch was more than just a secretary. He had great influence on Jeremiah (cf. chapter 45).

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:5 "who had returned from all the nations to which they had been driven away, in order to reside in the land of Judah"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 43:5 "who had returned from all the nations to which they had been driven away, in order to reside in the land of Judah" They were afraid because of Ishmael's ruthless acts against Gedaliah and the Neo-Babylonian honor guard. These covenant people had returned to live in the land of Judah; how ironical that now they were fleeing to Egypt.

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:6 "together with Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 43:6 "together with Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch" The prophet and his scribe were forced to accompany them in the face of God's warning.

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:7 "Tahpanhes"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 43:7 "Tahpanhes" This is one of the border cities (i.e. in Egyptian, "the Fortress of Penhase") in the eastern delta region on the caravan route to Palestine. It was just barely into Egypt's national boundary.

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:8-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 43:8-13 This paragraph describes the Neo-Babylonian invasion and destruction of Egypt as far as Heliopolis (Hebrew, "House of the Sun"). Jeremiah is again giving a very specific prophecy to prove/validate his role as prophet (possible date is 568-567 B.C.).

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:10 "Lord of hosts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
43:10 "Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

▣ "My servant" See SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

▣
NASB, NJB, REB  "canopy"
NKJV, Peshitta  "royal pavilion"
TEV, NET  "royal tent"
JPSOA  "pavilion"
LXX  "his weapons"

The BDB 1051 and KB 1636 suggest that this term (found only here in the OT) could mean

  1. royal pavilion
  2. canopy
  3. carpet
  4. scepter (from Akkadian root)

The first three suggestions assume an Assyrian VERB, "to spread out." The point is that a special royal structure in Egypt will become a Neo-Babylonian camp.

Herodotus, Nebuchadnezzar II annals, and Ezek. 29:19-21 all speak briefly of a Neo-Babylonian invasion of Egypt in 568 B.C.

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
43:11 This is a literary way of expressing YHWH's sovereignty (cf. Jer. 15:2) through Nebuchadnezzar II (called YHWH's servant in Jer. 43:10).

The translation of Jer. 43:12a reflects this by the NRSV and REB having "he" and the MT having "I." Nebuchadnezzar's army will do it but the real power and will are YHWH's. The UBS Text Project, p. 289, gives "I" a "B" rating.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 43:12 The idols and their temples will be burned and their gold, silver, and jewels taken to Babylon.

entries.title: Jeremiah 43:13 "the obelisks of Heliopolis"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
43:13 "the obelisks of Heliopolis" This city was called "On" by the Egyptians and "Beth-Shemesh" (i.e. "house of the Sun") by Jeremiah. It was known for its royal/religious pillars or obelisks.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:1 The cities of Migdol and Tahpanhes are in the eastern delta region. Memphis is about 100 miles up the Nile. The Land of Pathros is another 100 miles up the Nile (i.e. city of No-Amon). These locations would represent most of Egypt.

It is surprising that the expected full phrase "the word. . .from the Lord" is shortened but it still reflects the full revelatory formula of Jer. 7:1; 11:1; 18:1; 21:1; 30:1; 32:1; 34:1,8; 35:1; 40:1.
