CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. There is little historical evidence for an invasion of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar II.
    1. fragment of Nebuchadnezzar annals from the 37th year (568-567 B.C.)
    2. Herodotus, History
    3. Ezekiel 29:19-21

  2. The invasion may have been a punitive raid which, after initial success, was suspended. After this the political relationship between Egypt and Neo-Babylon improved.

  3. There was another military campaign against Egypt by Nabonidus (550-539 B.C.) in the closing days of the Neo-Babylonian Empire which lasted ten years.

  4. Jeremiah 43 and 44 are a literary unit but deal with two different groups of Judean refugees.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:2 "the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:2 "the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel" This extended title using YHWH and Elohim is repeated four times in this chapter (cf. Jer. 44:2,7,11,25). He is creator and covenant-making Deity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C., D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:3 Israel and Judah's problem was covenant disobedience.

  1. not listening to and obeying YHWH (cf. Jer. 44:23)
  2. going after other gods (cf. Jer. 44:3,5,15-19)

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (shema)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

▣ "burn sacrifices" This VERB (BDB 882, KB 1094, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) can mean (cf. Jer. 1:16)

  1. the smoke of a sacrifice
  2. the smoke of incense (cf. Jer. 44:17-18)

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:4 "again and again"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:4 "again and again" This is literally "rising early and sending" (cf. Jer. 7:13,25; 25:4; 26:5; 35:15). The Judeans knew YHWH's will through previous revelations to the Patriarchs and Moses/Joshua, as well as the messages of the prophets.

▣ "My servants the prophets" See SPECIAL TOPIC: SERVANT LEADERSHIP

▣ "abominable thing" For this phrase see Jer. 16:18; 32:34,35>

SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:6 The fall of Judah was not because of the power of the Babylonian god Marduk or the power of the Babylonian army. It was Judah's continued covenant disobedience that caused YHWH to bring to bear the "curses" of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:7 This verse is parallel to Jer. 42:20 (cf. Jer. 26:19). One's choices determine the consequences (cf. Deut. 30:15,19). These Judeans' choice will bring their lineage to an end (hyperbolic, some did survive)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:8 The idolatry (i.e. "the work of your hands," cf. Isa. 2:8; 17:8; 39:17; Jer. 25:6) of the Judeans continues in Egypt! These Jews changed the worship of the gods of Canaan to the gods of Egypt (cf. Jer. 2:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY, #6

▣ "become a curse and a reproach among all the nations of the earth" See full note at Jer. 42:18 (#4, BDB 887). The covenant people were to be a blessing to all the nations (cf. Gen. 12:3), but they had become a curse. They were meant to reveal the mercy and goodness of YHWH to the nations, but all they revealed was His anger (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ Idolatry spread to all levels of society! See note at Jer. 42:18.

▣
NASB, MT  "his wives"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV, REB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "of their wives"
NJB  "of your princes"
LXX  "of your rulers"

The UBS Text Project, p. 290, gives the MT a "B" rating. Wives were very involved in the worship of the Queen of Heaven (see note at v. 19).

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:10 "But they have not become contrite"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:10 "But they have not become contrite" The VERB (BDB 193, KB 221, Pual PERFECT) usually means "to crush"; here it is uniquely used to denote a crushed, repentant spirit.

Their lack of repentance is characterized as

  1. they have not feared YHWH
  2. they have not walked in His revelation (i.e. law, statutes)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:11 "I am going to set My face against you for woe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:11 "I am going to set My face against you for woe" This is vocabulary from Leviticus 26 (i.e. the cursings and blessings connected to covenant obedience, cf. Jer. 44:27). This phrase was used earlier in Jer. 21:10 (cf. Amos 9:4). A similar phrase is used in Jer. 44:27. YHWH will personally bring His people to judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FACE TO FACE

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:12 "remnant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:12 "remnant" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (three senses), A. #2

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:12-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:12-13 This is a repeat of Jer. 42:15-18,22.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:14 "for none will return except a few refugees"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:14 "for none will return except a few refugees" A small number will survive and return to Palestine (cf. Jer. 44:28). The Judeans who will be spared and returned are the ones taken to Babylon.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:16 As the Judean remnant in Judea would not listen (cf. Jer. 42:14-17; 43:2), so too, the ones already in Egypt.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:17 "we will certainly carry out every word"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:17 "we will certainly carry out every word" The VERB is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB from the same root (BDB 793, KB 889). This same intensive form is in Jer. 44:25 (twice). It denotes their strong intent to offer idolatrous sacrifices!

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:17-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:17-19 These Judeans attribute their current condition to their lack of idolatrous sacrifices, which Josiah stopped! O my, when light becomes darkness, how great is the darkness!

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:18 The historical period these idolaters are referring to must have been the reign of Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, who reigned 55 years and was the most wicked king of Judah. Josiah tried to bring the idolatry to an end (cf. 2 Kings 23) but at his death it returned!

These three kings (i.e. Hezekiah, Manasseh, and Josiah) may be the background to Ezekiel 18.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:19 The queen of heaven (i.e. female fertility goddess, cf. Jer. 7:18; 44:17,19,25; 2 Kgs. 17:16; possibly Ishtar or Astarte/Asherah) was a popular idol for women in the Ancient Near East. Notice the number of times "wife" or "women" is used in this chapter (cf. Jer. 44:9 [twice],15,19,20,24,25).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:20-30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:20-30 This is the last message of Jeremiah recorded in the book. He was in Egypt and was confronted again with widespread idolatry by the Judeans, a total disregard for YHWH's revelation/covenant.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:21 "the people of the land"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:21 "the people of the land" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PEOPLE OF THE LAND

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:22 This is similar to the warnings of Jer. 25:9,11,18,38; 29:18; 42:18; 44:13.

▣ "the abominations" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ABOMINATION

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:23 "not obeyed the voice of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:23 "not obeyed the voice of the Lord" The voice was communicated through Jeremiah (i.e. "the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah").

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

▣ "walked" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY.

▣ "His law, His statutes or His testimonies" See SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION, II.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:25 This verse repeats the committed promises of the Judean idol worshipers of Jer. 44:17 to continue their rebellious worship practices (here two intensified IMPERFECT VERBS and matching INFINITIVE ABSOLUTES).

▣ "the Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: The Lord of Hosts

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:26 The committed vows of idolatry by the Judean families in Egypt are now matched by the commitment (i.e. vow) of YHWH to bring judgment on them (cf. Jer. 44:27). They shall never call on His name again.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CALL ON HIS NAME

▣ "As the Lord God lives" This phrase contains two titles for Israel's Deity.

  1. Lord (Adon) ‒ SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (Adon and Aiōnios)
  2. God (YHWH) ‒ SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

This is an oath formula usually used in a worship setting to affirm the truthfulness of one's statement.

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:27 "I am watching over them for harm and not for good"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:27 "I am watching over them for harm and not for good" The VERB (BDB 1052, KB 1638, Qal PARTICIPLE) is a recurrent theological word in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 1:12; 31:28 [twice]) denoting YHWH's focused attention to those who

  1. do His will
  2. disobey His will

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:28 "remnant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 44:28 "remnant" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE REMNANT (three senses)

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:29 "My words will surely stand against you for harm"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:29 "My words will surely stand against you for harm" The VERB (BDB 877, KB 1086) is an INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and an IMPERFECT VERB denoting emphasis. This very form was used in Jer. 44:25 related to the idolaters' promise to continue to offer sacrifices. Now it is used of the certainty of YHWH's judgment.

▣ "sign" See SPECIAL TOPIC: SIGN (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 44:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
44:30 YHWH will judge Pharaoh Hophra (cf. Jer. 43:9-13 and 46:25; also note Ezek. 29:3). Pharaoh Hophra (Herodotus called him Apries) reigned from 588 to 569 B.C. (Jewish Study Bible has 589-570 B.C.), when he was killed in a rebellion led by one of his own officials. He was succeed by Amasus (569-525 B.C.).

Hophra was the Pharaoh who encouraged Zedekiah to rebel against Nebuchadnezzar. He was the one who sent the Egyptian army into Palestine during the siege of Jerusalem (cf. Jer. 37:5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF EGYPT

▣ "into the hand" See SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 45:1 "in the fourth year of Jehoiakim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
45:1 "in the fourth year of Jehoiakim" The date for this would be 605 B.C. This was the same year Neo-Babylon defeated the remnants of the Assyrian army and the Egyptian army at Carchemish in northern Syria (cf. Jer. 46:2). The power in the ANE changed!

The historical setting for this brief chapter is chapter 36.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

▣ "when he had written down these words in a book at Jeremiah's dictation" It is uncertain if this phrase refers to

  1. Jeremiah's first dictation to Baruch ‒ Jer. 36:4
  2. Jeremiah's expanded rewriting‒ Jer. 36:32

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 45:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
45:3 Baruch was grieving over the current state of affairs (i.e. for the king burning Jeremiah's scroll, see chapter 36).

  1. "woe is me!" (cf. Jer. 4:13,31; 6:4; 10:19; 13:27; 15:10; 22:13; 23:1; 48:1,46; 50:27, obviously a cultural idiom of despair)
  2. the Lord has added sorrow to my pain
  3. I am weary with my groaning
  4. I have found no rest

entries.title: Jeremiah 45:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
45:4 This verbiage reflects Jeremiah's call in Jer. 1:10 (cf. Jer. 18:7-10; 24:6; 31:28; 42:10). The curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 have come to reality! A reverse "exodus" has occurred in parallel to the removal of the Canaanite population who had previously inhabited Canaan (cf. Gen. 15:16). Their idolatry caused them to be exiled, so too, now Judah's idolatry has caused her to be exiled.

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

▣ "the whole land" Context clarifies that erets (BDB 75, KB 90) refers to

  1. Canaan
  2. also possibly Egypt

SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY EARTH

SPECIAL TOPIC: WORLD (several terms)

entries.title: Jeremiah 45:5 "But you, are you seeking great things for yourself?"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
45:5 "But you, are you seeking great things for yourself?" This is always an appropriate question for fallen, self-centered humanity. Believers must remember that all things are in our God's hands. We are only stewards. Our only appropriate response is, "I am available!" or "Here am I, send me."

A good biblical example of a person who recognized his spiritual stewardship (at least at first) was Solomon (cf. 1 Kgs. 3:9,11).

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NET  "you seek great things for yourself?"
TEV  "Are you looking for special
  treatment for yourself?"
NJB  "you ask for special treatment!"
REB, Peshitta  "you once sosught great things for
  yourself"
JPSOA  "do you expect great things for
  yourself?"

This phrase is not clarified in context. The translation options show the theories.

  1. Baruch expected special treatment (i.e. did not have to go to Egypt)
  2. Baruch was upset that he did not receive some honor with Jeremiah (i.e. recognized as a spiritual leader and compiler/editor of Jeremiah's prophecies)
  3. Baruch was hoping to escape the prophesied judgment of Judeans in Egypt
  4. he expected to be rewarded for supporting Jeremiah's oracles (cf. Jer. 43:3)

▣ "I am going to bring disaster on all flesh" This hyperbolic idiom is also found in Jer. 25:31 and Isa. 66:16. It is difficult for modern westerners to interpret ANE poetry because of our tendency toward literalism. A book that has really helped me in this genre is D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic. I commend it to you!

▣ "but I will give your life to you as booty" YHWH promises to spare Baruch's life in the midst of the judgment which will fall on the Judeans in Egypt.

This military imagery (i.e. "booty") occurs several times in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 21:9; 38:2; 39:18).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This begins the literary unit of the book dealing with YHWH's judgment on the surrounding nations (cf. Jer. 1:5,10; 25:15-38).

  2. These nations would never hear/read these prophecies. YHWH is addressing them in a literary way to show that He is the only God, the God of all the earth (i.e. Deut. 32:8).
    SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM
    SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

  3. The nations addressed are
    1. Egypt
    2. Philistia
    3. Phoenicia
    4. Moab
    5. Ammon
    6. Edom
    7. Syria
    8. Kedar and Hazor
    9. Elam
    10. Neo-Babylon

  4. There are several other places in the Prophets where YHWH addresses His judgment on the surrounding nations of the ANE.
    1. Isa. 13-23 ‒ Old Babylon, Philisita, Moab, Syria Ethiopia, Egypt, Edom, Arabia, Phoenicia, Tarshish
    2. Jer. 25:15-38 ‒ Egypt, Uz (Moab, Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Arabia [and desert people], Elam, Media, Babylon [Sheshach])
    3. Ezek. 25-32 ‒ Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Phoenicia, Egypt, Neo-Babylon, Assyria, Elam, Meshech-Tubal
    4. Amos 1-2 ‒ Syria, Philistia, Phoenicia, Edom, Ammon, Moab (even Israel and Judah)
    5. Obadiah ‒ Edom
    6. Nahum 2-3 ‒ Assyria, Egypt, Ethiopia
    7. Zeph. 2:4-15 ‒ Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia, Assyria

  5. Chart of Prophecies Against Nations and Regions (Jeremiah 46-49)

    Nations Chapter

  6. Jeremiah 46 describes Egypt's defeat by Nebuchadnezzar II's army at Carchemish in Syria (i.e. 605 B.C.). It is poetic and contains numerous commands.
    1. Jer. 46:3-4 (IMPERATIVES)
      1. line up the shield and buckler
      2. draw near for the battle
      3. harness the horses
      4. mount the steeds
      5. take your stand with helmets on (the only Hiphil in a series of Qal IMPERATIVES)
      6. polish the spears
      7. put on the scale-armor
    2. Jer. 46:6 (IMPERFECTS used as JUSSIVES)
      1. let not the swift man flee
      2. let not the mighty man escape
    3. Jer. 46:8 (two IMPERFECTS used as COHORTATIVES and one COHORTATIVE)
      1. I will rise
      2. I will cover
      3. I will surely destroy
    4. Jer. 46:11 (Qal IMPERATIVES)
      1. go up
      2. obtain
    5. Jer. 46:14 (4 Hiphil IMPERATIVES, 1 Qal)
      1. declare in Egypt
      2. proclaim in Migdol
      3. proclaim (Qal) also in Memphis and Tahpanhes
      4. take your stand
      5. get yourself ready
    6. Jer. 46:16 (Qal IMPERATIVE and COHORTATIVE)
      1. get up
      2. let us go back

  7. Jer. 46:2-12 deals with the battle at Carchemish (i.e. in Syria to the west of Haran on the headwaters of the Euphrates River) in 605 B.C.
    Jer. 46:13-26 deals with Nebuchadnezzar's military invasion in 568-567 B.C. Egypt was completely conquered by Persia in 525 B.C.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:2 "Pharaoh Neco"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:2 "Pharaoh Neco" Necho II (609-593 B.C.; of the Twenty-Sixth Dynasty) marched through Judah to confront Nebuchadnezzar II at Carchemish in Syria. Josiah attempted to stop him and was wounded at Meggido. Josiah later died of his wounds (i.e. 609 B.C.). Pharaoh Necho's army was defeated (partially because Josiah delayed him which allowed Neo-Babylon to defeat the remaining Assyrian army). As Pharaoh Necho II returned to Egypt he stopped at Jerusalem and exiled King Jehoahaz, Josiah's successor of only three months (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:28-37; 2 Chr. 35:20-36:4). Necho II placed Jehoiakim (a relative of Josiah) on Judah's throne as his surrogate (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:29ff).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF EGYPT

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:3-4 "line up"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 46:3-4 "line up" These IMPERATIVES (see Contextual Insights, E) were orders given by Egyptian officers to the Egyptian soldiers.

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:4 "helmets"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 46:4 "helmets" These helmets (BDB 464) were rarely worn, therefore, this denotes that the soldiers were to "immediately prepare for battle."

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:5 What powerful poetry of fear and defeat. It reminds me of Nahum 2.

Line 7, "terror is on every side," is an often repeated phrase in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 6:25; 20:3,10; 49:29; Lam. 2:22; see BDB 159 II, KB 544).

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:7-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 46:7-8 These two verses seem to reflect the arrogant attitude of the Egyptian army; they used the annual overflowing of the Nile as the imagery of victorious military conquest. But it is all a myth, a false hope. In reality the Egyptian army and her mercenaries flee before the Babylonian military. Instead of the Nile overflowing its banks, it retreats!

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:9 This verse identifies several regional elements of the Egyptian army.

  1. Cush ‒ BDB 468 I; Ethiopia (southern Egypt)
  2. Put ‒ BDB 866, Libya (northeast Africa)
  3. Lud ‒ BDB 530, Lydia (western Asia Minor)

It is uncertain if they were mercenaries (cf. Jer. 46:21) or defeated armies that joined Egypt's victorious army.

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:10 "the Lord God of hosts"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:10 "the Lord God of hosts" (twice) The first title "Lord" is the term Adon (BDB 10) which denotes "owner," "master," "lord," "husband."

The second title is literally "YHWH Sabbaoth." YHWH is usually noted in English Bibles as all capitals, Lord (cf, Ps. 110:1).

Verse 10 may be the Divine response to Pharaoh Necho II killing Josiah and replacing (exiling) his heir who reigned only three months!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

▣ "the sword" Often in poetic passages in the OT the "sword" is personified. The sword of the Neo-Babylonians is the sword of YHWH.

▣
NASB  "a slaughter for the Lord"
NKJV  "the Lord. . .has a sacrifice"
NRSV  "the Lord. . .holds a sacrifice"
NJB  "the Lord. . .is holding a sacrificial feast"
JPSOA  "the Lord. . .is preparing a sacrifice"

The UBS' A Translator's Handbook On Jeremiah (p. 847) has a good comment on this phrase. The picture is that of a sacrificial feast in which the worshiper is allowed to eat part of the animal that has been sacrificed. The same idea is conveyed in Ezek. 39:17-20; Zeph. 1:7.

Over the last few years I have become aware that YHWH has regularly used foreign nations to

  1. punish His people
  2. destroy other nations

This imagery drawn from ANE battles has become imagery of YHWH's control of all nations.

This insight has changed my understanding of the fall of Jerusalem to the Romans in A.D. 70, as well as my understanding of

  1. Jesus' Olivet Discourse (i.e. Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21)
  2. Paul's discussion of the "Man of Lawlessness" (2 Thess. 2)
  3. John's book of Revelation

I hope you will evaluate my exegetical commentaries on these texts, as well as the following Special Topics.

  1. SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING
  2. SPECIAL TOPIC: COMING ON THE CLOUDS
  3. SPECIAL TOPIC: SOON RETURN
  4. SPECIAL TOPIC: A DELAYED SECOND COMING
  5. SPECIAL TOPIC: THE ANY MOMENT RETURN OF JESUS vs. THE NOT YET

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:11 Gilead was widely known for its healing balms (cf. Jer. 8:22). But there was no balm for Egypt (cf. lines 3, 4). She is doomed to defeat and shame.

▣ "virgin daughter of Egypt" This is the NOUN CONSTRUCT of "virgin" (BDB 413) and "daughter" (BDB 123 I). The CONSTRUCT "daughter(s) of _________" is a way to refer to a nation.

  1. Zion/Jerusalem/Judah ‒ Ps. 9:14; Isa. 1:8; 10:32; 16:1; 37:22; 52:2; 62:11; Jer. 4:11; 6:2,23,26; 8:11,19,21,22; 9:1,7; 14:17; Lamentations (many times); Micah 1:13; 4:8,10; Zeph. 3:14; Zech. 2:10; 9:9
  2. Israel ‒ 2 Sam. 1:24; Ezek. 16:55
  3. Tyre ‒ Ps. 45:12; Isa. 23:12
  4. Babylon/Chaldea ‒ Ezra 2:61; Ps. 137:8; Isa. 47:1,5; Jer. 50:42; 51:33; Zech. 2:7
  5. Egypt ‒ Jer. 46:24
  6. Tarshish ‒ Isa. 23:10
  7. Philistia ‒ Ezek. 16:27,57
  8. all nations ‒ Ezek. 32:16

When the term "virgin daughter" is used it seems to emphasize the vulnerability of the nation addressed.

  1. Zion ‒ 2 Kgs. 19:21; Isa. 37:22; Jer. 14:17; Lam. 2:10,13
  2. Israel ‒ Jer. 18:13; 31:4,21; Amos 5:2
  3. Babylon ‒ Isa. 47:1
  4. Egypt ‒ Jer. 46:11

In 2 Kgs. 19:21 both forms are found in poetic parallel. Also note the changing meaning of "Israel," sometimes referring to all of the covenant people, descendants from Jacob/Israel, and in other contexts (i.e. the Divided Monarchy, 922 B.C. ‒ 722 B.C.) it refers to the Northern Ten Tribes (i.e. Israel, Samaria, Ephraim).

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:12 "The nations have heard of your shame"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:12 "The nations have heard of your shame" This is exactly the opposite of YHWH's intended purpose for His covenant people (cf. Gen. 12:3; Ezek. 36:22-36). YHWH wanted the descendants of Abraham to reflect His character to the world and, thereby to attract the world to Himself. This is still His purpose for His people.

▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NEB, TEV. Peshitta, JPSOA, NET  "shame"
REB, NEB  "cry"
  1. your shame ‒ קלונך (BDB 885, cf. Jer. 13:26)
  2. your voice ‒ קולך (BDB 876)

The UBS Text Project, p. 293, gives #1 a "B" rating. The NEB and REB seem to think "voice" is a better parallel to the next poetic line, which has "outcry" (BDB 846, i.e. a cry of distress or grief, cf. Jer. 14:2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:13-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 46:13-26 As Jer. 46:1-2 describes the battle at Carchemish in Syria in 605 B.C., Jer. 46:13-26 describes a later invasion of Egypt itself (cf. Jer. 43:11-12).

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:14 All of these locations are mentioned in Jer. 44:1 as places where the doomed Judeans were living.

46:15
NASB, Peshitta  "become prostrate"
NKJV, JPSOA  "swept away"
NRSV, NJB, REB, LXX  "Apis (Haf) fled"
TEV  "Apis fallen"

There are several translation issues with this verse.

  1. "mighty ones" (BDB 7) can refer to
    1. soldiers (NIV, NET Bible)
    2. the Egyptian bull god, Apis (LXX, RSV, NEB, NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 234)
  2. the VERB is SINGULAR (BDB 695, KB 749, Niphal PERFECT), but the NOUN PLURAL. The LXX divides the VERB (נסחף) into two words (נס חף ) which means "Hap (Apis) has fled." The UBS Text Project supports this division by giving it a "B" rating (p. 293).
  3. The defeat of the Egyptian soldiers or bull god (possibly a reference to Pharaoh as the incarnation of Egypt's gods) is attributed to YHWH (line 2).
46:16
NASB  "They have repeatedly stumbled"
NKJV, JPSOA  "He made many fall"
NRSV  "Your multitude stumbled and fell"
TEV  "Your soldiers have stumbled and fallen"
NJB  "he has caused many to fall"
REB  "the rabble of Egypt stumble and fall"
LXX  "your multitude was weak and fell"
Peshitta  "Multitudes of them are fallen"

The MT has "he made many stumble" (Hiphil PERFECT, BDB 505, KB 502 and Qal ACTIVE PARTICIIPLE, BDB 656, KB 709, both MASCULINE SINGULAR). The "he" is YHWH from Jer. 46:15.

Some translations assume it is a collective reference to the Egyptian army.

46:17
NASB, NKJV, NET  "a big noise"
NRSV, LXX  "braggart"
NJB  "Much-noise"
REB  "Bombast"
Peshitta  "Pharaoh the Lame. . .the troublemaker"

The Hebrew word (BDB 981, KB 1370 II) means

  1. roar of water (i.e. battle) ‒ Isa. 17:12; Jer. 48:45; 51:55; Amos 2:2; Hosea 10:14; here, imagery of "crash"
  2. uproar of battle ‒ Ps. 74:23; Isa. 17:12-13; 25:5
  3. festival uproar ‒ Isa. 5:14

It is used here as a possible play on Pharaoh's name or a ridicule of his military appearing and then disappearing (Jer. 37:5).

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:18 ". . .the King
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:18 ". . .the King

 Whose name is the Lord of hosts" YHWH, the covenant Deity, has always been "king" (cf. 1 Sam. 8:7). The Judean kings (cf. Gen. 49:10) from the line of Jesse/David (cf. 2 Samuel 7; 1 Chronicles 17) have only served as earthly representatives of Him.

The opening phrase, "As I live," functions in two ways.

  1. a word play on the Hebrew VERB "to be" and YHWH (i.e. the ever-living, only-living Deity)
  2. it is an idiom introducing an oath. An oath by YHWH in His name is a powerful promise that His words will come to be (i.e. Isa. 55:9-11)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH (OT)

▣ "Mount Tabor. . .Mount Carmel" These are references to the topological features that dominate a landscape. They are used here as imagery of overwhelming power (i.e. the Neo-Babylonian army against the Egyptian army).

46:19
NASB, LXX  "It will even be burned down"
NKJV, TEV, REB  "a ruin"
NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "desolate"

The Hebrew VERB (BDB 428, KB 429, Niphal PERFECT with waw) means "to kindle" or "to burn" (cf. Jer. 2:15; 11:16; 17:27; 21:14; 43:12; 49:2,27; 50:32; 51:30,58), but it is also used of "ruin" or "waste" (cf. Jer. 4:7; 9:11).

46:20
NASB  "horsefly"
NRSV, REB, NJB, JPSOA  "gadfly"
JPSOA footnote  "butcher"
TEV  "destruction"
Peshitta  "an army"
NET  "like swarms of stinging flies"

The MT has a NOUN (BDB 903, KB 1148) that occurs only here. A similar Aramaic and Arabic root denotes a biting insect. In context, it is obvious it refers to the invading Neo-Babylonian army.

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:21-23 "her mercenaries"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:21-23 "her mercenaries" They are mentioned in Jer. 46:9. Even these experienced, hired soldiers act like defenseless, pampered calves! They all flee (cf. Jer. 46:5) in the face of Nebuchadnezzar's army ("horsefly" of Jer. 46:20), as do the Egyptian soldiers, symbolized as a slithering snake in Jer. 46:22.

Notice the different imagery used to describe neo-Babylon's army.

  1. woodcutters with axes
  2. more numerous than locusts

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:22 "like a serpent"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:22 "like a serpent" Serpent imagery is recurrent in the Bible. It can be positive or negative. This particular usage seems to reflect in a negative way the serpent insignia on the crown of Pharaoh. Instead of a "striking" serpent, there is a fleeting serpent.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERPENT

▣ "as woodcutters with axes" The imagery of "cutting down trees" is recurrent in the Bible. It, like "serpents," has a wide usage. Only context can tell if it is

  1. an image of judgment (cf. Isa. 10:33-34)
  2. an image of idolatry (cf. Jer. 10:2-4)
  3. an image of the purposeful results of invasion
    1. wood for siege works
    2. a way to devastate a defeated country

This one denotes the power of the Neo-Babylonian army against the feeble Egyptian army.

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:25 This verse seems to repeat itself. The LXX shortens it to "Behold, I am avenging Amon, her son, on Pharaoh and on those who trust in him."

Amon (BDB 51 I) was supposed to be the "king of the gods." The three gods, Ra, Ptah, and Amon, are often combined. As the worship of Apis (cf. Jer. 46:15) was centered in Memphis, the worship of Amon was centered in Thebes.

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:25-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:25-26 In this chapter several prose verses introduce a poetic section.

  1. Jer. 46:1-2, then poem Jer. 46:3-12
  2. Jer. 46:13, then poem Jer. 46:14-24
  3. Jer. 46:25-26, about the previous poem

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 46:26 Egypt will be completely destroyed (cf. Ezek. 29:8-12) but it will be reinhabited (cf. Ezek. 29:13-14).

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:27 The first two VERBS are IMPERFECTS used in a JUSSIVE sense. The exiles in Babylon (not Egypt) are commanded not to be afraid. YHWH will save (BDB 446, KB 448, Hiphil PARTICIPLE, cf. Jer. 23:3-4; 29:14) them!

Notice the VERBS used to describe YHWH's people in Babylonian exile.

  1. do not fear (Jer. 46:28; see SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR)
  2. do not be dismayed
  3. I am going to save you (see SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION [OT])
  4. you shall return
  5. you shall be undisturbed
  6. you shall be secure
  7. no one will make you tremble

A new day of restoration and security is promised!

In the literary unit of judgment on the nations there are several passages related to the exiles of Judah (cf. Jer. 50:4-10,17-20; 51:36-40,50-53).

Remember, the term "remnant" is used in Jeremiah of three groups of Judeans.

  1. those taken to Babylon
  2. those left in Judah after the exile
  3. those who fled to Egypt

The prophets affirm that #2, 3 will be destroyed but YHWH will save and restore #1 to Canaan and restart the Patriarchal covenants.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:27-28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 46:27-28 The parallel to these verses is in Jer. 30:10-11. This section of Jeremiah is called "The Book of Hope." It addresses the Judeans who have been exiled to Babylon.

entries.title: Jeremiah 46:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
46:28 The basis of the Babylonian exiles' hope is YHWH (notice the number of "I's") and His promises (cf. 2 Sam. 7:8-16).

  1. I am with you
  2. I shall make a full end of all the nations where you were exiled
  3. I shall not make an end of you
  4. I shall correct you properly

Discipline but not judgment. This is similar to YHWH's promise to David's royal descendants in 2 Samuel 7:14.

Jer. 46:27-28 is very similar theologically to Jer. 30:10-11. The theme of restoration is repeated for emphasis!

YHWH is not a respector of persons or status. Sin brings judgment, but even in appropriate judgment, there is mercy and hope!

entries.title: Jeremiah 47:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
47:1 This first verse dates the prophecy (i.e. "before Pharaoh conquered Gaza"). There are several other places where the destruction of Philistia is prophesied (cf. Isa. 14:29-31; Ezek. 25:15-17; Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:6-8; Zeph. 2:4-7; Zech 9:5-7).

Herodotus (Hist. II, 159) mentions that Pharaoh Necho II conquered a Philistine city (i.e. Gaza) about 609 B.C. This would link up with his replacing Josiah's heir (Jehoahaz) with another puppet king (Jehoiakim), also in 609 B.C. The problem with this date is that Nebuchadnezzar II did not invade until 601 B.C.

The Expositors Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 655, lists three possible dates for the invasion of Neo-Babylon (if the MT is correct).

  1. 609 B.C. ‒ same time as the death of Josiah by Necho II
  2. 604 B.C. ‒ after the defeat of the Egyptian army at Carchemish
  3. still later in the reign of Pharaoh Hophra (or Apries, 588-569 B.C.), when he invaded Phoenicia and Philistia, which were on the way (i.e. southern coast)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 47:2 "waters. . .from the north"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
47:2 "waters. . .from the north" The invasion of Neo-Babylon into Palestine has been characterized by several images.

  1. overflowing boiling pot pouring south (cf. Jer. 1:13-14)
  2. biting fly from the north (cf. Jer. 46:20)
  3. here as a flooding river (Egypt is often described as the flooding Nile)

The imagery of an invading nation as an overflowing river is common in the OT.

  1. Assyria ‒ Isa. 8:8-9
  2. Egypt ‒ Jer. 46:7-8; Amos 8:8; 9:5

entries.title: Jeremiah 47:2e-3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
47:2e-3 This describes the actions of the Philistines.

  1. the men cry out, Jer. 47:2e
  2. every inhabitant of the land will wail, Jer. 47:2f
  3. fathers have not turned back for their children, Jer. 47:3c
  4. their hands are limp, Jer. 47:3d

What has terrified them?

  1. the noise of the galloping hooves of his stallions, Jer. 47:3a
  2. the tumult of his chariots, Jer. 47:3b

entries.title: Jeremiah 47:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
47:4 All of the small nations on the Mediterranean coast (the only possible land route from Mesopotamia to Egypt because of the desert in between) will be invaded and defeated.

▣ "The remnant of the coastland of Caphtor" The Philistines were from Caphtor (cf. Deut. 2:23; Amos 9:7). However, "Caphtor" here may be a reference to

  1. all the islands of the eastern Mediterranean
  2. a region of northern Egypt
  3. the island of Crete (best guess)
  4. less likely, but possibly, the island of Cyprus

entries.title: Jeremiah 47:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
47:5 There were five independent city-states which made up Philistia (i.e. same political structure as Greece).

  1. Gaza
  2. Ashkelon
  3. Ashdad
  4. Gath
  5. Ekron
▣
NASB, NKJV, JPSOA  "O remnant of their valley"
NRSV  "O remnant of their power"
NJB  "you who remain in the valley"
LXX, RSV  "the remaining Enakim" (i.e. "Anakites,"
  cf. Josh. 11:22)
REB, NET  "the remnant of the Philistine power"

The NASB reflects the MT.

  1. The NRSV and REB assume a different root found in Ugaritic (AB, p. 310).
  2. The REB assumes that Ashkelon was the only remaining undefeated Philistine city-state.
  3. The LXX is an emendation about the giants found at Gaza, Gath, and Ashdad in Josh. 11:22.
  4. The UBS Text Project, p. 296, gives "of the Anakim" a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS

▣ "gash yourself" This was part of

  1. their idol worship (see SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE)
  2. their mourning rites (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES)

Because of the parallelism with Jer. 47:5a, probably #2 is correct.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

entries.title: Jeremiah 47:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
47:6 This verse addresses the personified sword of YHWH (cf. Jer. 12:12; Isa. 34:6; Amos 9:4).

The question is asked (apparently by those being conquered) how long will it

  1. not be quieted
  2. withdraw into its sheath
  3. be at rest
  4. stay still

The last three are IMPERATIVES!

entries.title: Jeremiah 47:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
47:7 Verse 7 is an answer to the question of Jer. 47:6 (i.e. LXX text). There is no rest for YHWH's sword because the conquest of Palestine by Neo-Babylon is His will (i.e. "He has assured it," BDB 416, KB 419, Qal PERFECT). YHWH is in charge of world history! He now uses Babylon, as He previously used Assyria (i.e. Isa. 10:5) and will use Persia (i.e. Isa. 44:28; 45:1-3) in the future, to accomplish His purposes.

▣ "against Ashkelon" The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT) has a good brief article about this on page 679.

  1. From Babylonian Chronicle ‒
    1. Nebuchadnezzsar II attacked surprisingly in the rainy season (i.e., Kislev)
    2. Walls of the city were breached and the soldiers ransacked and burned the city, turning it into a mound of ruins.
  2. From archaeology, the date of the destruction was about 604 B.C. See Biblical Archaeology Library
  3. Ashkelon was a major port for Mediterranian maritime trade with Egypt. Neo-Babylon's control of Philistia was a real problem for Egypt.

The NET Bible, p. 1424, #5, suggests that although Ashkelon was destroyed in 604 B.C., this prophecy dates from 609 B.C., in which Pharaoh Necho II marched through Judah to aid the remnant of the Assyrian army, but both Egypt and Assyria were defeated at Carchemish in 605 B.C. by the Neo-Babylonian army.

 

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:1 "Moab"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:1 "Moab" The etymology of the name (BDB 555, KB 554) is uncertain. Genesis 19:37 seems to connect it to Lot's daughter, linking the child to her father, "from my father" or "water of my father." This is the type of popular etymology so common in the OT. Lot's incestuous child becomes the designation of a nation (as does the other daughter's son, Ammon (cf. Gen. 19:38). Their territory was between the Zered and Arnon Rivers on the eastern side of the Dead Sea.

▣ "Nebo" This term (BDB 612) has several biblical orientations.

  1. a Babylonian deity (cf. Isa. 46:1), sometimes spelled "Nabu." He was the eldest son of Marduk.
  2. a mountain in Moab just east of the top of the Dead Sea, in the plains of Moab from which Moses was allowed to view (but not enter) the Promised Land (cf. Deut. 32:48-52). He died there and was buried by God (cf. Deuteronomy 34). The mountain was also known as Pisgah (cf. Deut. 34:1).
  3. a city on the plains of Moab (cf. Num. 32:3,38; Isa. 15:2; Jer. 48:1,22)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEBO

▣ "Kiriathaim" This city (not to be confused with Kiriath-Jearim) is located on the eastern side of the Jordan River on the plateau of Moab (cf. line 5) in the tribal allocation of Reuben (cf. Num. 32:37; Josh. 13:19; Jer. 48:1,23; Ezek. 25:9). The name itself (BDB 900) means "double city" (see MacMillan Bible Atlas, p. 210).

▣
NASB  "the lofty stronghold"
NKJV  "the high stronghold"
NRSV, NET  "the fortress"
TEV  "its mighty fortress"
NJB  "the citadel"
REB, JPSOA footnote  "Misgah"
LXX  "Hamasagab"
JPSOA  "the stronghold"

This word (BDB 960, KB 640) basically means "high refuge" (cf. Isa. 33:16). However, it has the ARTICLE which is unusual—"the fortress"—unless it is referring to all of the plateau of Moab (cf. Jer. 48:8d). Also, the NOUN for fortress is MASCULINE in gender, but all the VERBS used in Jer. 48:1 (except for the first one, "say") are THIRD PERSON FEIMININE SINGULAR. There are two other cities listed in Jer. 48:1. These FEMININE forms fit a place name (cf. LXX and REB). Unfortunately this place name appears nowhere in ancient literature.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This is a lengthy condemnation of Moab (cf. Isaiah 15-16) made up of several different poems and comments about their judgment. Moab, Ammon, and Edom were relatives of the Israelites.
    1. Moab ‒ judged in Jeremiah 48 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MOAB)
    2. Ammon ‒ judged in Jer. 49:1-6 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: AMMON)
    3. Edom ‒ judged in Jer. 49:7-22 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL)

  2. There are many (17 or 18) IMPERATIVES in this chapter. Several of them involve the text of the MT. However, there are several Qere suggested readings. The Masoretic scholars (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MASORETIC TEXT) recognized about one thousand places in the OT where one form is in the text but another is suggested in the margin. There are five of these in this chapter and three are related to the gender of the IMPERATIVES.
    1. Jer. 48:18, "sit" (BDB 442, KB 444)
      1. Qal PARTICIPLE MASCULINE PLURAL (Kethiv)
      2. Qal IMPERATIVE FEMININE SINGULAR (Qere)
    2. Jer. 48:20, "wail" (BDB 410, KB 413)
      1. Hiphil IMPERATIVE FEMININE SINGULAR (Kethiv)
      2. Hophol IMPERATIVE MASCULINE PLURAL (Qere)
    3. Jer. 48:20, "cry out" (BDB 277, KB 277)
      1. Qal IMPERATIVE FEMININE SINGULAR (Kethiv)
      2. Qal IMPERATIVE MASCULINE PLURAL (Qere)
        This same "FEMININE" vs. "MASCULINE" issue is also involved in Jer. 48:27.
      3. Niphal PERFECT FEMININE SINGULAR (Kethiv)
      4. Niphal PERFECT MASCULINE PLURAL (Qere)
        The issue involves the proper gender when addressing a nation or inhabitants of a city.

  3. Notice how many cities are listed in this chapter.
    1. Nebo, Jer. 48:1, 22 (cf. Isa. 15:2)
    2. Kiriathaim, Jer. 48:1, 23 (cf. Ezek. 25:9)
    3. Heshbon, Jer. 48:2,34, 45 (cf. Isa. 15:4; 16:8,9)
    4. Dimon/Dibon ("Madmen"), Jer. 48:2, 18, 22 (cf. Isa. 15:2,9)
    5. Horonaim, Jer. 48:3, 5, 34 (cf. Isa. 15:5)
    6. Luhith, Jer. 48:5 (cf. Isa. 15:5)
    7. Aroer, Jer. 48:19 (possibly Jer. 48:6, cf Deut. 2:36; 3:12; 4:48)
    8. Holon, Jer. 48:21 (possibly Horon, cf. Isa. 15:5 and same as #5)
    9. Jahzah, Jer. 48:21, 34 (cf. Isa. 15:4)
    10. Mephaath, Jer. 48:21 (cf. Josh. 13:18; 21:37)
    11. Beth-diblathaim, Jer. 48:22
    12. Beth-gamul, Jer. 48:23
    13. Beth-meor, Jer. 48:23
    14. Kerioth, Jer. 48:24, 41 (cf. Amos 2:2)
    15. Bozrah, Jer. 48:24
    16. Kir-heres, Jer. 48:31, 36 (one of Moab's capitals, cf. Isa. 16:7, 11)
    17. Sibmah, Jer. 48:32 (cf. Isa. 16:8,9)
    18. Jazer, Jer. 48:32 (cf. Isa. 16:8,9)
    19. Elealeh, Jer. 48:34 (cf. Isa. 15:4; 16:9)
    20. Zoar, Jer. 48:34 (cf. Isa. 15:5, RSV and NEB have it in Jer. 48:4)
    21. Eglath-shelishiyah, Jer. 48:34 (cf. Isa. 15:5)
    22. Sihon, Jer. 48:45 (name of an Amorite king who lived in Heshbon, #3)

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:2 "Heshbon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:2 "Heshbon" This city (BDB 363 II) is in northern Moab but it was in an area contested by Ammon (cf. Num. 21:25). Apparently it is involved in a conspiracy against Moab, possibly by the Ammonites. However, it is probably better to see it as a reference to a campsite of the Neo-Babylonian army.

There is a word play between the name of Heshbon (BDB 363 II, חשׁבון) and the VERB "devised calamity" (lit. "think," BDB 362, KB 359, Qal PERFECT, חשׁב).

▣ "Madmen" There is considerable doubt about the meaning of this word (מדמן, BDB 199, KB 226-227). Do not confuse it with the English meaning.

  1. The Hebrew term emphasizes the VERB (BDB 198 I, KB 226 I) "be silenced" (cf. LXX, Peshitta)
    1. madman (BDB 199) ‒ מדםן
    2. VERB ‒ דמס
  2. a play on "dung hill" (BDB 199 I, KB 226, דמן, cf. Isa. 25:10)
  3. a city's name (in Moab, BDB 199), found only in Jer. 48:2
  4. a play on the city "Dimon" (BDB 192, דימון, cf. Isa. 15:9), a variant of Dibon (BDB 192, cf. Isa. 15:2)

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:3 "Horonaim"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:3 "Horonaim" The term (BDB 357) means "two hollows," "two caves," or "two ravines." This city's name is found only in Isa. 15:5 and Jer. 48:5,34 although RSV translates 2 Sam. 13:34 as a form of this word. It was located on the major trade route called "The King's Highway."

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:4 "Her little ones"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:4 "Her little ones" The LXX, RSV, and NRSV think this word (צעירה [translated "servants" in Jer. 14:3], BDB 859) should be translated by a city's name, Zoar (צער, BDB 858, cf. Jer. 48:34 and Isa. 15:5). The LXX also has a place name here (i.e. Zogora).

The UBS Text Project, p. 297, gives the Qere reading, "her little ones" or "youths," a "B" rating. In this way the grammar of the Hebrew fits better (NET Bible).

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:5 "Luhith"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:5 "Luhith" This Moabite city (BDB 532) is linked to Horonaim as a place of ascent and descent, probably close to the Dead Sea.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:6 The cities of Moab are doomed. They are commanded to

  1. flee ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. save your lives ‒ Piel IMPERATIVE
  3. give wings ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
▣
NASB, NKJV  "like a juniper"
NRSV, LXX  "like a wild ass"
TEV, NJB  "like a wild donkey"
JPSOA  "like Aroer"
REB  "like one destitute"
Peshitta  "like a plant"
NET  "like a lonely shrub"

The MT is uncertain, as the various options show. Aroer (cf. Jer. 48:19b) is the name of a city in Moab (BDB 792 II) and the parallelism of other cities seems to favor this option.

However, a similar word "shrub" or "juniper" is used in Jer. 17:6 (BDB 792 I).

"Aroer" ‒ כערוער (BDB 792 II, a city in Moab), as in Jer. 48:19

"wild ass" ‒ כערוד (KB 882) in LXX and Aquila, cf. Jer. 2:24; 14:6 (different Hebrew word)

"juniper" ‒ כערער (BDB 792 I, KB 883, cf. Jer. 17:6) in MT which UBS Text Project, p. 298, gives a "C" rating (considerable doubt)

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:7 "For because you trusted in. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:7 "For because you trusted in. . ." Several things are mentioned that Moab trusted (BDB 105, KB 120, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT).

1. NASB "our own achievements"
NKJV "works"
NRSV, LXX "like a wild ass"
TEV, NJB "like a wild donkey"
JPSOA "like Aroer"
REB "like one destitute"
Peshitta "like a plant"
The MT has "deeds" or "works" (BDB 795), which could refer to a number of things.
2. "treasures" JPSOA sees both #1 and #2 as parallel
3.  they also trusted in their national idol Chemosh who would utterly fail them (cf. Jer. 48:13,35)

The pride, arrogance, and idolatry of Moab is clearly seen in Jer. 48:29-30,42.

▣ "Chemosh" This was the national deity of the Moabites (cf. Num. 21:29), where Moab is called "the people of Chemosh." In Jdg. 11:24 this deity is linked to Ammon. Solomon brought this cult into Jerusalem in 1 Kgs. 11:7; 2 Kgs. 23:13, on behalf of his young Canaanite wives.

The etymology of the name itself (BDB 484) is uncertain. Some scholars assume "destroyer," or "subduer," while other scholars see it linked to a "fish god." Most of our information about this Canaanite deity comes from the Mesha Stele called "the Moabite Stone," discovered in 1868 at Dibon.

The text of 2 Kgs. 3:21-27 (esp. Jer. 48:27) strongly suggests that Chemosh was worshiped with child sacrifice, as were Molech and Ba'al, two other Canaanite fertility gods.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHEMOSH

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH

▣ "Chemosh will go off into exile" This could refer to:

  1. In the capture of a nation by an invader, the nations gods (i.e. idols) were carried away and put in the major temple of the invaders (i.e. Jer. 43:12).
  2. Because of the two groups of citizens (i.e. priests and princes), this may be imagery for a total exile of all the nation of Moab by Nebuchandezzar II.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:8 Moab's doom was by the word of YHWH (cf. Jer. 48:15c). His instrument was Neo-Babylon. See my additional note at Jer. 46:10.

48:9
NASB, NKJV, NJB, JPSOA  "Give wings"
NRSV  "Set aside salt"
TEV, NET  "Set up a tombstone"
LXX  "give signs"
REB  "give a wearning signal"
Peshitta  "give a garland"

There are several options on how to understand this line of poetry.

  1. the MT has "wings" (BDB 851 II), a unique meaning from a supposed Aramiac root used only here
  2. LXX, TEV, and REB see the VERB as a road marker (BDB 846, cf. Jer. 31:21)
  3. the NRSV assumes a Ugaritic root, "salt," which would fit the context of judgment (cf. Jdgs. 9:45)
  4. TEV, NET see 2 Kgs. 23:17, "to me (BDB 868) as the source of the imagery"
▣
NASB, NJB  "For she will flee away"
NKJV  "that she may flee and get away"
NRSV  "For she will surely fall"
TEV  "it will soon be destroyed"
REB  "For she will be laid in ruins"
JPSOA  "For she must go hence"
Peshitta  "she shall surely be destroyed"

It is obvious from the different translation options that there is some confusion on which Hebrew root was original.

  1. נצא ‒ "to fly," BDB 661, KB 714
  2. נצה ‒ "to fall into ruins" ‒ BDB 663 III, cf. Jer. 4:7
  3. יצא ‒ "to surrender," BDB 423, #2 a., cf. Jer. 38:17,21 (i.e. to exile, Jer. 29:16)

The UBS Text Project, p. 299, gives option #1 a "C" rating, meaning the committee could not decide which was original.

If "wings" in the first line of v. 9 is original, then option #1, "fly," seems the best contextual parallel.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:10 Many English translations mark this as a parenthesis (cf. TEV, NJB, NET). It is addressed to the Neo-Babylonian invaders, admonishing them to fully execute YHWH's judgment on every city in Moab. Show no mercy (i.e. Holy War terminology)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:11 Moab paid tribute to Assyria and when Neo-Babylon invaded, Moab supported them. Therefore, her towns and villages were spared. But a day will come when destruction and judgment from YHWH comes (v. 12).

The imagery from the production of wine:

  1. wine must not be left undisturbed because it settles (i.e. "on it dregs")
  2. wine must be poured from vessel to vessel several times over time
  3. The last two poetic lines of v. 11 are a summary of their protected status in the past.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:11-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:11-12 This is imagery drawn from the wine industry. Notice how this is also seen in Jer. 48:26 and 33. Because of these allusions to wine making several of Jeremiah's poems, given at different times, may have been joined together in one context.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:11-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:11-20 Notice that all the English translations have different ways to divide this chapter into paragraphs/strophes. It is often difficult to distinguish between prose and poetry. Even though these divisions are not inspired (i.e. marked in the original text) they serve the hermeneutical purpose of determining the literary units and how they relate to each other. Every paragraph/strophe has one main truth. This information is crucial in trying to find and follow the original inspired author's intent. See "Bible Interpretation Seminar" online at www.freebiblecommentary.org.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:12 This verse continues the imagery from the wine industry, but the statements are negative.

  1. NASB ‒ "those who tip vessels," BDB 858, KB 1040, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  2. NASB ‒ "and they will tip him over," BDB 858, KB 1040, Piel PERFECT with waw
  3. NASB ‒ "and they will empty his vessels," BDB 937, KB 1227, Hiphil IMPERFECT
  4. NASB ‒ "and shatter their jars," BDB 658, KB 711, Piel IMPERFECT

Each of these is a normal, needed part of producing wine, but #4 is obviously a judgment. In the past, Moab was spared invasion and exile, but no more!

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:13 Idol worship brought shame and humiliation, to Israel and to Moab (i.e. Jer. 48:35; Isa. 44:10-11; 45:16; SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME).

The allusion to Bethel:

  1. a title for a Semitic deity used by the Jewish inhabitants of Elephantine, an island in the Nile River (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 680)
  2. a place name where Jeroboam I set up a rival temple site at the city of Bethel (a few miles north of Jerusalem) where the symbol of YHWH (i.e. a golden calf, cf. Exodus 32), over time, became a Canaanite fertility site (cf. 1 Kgs. 12:25-33)
  3. Verse 13 seems to denote the worship of two deities—Chemosh and Bethel, which supports option #1 above.

As fallen humans trust (BDB 105) in the power of manmade gods and reject or ignore the one true God, there is no hope, confidence, or security! Idols cannot affect reality!

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:15-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:15-16 The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 680, says the Josephus notes that five years after the fall of Jerusalem to the Neo-Babylonian army (i.e. 586 B.C.), Nebuchadnezzar II subdued both Moab and Ammon. I have not been able to find the reference in Josephus' Antiquities of the Jews

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:17 "scepter. . .staff"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:17 "scepter. . .staff" These are both royal symbols of power.

  1. scepter ‒ BDB 641, a staff or rod
  2. staff ‒ BDB 596

They could refer to

  1. a shepherd's staff (cf. Gen. 32:10)
  2. a traveler's stick (cf. Exod. 12:11)
  3. riding stick (cf. Num. 22:27)
  4. weapon (cf. 1 Sam. 17:40; Ezek. 39:9)
  5. diviner's rod (cf. Hosea 4:12)
  6. kingly power (i.e. Messianic in Zechariah 11)

Here it refers to the kingdom of Moab.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:17-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:17-20 This part of a larger poem addresses two groups.

  1. those who live near Moab
  2. those who have heard of it

These two groups are collectively personified and give advice to Moab.

  1. mourn, Jer. 48:17 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. say, Jer. 48:17 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. come down, Jer. 48:18 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. sit, Jer. 48:18 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE(Qere)
  5. stand by, Jer. 48:19 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. keep watch, Jer. 48:19 ‒ Piel IMPERATIVE
  7. ask, Jer. 48:19 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  8. say, Jer. 48:19 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  9. wail, Jer. 48:20 ‒ Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  10. cry out, Jer. 48:20 ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE
  11. declare, Jer. 48:20 ‒ Hiphil IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:18-28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:18-28 The Jewish Study Bible (p. 1022) asserts that this poem/oracle is based on the imagery of a woman being raped (i.e. Moab by Neo-Babylon), possibly because there are so many FEMININE SINGULAR forms.

48:18
NASB, NRSV, NJB, REB  "sit on the parched ground"
NKJV, JPSOA  "sit on the ground in the dust"
LXX  "sit on the moist ground"
Peshitta  "sit in disgrace"
AB  "sit in filth [?]"

The footnote in the AB (Anchor Bible Commentary by John Bright) lists the options as (p. 315):

  1. basso'ah ‒ filth/excrement, KB 992 (requires emendation)
  2. bassama ‒ thirst (MT), BDB 854 (of a person or animal)
  3. bassame ‒ on parched ground (cf. Isa. 44:3; BDB 854 [i.e. no rain equals imagery for destruction of Dibon])

The JPSOA footnote says "Meaning of the Heb. uncertain" (p. 1022). Often in poetry one must rely on

  1. context (i.e. parallelism and strophe emphasis)
  2. cognate roots in other Semitic languages
  3. parallel passages (for Jeremiah 48 use Isaiah 15-16)

The Expositor's Bible Commentary (p. 662) has a chart that shows the relationship between Isaiah 15-16 and Jeremiah 48.

  1. Isa. 15:2 ‒ Jer. 48:1
  2. Isa. 15:2-3 ‒ Jer. 48:37
  3. Isa. 15:3 ‒ Jer. 48:38
  4. Isa. 15:4 ‒ Jer. 48:21,5
  5. Isa. 15:4-6 ‒ Jer. 48:5,34
  6. Isa. 15:5 ‒ Jer. 48:3
  7. Isa. 15:5; 16:7,11 ‒ Jer. 48:31
  8. Isa. 15:7 ‒ Jer. 48:36
  9. Isa. 16:6 ‒ Jer. 48:29
  10. Isa. 16:8-9 ‒ Jer. 48:32
  11. Isa. 16:10 ‒ Jer. 48:33
  12. Isa. 16:11 ‒ Jer. 48:36
  13. Isa. 16:12 ‒ Jer. 48:35

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:21-24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:21-24 The cities of Moab are listed.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:25 Two ancient images are used to describe Moab's total defeat.

  1. her "horn" (BDB 901, KB 1144) has been cut off (BDB 154, KB 180, Niphal PERFECT, cf. Ps. 75:11)
  2. her arm broken (BDB 990, KB 1402, Niphal PERFECT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:26 Excessive wine drinking is used as imagery for judgment (cf. Jer. 52:27; Isa. 19:14).

  1. make him drunk (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM)
  2. wallow in his vomit (lit. "splash," see BDB 706, Qal #3, meaning used only here, usually the VERB means to "clap" one's hands in joy or one's thigh in grief)

The reasons for YHWH's judgment of Moab:

  1. he is arrogant toward YHWH, Jer. 48:26, 42
  2. he is prideful, Jer. 48:29 (cf. Isa. 16:6)
  3. his idle boasts are futile, Jer. 48:30
▣
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, NJB  "wallow in his vomit"
TEV  "roll in its own vomit"
REB  "Let Moab overflow with his vomit"
Peshitta  "Moab also shall wallow in his filth"
JPSOA  "Moab shall vomit till he is drained"

This VERB (BDB 706, KB 765, in Qal) has several connotations.

  1. to slap one's thigh in grief or sorrow ‒ Jer. 31:19; Ezek. 21:12 (KB 765 I, Qal #2)
  2. to clap the hands (KB 765, Qal #1)
    1. in self righteousness ‒ Job 34:37
    2. in astonishment ‒ Job 27:23; Lam. 2:15
  3. to splash ‒ KB 765 II, Jer. 48:26, implying to fall into one's vomit with a big splash (possibly old south Arabic)

This is a good example of how the same root can have diverse meanings in specific contexts. Remember, context, context, context determines meaning ‒ not lexicons!

▣
NASB, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA  "laughingstock"
NKJV, REB, Peshitta  "derision"

This word (BDB 966) denotes joyous laughter (Job 8:21; Ps. 126:2; Eccl. 2:2; 10:19), but when used in sarcasm it denotes derision (cf. Jer. 20:7; Lam. 3:14; Job 12:4).

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:27
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:27 What Moab did to Israel is now done to them (i.e. reversal)! For an example of this kind of derision see Lamentations 2:15-17!

▣
NASB, NKJV  "shake your head in scorn"
NRSV, REB, NJB  "you shook your head"
TEV  "how you made fun of the people of
  Israel"
Peshitta  "was not Israel a derision to you"
JPSOA  "shake your head" (footnote, "in
  mockery")
NET  "you shook your head in contempt"

"Shaking the head" (BDB 626, KB 678) can be positive or negative.

  1. positive ‒ Job 42:11; Isa 51:19 (KB), where it is a sign of sympathy
  2. negative ‒ Job 16:4; Ps. 22:7; 109:25; Isa. 37:22; Jer. 18:16; Lam. 2:15; Zeph. 2:15
  3. a sign of excitement (a suggestion of BDB) in Jer. 48:27, but notice most of the translation options see it as showing a dismissiveness, giving Ps. 64:8 as an example

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:28 This verse has three Qal IMPERATIVES. They use imagery involving the inhabitants of Moab, to seek safety in the uninhabited places (i.e. crags, caves, cf. Jer. 16:16; Jdg. 6:2; 1 Sam. 13:6; Isa. 2:19).

▣
NASB  "Beyond the mouth of the chasm"
NKJV  "in the sides of the cave's mouth"
NRSV  "on the sides of the mouth of the gorge"
TEV, NET  "in the sides of a ravine"
REB  "in the rock-face at the mouth of a cavern"
NJB  "in the walls of the gaping gorge"
Peshitta  "in the sides of the mouth of a crag"
JPSOA  "in the sides of a pit"

The MT has the CONSTRUCT BDB 804 plus BDB 809. The second NOUN (KB 924) could mean

  1. a man-made pit (cf. Isa. 24:17; Jer. 48:43)
  2. a grave (cf. 2 Sam. 18:17)
  3. an animal trap (cf. Isa. 24:18)
  4. a deep ravine

Here, option #4 fits best and describes Moab's sense of security of being on a high, rocky plain. Doves thought they were safe by building nests on rocky cliffs, so too, Moab.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:29 This is similar to Isa. 16:6. Moab's judgment is discussed in Isaiah 15-16. There are many literary parallels and allusions between Jeremiah 48 and Isaiah 15-16. Isaiah wrote before Jeremiah.

The UBS A Translator's Handbook on Jeremiah (p. 888) mentions that there are several NOUNS used to describe the pride of Moab.

  1. the pride of Moab (BDB 144)
  2. he is very proud (BDB 144 and 547)
  3. his haughtiness (BDB 147)
  4. his pride (BDB 144)
  5. his arrogance (BDB 144)
  6. his self-exaltation (lit. "elevation of his heart," BDB 927 CONSTRUCT BDB 524)

This purposeful repetition is to powerfully communicate the prideful attitude of Moab (cf. Jer. 48:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:29-39
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:29-39 The Jewish Study Bible (p. 1022) notes that these verses are written in a 3/2 beat, which characterized funeral songs. This is the lament form often used in prophetic literature in the sense of "woe."

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT), IV. E.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:31-32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:31-32 The "I" refers to YHWH (cf. Jer. 48:30-36; 31:20; Isa. 16:11; Hosea 11:8-9). He continuously grieves over the necessity of judgment on Moab, part of the tribal inheritance of His people. Judgment is YHWH's strange work (cf. Isa. 28:21)! He desires to bless, prosper, and restore!

Notice the powerful, remorseful parallel.

  1. I wail ‒ BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERFECT
  2. I cry out ‒ BDB 277, KB 277, Qal IMPERFECT
  3. I mourn ‒ BDB 211, KB 237, Qal IMPERFECT (form is THIRD PERSON but parallelism is FIRST PERSON)

The NASB Study Bible (p. 1132) asserts that the FIRST PERSON PRONOUN should refer to the prophet and uses Isa. 15:5 and 16:9 as examples.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:32 Lines 3 and 4 are repeated from Isa. 16:8. The MT has "sea of Jazer" but the LXX and Isa. 16:8 do not. The "sea" in line 1 would refer to the Dead Sea.

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:33
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:33 There seem to be two different groups "shouting."

  1. the joy of wine makers (will cease)
  2. the shout of conquering soldiers
  3. also note the "cry" of ruin and destruction in v. 34

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:34
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:34 The geographical locations are uncertain, but the meaning is obvious — the outcry of judgment is heard far and wide!

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:35
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:35 YHWH's judgment on Moab is related to their idolatry.

  1. they offer sacrifice on the high place
    1. central sanctuary, cf. Isa. 16:12
    2. local high places, cf. Jer. 11:13
  2. burn incense to his god

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:37-38
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:37-38 These were signs of mourning (cf. Jer. 4:8, see SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES). It is possible they were also denoting idol rituals (i.e. "gashes on their hands," cf. Jer. 16:6, or "on house tops," cf. Jer. 19:13; 32:29) or possibly even the corrupted worship of YHWH (cf. Jer. 41:5).

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:39 "turned back"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:39 "turned back" This VERB (BDB 815, KB 937, Hiphil PERFECT) can refer to

  1. humiliation
  2. retreat in battle

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:40
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:40 This refers to Nebuchadnezzar's army (cf. Jer. 4:13; 49:22; Ezek. 17:3,12; Hosea 8:1).

48:41
NASB, NKJV, LXX, JPSOA, Peshitta  "Kerioth"
NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, NET  "the towns"

The Hebrew root, קריה (BDB 900) means "city." The form in the text, הקריות, is used of a proper name in v. 24 (BDB 901) and Amos 2:2 (but a different Hebrew word for "strongholds") and also on the Moabite Stone. "The towns" fits this verse better.

▣ "like. . .a woman in labor" See note at Jer. 30:6 and SPECIAL TOPIC: BIRTH PAINS

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:43-44
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 48:43-44 This same terminology is used in Isa. 24:17-18, possibly a well known proverbial saying because it is a sound play on the three words (BDB 808, 809, 809 I). Imagery from hunting techniques are used of YHWH's judgment (cf. Amos 5:19). There is no escape, no help, no hope!

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:45 "the forehead of Moab"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:45 "the forehead of Moab" This may be an allusion to Num. 24:17, which is one of the prophecies of Balaam. "Forehead" (BDB 802), like "rod" and "staff" of Jer. 48:17, is a symbol of royal power.

It is also possible that "forehead" is parallel to "crown of the head" (BDB 869), meaning the heads of the rebellious Moabites were crushed (i.e. killed in battle).

There is a possibility both "forehead" and "skulls" are imagery for the mountains or fortresses of Moab (TEV).

entries.title: Jeremiah 48:47
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
48:47 As YHWH grieves over His need to judge (cf. Jer. 48:31,36), now He promises a future day of hope (cf. Jer. 12:14-17). It must be remembered that YHWH chose Abraham/Israel to choose the world.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LAST DAYS

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:1 "Ammon"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:1 "Ammon" These people (like Moab) were descendants of Lot by his own daughter (cf. Gen. 19:38). Therefore, they were relatives of Abraham's family. Their territory was northeast of Moab on the eastern side of Jordan. A group known as "Amorites" lived next to the Jordan River and the Ammonites to the east, closer to the desert. Their capital was Rabbath. They were a potent rival to King Saul, but a vassal to Kings David and Solomon.

The Jerome Biblical Commentary (p. 334) reminds us that Ammon

  1. rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem (cf. Ezek. 25:1-7)
  2. their king, Baalis, encouraged Ishmael to assassinate the new Babylonian governor, Gedaliah (cf. Jer. 40:11-16)

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMMON

49:1,3
NASB, MT  "Malcam"
NKJV  "Milcham"
NRSV, NJB, JPSOA, REB  "Milcom"
TEV  "Molech"
Peshitta (JPSOA footnote)  "Malcom"
LXX  "Melchol"

The MT has "their king." All of these names are a word play on the Hebrew word for "king," מלך (BDB 572). In 1 Kgs. 11:5,33, this Ammonite national deity is called "Milcom," but in Jer. 49:7 "Molech" (cf. 1 Kgs. 11:7), which is the more common name of this fertility god.

The UBS Text Project (p. 304) gives "Milcom" a "B" rating.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOLECH

▣ "Gad" This refers to the tribal allocation of Gad (cf. Num. 32:33-37; Josh. 13:24-28). It included the territory of the Amorites and part of the territory of Ammon.

The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of the tribe of Manasseh asked for and received their tribal inheritance on the eastern side of the Jordan River (cf. Josh. 13:8).

The exact reference to Ammon expanding into the territory once held by the tribe of Gad is during the period of Assyrian power (i.e. Tiglath-pileser III in 734-732 B.C., cf. 2 Kgs. 15:29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA
