READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter deals with the prophecies against
    1. Ammon, Jer. 49:1-6
    2. Edom, Jer. 49:7-22
    3. Syria, Jer. 49:23-27
    4. Kedar and Hazor, Jer. 49:28-33
    5. Elam, Jer. 49:34-39

  2. Many cities are listed, as in chapter 48 (judgment on Moab).
    1. Ammon, Jer. 49:1-6
      1. Rabbah, Jer. 49:2,3
      2. Heshbon, Jer. 49:3
      3. Ai, Jer. 49:3
    2. Edom, Jer. 49:7-22
      1. Teman, Jer. 49:7
      2. Dedan, Jer. 49:8
      3. Bozrah, Jer. 49:13,22
    3. Syria, Jer. 49:23-27
      1. Damascus, Jer. 49:23,34,27
      2. Hamath, Jer. 49:23
      3. Arpad, Jer. 49:23
      4. "the city of praise, "the town of My joy," Jer. 49:25 (i.e. Damascus)

  3. As there was a ray of hope and restoration related to Moab in Jer. 48:47 (cf. Jer. 12:14-17), so now there is also a ray of hope and restoration for
    1. Ammon, Jer. 49:6
    2. Elam, Jer. 49:39

  4. There is a recurrent emphasis on YHWH speaking.
    1. thus says the Lord, Jer. 49:1a, 2g, 12a, 18, 28
    2. declares the Lord, Jer. 49:2a, 6c, 13b, 16h, 31b, 32d, 38c, 39c
    3. declares the Lord God of hosts, Jer. 49:5b
    4. thus says the Lord of hosts, Jer. 49:7b, 26c, 35a
    5. a message from the Lord, Jer. 49:14
    6. It is possible that Jer. 49:25 is also a word from YHWH, but not probable; see note.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:2 "a trumpet"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:2 "a trumpet" The word is not in the MT, only the CONSTRUCT "cry of battle" (BDB 929 CONSTRUCT BDB 536). It may refer to

  1. a particular battle cry (Josh. 6:5-6; Jdgs. 7:16-18; Ezek. 21:22)
  2. the blast of a trumpet (cf. Jer. 4:19; 20:16; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL)

▣ "towns" This term (BDB 123 I) is literally "daughters," but is often used in an idiomatic way (i.e. BDB 123 I, #4) for "surrounding villages" (cf. Num. 21:25,32; Jdg. 1:27; Neh. 11:25-31). In Jer. 49:3 it is difficult to know if the word means

  1. inhabitants of Rabbah
  2. villages around Rabbah

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:3 This series of IMPERATIVES calls on the Ammonites to grieve over their defeat and exile.

  1. wail ‒ BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  2. cry out ‒ BDB 858, KB 1042, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. gird. . .sackcloth ‒ BDB 291, KB 291, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. lament ‒ BDB 704, KB 763, Qal IMPERATIVE
  5. rush back and forth ‒ BDB 1001, KB 1439, Hithpolel IMPERATIVE or possibly "gash yourselves," REB, cf. Jer. 48:37; this line is missing in the LXX)

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "Ai" A city by this name is unknown in Ammon. NJB changes it to "Ar." The LXX has "Gai." The best explanation comes from R. K. Harrison (Tyndale OT Commentary, "Jeremiah," p. 179). He notes that when "Ai" is used for a city it always has the ARTICLE, but there is no ARTICLE here. The word itself (BDB 743) means "ruins" and, therefore, is a reference to Heshbon's destruction.

The UBS Text Project, p. 304, gives "Ai" a "B" rating.

▣ "sackcloth" See SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.

▣
NASB  "rush back and forth inside the walls"
NKJV  "run to and fro by the walls"
NRSV  "slash yourselves with whips"
TEV  "run about in confusion"
REB  "score your bodies with gashes"
NJB, JPSOA  "run to and fro among the sheep-pens"
Peshitta  "be disquieted"
NET  "run about covered with gashes"

The VERB (BDB 1001, KB 1439, Hithpoel IMPERATIVE implies a quick movement.

The next word in the MT is walls or hedges (BDB 155 I). Therefore, this would represent the frightened movement of the soldiers guarding the fortified cities.

As you can see from the variety in the translations, there is a popular emendation from "walls" to "gashes." This would refer either to

  1. signs of grief and fear
  2. idolatry practices to attack their deities

The only difference in the words is the common "r" ‒ "d" confusion.

  1. within the walls #8210; בגדרות
  2. with gashes ‒ בגדדות

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:4 Ammon had some knowledge of YHWH. Instead of trusting in Him they trusted in

  1. their geography (i.e. fertile valleys, lit. "flowing," BDB 264, KB 206)
  2. their treasures (i.e. possibly revenue from trading routes, cf. Jer. 48:7)

The JPSOA translates the first two lines as:

"Why do you glory in strength,

Your strength is drained"

They interpret the Hebrew root (BDB 770) "valley" as coming from an Akkadian root for "strength" (cf. NRSV, TEV, REB, NET).

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:5 Josephus (Antiq. 10.9.7) mentions that Ammon was devastated by Nebuchadnezzar II in his twenty-third year (i.e. 582 B.C.).

▣ "Lord of Hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:6 This is another promise of restoration like Jer. 48:47 (cf. Jer. 12:14-17). The same terminology is also used of Elam in Jer. 49:39. These promises have an eschatological orientation, not limited to these specific nationalities, but to the promised inclusion of "the nations" through Israel's God and His Messiah (i.e. Ps. 22:27; 66:1-4; 86:8-10; Isa. 2:2-4; 12:4-5; 25:6-9; 42:6-12; 45:22-23; 49:5-6; 51:4-5; 56:6-8; 60:1-3; 66:23; Micah 4:1-4; Mal. 1:11; John 3:16; 4:42; 1 Tim. 2:4; Titus 2:11; 2 Pet. 3:9; 1 John 2:1; 4:14)! Hallelujah, hallelujah, hallelujah!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:7 "Edom"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:7 "Edom" There is no hope given to Edom, as there is to the other nations. Edom was a perennial enemy of Judah.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

▣ "wisdom. . .good counsel" There are several words used to describe Edom's reputation of having "wise men" (use of three questions). Job was probably from Edom (i.e. "the land of Uz," and one of his friends from Teman, a city in Edom).

  1. wisdom (BDB 315)
  2. counsel (BDB 420)
  3. the prudent (BDB 106, KB 122, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)

Jeremiah 9:23-24 is very clear that true wisdom is inseparably linked to a knowledge of YHWH.

▣ "Teman" This NOUN (BDB 412) means "south" (cf. Josh. 12:3; 13:4) or "south wind" (cf. Ps. 78:26). It is used as a designation for

  1. a descendant of Esau, Gen. 36:11; 1 Chr. 1:36
  2. an Arabian clan, Gen. 36:15; 1 Chr. 1:53
  3. a territory or country, Gen. 36:34; Obadiah Jer. 49:9
  4. a city, Jer. 49:7,20; Ezek 25:13; Amos 1:12
▣
NASB  "decayed"
NKJV, NRSV, NJB  "vanished"
TEV  "disappeared"
JPSOA, AB  "gone stale"
REB  "dispersed abroad"
Peshitta  "taken away"
NET  "turned bad"

This VERB (BDB 710, KB 769) in Qal means "to be loosed." This is the only occurrence of the VERB in Niphal. The root has several senses and different lexicons list them differently.

  1. BDB 710
    1. VERB
      (1) Qal ‒ go free, be unrestrained
      (2) Niphal ‒ let loose in the sense of dismissed
    2. NOUN ‒ excess (cf. Exod. 26:12)
  2. KB 769 ‒ VERB
    1. to stink (Syrian)
    2. to stop
    3. obstinance
    4. falsehood
    5. hanging down
    6. projecting
    7. lounge around

KB #a. seems to fit the VERB form and context best (KB 769 II), but it is found only here, which makes certainty impossible.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:8 This is another series of IMPERATIVES, like Jer. 49:3, related to Edom's judgment.

  1. flee away ‒ BDB 630, KB 681, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 49:24; 46:21
  2. turn back ‒ BDB 815, KB 937, Hophal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 49:24; 46:21
  3. dwell in the depths IMPERATIVE BDB 770, KB 847, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (i.e. an attempt to hide, cf. Jer. 49:10, or possibly to leave the trans-Jordan plateau and return to their original homeland, cf. NET Bible, p. 1432, #5)

▣ "Dedan" This was an Arabian tribe connected with Sheba (cf. Gen. 25:3; 1 Chr. 1:32). They are somehow related to Edom in Jer. 25:23 and Ezek. 25:13. The best guess is that a group/city/clan of them had settled in the territory of Edom; not that Edom's influence had spread that far south and east.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:9-10 This is very similar to Obadiah 5-6.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:9 "gleanings"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:9 "gleanings" This term (BDB 760) is from Lev. 19:9-10; 23:22; Deut. 24:20-22, where it describes YHWH's provision for the poor as it relates to harvesting a field. The grain which was not gathered the first time through and the grain in the corners was left for the poor to harvest enough to eat but not to gather in quantities to sell.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:10 There is a play on the word "offspring" (lit. "seed," BDB 282) connected to "gleaning." Edom will be completely and utterly destroyed, nothing left.

▣ "and he is no more" This represents the MT. Some versions of the LXX change this to "and there is none to say," which gives a context to Jer. 49:11, thereby making specific who the speaker is (i.e. the invaders).

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:11 Is Jer. 49:11 (1) another ray of hope linked to Jer. 49:12 or (2) an affirmation of complete destruction of even the most vulnerable? The context fits #2 best (cf. Jer. 49:20).

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:12 "the cup"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:12 "the cup" The word "cup" (BDB 468) is often an idiom for judgment. As one drinks and becomes drunk with its physical and emotional consequences (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM), the idiom of "cup" became a way to describe poor choices and their consequences. Some examples of this idiom:

  1. Job 21:20
  2. Psalm 60:3; 75:8
  3. Isa. 29:9; 51:17; 63:6
  4. Jer. 25:15-16,28; 49:12
  5. Lamentations 4:21
  6. Ezek. 23:32-34

It is used in the NT of

  1. Jesus ‒ Matt. 20:22; 26:38-42; Mark 14:36; Luke 22:47; John 18:11
  2. the beast ‒ Rev. 14:10; 16:19; 19:15

▣ "certainly drink" There are three INFINITIVE ABSOLUTES and IMPERFECT VERBS of the same roots used for emphasis in this verse.

  1. certainly drunk ‒ BDB 1059, KB 1667 (three INFINITIVES and two IMPERFECTS)
  2. same as #1
  3. completely acquitted ‒ BDB 667, KB 720 (one INFINITIVE and two IMPERFECTS)

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:13 "I have sworn by Myself"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:13 "I have sworn by Myself" There is no one greater to swear by than YHWH Himself (i.e. "as I live," cf. Jer. 22:5; 44:26; 51:14; Gen. 22:16; Isa. 45:23; Amos 6:8; Heb. 6:13,18). Oath taking was a cultural way of affirming the absolute trustworthiness/truthfulness of a statement or promise.

▣ "Bozrah" This was a major city (possibly the capital in the seventh century) in Edom. The "Bozrah" mentioned in Jer. 48:24 is an unknown site in Moab. The root for the city's name (BDB 131 II) is related to the VERB for "grape-gathering" (lit. "those who cut off") in Jer. 49:9 (BDB 130, KB 148, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE).

▣ "an object of horror, a reproach, a ruin and a curse" This is a series of terms used to describe people's reaction to God's judgment.

  1. "a curse" ‒ BDB 46, #4, "execration" ‒ Num. 5:27; Deut. 29:21; Jer. 29:18; 42:18; 44:12
  2. "a horror" ‒ BDB 1031 I, "appallment,"
    "horror" ‒ Deut. 28:37; 2 Kgs. 22:19; 2 Chr. 29:8; 30:7; Jer. 5:30; 25:9,11,28,38; 29:18; 42:18; 44:12,22; 49:13,17; 50:23; 51:37,41; Micah 6:16; Zeph.2:15
  3. "a reproach" ‒ BDB 357, #3 ‒ "a Taunt" ‒ Ps. 31:11; 44:13; 69:10; 79:4; 89:41; 109:25; Isa. 30:5; Jer. 6:10; 20:8; 24:9; 29:18; 42:18; 44:8,12; 49:13; Ezek. 5:14,15; Dan. 9:16; 12:2
  4. "an imprecation (i.e. curse)" ‒ BDB 887 ‒ Deut. 11:26,28; 21:23; 23:5; 28:15,45; 2 Kgs. 22:19; Ps. 109:17,18; Jer. 24:9; 25:18; 29:22; Zech. 8:13
  5. "a ruin" ‒ BDB 351 II, cf. Ezek. 29:10; 38:8; Zeph. 2:4

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:14 There is a literary relationship between this verse and the opening verses of Obadiah. I assume that Jeremiah has influenced Obadiah and, thereby makes Obadiah an early post-exilic prophet (which goes against the order of the book in the scroll of the Minor Prophets; see SPECIAL TOPIC: POST EXILIC CHART).

YHWH's prophet is calling on a foreign invader to decimate Edom.

  1. gather yourselves ‒ BDB 867, KB 1062, Hithpael IMPERATIVE
  2. come against her ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. rise up for battle ‒ BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Obad. 1:1
49:16
NASB  "As for the terror of you"
NKJV  "Your fierceness"
NRSV  "the terror you inspire"
TEV  "your pride"
NJB  "your reputation for ferocity"
JPSOA  "your horrible nature" (footnote says "meaning
  of Hebrew uncertain")
REB  "your overbearing arrogance"

This word (BDB 814) occurs only here. Most lexicons relate it to the VERB listed just above it in BDB "shuddering" (i.e. in fear, cf. Job 21:6; Ps. 55:5; Isa. 21:4; Ezek. 7:18).

The AB (p. 331) speculates that it may relate to the name of an idol (BDB 814), possibly mentioned in 1 Kgs. 15:13 (twice), because the NOUN is FEMININE but the VERB ("deceive," BDB 674 II, KB 728, Hiphil PERFECT) is MASCULINE.

▣ "arrogance" Edom thought her topography (i.e. a high table land or plateau) would make her immune to invasion but she was mistaken. Just as Moab was mistaken.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:17 "an object of horror. . .hiss"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:17 "an object of horror. . .hiss" See note at Jer. 49:13 for other words used to describe ANE shame and reproach. Here

  1. everyone who passes by it will be horrified ‒ BDB 1030, KB 1563, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Lev. 26:32; Jer. 18:16; 19:8; 50:13
  2. everyone who passes by it will hiss ‒ BDB 1056, KB 1656, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. 1 Kgs. 9:8; Jer. 19:8; 50:13; Lam. 2:15

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORROR, REPROACH, RUIN, CURSE

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:18 "like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah with its neighbors"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:18 "like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah with its neighbors" Sodom and Gomorrah were the wicked cities destroyed by God in Genesis 19. Their destruction and lack of habitation became a cultural idiom (cf. Deut. 29:23; Isa. 1:9-10; 13:19; Jer. 23:14; 50:40; Lam. 4:6; Ezek. 16:46,48,49,53,55,56; Amos 4:11; Zeph. 2:9; Matt. 10:15; 11:23-24; Rom. 9:29; 2 Pet. 2:6; Jude Jer. 49:7; Rev. 11:8).

▣ "a son of man" This is the Hebrew CONSTRUCT ben-adam (i.e. Ezek. 2:1), which meant human person (i.e. Job 25:6; Ps. 8:4; Ezek. 2:1; Dan. 8:17). In this verse it is parallel to "no one."

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SON OF MAN, I.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:19 "like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:19 "like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan" At one time the Jordan River valley was heavily forested and had many wild lions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣ "whoever is chosen I shall appoint over it" This phrase is uncertain in the MT. Nebuchadnezzar II was YHWH's choice for judgment and Cyrus II was HIs choice for restoration (cf. Isa. 44:28; 45:1-7).

Some commentators change this phrase so as to refer to the imagery of a shepherd trying to protect the sheep from the lion (AB footnote e, p. 329).

▣ "For who is like Me" See SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

▣
NASB  "who will summon Me into court?"
NKJV, REB  "who will arraign Me?"
NRSV, JPSOA  "who can summon Me?"
TEV  "who would dare challenge me?"
NJB  "who can haul me into court?"
Peshitta  "who can testify against me?"
NET  "there is no one who can call me
  to account"

The UBS Text Project, p. 308, makes two suggestions.

  1. and who will summon me ‒ ומי יעידני
  2. and who will be my equal ‒ ומי יעודני

The VERB in the MT (BDB 416, KB 419) is in the Hiphil stem that means to appoint someone to a certain place. The second option is in the Hophal stem and means to set before.

Both fit the context. The UBS Text Project cannot decide which is original and gives option #1 a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:19-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:19-21 This is very similar to Jer. 50:44-46, obviously common cultural idioms.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:20 "the plan of the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:20 "the plan of the Lord" History and nations are in YHWH's control! He establishes and destroys (cf. Jer. 1:10). His ultimate plan is the redemption of all human beings.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "Teman" This was a city in the southern region of Edom. The imagery denotes the complete exile of this city and region (cf. vv. 7,20; Amos 1:12). See full note at v. 7.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:21 "at the Red Sea"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:21 "at the Red Sea" This geographical location is uncertain. Please see the Special Topic below.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE RED SEA

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:22 "He will mount up and swoop like an eagle"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:22 "He will mount up and swoop like an eagle" Nebuchadnezzar's army is depicted in this imagery in Jer. 4:13; 48:40; and Lam. 4:19. It denoted a swift, powerful, deadly attack.

▣ "Bozrah" This was an ancient capital of Edom, mentioned several times in judgment oracles (cf. Isa. 34:6; 63:1; Jer. 49:13,22; Amos 1:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EDOM AND ISRAEL

▣ "a woman in labor" This was a recurrent idiom of fear and anguish (cf. Jer. 4:31; 30:6; 48:41; Isa. 13:8; 26:17; Micah 4:9-10). At that moment they were helpless!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIRTH PAINS

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:23 "Damascus"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:23 "Damascus" This was the capital of the Syrian kingdom (i.e. Aramean kingdom, cf. Gen. 14:15; 15:2; 1 Kings 11:24; 15:18; 19:15; 20:34; 2 Kings 8:7,9; 14:28; 16:10-12; Isa. 7:8). It was north/northeast of Israel. It was part of the land bridge between Mesopotamia and Egypt. Caravans and armies took this route because of the desert to the east of Palestine. It was conquered by the Assyrian king, Tiglath-pileser in 733 B.C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA

▣ "put to shame" See SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:23-24 "they have heard bad news"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:23-24 "they have heard bad news" This refers to the invasion of the Neo-Babylonian army. Notice the series of words used to describe their fear.

  1. put to shame
  2. heard bad news
  3. disheartened
  4. anxiety (this line of poetry is uncertain)
  5. cannot be calmed
  6. helpless
  7. turned away to flee
  8. panic has gripped her
  9. distress
  10. pangs

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:24 "like a woman in childbirth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:24 "like a woman in childbirth" This is a recurrent image (BDB 408) for fear and pain (cf. Jer. 6:24; 13:21; 22:23; 49:22; 50:43; Ps. 48:6; Isa. 13:8; 21:3; 42:14; Hosea 13:13; Micah 4:9,10).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIRTH PAINS

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:25 It is hard to know who is speaking these words.

  1. YHWH
  2. people of Syria

There is no reason why Damascus should be called "the city of praise" or "the town of My joy" by YHWH. Poetry is so condensed and figurative that it is often difficult to follow who is speaking. In the judgment of the nations poems of those who are being judged are often quoted as hypothetical of what they would/might have said.

▣ "has not been deserted" This goes against the rest of the context of judgment. Many scholars see the "not" (Hebrew לא, BDB 518) as a grammatical feature called "an emphatic lamedh" (Hebrew L) and, therefore, meaning, "has been completely deserted."

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:26 This is very similar to Jer. 50:30, obviously cultural idioms and war imagery (cf. Jer. 49:27; Amos 1:4) is/are repeated often in ANE poetry.

▣ "the Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: The Lord of Hosts

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:27 "Ben-hadad"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:27 "Ben-hadad" This means "son of Hadad." Hadad was one of the fertility gods of the Ancient Near East (i.e. a storm/rain god, like Ba'al). Many of the kings of Syria were called by this name.

  1. 1 Kings 15:18,20; 2 Chr. 16:2,4
  2. 1 Kings 20 (mentioned by name 13 times)
    2 Kings 6:24; 8:7,9
  3. 2 Kings 13:3,24,25; Amos 1:4

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:28 "Kedar"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:28 "Kedar" This name (BDB 871) originally referred to the second son of Ishmael (cf. Gen. 25:13; 1 Chr. 1:29). The family became a desert, nomadic clan (Bedouin) that lived in tents in northern Arabia (cf. Jer. 49:29; Ps. 120:5; Song of Songs 1:5; Isa. 60:7).

Joesphus (Apion I.19) quotes a Babylonian historian, Berossus, saying that Nebuchadnezzar II took over the area where they lived and controlled the caravan routes (International Dictionary of the Bible, vol. 3, pp. 3-4).

▣ "the kingdoms of Hazor" This does not refer to the Canaanite city that was defeated by both Joshua (cf. Josh. 11:1-15) and later Deborah/Barak (cf. Judges 4-5). The Hebrew word (BDB 347) could also be understood as "unwalled villages" (BDB 347, cf. Gen. 25:16; Isa. 42:11).

This refers to Arabian desert dwellers to the east of Ammon who were conquered by Nebuchadnezzar II in about 598 B.C. This event is also recorded by Josephus.

Nebuchadnezzar II is commanded by YHWH to conquer.

  1. rise ‒ BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. go up ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. devastate ‒ BDB 994, KB 1418, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. commands #1 and #2 are repeated in Jer. 49:31

▣ "the men of the east" This descriptive phrase can refer to different people groups on the eastern side of the Jordan (cf. Gen. 29:1; Jdg. 6:3,33; 7:12; 8:10; 1 Kgs. 4:30; Job 1:3; Isa. 11:14; Jer. 49:28; Ezek. 25:4,10).

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:29 "Terror on every side"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:29 "Terror on every side" This phrase is used several times in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 6:25; 20:3,10; 46:5; 49:29; Lam. 2:22). This would be similar imagery to "the four winds" of Jer. 49:36.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:30 This is another series of three IMPERATIVES directed to Kedar and Hazor.

  1. run ‒ BDB 630; KB 681, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. flee ‒ BDB 626, KB 678, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. dwell in the depths ‒ BDB 770, KB 847, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

This was common imagery; see Jer. 49:8.

▣ "a plan" Nebuchadnezzar's plan is really YHWH's plan (i.e. Jer. 49:20; 51:10,11; Isa. 14:24). Nebuchadnezzar II is His instrument of judgment, as Cyrus II will later be His instrument of restoration.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:32 "who cut the corners of their hair"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:32 "who cut the corners of their hair" This was a practice of several desert tribes (cf. Jer. 9:26; 25:23). It is uncertain if it was idolatrous (cf. Lev. 19:27) or societal i.e. a ritual or a standard of appearance).

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:33 "a haunt of jackals"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:33 "a haunt of jackals" It is possible that the references to the destruction and lack of human habitation was

  1. an idiom of complete and continuing devastation (cf. Isa. 34:10)
  2. the presence of the demonic (i.e. cursed place, cf. Jer. 9:11; 10:22; Isa. 34:11-15

The NEB, based on new archaeological finds, was the first English translation to see these animals as possibly the demonic behind pagan idols.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DEMONIC (OT)

▣ "a son of man" See note at Jer. 49:18.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SON OF MAN

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:34 "Elam"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:34 "Elam" This represents the highland area east of the Tigris River. Over the centuries its territory expanded and contracted. Both Susa/Shushan and Persepolis were in its territory. Today it would be in Iran.

The Jerome Biblical Commentary (p. 335) mentions an account found in the "Babylonian Chronicles" that tells of Nebuchadnezzar II defeating an Elamite king in about 597 B.C. The exiles in Babylon may have been hoping that Nebuchadnezzar II would be defeated by Elam. This hope was dashed!

▣ This prophecy is dated in the same time frame as Jer. 28:1. Zedekiah reigned from 597 B.C. to the fall and destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:35 "break the bow"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:35 "break the bow" This was an idiom for the destruction of a nation's military power (cf. Jer. 51:56; Psa. 46:9; Isa. 22:6). Apparently Elam was famous for its archers.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:36 "the four winds of heaven"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:36 "the four winds of heaven" The number "four" is often used to represent the whole world. The inhabitants of Elam will be scattered out of existence but notice God's promise in Jer. 49:39. See note at Jer. 49:6, where the same terminology and promise is given to Ammon (but not to Edom).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #2

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:37
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:37 Again common imagery is used as before in Jer. 9:16.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:38 "I will set My throne in Elam"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 49:38 "I will set My throne in Elam" This seems to be a reference to Nebuchandezzar's control of the area, functioning as YHWH's chosen vessel of judgment.

entries.title: Jeremiah 49:39
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
49:39 This is a repeated promise and hope (cf. Jer. 30:3,18; 31:23; 32:44; 33:7,11,26; 48:47; 49:6,39). See full note at Jer. 48:47 and 49:6. This seems to be an eschatological reference (cf. Deut. 30:3-5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE LAST DAYS

▣
NASB, NRSV   "I shall restore"
NKJV   "I will bring back"

The MT has "return" (BDB 996, KB 1477, Qal IMPERFECT but the Qere form is Hiphil IMPERFECT of the same VERB).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Jeremiah 50 and 51 make up a literary unit which describes both
    1. the fall of Babylon (both the capital and the nation as a whole)
    2. the restoration of God's people to their land (cf. Jer. 50:4-5,6-10,17-20,33-34; 51:36-40)

  2. This prophecy is characterized by YHWH's (through His prophet) commands to
    1. the destroyer of Babylon (i.e. Persia, Cyrus II, cf. Isa. 44:28; 45:1), Jer. 50:2,14,21,26-27,29
    2. the Jewish exiles, Jer. 50:8

  3. The destruction of the Fertile Crescent Empire in the delta region known as Babylon is described in several places in Isaiah. The interpretive problem is that there was an "old Babylon" and a "new Babylon." Isaiah wrote during the eighth century B.C. when "old Babylon" was in existence. It is difficult to know if Isa. 13; 14:22-27; 21:1-9; 47:5,9; 48:14 refer to it or to Neo-Babylon (see SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON).
     This in no way questions predictive prophecy, as Isa. 44:28; 45:1 clearly demonstrate, but the historical setting is crucial so as to ascertain the original inspired author's intent.

  4. A good brief historical survey of this chapter, written by John Walton, is found in IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), pp. 683-685.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:2 This verse is characterized by

  1. a series of IMPERATIVES from YHWH to publicize Neo-Babylon's demise
    1. declare ‒ BDB 616, KB 665, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    2. proclaim ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (twice)
    3. same as #2
    4. lift up a standard ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 51:12,27
    5. do not conceal ‒ BDB 470, KB 469, Piel IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    6. say ‒ BDB 55, KB 65, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. a series of PERFECTS denoting a complete action (i.e. PROPHETIC PERFECTS) of events yet to occur, but which surely will occur because of YHWH"s stated will
    1. Babylon has been captured ‒ BDB 539, KB 530, Niphal PERFECT
    2. Bel has been put to shame ‒ BDB 101, KB 116, Hiphil PERFECT (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BEL)
    3. Marduk has been shattered ‒ BDB 369, KB 365, Qal PERFECT (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK)
    4. her images have been put to shame ‒ same as #b
    5. her idols have been shattered ‒ same as #c

▣ "Bel" Below are my notes from Isa. 46:1. Bel, like Ba'al, means "lord," "master," "owner."

Isa. 46:1 "Bel" Bel (BDB128, KB 132, Akkadian for "lord") is a similar title to the Canaanite title Ba'al. This is an allusion to the chief god of the Akkadian pantheon (Enlil, who was called "lord"). As Babylon came to power the chief deity's name was changed to Marduk (BDB 597, cf. Jer. 50:2).
SPECIAL TOPIC: MARDUK

▣ "Nebo" This was the son of Marduk (named only here in the OT) and was the god of learning and writing (BDB 612). Bel and Nebo can be seen in many of the Babylonian names of the period (Nebuchadnezzar [Dan. 1:1]; Nebushazban [Jer. 39:13]; Nebuzaradan [Jer. 39:9]; Nabopolassar [first king of Neo-Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar's father]; Nabonidus [Beshazzar's father, last king of Neo-Babylon]; Belteshazzar [Dan. 1:7]; Belshazzar [Dan. 5:1]). These were the two chief gods of the Babylonian pantheon.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEBO

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

▣
NASB, TEV, NJB, REB  "Marduk"
NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA  "Merodack"
Peshitta  "Merodach"

The MT has "Merudack" (BDB 597). It is another way to transliterate the consonants for Marduk. The Sumerian pantheon is fluid. Originally the title "lord" was applied to Enlil, but when the city of Babylon became more important, her chief deity, Markuk, took the place of Enlil/Bel as the head of the pantheon. For a further outline of these Sumerian gods and their myths, see my commentary on Genesis 1-11, the introduction, online at www.freebiblecommentary.org.

The last king of Babylon (i.e. Nabonidus) depreciated Marduk for the worship of the moon goddess. When the Persians attacked the city of Babylon they were supported by the priests and followers of Marduk.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:3 As the covenant people had to fear the enemy from the north (i.e. Jer. 1:13-15; 4:6; 6:1,22), now that very enemy (i.e. Neo-Babylon) must fear another instrument of God's judgment from the north (i.e. Cyrus II and the armies of Persia, cf. Isa. 44:28; 45:1).

Notice the two PROPHETIC PERFECTS," like the five of Jer. 50:2.

  1. have wandered off ‒ BDB 626, KB 678, Qal PERFECT
  2. have gone away ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal PERFECT

Neo-Babylon's judgment is sure because YHWH wills it, plans it, and will bring it to pass.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA

▣ "an object of horror" See SPECIAL TOPIC: HORROR, REPROACH, RUIN, CURSE.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:4-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:4-5 These verses are a ray of hope and promise that YHWH will restore His covenant people to their promised homeland.

Notice that the returnees are repentant descendants of both Israel and Judah. Also notice they came for the purpose of finding and fellowshiping with their covenant God. This new day of fellowship through repentance and faith is the essence of the "new covenant" of Jer. 31:31-34.

The NASB version translated the second VERB of Jer. 50:5 (BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE) in a future sense, "they will come," but it is an IMPERATIVE "come" (UBS Text Project gives the IMPERATIVE a "B" rating, p. 314). This is the invitation to faith, repentance, and intimate worship which brings the exiles home to the temple and the Promised Land. There is both Divine sovereignty and human free will involved.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

SPECIAL TOPIC: ELECTION/PREDESTINATION AND THE NEED FOR A THEOLOGICAL BALANCE

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:5 "an everlasting covenant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:5 "an everlasting covenant" Be careful of reading English definitions into these Hebrew words.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL COVENANTS (OT)

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:6-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:6-10 This is a poem that describes

  1. the past sins of the covenant people, both their leaders and general populous (i.e. fertility worship, Jer. 50:6 and faithlessness to YHWH, Jer. 50:7)
  2. YHWH commands for them to leave Babylon (Jer. 50:8; Isa. 48:20) because God is bringing a destroyer from the north (i.e. Persia, Jer. 50:9-10)

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:7 "their adversaries have said. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:7 "their adversaries have said. . ." The prophet states what Judah's adversaries think is the reason the God of Abraham will not judge them for their treatment of His people.

  1. they are guilty
  2. they have sinned against their God (i.e. idolatry)
    1. who is the habitation of righteousness (cf. Jer. 31:23; SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS)
    2. who is the only hope of their fathers (cf. Jer. 14:8; 17:13)
    3. who provides them a resting place (v. 6, line e; Jer. 33:12; 50:19)

But, the adversary (i.e. Neo-Babylon) will be judged (cf. Jer. 50:11,16).

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:8 "Babylon. . .the Chaldeans"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:8 "Babylon. . .the Chaldeans" These are two ways of referring to the peoples/nations of the southern area of the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers (cf. Jer. 50:1,8,35,45). The terms "Babylonian" and Chaldean" are parallel.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHALDEANS

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:9 There is a sound play between the first three VERBS of Jer. 50:9.

  1. עוה ‒ BDB 734, KB 802, "arouse"
  2. עלה ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, "bring up"
  3. ערך ‒ BDB 789, KB 884, "draw up their battle lines"

▣ "a horde of great nations" The Persian army was made up of Medes and Persians and the mercenaries of conquered armies (cf. Jer. 51:27-28).

▣
NASB, NKJV, LXX  "an expert warrior"
NRSV, JPSOA  "a skilled warrior"
TEV  "skillful hunters"
NJB  "experienced soldiers"
Peshitta  "expert archer"

The MT has the VERB "miscarry" (BDB 1013, KB 1491, Hiphil PARTICIPLE, i.e. "make childless"). Most translations take it from another root "skilled" (BDB 968). The first letter in MT is שׁ, but in the other versions, שׂ. The rest of the consonants are the same. These were lethal archers!

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:11 There are several suggestions from the Masoretic scholars (Qere) about changing the VERBS in the MT (Kethiv), which are FEMININE SINGULAR to MASCULINE PLURAL.

  1. you are glad
  2. you are jubilant
  3. you skip about (NET, "like calves in a pasture")
  4. neigh like stallions (lit. "mighty ones")

When you read Jer. 50:12-13 you see where the FEMININE understanding came from in Jer. 50:11. Verse 11 addresses the people of Neo-Babylon who have had such victory and easy living. All of that will change (cf. Jer. 50:12-16)!

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:13 "will be horrified. . .will hiss"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:13 "will be horrified. . .will hiss" This imagery is recurrent; see notes at Jer. 18:16-17 and 49:17.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORROR, REPROACH, RUIN, CURSE

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:14 In Jer. 50:14-16 YHWH uses IMPERATIVES to address the invading and victorious Persian army. This verse uses imagery from archery.

  1. "bend the bow" (lit. "tread" so as to bend the bow for the string)
  2. shout
  3. do not be sparing with your arrows
  4. the LXX refers to archers in Jer. 50:29

The reason for the military attack is that Babylon sinned against YHWH.

  1. Jer. 50:29-32 ‒ arrogance
  2. Hab. 2:8,17 ‒ murder
  3. Jer. 50:38; Hab. 2:19 ‒ idolatry

As she did to others, so now it will be done to her (cf. Jer. 50:15f, 29f).

50:15
NASB   "pillars"
NKJV, Peshitta   "foundations"
NRSV, LXX   "bulwarks"
NJB, JPSOA, REB   "bastions"
NET Bible   "towers"

The word in the MT (אשׁיה, BDB 78, KB 94) occurs only here. A similar word, אשׁדה (BDB 78), meaning "foundation," is found in Deuteronomy and Joshua. The KB lists several cognate options.

  1. Assyrian ‒ tower
  2. Aramaic ‒ wall
  3. Syrian ‒ pillar
  4. Arabian ‒ columns

It refers to some type of protective structure/fortification.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:16 The first two lines predict the complete collapse of commerce and food production.

The next three lines are a warning for all foreigners to flee.

  1. mercenaries
  2. merchants 
  3. possibly even exiles/captives who could

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:17 "Israel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:17 "Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (THE NAME)

▣ "lions" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

▣
NASB, NKJV, TEV, NJB, Peshitta  "Nebuchadnezzar"
NRSV, JPSOA, REB  "Nebuchadrezzar"
LXX  (omits the name but has)
  "king of Babylon"

Both of these refer to the same person, son of Nabopolassar. There are several forms of his Babylonian name in Hebrew letters. It is difficult to transliterate names from one language to another.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:17-20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:17-20 This prose paragraph connects with Jer. 50:4-5. God's people are coming home!

This paragraph lists the covenant people's two main enemies of this period.

  1. Assyria who took the northern ten tribes into exile with the fall of Samaria in 722 B.C.; see SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA
  2. Neo-Babylon who took Judah into exile with the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.; see SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON

The nation that God will use to bring judgment on these two Mesopotamian powers and restore His people is Persia, under Cyrus II (cf. Isa. 44:28; 45:1; SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA).

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:20 This is such an important theological text. The faithful remnant of YHWH's people have been forgiven (i.e. Jer. 31:31-34; 33:8; 36:3) and restored!

In the future period ("in those days") a repentant and obedient Israel and Judah will be united in restoration and forgiveness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (three senses)

SPECIAL TOPIC: POST EXILIC CHART

▣ "search will be made" This search (BDB 134, KB 152, Pual IMPERFECT) for the sins of God's covenant people obviously asks the question, "Who would do this?"

  1. enemies of Israel and Judah (i.e. the surrounding nations)
  2. Satan, the accusor of of God's people (and all people)
    SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN
  3. the heavenly countil (SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS)

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:21 "Merathaim. . .Pekod"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:21 "Merathaim. . .Pekod" There seems to be a word play between these terms and some people/areas of Babylon (i.e. south and east). The word play is difficult to bring into English in a meaningful way. Poetry often uses the sound association to make a point to its original hearers/readers.

Merathaim would mean "double rebellion" (BDB 601) and Pekod would mean "punishment" or "visitation" (BDB 824). YHWH will judge all of Neo-Babylon and its surrounding allies.

▣ "utterly destroy" This is an important VERB. Below is my note from Deut. 3:6. It is available online free at www.freebiblecommentary.org in OT Studies section, under Written Commentaries.

Deuteronomy 3:6

NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "utterly destroyed"
TEV  "destroyed"
NJB  "the curse of destruction"
REB  "under solemn ban"
JPSOA  "doomed"

This VERB (BDB 355, KB 353) is used twice in this verse (Hiphil IMPERATIVE and Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE). Its basic meaning is to devote something to God whereby it becomes too holy for human use and must be destroyed. It is regularly used in "holy war" contexts (cf. Jer. 2:34; 7:2; Exod. 22:20; Josh. 6:17,21) to assert that the victory and, thereby, the spoils belong to YHWH. In these conquest contexts the things devoted to God are Canaanites and their property. They are judged because of their abominable sins and unwillingness to repent (cf. Gen. 15:16; Lev. 18:24-26; Deut. 9:5).

For a good discussion of "holy war" see Ancient Israel, by Roland deVaux, vol. 1, pp. 258-267.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:21-28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:21-28 YHWH calls on (i.e. commands) His instrument of judgment (i.e. Persia) to attack and conquer Neo-Babylon.

  1. go up against it, Jer. 50:21 ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. slay, Jer. 50:21 ‒ BDB 352, KB 349 (lit. "attack"), Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. utterly destroy, Jer. 50:21 ‒ BDB 355, KB 353, (lit. "under the ban"), Hiphil IMPERATIVE (see SPECIAL TOPIC: UTTERLY DESTROY)
  4. do according to all that I have commanded you, Jer. 50:21 ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE
  5. come to her, Jer. 50:26 ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  6. open up her barns, Jer. 50:26 ‒ BDB 834, KB 986, Qal IMPERATIVE
  7. pile her up, Jer. 50:26 ‒ BDB 699, KB 757, Qal IMPERATIVE
  8. utterly destroy, Jer. 50:26 ‒ same as #3
  9. let nothing be left, Jer. 50:26 ‒ BDB 224, KB 243, Qal JUSSIVE
  10. put. . .to the sword, Jer. 50:27 ‒ same as #2
  11. let them go down to slaughter, Jer. 50:27 ‒ BDB 432, KB 434, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:23-24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 50:23-24 There is a series of seven PERFECT TENSE VERBS that describe Neo-Babylon's fall and destruction as if it already happened (PROPHETIC PERFECTS).

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 50:24 One wonders if this verse, especially line 2, is a historical prediction about the unexpected fall of the city of Babylon in 539 B.C. by Cyrus II's army. They took the city by surprise with almost no opposition (cf. Jer. 51:8; Daniel 5).

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 50:25 This imagery describes YHWH as having an armory of stored weapons. This is referring to the weaponry of the Persian army acting as YHWH's instrument of wrath (cf. Isa. 44:28; 45:1).

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:28 Notice how YHWH and His temple are identified together. As His "name" stands for Him, so too, "the place He caused His name to dwell" (repeated phrase in Deuteronomy).

The UBS Translator's Handbook on Jeremiah asserts that this verse is a parenthesis (TEV, NET Bible) referring to the returning Jewish exiles sharing how YHWH judged Babylon (p. 946).

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:29 "she has become arrogant against the Lord"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:29 "she has become arrogant against the Lord" Jeremiah 50:29-32 is a poem about Neo-Babylon's arrogance (BDB 267, KB 268). Daniel 4 is addressed to Nebuchadnezzar II on this same issue.

▣ "the Holy One of Israel" Notice that this phrase and "the Lord God of hosts," both covenant titles for Israel's Deity, are named in this condemnation of Neo-Babylon's arrogance.

The title is used often in Isaiah, but rarely in Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 51:5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:33-40
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 50:33-40 This poem is directed at the Jewish exiles and promises that their God will defeat their Babylonian captors and bring them home.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:34
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:34 Notice the names of God.

  1. Redeemer (see SPECIAL TOPIC: RANSOM/REDEEM and SPECIAL TOPIC: KINSMAN REDEEMER)
  2. God (Elohim (see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.)
  3. Lord of hosts (twice) (see SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS)

▣ "He will vigorously plead their case" This is the INFINITIVE ABSOSLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 936, KB 1224), which denoted a vigorous legal defense (cf. 1 Sam. 24:15; Ps. 35:1; 119:154; Isa. 50:8-9; 51:22; Micah 7:9). One wonders if the title for Jesus and the Spirit as "advocate" came from this imagery. Below is my note from 1 John 2:1.

1 John 2:1 "we have an Advocate with the Father" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE which refers to Jesus' ongoing intercession as our heavenly Advocate (paraklētos). This was a legal term for a defense lawyer or "one called alongside to help" (from para, beside and kaleō, to call). It is used in the upper room discourse in the Gospel of John, for the Holy Spirit, our earthly, indwelling advocate (cf. John 14:16,25; 15:26; 16:7). However, this is the only use of the term for Jesus (although it is implied in John 14:16; Rom. 8:34; Heb. 4:14-16; 7:25; 9:24). Paul used this same concept for the intercessory work of Christ in Rom. 8:34. In this same passage he also speaks of the intercession of the Holy Spirit in Rom. 8:26. We have an Advocate in heaven (Jesus) and an Advocate within (the Spirit), both of whom the loving Father sent on His behalf.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:35-37
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:35-37 There is a repeated pattern (i.e. "a sword against. . ."):

  1. the Chaldeans, Jer. 50:35
  2. inhabitants of Babylon, Jer. 50:35 (parallel)
  3. her officials, Jer. 50:35
  4. her wise men, Jer. 50:35 (parallel)
  5. the oracle priests, Jer. 50:36
  6. her mighty men, Jer. 50:36
  7. their horses, Jer. 50:37
  8. their chariots, Jer. 50:37
  9. all the foreigners (possibly mercenary military), Jer. 50:37
  10. her treasures, Jer. 50:37
  11. Jer. 50:38 could also have "sword" (REB, JPSOA footnote, BDB 352) instead of "drought" (MT, NASB, NRSV, BDB 351); both have the same CONSONANTS (BDB 351, KB 352)

YHWH's judgments fall on every aspect of Babylonian society!

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:38 "they are mad over fearsome idols"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:38 "they are mad over fearsome idols" The word translated "mad" could also mean "glory in" (cf. REB). Both make sense in this context. The difference is only one vowel in the Hebrew text.

  1. the idols are afraid (as are their priests, cf. Jer. 50:36)
  2. the idol worshipers glory in their idols but to no avail (cf. Jer. 50:36a). Terror falls on all!

The UBS Text Project (p. 318) gives the text followed by NASB a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:39-40
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:39-40 These two verses bring together two idioms of destruction.

  1. the presence of wild animals in her ruins, which was a symbol of
    1. complete destruction
    2. no human habitation
    3. the presence of the demonic (cf. Ps. 74:14; Isa. 13:21; 23:13; 34:14)
  2. the allusion to the complete destruction of the cities of the plain in Genesis 19 and it's perpetual non-habitation (cf. Jer. 49:18)

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:41
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 50:41 The Persian army, like the Neo-Babylonian army, was made up of many mercenary soldiers.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:41-43
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:41-43 As Babylon was "a people from the north" to judge God's people (cf. Jer. 1:13-15; 4:6; 6:1,22), now a people from the north (i.e. Persia) will come and defeat them! As they did to others now it will be done to them (cf. Jer. 50:15, 29).

These verses are very similar to Jer. 6:22-24, where YHWH's judgment is directed at Jerusalem, but now Neo-Babylon.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:42
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 50:42 This describes in poetic terms the Persian army.

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:43
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
50:43 As other nations feared the Neo-Babylonians, now they fear.

  1. hands hang limp (cf. Jer. 6:24)
  2. distress like child birth (cf. Jer. 4:31; 6:24; 13:21; 22:23)

entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley

50:44 "lion" See SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

entries.title: Jeremiah 50:44-46
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 50:44-46 This prose section continues the context of Babylon's defeat. Jeremiah 50:44-45 is very similar to Jer. 49:19-20. See notes there.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:1 "Leb-Kamai"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:1 "Leb-Kamai" This is a CONSTRUCT of "heart" (BDB 524) and the VERB "arise" or "stand up" (BDB 877, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE). It could be translated literally as

  1. UBS Text Project ‒ "heart of my adversaries"
  2. NKJV (footnote) ‒ "the midst of those who rise up against Me"
  3. AB ‒ "the heart of those who rise up against Me"

The LXX and most English commentators and translations take it as an Atbash cipher (letters of the alphabet are reversed to make them into a code) for "Kasdim" (i.e. Chaldean referring to Babylon). Another cipher for Babylon is "Sheshach" of Jer. 25:26 or "Sheshak" of Jer. 51:41. The Apostle John used a similar code mechanism in Revelation 18, where "Babylon" refers to Rome.

NASB  "that spirit of a destroyer"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, LXX,
 REB, JPSOA, Peshitta
 "a destroying wind"
NET  "a destructive word"

The Hebrew word ruah (BDB 924) can mean "wind," "breath," or "spirit." Only context can determine which is intended by the original author. In this context (i.e. Jeremiah) "wind" fits best (cf. Jer. 4:11-12; 13:24; 18:17; 22:22; 49:32,36). Jeremiah 51:11b demands a translation of "spirit." Context, context, context!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

51:2
NASB, TEV  "foreigners"
NKJV, NRSV, NJB, REB  "winnowers"
JPSOA  "strangers"
Peshitta  "destroyers"

The MT has "strangers" (BDB 266 I, cf. Jer. 5:19; 30:8; 51:2,51; Lam. 5:2), but other ancient versions read "winnowers" (BDB 279, cf. Jer. 4:11; 15:7; the same root is translated "scatter" in Jer. 49:32,26). The UBS Text Project, p. 320, gives "strangers" a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

The LXX translates this term as "spoilers" or "insolent men."

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:3 This verse is uncertain. It could be addressing the invaders to charge ahead or it could address the defenders that all their efforts are useless. The invaders are called on

  1. not to spare (BDB 328, KB 328, negated Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE, cf. Jer. 51:4)
  2. to devote to God (BDB 355, KB 353, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, i.e. put under the ban, cf. Jer. 25:9; 50:21,36; see SPECIAL TOPIC: CURSE)

All of Neo-Babylon's defenders are helpless, just as they mercilessly defeated others, so now no mercy to them!

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:4 "pierce"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:4 "pierce" This VERB (BDB 201, KB 230, Pual PARTICIPLE) denotes a badly wounded person (cf. Jer. 37:10).

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:5 In light of Jer. 33:24-26, this is an important affirmation that YHWH has not permanently rejected the descendants of Abraham, but only temporarily judged them for their sin (cf. Isa. 54:7-8; also note Romans 9-11).

▣ "Lord of hosts" See SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts.

▣ "the Holy One of Israel" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HOLY ONE.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:6 There is a series of IMPERATIVES very similar in meaning to Jer. 50:8.

  1. flee ‒ BDB 630, KB 681, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. save ‒ BDB 572, KB 589, Piel IMPERATIVE
  3. do not be destroyed ‒ BDB 198, KB 226, negated Niphal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

YHWH commands the Jewish exiles to leave Babylon before His judgment comes! One wonders how exiles could leave before Persia's victory and Cyrus' decree. Possibly they could leave the capital city of Babylon, not the country.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:7 Babylon served as YHWH's instrument of judgment. The "cup" was an idiom for judgment (i.e. drunkenness, cf. Jer. 25:15; Hab. 2:16; Rev. 14:8, see note at Jer. 49:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CUP

▣ "the nations are going mad" This VERB (BDB 237, KB 248, Hithpoel IMPERFECT) is also used in Jer. 25:16. This is imagery of drunkenness used for divine judgment.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WINE AND STRONG DRINK

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:8 This is sarcasm addressed to Neo-Babylon's subservient nations.

  1. wail over her ‒ BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  2. bring balm for her pain ‒ BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:9 All the efforts to heal Neo-Babylon by the subservient nations were to no avail. Therefore,

  1. forsake her ‒ BDB 736, KB 806, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. let us each go to his own country ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense (cf. Jer. 50:16; Isa. 13:14)
    1. mercenaries
    2. merchants

▣ "has reached to heaven. . .up to the very skies" Poetry is difficult to interpret because of its brevity and imagery.

 These VERBS seem to imply that

  1. the sins of Neo-Babylon have come to YHWH's notice
    1. sins of the people who were building the tower of Babel ‒ Gen. 11:5
    2. sins of the people of Sodom and Gomorrah ‒ Gen. 18:20-21
    3. sins of the covenant people ‒ Ezra 9:6
  2. YHWH's judgment of Babylon is so extensive that it symbolically reaches to the heavens

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:10 As Jer. 51:5 promised YHWH's forgiveness and restoration, Jer. 51:10 demands that the covenant people share His victory in Zion.

  1. come ‒ BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. let us recount ‒ BDB 707, KB 765, Piel COHORTATIVE, cf. Jer. 50:28; Isa. 40:2
    1. in Zion
    2. the work of YHWH

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:11d
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:11d This last line of poetry repeats the message of Jer. 50:28. Neo-Babylon will be destroyed with its magnificent pagan temples, as they destroyed YHWH's temple (i.e. 586 B.C.).

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:11-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:11-14 This poem addresses the invading army. TEV attributes the commands to the Persian army officers.

  1. sharpen the arrows, Jer. 51:11 ‒ BDB 140, KB 162, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  2. fill the quivers, Jer. 51:11 ‒ BDB 569, KB 583, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. lift up a signal, Jer. 51:12 ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. post a strong guard, Jer. 51:12 ‒ BDB 304, KB 302,, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  5. station sentries, Jer. 51:12 ‒ BDB 877, KB 1086, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  6. place men in ambush, Jer. 51:12 ‒ BDB 465, KB 464, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

However, #3-#6 could refer, in sarcasm, to the ineffective Neo-Babylonian defenders (cf. Jer. 51:13). The reason they are ineffective is because YHWH is now against them (cf. Jer. 51:12e-f, 14).

51:11
NASB, NRSV, NJB, JPSOA, REB  "fill the quivers"
NKJV  "gather the shields"
TEV  "get your shields ready"
Peshitta  "gather the quivers"

The MT has "fill the shields" (BDB 1020), but KB (1522-23) shows that this root was used in the Dead Sea Scrolls for "quiver." There is an Akkadian root with the same meaning. "Quiver" fits this context best in linking with

  1. the previous line of poetry
  2. the VERB "fill"

The word "shields" in the Dead Sea Scrolls could refer to a throwing (i.e. spear), slinging, or shooting (i.e. arrow) weapon.

▣ "the kings of the Medes" The invader from the north is now identified (i.e. Medo-Persia under King Cyrus II, "Cyrus the Great"). The MT has "kings" (PLURAL) but the LXX has the SINGULAR. Cyrus' empire was made up of several small nations, or it may be the Hebrew grammatical feature called the "PLURAL OF MAJESTY," denoting Cyrus' greatness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF PERSIA

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:13 "you who dwell by many waters"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:13 "you who dwell by many waters" This phrase refers to the southern part of Babylon which was made up of marshes formed at the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers.

▣ "measure" This is literally "cubit" (BDB 52 II). The phrase, line 4, refers to the thread being cut from a loom. Here it is an idiom for death (cf. Job 6:9; Isa. 38:12).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CUBIT

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:14 "the Lord of hosts has sworn by Himself"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:14 "the Lord of hosts has sworn by Himself" This concept goes back to Gen. 22:16 and 26:3. There is no one or no power greater than YHWH, so to swear (BDB 989, KB 1396, Niphal PERFECT) by Him is the ultimate oath. This same imagery is used in Jer. 22:5; 44:26; 49:13 and Isa. 14:24; 45:23; 62:8. That which YHWH purposes (cf. Jer. 51:12e), He will perform (cf. Jer. 51:12e)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord of Hosts

▣ "locusts" "Locusts" are often used as imagery for invading armies (i.e. Joel 2:25).

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:15 "stretched out the heavens"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:15 "stretched out the heavens" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:15-19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:15-19 This is a comparison of YHWH, the God who knows and acts, with the idols who are blind, dumb, uninformed, and cannot act!

Notice the attributes of YHWH listed.

  1. creator, Jer. 51:15
  2. provider, Jer. 51:16
  3. covenant God of Jacob, Jer. 51:19

Notice the characterization of the idols.

  1. made by mankind, Jer. 51:17
  2. worthless to help, even provide false hope, Jer. 51:18

This strophe is paralleled in Jer. 10:12-16. These truths were a recurrent theme of YHWH's reality versus the idols of the nations' non-existence.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:15-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:15-23 The NASB sees this as one literary unit but most other English translations see Jer. 51:15-19 and Jer. 51:20-23 as separate. There is no textual marker to ensure the division of ancient texts into literary units. However, the task is primary in interpretation. This is where checking several modern versions can be helpful (see the paragraph divisions on the first page of each chapter).

"Bible Interpretation Seminar"

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:17 "put to shame"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:17 "put to shame" See SPECIAL TOPIC: SHAME

▣ "there is no breath in them" This same phrase describing the lifeless idols is in Jer. 10:14. The word "breath" is ruah, translated "spirit" in Jer. 51:11. The prophets regularly "make fun of" and ridicule the non-existence of pagan idols (i.e. Isa. 40:18-20; 41:6-7; 44:9-11,12-17; 46:5-7). They "cannot"; YHWH can and does!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:20-23
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:20-23 The only true God (see SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM) will bring judgment on Babylon by His chosen instrument (i.e. war-club, lit. "hammer," BDB 659 and BDB 536), Persia and Cyrus II, who are named by a specific prophecy in Isa. 44:28; 45:1.

  1. destroy nations
    destroy kingdoms
  2. shatter horse and its rider
    shatter chariot and its rider
  3. shatter man
    shatter woman
  4. shatter old men
    shatter youth
  5. shatter young men
    shatter virgins
  6. shatter the shepherd
    shatter his flock
  7. shatter the farmer
    shatter his team
  8. shatter governors
    shatter prefects

All levels of society will be "shattered" (BDB 658, KB 711, nine Piel PERFECTS).

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:24-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:24-26 This poem (Jer. 51:25-26) describes the destruction of Neo-Babylon ("O destroying mountain") in highly figurative language. The two books that have helped me understand this genre are by

  1. D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic
  2. Fee and Stuart, How to Read the Bible For All Its Worth, esp. chapter 10

It is possible that this imagery relates to the Babylonian sky gods who were worshiped on the tops of ziggurats (i.e. the tower of Babel, Genesis 11). These manmade mud brick structures dominated the flat river plains of Babylon's chief cities. Each one had their own god and tower. The great ziggurat of Marduk was in the city of Babylon.

The violent and complete destruction of the city of Babylon did not occur in 539 B.C., when the city was taken without a fight and with minimal destruction, by the Persian army. However, it did occur later in history (i.e. by Xerxes I in 482 B.C.).

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:25 "O destroying mountain"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:25 "O destroying mountain" This imagery is uncertain. It is obviously figurative language referring to Babylon as a military victor. But why "mountain"?

  1. the home of the gods (i.e. divine empowerment, i.e. Isa. 14:13)
  2. the God of Mt. Moriah (i.e. the Jewish temple, i.e. Isa. 2:2-3)
  3. the military advantage of "higher ground"
  4. the awesome physical sites of mountains and their strength
  5. root of the mountains as the entrance to the underworld
  6. imagery used of a mountain where pagan altars were located (cf. 2 Kgs. 23:13)

This destroying mountain will be destroyed (i.e. fire) by YHWH. He sends and uses Neo-Babylon but also holds them responsible!

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:26 This is imagery of a complete and lasting destruction (cf. Jer. 50:13). Usually in the ANE the sites of major cities were advantageous sites (i.e. water, protection, fertility), so destroyed cities were quickly rebuilt, often using the building material lying around. This verse prophesies no habitation. Note the ruins of Babylon today!

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:27 "Ararat"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:27 "Ararat" This nation (BDB 76) is located around Lake Urmia. Today its territory is in Armenia, Russia, and Iran. It was known as Urartu by the Assyrians. This ethnic group participated in the Persian attack on Neo-Babylon.

▣ "Minni" This (BDB 585 I) refers to the people group south of Lake Van. They were later known as Scythians but at this time as "Mannaeans."

▣ "Ashkenaz" This group of people (BDB 79) is mentioned in Gen. 10:3; 1 Chr. 1:6, living east of Lake Urmia. They are also part of what later became the Scythians.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:27-32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:27-32 YHWH calls on the Persian Empire to take up arms against Neo-Babylon in a series of IMPERATIVES.

  1. lift up a signal ‒ BDB 669, KB 724, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 51:12; 50:2; Isa. 5:26; 13:2
  2. blow a trumpet ‒ BDB 1075, KB 1785, Qal IMPERATIVE
  3. consecrate the nations ‒ BDB 872, KB 1073, Piel IMPERATIVE
  4. summon. . .kingdoms ‒ BDB 1033, KB 1570, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  5. appoint a marshal ‒ BDB 823, KB 955, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Jer. 49:19; 50:44
  6. bring up horses ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
  7. in Jer. 51:28a #3 is repeated

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:30
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:30 This is ANE imagery of dis-spirited soldiers.

  1. they have ceased fighting
  2. they stay in the stronghold
  3. their strength is exhausted
  4. they are like women

Their fortifications are breached.

  1. set on fire
  2. gate bars broken

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:31-32
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:31-32 This is a message to be delivered to the king of Neo-Babylon by the city's defenders.

  1. the city is captured
  2. fords seized
  3. marshes burned
  4. soldiers terrified

There was no way to escape!

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:33
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:33 It is uncertain if this should be a separate literary unit or part of Jer. 51:27-32. The speaker of Jer. 51:20-32 is YHWH, so too, here. Neo-Babylon's fate is set. Her doom is sure! What she did to others will be done to her.

▣ "threshing" This is often used in judgment imagery (cf. Isa. 21:10; 41:15-16).

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:34-39
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:34-39 Jerusalem/Judah (Jer. 51:35d) is personified as a devastated people (Jer. 51:34).

  1. Neo-Babylon has devoured me ‒ BDB 37, KB 46, Qal PERFECT
  2. Neo-Babylon has crushed me ‒ BDB 243, KB 251, Qal PERFECT
  3. Neo-Babylon has set me down as an empty vessel ‒ BDB 426, KB 427, Hiphil PERFECT
  4. Neo-Babylon has swallowed me like a monster ‒ BDB 118, KB 134, Qal PERFECT
  5. Neo-Babylon has filled his stomach with my delicacies ‒ BDB 569, KB 583, Piel PERFECT
  6. Neo-Babylon has washed me away ‒ BDB 188, KB 216, Hiphil PERFECT

Every one of these (except #5) has a Kethiv and Qere form related to PLURAL or SINGULAR.

51:34
NASB   "washed me away"
NKJV   "spit me out"
NRSV, REB   "spewed me out"
TEV   "threw the rest away"
NJB   "threw me out"
JPSOA   "rinsed me out"
LXX    —omit—
Peshitta   "has caused me to go astray"

The MT has the VERB "rinse" or "cleanse away" (BDB 188, KB 216, Hiphil PERFECT). The VERB can refer to

  1. ritual washing ‒ 2 Chr. 4:6; Ezek. 40:38
  2. cleansing ‒ Isa. 4:4
  3. here the context seems to demand a mouth rinse and expulsion of the liquid

The point is Babylon used Jerusalem and then spit her out as useless!

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:35a
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:35a This is praying/wishing that what Neo-Babylon did to Jerusalem/Judah, others will do to her (cf. Jer. 50:15,29). The speaker is personified Jerusalem.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:36-40
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:36-40 YHWH describes what He will do to Neo-Babylon and for Judah.

  1. for Judah
    1. plead your case, Jer. 50:34; 51:36 (i.e. act as your advocate)
    2. exact full vengeance on her behalf
  2. to Neo-Babylon
    1. dry up her sea (i.e. commerce)
    2. become a heap of ruins
    3. become a haunt of jackals, cf. Jer. 49:33
    4. become an object of horror
    5. become an object of hissing
    6. make them the food of a banquet
    7. make then drunk (lit. "rejoice"), cf. Jer. 51:57
    8. make them sleep forever
    9. make them sacrificial animals

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORROR, REPROACH, RUIN, CURSE

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:38-39
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:38-39 The context demands that this refers to Neo-Babylon. They are enjoying their spoils in Jer. 51:38. However, their victories make them vulnerable to excess (drunkenness), which leads to destruction and death (Jer. 51:39, lines 3 & 4, Jer. 51:40).

In Jer. 51:40 the Neo-Babylonians are like animals being led to slaughter. They cannot defend themselves. As they treated others, now they will receive!

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

SPECIAL TOPIC: WINE AND STRONG DRINK

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:39 "May sleep a perpetual sleep
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:39 "May sleep a perpetual sleep

And not wake up" One cannot build doctrine about the afterlife based on verses such as this.

  1. OT has little information about the afterlife
  2. sleep is an OT euphemism for death
  3. "perpetual" (i.e. 'olam) must be interpreted in light of the larger context
    SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam and aiōnios)
  4. this phrase is a result of "drunkenness"

See F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 30-31 and William Hendricksen, The Bible On the Life Hereafter.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:41 "Sheshak"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:41 "Sheshak" See full note at Jer. 25:26. This is another atbash cipher.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:41-44
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:41-44 Another poem of YHWH's judgment on Neo-Babylon (there are several separate poems in this chapter brought together by topic). Most of the VERBS are PROPHETIC PERFECTS describing future events as completed actions.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:42
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:42 Babylon was a country of rivers, canals, and marshes (cf. Jer. 51:13a); her waterways are disrupted as an idiom of divine judgment (cf. Jer. 51:36). YHWH, the creator God, controls the waters (cf. Jer. 5:22; 31:35). The nation of "waters" will be dry (Jer. 51:43b).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:44 "Bel"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:44 "Bel" See note at Jer. 50:2.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BEL

▣ "what he has swallowed" This is the imagery of eating used to describe conquest. As Neo-Babylon "ate" Jerusalem in Jer. 51:34, then spit her out, so too, now Neo-Babylon. Her deities must regurgitate!

▣ "even the wall of Babylon has fallen down" This prophecy of complete destruction of the city of Babylon (cf. Jer. 50:15; 51:58) is a hyperbolic description of Persia's defeat, but literal for future events. See note on the genre of prophecy at Jer. 51:24-26.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:45-48
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:45-48 This is another poem with two emphases.

  1. YHWH calls for His people to leave the city of Babylon before His judgment comes (cf. Jer. 50:8; 51:6)
  2. YHWH will punish Neo-Babylon

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:46
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:46 This may relate to Jer. 50:28. There are two reports circulating.

  1. Judah/Israel's restoration (cf. Isa. 48:20)
  2. Neo-Babylon's fall

▣ "lest your heart grow faint" The faith challenge to God's people is "do not fear, do not lose heart," because I am with you; I am in control (cf. Deut. 3:22; 7:18; 20:3; 31:6,8; Josh. 1:6,7,9; Isa. 43:5; Jer. 46:27,28). This same admonition is for the people of faith today!

The Jerome Biblical Commentary (p. 336) and NASB Study Bible (p. 1142) assert that this verse is reflected in Jesus' eschatological discourse of Matt. 24:6ff.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:48 "heaven and earth"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:48 "heaven and earth" These are the two ancient witnesses (cf. Isa. 44:23; 49:13). They summarize all creation (cf. Gen. 1:1). "Heaven" refers to the atmosphere above the earth.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

▣ "from the north" See notes at Jer. 50:3,9,41, which build on Jer. 1:13-15.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:49
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:49 Notice Neo-Babylon is reaping the judgment of YHWH because of its treatment of the covenant people (i.e. their treatment of the temple, cf. Jer. 51:51; 50:28c; Lam. 1:10; 2:6-7). The irony is that it was YHWH who sent Neo-Babylon but still she is responsible for her actions.

There is another way to interpret this phrase. It is possible to make it parallel to Jer. 51:47. If so, it is not just "for the slain of Israel," but for all the slain of all the nations.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:49-51
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:49-51 This poem is addressed to the remnant of the exiles who returned to Judah under Cyrus' decree in 538 B.C. I believe Jer. 51:52-53 should go with Jer. 51:49-51.

SPECIAL TOPIC: REMNANT (THREE SENSES)

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:50
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:50 YHWH commands His exiled people in Babylon to think of Jerusalem/temple and leave their captivity.

  1. depart ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. do not stay ‒ BDB 763, KB 840, negated Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  3. remember the Lord from afar ‒ BDB 269, KB 269, Qal IMPERATIVE
  4. let Jerusalem come to your mind ‒ BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

The exiles of Nebuchadnezzar's previous deportations (i.e. 605, 597 B.C.) heard of the atrocities that occurred in 586 B.C. with the fall and destruction of Jerusalem and the temple (cf. Jer. 51:51), but they are encouraged now to remember YHWH!

The vast majority of exiled Jews did not return under the leadership of Sheshbazzar, Zerubbabel/Joshua, Ezra, and Nehemiah in the Persian period.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:53
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:53 The imagery of geographical high places which was used of Edom does not fit Babylon, which was located mostly in the Tigris/Euphrates River valley and plain. It is imagery which may reflect her trust in the gods of the sky who they worshiped from their manmade towers, ziggurats (possibly related to Genesis 11, "the Tower of Babel").

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:54
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:54 There are no VERBALS in Jer. 51:54, just stark NOUNS.

  1. hark ‒ BDB 876
  2. cry ‒ BDB 277
  3. great destruction ‒ ADJECTIVE, BDB 152 and NOUN, BDB 991

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:54-58
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 51:54-58 This is another in a series of POETIC PROPHECIES about the fall of Neo-Babylon.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:56 "a God of recompense"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:56 "a God of recompense" This characterization of YHWH as One who holds humans accountable for their actions is a recurrent theme (cf. Jer. 51:6; Isa. 35:4; 59:18 [twice]; 66:6; Lam. 3:64). For a full list of all the places in Scripture where this truth is revealed, see the note at Jer. 17:10.

▣ "He will fully repay" This is an intensified grammatical form. The INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root (BDB 1022, KB 1532) are used.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:58 "will be completely razed"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:58 "will be completely razed" As Jer. 51:56 had an intensified grammatical form, so too, here (i.e. INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE and IMPERFECT VERB of the same root, BDB 792, KB 889).

This purposeful hyperbole is a common feature of prophetic and apocalyptic literature (see D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks). It was not meant to be taken in a modern, western literalism. In fact, Cyrus II did not destroy the walls of the city of Babylon. The amazingly huge, thick double walls of Babylon (cf. Herodotus 1.178ff) were destroyed by Xerxes I in 482 B.C.

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:59-64
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:59-64 This is a concluding prose section relating a message sent by Jeremiah by the hand of Seraiah (possibly Baruch's brother, cf. Jer. 32:12) to the exiles already in Babylon (i.e. 605, 597 B.C.).

When the visit occurred in 594/3 B.C. (Zedekiah began to reign in 597 B.C.). This is the only mention of this visit in the Bible. Possibly it was when Zedekiah tried to convince Nebuchadnezzar II of his loyalty and denial of any duplicity in the alliances/revolts of the far western nations.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

entries.title: Jeremiah 51:63
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
51:63 This was done for one of two reasons (or maybe both).

  1. as a symbol of Neo-Babylon's destruction
  2. as a way to protect the message from causing a reaction from the Babylonian captors (i.e. note the ciphers of Jer. 25:26; 51:1,41).

One wonders how much of Jeremiah 50-51 was included on that scroll. It seems that many poems from different periods of Jeremiah's life were brought together by topic in these two chapters (by Baruch or a later editor).

Also note the cultural emphasis on oral presentation versus written. The ANE was made up of oral societies (for the most part). For a good discussion, see John H. Walton and D. Brent Sandy, The Lost World of Scripture.

51:64
MT, NASB, NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "Thus far are the words
  of Jeremiah"
TEV  "The words of Jeremiah
  end here"
REB "Thus far are the collected
  sayings of Jeremiah"
LXX, JPSOA    —omit—

There is no VERB. Many scholars believe this is an editorial comment to separate chapter 52 (destruction of Jerusalem, cf. 2 Kgs. 24:10-25:30) from Jeremiah's writings. The faith presupposition of "inspiration" must cover the editing and compiling of OT books.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

entries.title: Jeremiah 52:1 "Hamutal"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
52:1 "Hamutal" The meaning of the name is uncertain (BDB 327, KB 326). She was the wife of King Josiah and mother of

  1. Jehoahaz ‒ 2 Kgs. 23:31
  2. Zedekiah ‒ 2 Kgs. 24:18; here

entries.title: Jeremiah 52:1-3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
52:1-3 This information is also found in 2 Kgs. 24:18-20 and 2 Chr. 36:11-21. Zedekiah reigned from 597 B.C. ‒ 586 B.C.

Zedekiah succeeded Jehoiachin who was exiled by Nebuchadnezzar II after only three months (cf. 2 Kgs. 24:8-17). At that time Nebuchadnezzar II made his uncle, named Mattaniah, a puppet king of Judah in his place. The uncle was given the throne name "Zedekiah." He was the youngest of the children of Josiah to reign (i.e. Jehoahaz, exiled by Pharaoh Necho and Jehoiakim, cf. 1 Chr. 3:15). He was a spiritually weak and easily manipulated person, as the writings of Jeremiah clearly show.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED KINGDOM

entries.title: Jeremiah Contextual Insights
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
